artigo.texto: The Volusia County Council on Tuesday, Oct. 6, held the first of two required public hearings on a proposed ordinance to prohibit large-scale data centers in unincorporated Volusia County, continuing a process that began in August to address community concerns about water resources, infrastructure, energy demand, and compatibility with surrounding communities. This is the latest step in a process that began Aug. 17, when council members directed staff to develop regulations addressing large-scale data centers, which State law defines as a facility at a single location with an anticipated monthly peak electrical load of 50 megawatts or more. The ordinance is scheduled to go before the Planning and Land Development Regulation Commission on Thursday, Oct. 15, then return to the county council for the second and final public hearing Tuesday, Oct. 20. If adopted after the final hearing, the ordinance would take effect upon filing with the Florida Department of State. No new applications The County has not accepted new applications for large-scale data centers in unincorporated Volusia County since Aug. 17, when the Council directed staff to pursue a prohibition. That hold will remain in place until the Council takes final action on the proposed ordinance. If ultimately adopted, the ordinance would make large-scale data centers prohibited use throughout unincorporated Volusia County. The county would not accept or process applications, development approvals, comprehensive plan amendments, rezonings, permits, site plans, or other County approvals associated with establishing, constructing, expanding, or operating a large-scale data center. The prohibition would apply only within unincorporated Volusia County and would not govern land-use decisions within municipalities.

artigo.texto: Mumbai: The Brihanmumbai Electric Supply and Transport (BEST) undertaking is set to roll out a new generation of Olectra Greentech electric buses in Mumbai. The buses are equipped with advanced Blade Battery technology, which is expected to offer a longer range and enhanced safety. The first batch of 25 buses is expected to become operational by the end of the month, The Times of India reported. The buses are equipped with lightweight batteries that will enable them to operate for up to two days on a single charge. Batteries designed to conserve energy The batteries use lithium iron phosphate technology and are integrated into the bus chassis. They are reported to be capable of storing at least 30 percent more energy compared with batteries installed in existing air-conditioned buses. The new buses are also designed to offer improved safety and a longer range while operating at lower costs. Olectra supplying buses to BEST Olectra Greentech Limited is supplying the Blade Battery-based electric buses to BEST as part of efforts to meet Mumbai's public transport requirements. Technology designed for enhanced safety A senior Olectra Greentech official was quoted as saying by The Times of India: “Blade battery is designed to withstand extreme climatic conditions and is much safer even when severely damaged during accidents. It has very slow heat generation and no oxygen release. It is also more compact, increasing space utilisation in the battery pack by over 50%." Buses equipped with the similar battery technology are also operating in other cities across the globe, including London and Singapore, according to the report. artigo.texto: President Donald Trump recently told communities that if they reject data centers, they are choosing “poverty, crime and squalor” and want to end up “backwards and poor.” I, like many, found that language deeply disturbing. But sadly, not unfamiliar. Over the last year, I have sat in county council meetings in Kershaw, Marion, Colleton, Marlboro, Orangeburg and Fairfield counties, supporting communities concerned about how much water data center companies will need, how much higher projects will eventually make their light bills, why we are offering tax breaks and how many permanent jobs will actually be created that locals are qualified for. I have watched those questions be sidestepped, again and again, in tones not unlike the president’s. South Carolinians don’t get to shop around for their electric utility; where you live determines your provider, which gives utilities unfair influence over rates. Energy burdens for low- and moderate-income households can reach extraordinary levels, with families paying nearly 25 percent of their income for energy in some parts of our state. I spend time with families living in older homes with bad insulation, drafty doors and windows and inefficient appliances, paying top-dollar for energy that’s literally leaking out. We’ve been demanding serious weatherization and efficiency programs for years. But as data center developers began circling South Carolina, the conversation in Columbia shifted quickly from helping families use less energy to finding ways to produce a lot more of it. Last year the General Assembly passed H.3309, the S.C. Energy Security Act, which authorized Dominion Energy and Santee Cooper to pursue a large new natural-gas plant at the old Canadys coal site, and created an expedited review process for certain other energy infrastructure. This year lawmakers took up S.867, a bill that would have addressed data center siting, water use, infrastructure, noise and light, and who pays for utility upgrades. It did not become law, and the projects kept coming. So here we are. I’ve watched communities across the state push back, ask for moratoriums, demand information about incentives and tell local elected officials that their responsibility is to the people who already live there, not simply to lobbyists and developers promising billions of dollars in investment. The Post and Courier recently reported that projected average water use for the NorthMark project in Spartanburg had climbed to 1.4 million gallons a day after earlier paperwork listed a much lower figure. At a Senate hearing this spring, I heard a Google representative explain that its Berkeley County data center “only” uses about 750 million gallons of water yearly. Even that's obscene. Farmers need water to irrigate crops. Families need utility bills they can afford. People who grew up fishing, swimming and worshipping along these rivers have every reason to ask what happens when another enormous user moves in. There’s a national story here, too; the Democratic Party has put our state first on its 2028 primary calendar. Candidates will spend time here talking affordability, working people, jobs and whatever version of the future economy tops their list of priorities. My hope is that they’re also aware of what’s happening in these county council chambers. The artificial intelligence argument looks different when it’s no longer about extinction, data leaks or a stock price, but about a power plant down the road, water permits, a county tax deal and whether the people living nearby knew about it before ink dried on the non-disclosure agreement. South Carolina needs investment, yes. We also need homes cheaper to heat and cool, utility bills people can afford, and jobs that last longer than construction phases. If lawmakers can move this quickly to accommodate hundreds of megawatts of new demand, they can bring some of that urgency to weatherization, energy efficiency and the South Carolinians who’ve been asking for relief for years. The people I’ve met across our state are doing exactly what we should want people to do when someone comes to town promising billions of dollars: asking questions before shovels hit the dirt. In 2028, presidential candidates will come here (some already have) and talk about the struggles and futures facing working people. They should start in these communities, listening to people who will actually have to live next door to whatever version of progress gets built. Zakiya Mickle is the founder of The Ubuntu Collective, a S.C.-based social action business focused on building collective power and advancing liberation.

artigo.texto: CATL World's largest battery manufacturer According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Advanced Energy Storage Systems market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global Advanced Energy Storage Systems market is undergoing a structural transformation from a policy-supported niche to a demand-pull cornerstone of modern energy infrastructure. As renewable penetration rises and grid operators confront intermittency, the economic case for storage has shifted from subsidy-driven to necessity-driven. Between 2026 and 2035, the market will be shaped by the imperative to integrate variable renewables, defer transmission upgrades, and enhance grid resilience. System integration and power conversion subsystems are emerging as critical value capture points, often determining project bankability more than the storage medium itself. A fundamental bifurcation is occurring: short-duration, high-cyclicity applications compete on $/kW and $/kWh metrics, while long-duration and resilience applications compete on total cost of ownership, safety, and site-specific integration complexity. Supply chain resilience has become a baseline requirement, and qualification burdens for new chemistries create time-to-market disadvantages. Procurement is shifting from component purchasing to performance-guaranteed, service-based contracts, forcing manufacturers to assume long-term operational risk. Geographic specialization is intensifying, creating complex trade dependencies. Safety protocols are evolving from afterthoughts to primary design constraints, influencing insurance, permitting, and deployment feasibility. This report provides a structured, commercially grounded analysis of these dynamics, offering decision-makers a clear view of deployment demand, technology positioning, manufacturing exposure, project economics, and competitive structure through 2035. The baseline scenario for the Advanced Energy Storage Systems market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates robust expansion, driven by the accelerating integration of renewable energy sources and the urgent need to modernize aging grid infrastructure. As solar and wind capacity grows, the intermittency challenge becomes more acute, making storage an indispensable component of reliable power systems. Utilities and grid operators are increasingly procuring storage to defer costly transmission and distribution upgrades, provide frequency regulation, and enhance resilience against extreme weather events. The commercial and industrial sector is also emerging as a significant demand center, motivated by energy cost management, sustainability targets, and the need for backup power. Technological advancements, particularly in lithium-ion chemistry and power conversion systems, are driving down costs and improving performance, further bolstering the economic case. However, the market faces headwinds from supply chain constraints, particularly in critical minerals and battery cell manufacturing, which could temper growth in certain regions. Policy support remains a key enabler, but the trend is toward market-based mechanisms that reward storage for its grid services. The competitive landscape is expected to consolidate, with integrated system providers gaining share over component suppliers. By 2035, the market is projected to reach a significantly higher level of deployment, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 15.2% from 2026 to 2035, and the market index (2025=100) rising to 420, reflecting a more than fourfold increase in market value. This outlook assumes no major disruptive technological shifts or severe geopolitical crises, but acknowledges that regional variations will persist based on policy environments and resource endowments. Electric utilities and grid operators represent the largest and fastest-growing end-use sector for advanced energy storage systems. The primary mechanism driving demand is the need to integrate increasing shares of variable renewable generation, such as solar and wind, while maintaining grid stability and reliability. As renewable penetration exceeds 30-40% in many regions, the intermittency challenge becomes critical, necessitating storage for frequency regulation, voltage support, and energy shifting. Utilities are also deploying storage to defer or avoid costly upgrades to transmission and distribution infrastructure, using storage as a non-wires alternative. Additionally, storage provides essential grid services like spinning reserve and black start capability. Through 2035, demand will be further propelled by the retirement of aging fossil fuel peaker plants, which storage can replace with cleaner, faster-responding capacity. Key demand-side indicators include renewable capacity additions, grid interconnection queue volumes, and capacity market prices. The trend is toward larger, longer-duration projects, with utilities increasingly procuring storage through competitive solicitations and power purchase agreements. However, the pace of deployment varies by region, depending on regulatory frameworks and market designs that value storage's multiple benefits. Current trend: Rapid growth driven by renewable integration and grid modernization. Major trends: Shift from pilot projects to large-scale, multi-hundred-megawatt deployments, Increasing use of storage as a non-wires alternative to defer transmission upgrades, Growth in long-duration storage procurement to address seasonal variations, Integration of storage with renewable generation in hybrid projects, and Adoption of performance-based contracts and capacity markets. Representative participants: NextEra Energy, Duke Energy, Southern Company, National Grid, Enel, and Iberdrola. artigo.texto: O satélite do Google subiu em 1º de outubro num Falcon 9 da SpaceX, o mesmo foguete que levou dois satélites feitos por alunos de escolas públicas do Brasil. É o primeiro teste em órbita do plano de montar data center movido a luz do Sol. O satélite do Google com quatro chips de inteligência artificial já está em órbita e respondendo. O protótipo do Project Suncatcher subiu na quinta-feira (1º) na missão Transporter-18 da SpaceX, e a empresa confirmou o contato no mesmo dia, em post assinado por Travis Beals, diretor do projeto. Segundo ele, a nave está “operando como esperado”. O aparelho foi construído em parceria com a Planet, empresa de imagens de satélite. A pergunta que ele precisa responder é simples de escrever e difícil de provar: um chip feito para data center em terra aguenta o espaço? O que o satélite do Google leva a bordo O protótipo tem quatro TPU, as unidades de processamento tensorial que o Google desenha para aprendizado de máquina e já usa nos próprios data centers. Segundo a NPR, os chips vão rodar uma versão do Gemma, o modelo aberto da empresa, para responder perguntas simples. Cada sessão dura 15 minutos, por limite de calor. - Computador raro Q1 de 1972 é encontrado sob caixas em casa de Londres, revela tecnologia Intel 8008 anterior ao Apple 1 e acaba vendido por mais de R$ 260 mil - Pesquisa brasileira mostra novo caminho para acelerar produção sustentável de amônia que pode ajudar a tornar mais eficientes processos industriais ligados aos fertilizantes agrícolas - Cientistas brasileiros usam drones e inteligência artificial para encontrar milho tolerante à seca e alcançam mais de 90% de acerto em parte dos testes - Volvo coloca VNL autônomo na rota Dallas–Houston, usa direção nível SAE 4 e mira escala com rede de 38 mil clientes para mudar o transporte de cargas nos EUA A NPR descreve o satélite do Google como do tamanho de uma geladeira. Ele fica numa órbita heliossíncrona, em que os painéis solares quase nunca entram na sombra. Isso dispensa baterias pesadas e energia de reserva. A meta é que a missão funcione por um ano. O próprio Beals chamou o voo de “um teste muito mínimo”. Primeiro a Planet coloca a nave para funcionar. Depois o Google liga as TPU do satélite e mede como elas se comportam com radiação, vibração e calor. Os números que o Google já mediu em terra Antes de o satélite do Google subir, a equipe publicou os testes de bancada. Eles ajudam a entender o tamanho do desafio: - Energia: na órbita certa, um painel solar rende até 8 vezes mais do que na superfície da Terra. - Lançamento: a subida dura cerca de 10 minutos, com cargas de até 10 g. Componentes isolados, como as TPU, podem sentir de 50 a 100 g. - Radiação: o chip Trillium (TPU v6e) foi testado num feixe de prótons de 67 MeV. A memória HBM só mostrou falhas depois de 2 krad(Si). A dose esperada em cinco anos de missão, com blindagem, é de 750 rad(Si). - Dose máxima: nenhuma falha permanente apareceu até 15 krad(Si), o maior valor testado num único chip. - Laser entre satélites: um demonstrador de bancada passou 800 Gbps em cada sentido, ou 1,6 Tbps no total, com um único par de transceptores. A conta da radiação mostra a folga. Dividindo 2.000 rad por 750 rad, o primeiro sinal de falha veio com 2,7 vezes a dose de cinco anos. Já os 15 krad sem dano permanente equivalem a 20 vezes essa dose. Os dados estão no post técnico do Google Research, de novembro de 2025, e o trabalho agora saiu revisado por pares na revista Joule. O problema do calor no vácuo Em terra, data center se resfria com ar ou água. Em órbita não existe ar. No vácuo, o calor só sai por radiadores, e por isso as sessões do Gemma ficam limitadas a 15 minutos. No satélite do Google, a saída testada é uma combinação de tubos de calor e radiadores. O conjunto passou por uma câmara de vácuo térmico, que imita o frio e o vácuo do espaço. Beals contou à NPR que os radiadores estão entre as peças mais pesadas do satélite do Google. Isso pesa no custo, porque cada quilo a mais encarece o lançamento. Brandon Lucia, professor de engenharia da Universidade Carnegie Mellon, lembrou outro ponto à NPR. Quando um chip quebra em um data center comum, um técnico entra e troca. Em órbita, segundo ele, custo e complexidade de manutenção sobem 10 ou até 100 vezes. Do protótipo à constelação de data center O satélite do Google é só o começo. A empresa imagina grupos de satélites voando muito perto uns dos outros, ligados por laser, cada um com dezenas de TPU. No modelo publicado, um aglomerado de 81 satélites voa a 650 km de altitude, num raio de 1 km. A distância entre vizinhos oscila entre 100 e 200 metros. A conta que decide o projeto é o preço por quilo. O Google calcula que o lançamento pode cair para menos de US$ 200 por quilo em meados da década de 2030. Nesse patamar, montar e operar um data center em órbita ficaria parecido com a conta de energia de um data center equivalente em terra, por quilowatt ao ano. O próximo passo é em 2027, com dois satélites em órbita para testar o laser entre eles. O próprio Beals freia a expectativa. Ele disse à NPR que não vê o modelo ficando mais barato nos próximos cinco anos. O mesmo foguete levou satélites de escolas brasileiras O Falcon 9 da Transporter-18 decolou da Base da Força Espacial de Vandenberg, na Califórnia, com 130 cargas. Entre elas estavam o EduSat-2 e o EduSat-3, montados por alunos de escolas públicas de Sorocaba (SP) e Fortaleza (CE). Os dois saíram do projeto AEB Escola em Órbita, da Agência Espacial Brasileira com a empresa Ideia Space. Em Sorocaba, a missão definida pelos alunos foi olhar para alagamentos e falhas de conectividade na região. A carona coletiva explica a mistura. Num voo desse tipo, a SpaceX divide o espaço do foguete entre dezenas de clientes, de gigantes da tecnologia a projetos de escola.

artigo.texto: FARGO, N.D. — During a debate Thursday evening, three of North Dakota’s U.S. House candidates voiced support for more transparency around AI data centers. Democratic candidate Trygve Hammer said there needs to be more caution around establishing data centers and that Congress must have a role in regulating them. ADVERTISEMENT “Corporations are using AI surveillance tools to drive up our prices and to drive down wages,” he said. “And they keep losing control of the AI agents they put out there. How long until they hack into something that could be truly dangerous? So we need regulation.” Independent Helene Neville asked if people know what the centers are doing, storing and the outcome of them. There isn’t a remediation plan. “I worked for Superfund sites (polluted areas requiring long-term cleanup) in Iowa, and we did soil, air, water samples, cancer cluster investigations,” she said. “We knew what was going on in the site, and then we had remediation protocols set up. None of that was done on data centers. We’re in the dark.” Independent Charles Tuttle said people should be concerned about the longevity of data centers. He has attended township meetings and county meetings around data centers and says one of the problems is there is too much secrecy. “Even on the local level, townships are the most powerful political subdivision there is, and we need to allow them to have the power that they are granted,” he said. The debate was the first of the 2026 midterms for Prairie Public, which hosted the debate live on its television service, radio and YouTube channel Thursday, Oct. 8. The only U.S. House candidate to not participate was Republican incumbent Julie Fedorchak, who withdrew from the debate in September. The debate was moderated by Dave Thompson, Prairie Public's news director. Candidates discussed various topics, including North Dakota farmers being increasingly dependent on both domestic and international markets and biofuel demands, changes to Social Security and Medicare, changes in campaign finance laws, continued action in the Middle East and Ukraine and rural hospitals and clinics. ADVERTISEMENT On the topic of supporting farmers to make them less vulnerable to tariffs, trade disputes and changing foreign demand, Tuttle said the U.S. has to make sure that it has fair and equal trade. He believes that biofuels and green energy don’t work. “We’ve got to stop using these things with tax incentives and giving welfare out to different people, winners and losers,” he said. “It’s got to stop because we don’t have the money to continue to do that.” Neville said the answer lies in stopping insider trading. “Halting, pausing, whatever it takes,” she said. Hammer said Congress needs to take control and get something done, such as through a farm bill that favors smaller operators. “The power of the tariff actually belongs to Congress, and those ag markets that went away with this trade war, that is on Congress,” he said. A recording of the debate is available on Prairie Public’s YouTube channel, titled “Face to Face: North Dakota U.S. House Debate 2026.”

artigo.texto: The Vandalia City Council moves forward with the process of eventually approving an ordinance for Battery Energy Storage Systems. During their meeting on Monday night, the Vandalia City Council discussed the matter and was probably their longest topic of discussion during Monday’s meeting. Alderman Kenny Lewey asked some questions about the need for the ordinance and City Attorney Ryan Connor and Mayor Doug Knebel this gets the ball rolling on the matter for the City of Vandalia. Mayor Knebel says, at this time with no ordinance in place, a company would not be able to put in a Battery Energy Storage System in Vandalia. Alderman Russ Stunkel asked if this is a matter where the City is getting their hand forced by the State and he got further explanation from Connor and City Administrator LaTisha Paslay on the matter. The matter was approved by the Vandalia City Council by a 5 to 2 vote with Aldermen Mike Hobler and Steve Barker voting No and Alderman Ken Hubler absent from the meeting. The ordinance will now be referred off to the Planning & Zoning Committee for review. After their review of the matter and possible changes, it would then come back to the Vandalia City Council for final approval.

artigo.texto: Notícias RESOLUÇÃO Custeio de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias entra em consulta A minuta de resolução sobre a base de custeio e a metodologia de rateio do Encargo de Reserva de Capacidade associado à contratação de Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia em baterias (Ercap-SAE) é tema da Consulta Pública nº 37/2026 e de workshop, conforme aprovado na 20ª Reunião Pública Ordinária da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (ANEEL), na terça-feira (06/10). É importante ressaltar que a proposta trata exclusivamente do Ercap-SAE e não dispõe sobre o Encargo de Reserva de Capacidade Geral (Ercap-Geral), pretendendo assegurar que os dois regimes coexistam sem sobreposição. A proposta de regulação busca garantir a sustentabilidade econômica dos projetos de armazenamento, essenciais para a expansão contínua das fontes renováveis variáveis na matriz elétrica nacional. Pela minuta, estarão sujeitos ao rateio do Ercap-SAE os titulares de outorga ou de registro de central geradora que se enquadrem como agentes da Câmara de Comercialização de Energia Elétrica (CCEE), excluindo a Micro e Minigeração Distribuída (MMGD) e o armazenamento autônomo. Está previsto, ainda, que a base de cálculo do encargo seja a energia efetivamente associada a cada agente de geração no período de apuração e que caberá ao Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) divulgar anualmente a classificação dos empreendimentos para aplicação no ano subsequente. Ainda pela minuta, o Ercap-SAE integrará a estrutura de financiamento da reserva de capacidade junto à Conta de Potência para Reserva de Capacidade (CONCAP). Como participar A Consulta Pública nº 37/2026 terá duração de 30 dias, de 08/10/2026 a 06/11/2026, quando poderão ser enviados subsídios e informações adicionais para o e-mail cp037_2026@aneel.gov.br. Os documentos que integram o processo, incluindo a Análise de Impacto Regulatório (AIR) e a minuta de resolução, estão disponíveis no portal da ANEEL, no menu Participação Social > Consultas Públicas. Durante o período da consulta, a ANEEL promoverá um workshop para apresentação da proposta e discussão da metodologia de rateio, dos índices e patamares de flexibilidade, dos critérios de enquadramento, da segregação entre o Ercap-Geral e o Ercap-SAE e dos mecanismos de apuração, repasse e liquidação. A data será oportunamente divulgada. O evento estará aberto à participação dos agentes setoriais, da Câmara de Comercialização de Energia Elétrica (CCEE), do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) e aos demais interessados.

artigo.texto: Finlândia freia construção de dois 'data centers' da Google por impacto ambiental Empresa responsável por obras não teria apresentado reltório de avaliação; agência do governo investiga corte de mais de 300 hectares de floresta Uma agência governamental finlandesa ordenou, nesta terça-feira (6), que a Google suspenda a construção de novos "data centers" em dois municípios da Finlândia no mais tardar em 23 de outubro de 2026, à espera de uma avaliação de seu impacto ambiental. Estes projetos fazem parte de um investimento de 13 bilhões de euros (R$ 72,7 bilhões) anunciado na Finlândia, o maior investimento da gigante tecnológica americana na Europa no âmbito da inteligência artificial. Durante uma visita na semana passada à cidade de Muhos, uma jornalista da AFP observou o ir e vir de retroescavadeiras. Em frente à fazenda de um dos moradores com quem conversou, a floresta tinha desaparecido de um terreno adquirido pela Google. - Caribe em Ipanema: Descoberta de bancos de algas calcárias cor-de-rosa surpreende pesquisadores; veja - Quer morar fora? Guia reúne informações sobre 36 países A agência finlandesa de supervisão exigiu, em um comunicado, que sejam suspensas "todas as medidas preparatórias suscetíveis de modificar de forma significativa o meio ambiente no âmbito dos projetos de 'data centers' previstos em Muhos e Kajaani", no noroeste do país. A agência abriu uma investigação pela suspeita de que a empresa Tuike Finland, que representa a Google, cortou mais de 300 hectares de floresta em Muhos sem realizar previamente a avaliação de impacto ambiental. As obras devem ser interrompidas até que seja feita esta avaliação, detalhou a agência. "Entendemos as preocupações expressas e reconhecemos que, neste caso concreto, não estivemos à altura de nossos próprios padrões, que são elevados", admitiu Sondre Ronander, porta-voz da Google, em uma mensagem enviada à AFP. "Estudaremos as conclusões da agência e seguiremos suas recomendações", acrescentou. Graças a um clima ameno, uma eletricidade relativamente estável e barata, produzida majoritariamente mediante energia nuclear, além de uma ampla capacidade eólica e hidrelétrica, a Finlândia experimentou recentemente um auge dos investimentos em "data centers".

artigo.texto: Geral Aneel aprova consulta pública sobre custeio da contratação de baterias no sistema elétrico Consulta pública ficará aberta até 9 de novembro de 2026 A diretoria da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) decidiu nesta terça-feira, 6, abrir consulta pública de 30 dias para o aprimoramento da proposta de custeio da contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, na modalidade de reserva de capacidade. A consulta ficará aberta de 8 de outubro a 9 de novembro de 2026. A área técnica da Agência apontou, em parecer de agosto, que a melhor alternativa para os custos da contratação de baterias é o rateio entre todos os geradores de energia. Contudo, a proposta é que o pagamento seja modulado em função do chamado Índice de Flexibilidade (IF). Com esse critério, aquelas usinas com maior flexibilidade pagariam menos (25% do encargo), enquanto aquelas com menor flexibilidade pagariam 100%. A alternativa, ainda de acordo com a área técnica, apresenta o “melhor equilíbrio” entre a aderência à finalidade do encargo, a estabilidade do custeio, a objetividade técnica e a viabilidade regulatória. O tema é controverso, especialmente porque há projetos de lei no Congresso buscando derrubar essa previsão de rateio dos custos. A Lei nº 15.269/2025, de modernização do setor elétrico, previu expressamente que os custos decorrentes da contratação de baterias sejam rateados apenas entre os geradores de energia elétrica, excluindo a possibilidade de custeio pelos consumidores. Os dois leilões de baterias, inéditos, estão previstos para dezembro deste ano. O diretor Gentil Nogueira, relator, comentou que a proposta em discussão trata da “norma perene”, que, se aprovada, poderá ser utilizada para o custeio dos sistemas de armazenamento que devem ser contratados no leilão de baterias marcado para dezembro. No entanto, ele salientou que o próprio edital do leilão, ainda a ser aprovado, pode trazer disciplina para esse custeio específico. O edital precisa ser aprovado até o fim de outubro, de maneira a cumprir a regra de publicação com 30 dias de antecedência. artigo.texto: BOSTON, Sept. 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Factorial Energy Inc. (“Factorial”) (Nasdaq: FAC), a global leader in solid-state battery technology, today announced a strategic partnership with Mitsui Kinzoku Company, Limited to support the industrialization of its Solstice™ all-solid-state battery platform. Mitsui Kinzoku is a leading producer of sulfide-based solid electrolytes for all-solid-state batteries, one of few companies worldwide with foundational technology in this space, and already the global leader in ultra-thin copper foil, with an estimated 90% share of the semiconductor market for that foil. That materials science expertise underpins its A-SOLiD™ sulfide solid electrolyte, unveiled in 2016 and advancing toward mass production at a dedicated plant in Saitama, Japan. "I am very pleased that we have been able to enter into this joint development agreement with Factorial," said Dr. Kiyotaka Yasuda, Senior Executive Officer, General Manager, Business Creation Division of Mitsui Kinzoku Company, Limited. "Batteries are a key technology for realizing an electrified society, but significant technical challenges still remain. That is precisely why we believe it is necessary to go beyond the extension of existing technologies and take on the challenge of creating new value. By leveraging Mitsui Kinzoku's long-established expertise in materials and manufacturing technologies and combining it with Factorial's advanced technological capabilities, we aim to accelerate the realization of next-generation batteries." Factorial remains the fabless innovator across the platform, leading cell design, process development, supply chain qualification, line integration, and manufacturing validation. “Battery innovation can't be done by one single company," said Siyu Huang, CEO of Factorial. "It's driven by the entire supply chain and, increasingly, by an entire industry coalition. Mitsui Kinzoku's foundational electrolyte technology brings critical materials expertise to our work to move Solstice™ toward commercial deployment. We're not just building a battery. We're building the connective thread that helps the whole industry move forward together.” As robotics, aerospace systems, and AI-enabled infrastructure ask more of the physical world, energy is fast becoming the defining constraint on what's possible. Factorial calls this the emergence of the energy layer - the battery infrastructure needed to power the next era of mobility, aerospace and physical intelligence. Built for that layer, Solstice™, Factorial's sulfide-based all-solid-state battery platform, delivers high energy density and improved thermal stability, with proprietary dry-cathode processing enabling more cost-effective manufacturing. This collaboration builds on Factorial's recent momentum, including strategic investments from IQT and POSCO Future M; its first commercial orders for passenger vehicles in January and for aerospace in July; expanded automotive and industrialization partnership programs; and its June 2026 Nasdaq listing under the ticker symbol FAC. Factorial Energy (Nasdaq: FAC) is a leading American solid-state battery innovator backed by IQT – the not-for-profit strategic investor for the U.S. national security community and America’s allies – and Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, Hyundai, and Kia. Through its proprietary FEST® and Solstice™ platforms, engineered for scalable manufacturing, Factorial delivers industry-leading performance across aerospace, energy storage and mobility applications. In 2026, Factorial's initial drone flight test achieved 30% longer range, and the company secured its first commercial orders in both aerospace and passenger vehicle applications. In automotive, Mercedes-Benz’ real-world road testing in a lightly modified test vehicle achieved over 1,200 km of range on a single charge, with the technology also successfully integrated into a fully built Dodge Charger Daytona demonstration vehicle in partnership with Stellantis.. For more information, visit www.factorialenergy.com. Mitsui Kinzoku is a Japan-based global materials company and a leading manufacturer of non-ferrous metals and advanced materials, providing innovative solutions primarily for the automotive and electronics industries. Leveraging its core strengths in non-ferrous metals, functional materials, and recycling technologies, the company develops and manufactures a wide range of high-performance products, including automotive components, semiconductor materials, battery materials, and engineered materials. With a strong focus on innovation, environmental responsibility, and resource circulation, Mitsui Kinzoku collaborates with partners around the world to create new value and will continue to contribute to the realization of a sustainable society. artigo.texto: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. While state lawmakers and both candidates in Wisconsin’s race for governor say they want individual communities to have the final say in data center development, local policymakers say that approach puts them in a tricky position. Dane County communities, including Madison and the county itself, have passed temporary moratoriums on data center development amid public opposition to the facilities. In Sun Prairie, which passed a moratorium on facilities of 10,000 square feet or larger in September, the city’s Utilities Commission received its first public comment on any topic in five years, commission chair Josh Christensen announced to the delight of its members. The topic was data centers, and resident Jenna Frost wanted to put in her two cents in a written comment in August. “She strongly wanted us to know that she is in support of a moratorium, would like to see transparency throughout any process and is very anti-data center,” Christensen said in summary. Public speculation about possible data center developments has also mounted. During a recent Sun Prairie City Council meeting, Mayor Steve Stocker asked staff members to dispel a rumor that the city’s proposal to acquire nearby marshland would pave the way for a data center. Property zoned for parkland can’t be developed. But whispers about possible data centers aren’t exactly unfounded. The state is home to at least 30 data centers, a report from the Wisconsin Policy Forum found. While most are older and smaller facilities, the state has seen growing interest in so-called “hyperscale” facilities from big technology companies like Microsoft, Oracle and Open AI. Seven such proposals, including a $12 billion facility near DeForest, have been blocked at the local level, but others, like those in Port Washington and Beaver Dam, have continued. Mike Peters, president of the nonprofit power provider WPPI Energy, recounted a meeting last fall when he asked the utility’s board members from the 51 communities WPPI serves whether they had been approached by data centers. “Half the hands went up in the room,” Peters said. “Data centers are out there knocking on the door of most of our members.” Often, they’re doing so quietly. Patrick Miles, chair of the Dane County Board, sponsored the resolution that set up an 18-month moratorium on hyperscale data center development in areas where the county has zoning authority, in large part as a way of creating transparency in an often opaque process. “Learning about their habit of using NDAs (non-disclosure agreements) when they’re talking with community decisionmakers, it’s no wonder that there’s so much distrust and concern,” Miles said. “It started becoming clear to me that we’re living in the Wild West. There aren’t guidelines. There aren’t guardrails.” The nature of the current data center prospecting and development process is frustrating local elected officials. Cynthia Richson, chair of Middleton’s Town Board, called it a “playbook” where well-resourced companies privately reach out to local officials to “one by one turn them.” “They like local officials who don’t know much because they’re kind of easy to persuade when you dangle a big pile of money in front of them, which is sad,” said Richson, who serves on Dane County’s Advisory Committee on Data Centers. “‘Taking advantage’ seems like how I would describe that (tactic) of sophisticated tech people.” Local officials have some tools at their disposal to regulate data center development. Both Richson and Madison City Council member Derek Field, who sits on the city’s Plan Commission, pointed to long-range planning and zoning as the primary way communities can limit or prohibit the facilities. Still, finding answers amid what Field called “the biggest land use discussion of our time” is challenging for local lawmakers in Wisconsin because of the pace of changing technology, a relative lack of reliable information, and an inability to act more broadly. Local leaders have also found themselves somewhat at odds with state lawmakers’ current approach to the issue, especially as the Legislature created a set of tax exemptions for data center developers in 2023. “I’m under no delusion that a (hypothetical) hyperscale data center that opens on the town of Cottage Grove side of our municipal boundary would have any less of an impact on the power rates we have to pay for the next 30 years,” Field said. “This is definitely a regional problem. I think we are struggling to figure out how to deal with those impacts locally when we can only legislate within Madison.” While the county’s task force started as a way of advising Dane County communities on data centers, Miles said it’s taken on an informal lobbying role. “What has evolved in this is also a need to (reach) another audience — state government — for us to identify gaps and weaknesses in state policy,” Miles said. ‘A significant disadvantage’ At a recent meeting of the county task force, Jim Hamilton, executive director of the Nuclear Decommissioning Collaborative, drew comparisons between nuclear power plants and hyperscale data centers, given the amount of land required, environmental questions, payment structures to local governments, and the need to retire equipment after a certain period of time. He advised members to “get everything up front” in agreements with developers so local communities aren’t left to pay for future costs when the payments stop. In Wisconsin, local governments cannot mandate developers to sign community benefit agreements that can require, for example, the use of union labor or renewable power sourcing as part of a conditional use permitting process. artigo.texto: The solar array on the Williston side of the GlobalFoundries campus, seen here, accounts for about one-third of the solar energy now generated on the campus. GlobalFoundries last week marked the delivery of approximately six megawatts of new on-site solar arrays and a 16-megawatt battery energy storage system at its campus in Essex Junction and Williston. Company leaders invited Gov. Phil Scott, Agency of Natural Resources Secretary Julie Moore and project developers from Encore Renewable Energy and Lightshift Energy to celebrate the occasion, which the company described in a news release as “a milestone in its clean energy journey.” “Together, the projects advance GlobalFoundries’ long-term energy strategy, support grid reliability and demonstrate a practical model for powering advanced manufacturing … The solar arrays and battery system help GlobalFoundries optimize energy use, manage costs and put underutilized industrial land to productive use.” The company’s “Journey to Zero” strategy comprises environmental efforts in energy, water usage and manufacturing emissions. “This site has been in the business of firsts for almost 70 years, and today we’re celebrating a new way of powering the semiconductor innovations we make,” said Dan Colello, vice president and general manager of GlobalFoundries’ Vermont campus. “The team took the time to thoroughly study, validate and design a solution that can work in harmony with the highly sensitive, advanced manufacturing equipment that powers our operations.” GlobalFoundries developed the project with Vermont regulators, the City of Essex Junction, VELCO and Green Mountain Power. The systems will come fully online in the coming months and are expected to be in service for over 20 years. “Economic growth should always be a priority of government as well as clean energy innovation and affordability,” said Gov. Scott. “And when we do it right, like everyone has done on this project, it helps us achieve our economic and environmental goals faster.” Chad Farrell, founder and president, Encore Renewable Energy, added: “This site is ready for its second act — an encore as a bright field, bringing new energy to the land and the regional power grid. These two solar projects show the potential in spaces that were once heavily used and then largely forgotten. The sun still shines on this land, and now more than 30 acres of it are delivering real value to GlobalFoundries, the region and the state.”

artigo.texto: With a few dozen data centers already up and running in Pennsylvania and proposals on the table for over 100 more, public opposition is growing — especially to the new hyperscale projects intended to support AI. Like his counterparts across the Chesapeake Bay region, Gov. Josh Shapiro is reading the room. According to a Quinnipiac University poll released in July, 74% of Pennsylvania voters say they would be against building an AI data center in their community. And on Aug. 18, Shapiro signed an executive order intended to give municipalities more control over data center development and to establish stricter guardrails for those projects. Governors in Maryland and Virginia have since followed suit. Shapiro’s order is “an important way to address concerns about consumer impacts, environmental impacts and public health impacts from data centers,” said Robert Routh, the state’s policy director for the Natural Resources Defense Council. Shapiro, a Democrat, was once a champion for data center development. In June 2025, his administration announced a $20 billion Amazon investment for AI infrastructure in Pennsylvania. “Our team worked closely with local leaders and Amazon to land this deal,” he said at the time. But with public outcry growing and the number of proposals multiplying, the Shapiro administration is attempting to place checks on the industry. In a May 2026 precursor to the executive order, Shapiro’s team announced the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development (GRID) initiative, intended to establish “strict standards that data centers must comply with to receive support from the commonwealth.” Those standards include commitments to economic development, energy affordability and transparency. They also address environmental protection, such as requirements for technologies that minimize water use and air pollution. In exchange, data center developers could expect speedier permitting through the PA Permit Fast Track Program. But compliance with GRID is voluntary. The new executive order adds teeth to the program and gives more power to local communities. Now, developers who sign a legally binding agreement with the state Department of Environmental Protection to meet GRID requirements can immediately submit permit applications for review. But DEP will not issue those permits until municipalities have approved the project. If a developer refuses to sign the agreement, DEP will not even begin reviewing its permit applications until local approval is secured. And the department will not issue any permits until all applications have been submitted. Developers who do not agree to GRID will also not qualify for the existing tax exemption on data center computer equipment. The order also removes all data center proposals from the PA Permit Fast Track Program, prohibits developers from using nondisclosure agreements and requires data center operators to report energy and water usage to DEP annually beginning in July 2027. “There are no AI data centers up-and-running right now in Pennsylvania,” Shapiro remarked at his executive order signing ceremony. And only two have completed DEP review, according to the department’s new Data Center Permit Tracker website. One of those is in Westmoreland County, and the other is one of two planned for Lancaster County. The expectation, one administration official said on background, is that these new requirements will help distinguish projects that may never be built from “projects that are serious, have financing and access to power and have a committed end user.” The order means that developers cannot use the state’s approval as leverage at the local level, said David Sanko, executive director of the Pennsylvania State Association of Township Supervisors. Developers, he adds, will no longer get their state permits first and then say, “Well, the state already says ‘okay.’ Why are you in the way?” Kirk Stoner, director of planning for Cumberland County, across the Susquehanna River west of Harrisburg, wishes the GRID guidance had come sooner. His county is home to the hotly contested $15 billion PAX-1 data center project in Middlesex Township. Some of the arguments over energy, water and air quality could have been more focused if there had been more definitive information on resource impacts to consider upfront, he said. But exactly how the executive order will play out in individual towns isn’t yet clear. “A lot of the ordinances that I’m seeing here in Cumberland County are really strict, and I’m not sure that there’s going to be a lot of projects moving forward to the state level,” Stoner said. A municipality might, for example, restrict data center development to a minimum lot size of 40 acres within an industrial zone that doesn’t contain available lots that size. Stoner said it begs the question, “At what point does the private sector and the data center industry start to push back on some of those and come in and challenge ordinances to say they’re exclusionary?” Stoner also wonders whether some municipalities might actually request that DEP complete reviews of environmental permits first, so they don’t waste time and concern citizens with projects that might ultimately be killed at the state level. Another question is how many data center developers will sign the GRID agreement. “In distinguishing speculative proposals from real projects, it’s important that rules are not changed midstream, impacting ongoing investment in verified and responsible data center projects,” said Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs for the Data Center Coalition, a trade association. “Companies have made plans, [and] communities have prepared for economic opportunities.” As of September 18, one month after the executive order was signed, a Shapiro administration official told the Bay Journal thatno data center developers had signed on. artigo.texto: O Data Center World Brasil ainda não terminou e já é considerado um sucesso, nas palavras de representantes da Informa Eventos, organizadora da exposição realizada no São Paulo Expo, em São Paulo. Pela primeira vez no Brasil, o evento tem 3,5 mil visitantes inscritos, superando em mil a meta dos organizadores, além de 42 empresas no segmento de infraestrutura de data centers, 100% dos espaços vendidos e um número superior a 110 reuniões agendadas conectando patrocinadores a grandes compradores finais. “Isso mostra o quanto pessoas são interessados em data center, quanto dinheiro tem aí, mas mais do que isto, quantas oportunidades tem aí para o desenvolvimento do país na geração de emprego e qualificação de mão-de-obra”, disse o diretor do Data Center World Brasil, Leonardo Benedicto. A feira é realizada em conjunto com o Futurecom, ambos da mesma organizadora e este um evento já consolidado no cenário de tecnologia, telecomunicações e segmentos associados. E neste cenário, o Rio Grande do Sul tem sido visto com bons olhos, na esteira de projetos como os de R$ 500 milhões da Parks para uma estrutura do tipo em Cachoeirinha, na região Metropolitana, e o Scala AI City, em Eldorado do Sul, de R$ 3 bilhões. Outra empresa envolvida com o RS que expõe na feira paulistana é a V.tal, responsável pelo cabo submarino Malbec, que ingressa no território gaúcho pelo município de Balneário Pinhal, no litoral Norte. Data Center World Brasil 2026 e participação da Kingston no evento “O Rio Grande do Sul tem projetos muito atrativos, assim como outros estados também têm”, pontuou Benedicto. Já o head de infraestrutura e tecnologia da Informa Markets, Fernando d’Ascola, destacou “corredores cheios, expositores felizes, muito encontro e muito networking” nos pavilhões 1 e 2 do São Paulo Expo, onde as feiras são realizadas conjuntamente. O Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), sancionado em setembro pelo governo federal, é bem visto pelo setor, além de discussões durante o evento pontuarem a necessidade de maior carga e disponibilidade de energia, especialmente renovável, de maneira principal visando ao avanço da inteligência artificial e da computação em nuvem. “Não basta ter projetos e investimentos. É preciso ter disponibilidade energética, conectividade e segurança para colocar essa infraestrutura de pé e mantê-la em operação. Dada essa dinâmica de mercado e às fortalezas únicas do Brasil no que diz respeito à abundância de água, matriz energética renovável, em especial que é uma vantagem competitiva, precisávamos ter um evento que fosse essa plataforma, e é para isso que o Data Center World Brasil chega”, disse Leonardo. Ele destacou ainda que o congresso busca “desmistificar mitos” relacionados a questão ambiental e mostrar a preocupação real do setor, combatendo visões distorcidas sobre o uso de água por meio de dados reais e curadoria técnica. Para conter esse impacto, a feira destacou tecnologias avançadas de climatização para data centers, como sistemas de refrigeração líquida, refrigeração evaporativa e gestão inteligente de efluentes e água.

artigo.texto: Tesla Megapack, CATL TENER and BYD MC Cube are competing for a rapidly expanding utility-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) market, but their strategies differ significantly. Tesla emphasizes factory-integrated hardware, deployment and energy-market optimization through Autobidder. CATL is pushing container energy density, long-duration efficiency and lifecycle performance. BYD combines Blade Battery technology, Cell-to-System integration and vertically integrated LFP manufacturing. For utilities and renewable-energy developers, however, the key question is not which company has the largest battery container. It is which BESS can deliver the lowest risk-adjusted lifetime cost and highest revenue from a project’s available land and grid connection. There is no credible public evidence that Tesla, CATL or BYD universally offers the lowest installed cost or highest ROI. Project bids, EPC scope, warranties, grid connection and revenue models are needed to determine that. This distinction becomes increasingly important as the world’s largest battery storage projects move from hundreds of MWh into multi-GWh territory. Tesla Megapack: Software Could Be Its Biggest Advantage Tesla’s four-hour Megapack configuration provides 979 kW of power and 3,916 kWh of energy per unit, with published round-trip efficiency of 93.7 percent. Its two-hour configuration provides 1,927 kW/3,854 kWh and 92 percent efficiency. Megapack is factory integrated with battery modules, inverters and thermal systems and ships ready for installation. The differentiator is increasingly software. Tesla’s Autobidder uses price, load and generation forecasting to automate bidding and dispatch in wholesale electricity markets. Tesla says Autobidder-optimized sites cover more than 30 projects and 10 GWh and can also be offered with revenue guarantees. That gives Tesla an important proposition for merchant BESS developers: combining hardware, servicing and revenue optimization. Tesla is also expanding manufacturing. Megapack 3 production is scheduled at Megafactory Houston during 2026 with planned manufacturing capacity of up to 50 GWh annually. Tesla advantage: standardized deployment plus a mature software and energy-trading layer. CATL TENER: Energy Density and Efficiency Lead the Pitch CATL has taken a different route by aggressively increasing the amount of energy that can be installed within a constrained site. The original TENER stores 6.25 MWh in a 20-foot container, using LFP cells with energy density of 430 Wh/L. CATL says the design increases energy density per unit area by 30 percent and reduces station footprint by 20 percent. CATL also claims TENER can achieve zero capacity and power degradation during its first five years under specified conditions. Developers need to evaluate the precise warranty and operating conditions behind that claim. TENER H pushes capacity to 9,008 kWh per container and supports two-, four- and eight-hour configurations. CATL says the four- and eight-hour versions achieve round-trip efficiency of up to 96 percent, while increasing land utilization by 45 percent. CATL also reported 125 GWh of ESS battery shipments during H1 2026, according to SNE Research data cited by the company. CATL advantage: high energy density, manufacturing scale and long-duration configurations. BYD MC Cube-T: Blade Battery Meets System Integration BYD’s MC Cube-T combines the company’s LFP Blade Battery technology with Cell-to-System architecture. MC Cube-T provides 6.432 MWh of capacity. BYD says the system reduces the number of parts and components by 36 percent while increasing space utilization by 98 percent. The technology is already moving into large projects. A 100 MW/400 MWh project in Central California using BYD MC Cube entered service in 2025. BYD also signed contracts with Saudi Electricity Company covering 12.5 GWh of grid-scale storage projects in 2025, taking their combined cooperation to 15.1 GWh including an earlier 2.6 GWh project. MC Cube-T is no longer BYD’s highest-capacity platform. Its Haohan platform reaches up to 14.5 MWh, illustrating the rapid increase in container-level energy density. BYD advantage: Blade Battery technology, vertical integration, CTS architecture and growing deployment scale. The scale of these platforms reflects the broader energy storage investment boom as utilities and renewable-energy developers increasingly treat BESS as core grid infrastructure. What Would a 200 MWh Project Require? Container capacity illustrates how architecture affects the number of major battery units required. These are simple energy-capacity calculations, not complete BESS designs. A real project must account for PCS configuration, redundancy, usable capacity, safety separation, transformers, access roads, augmentation and interconnection. Nevertheless, fewer battery units can potentially mean fewer foundations, cable runs and installation interfaces and a smaller overall footprint. For developers comparing project economics, battery storage costs in 2026 increasingly depend on much more than the price of cells or containers. CATL Leads on Published Container Density For land-constrained projects, CATL’s TENER H is notable because it reaches approximately 9 MWh per container. BYD MC Cube-T’s 6.432 MWh is also substantially above Tesla’s published approximately 3.9 MWh four-hour Megapack configuration. But container MWh alone should not determine procurement. Tesla integrates the inverter within Megapack, so comparing battery-container capacity alone can exaggerate differences between architectures. Developers need to compare total plant footprint for the same MW/MWh specification. The relevant commercial metric is ultimately usable MWh per acre, not simply MWh per container. Efficiency can also have a substantial lifetime impact. artigo.texto: Mercado global dos sistemas avançados de armazenamento de energia: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do Mercado de Sistemas Avançados de Armazenamento de Energia até 2035: modernização da rede e integração de renováveis impulsionam a expansão Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de Sistemas Avançados de Armazenamento de Energia, o mercado entra em 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de Sistemas Avançados de Armazenamento de Energia passa por uma transformação estrutural: de nicho sustentado por políticas públicas para pilar da infraestrutura energética moderna, puxado pela demanda. À medida que a participação das renováveis aumenta e os operadores de rede lidam com a intermitência, a lógica econômica do armazenamento deixou de ser movida por subsídios e passou a ser movida pela necessidade. Entre 2026 e 2035, o mercado será moldado pelo imperativo de integrar renováveis variáveis, adiar reforços na transmissão e ampliar a resiliência da rede. A integração de sistemas e os subsistemas de conversão de potência despontam como pontos críticos de captura de valor, muitas vezes determinando a bancabilidade do projeto mais do que o próprio meio de armazenamento. Ocorre uma bifurcação fundamental: aplicações de curta duração e alta ciclagem competem por métricas de US$/kW e US$/kWh, enquanto aplicações de longa duração e de resiliência competem pelo custo total de propriedade, pela segurança e pela complexidade de integração específica de cada local. A resiliência da cadeia de suprimentos tornou-se requisito básico, e as exigências de qualificação para novas químicas criam desvantagens de tempo de entrada no mercado. A compra está migrando da aquisição de componentes para contratos de serviço com desempenho garantido, forçando os fabricantes a assumir risco operacional de longo prazo. A especialização geográfica se intensifica, criando dependências comerciais complexas. Os protocolos de segurança deixam de ser uma preocupação secundária e passam a ser restrições primárias de projeto, influenciando seguros, licenciamento e viabilidade de implantação. Este relatório oferece uma análise estruturada e comercialmente fundamentada dessas dinâmicas, dando aos tomadores de decisão uma visão clara da demanda de implantação, do posicionamento tecnológico, da exposição industrial, da economia dos projetos e da estrutura competitiva até 2035. O cenário-base para o mercado de Sistemas Avançados de Armazenamento de Energia entre 2026 e 2035 prevê expansão robusta, impulsionada pela aceleração da integração de fontes renováveis e pela necessidade urgente de modernizar a infraestrutura de rede envelhecida. Com o crescimento da capacidade solar e eólica, o desafio da intermitência se agrava, tornando o armazenamento componente indispensável de sistemas elétricos confiáveis. Utilities e operadores de rede compram cada vez mais armazenamento para adiar reforços caros de transmissão e distribuição, prestar regulação de frequência e ampliar a resiliência contra eventos climáticos extremos. O setor comercial e industrial também desponta como importante centro de demanda, motivado pela gestão de custos de energia, por metas de sustentabilidade e pela necessidade de energia de reserva. Avanços tecnológicos, sobretudo na química de lithium-ion e nos sistemas de conversão de potência, reduzem custos e melhoram o desempenho, reforçando ainda mais a lógica econômica. O mercado, porém, enfrenta ventos contrários ligados a restrições da cadeia de suprimentos, especialmente em minerais críticos e na fabricação de células de bateria, o que pode moderar o crescimento em algumas regiões. O apoio de políticas públicas continua sendo viabilizador essencial, mas a tendência é de mecanismos de mercado que remunerem o armazenamento pelos serviços prestados à rede. Espera-se consolidação do cenário competitivo, com fornecedores de sistemas integrados ganhando participação sobre os fornecedores de componentes. Até 2035, projeta-se que o mercado alcance um nível de implantação significativamente maior, com taxa de crescimento anual composta (CAGR) de 15,2% entre 2026 e 2035, e o índice de mercado (2025=100) subindo para 420, o que reflete mais que quadruplicar o valor de mercado. Essa projeção não considera grandes rupturas tecnológicas nem crises geopolíticas severas, mas reconhece que persistirão variações regionais conforme os ambientes regulatórios e a dotação de recursos de cada região. Vetores e Restrições da Demanda Principais Vetores de Demanda - Os rápidos acréscimos de capacidade renovável, sobretudo solar e eólica, criam necessidade urgente de armazenamento para suavizar a intermitência e deslocar a oferta para os períodos de pico de demanda. - As iniciativas de modernização da rede e a necessidade de adiar reforços caros de transmissão e distribuição impulsionam a compra de armazenamento em escala de utility. - A queda dos custos de baterias e a melhoria da densidade energética, impulsionadas por escala e avanços tecnológicos, ampliam a viabilidade econômica dos projetos de armazenamento. - Compromissos corporativos de descarbonização e metas de sustentabilidade estimulam instalações de armazenamento comercial e industrial atrás do medidor. - A frequência crescente de eventos climáticos extremos e de interrupções na rede estimula a demanda por soluções de resiliência e energia de reserva. - Políticas governamentais de apoio, incluindo créditos fiscais de investimento e reformas de mercados de capacidade, aceleram a implantação de armazenamento em mercados-chave. artigo.texto: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. Maily Kocinski feels like she’s screaming into the void. She lives about four miles from where Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, is building a data center in Beaver Dam. The fifth grade teacher has struggled to know where to turn with her concerns about whether the data center development could be harming her water or land. And although Kocinski has been a dedicated Democratic voter, her experience as a data center neighbor is causing doubts about her choice in the Nov. 3 election for governor. Wisconsin has seen a boom of proposed hyperscale data centers, large facilities that house servers often used to power artificial intelligence technology. In addition to Meta’s $1 billion campus in Beaver Dam, data centers are being built in Port Washington and Mount Pleasant, and others have been proposed in DeForest, Janesville, Wisconsin Rapids and elsewhere. Data centers have become a divisive issue, but not in the left vs. right fashion typical in a battleground state like Wisconsin. The disconnect appears to be between a broad range of Wisconsinites and the public officials who want to represent them: For some voters, data centers are at the center of the universe. But for many lawmakers and political candidates, the issue is toxic. “That’s a very thorny, difficult thing for public officials. And whether they haven’t realized how big of an issue it is, or whether they are hesitant to acknowledge it because they’re still trying to figure it out, the reality is it’s a complicated situation for them,” said Brian Reisinger, a public affairs strategist and former Republican campaign adviser. “But for the voters right now — the voters don’t consider it complicated,” Reisinger said. Into the void Wisconsin voter opposition to data centers has been widespread in recent months, according to polling. A September poll from the Marquette University Law School found that 74% of Wisconsin voters who responded thought the costs of data centers outweighed their potential benefits, which was up from last October, when 55% felt that way, though slightly down from the 78% in August. Voters of all creeds shared this sentiment: 57% of Republicans, 83% of independents and 90% of Democrats felt the costs of data centers outweighed the benefits. “It’s hard to find an issue that has more people from the left, more people from the right, and those independent swing voters and split-ticket voters worked up than data centers,” said Reisinger. Wisconsin politicians from both sides of the aisle have more tepid feelings toward data centers than their voters do. While most want more regulations, you’d be hard pressed to find one who is staunchly for or against the developments. This includes the two main candidates running for governor, Democrat David Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany, who have similar ideas for how the state should address data centers. They both want to ban nondisclosure agreements — the secret-keeping deals some local government officials have made with developers — and say they want to protect utility customers and the environment. But Crowley and Tiffany both also oppose a statewide moratorium on the developments and say they want local governments to have the final say on whether to allow a data center in their community. They disagree marginally. Tiffany said he wants to fully eliminate subsidies included in the 2023-25 state budget, which exempted data center builders from sales and use taxes on equipment they bought to furnish the facilities. Crowley said he wants to scale back but not eliminate the subsidies, which could cost the state about $1.5 billion in lost tax revenue over five years, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Fiscal Bureau. Crowley has called for data centers to use 100% renewable energy, while Tiffany has been critical of that approach. Both claim the other is softer on data centers and regulating AI. The Cap Times requested interviews with both Crowley and Tiffany to discuss the specifics of their data center plans and how they would execute them, but both campaigns declined and sent prepared statements instead. “I’ve been clear that local communities should decide if a data center is right for them, and if they don’t want them, they should not be forced to accept them — no ifs, ands or buts. And if a community decides they want a data center, they need to be built with union labor and with full transparency and accountability, ensuring these data centers don’t pass on a single penny to (utility) ratepayers,” Crowley said in his statement. “We have some of the best farmland in America, and once it’s gone, we don’t get it back. As governor, I will end the data center subsidies, protect our farmland, and make sure America’s Dairyland does not become America’s Dataland,” Tiffany said in his statement. State lawmakers running for reelection agree that data centers need to be regulated and that there should be local control. Rep. David Steffen, a Republican from the Green Bay area who chairs the state Assembly’s energy and utilities committee, called data centers a “totally toxic issue” for voters. But he called himself “agnostic” on the issue. Instead of picking a side, he said he’s focusing on ensuring that the public understands data centers aren’t a “Death Star” designed to harm people. “It doesn’t have to fit for everyone. But just like any business, they should have the opportunity to come and at least speak to a community and say, ‘Hey, do you want this?’” Steffen said. “But I think actually there’s a great opportunity for unity on this particular issue,” he said. Steffen said he feels confident that, regardless of who wins the race for governor in November, the state will install data center regulations in the first 90 days of the new legislative session that starts in January. artigo.texto: Amazon investirá US$1 bi em cinco anos em comunidades de data centers dos EUA A Amazon Web Services investirá mais de US$ 1 bilhão em cinco anos nas comunidades norte-americanas onde opera data centers. A medida visa mitigar críticas e conter mais de 100 moratórias locais contra os impactos dessas instalações no consumo de eletricidade e água, agravados pela expansão da IA. O aporte financiará educação, capacitação profissional e preservação energética e hídrica, alinhando-se à meta da empresa de devolver mais água do que consome até 2030. A divisão de computação em nuvem da Amazon afirmou nesta sexta-feira que investirá mais de US$1 bilhão nos próximos cinco anos em comunidades dos Estados Unidos onde possui data centers e prometeu abordar os impactos desses centros no consumo de eletricidade e água. Os data centers, que fornecem o poder computacional para treinar e executar modelos de inteligência artificial, têm gerado oposição em comunidades de todo o país devido a preocupações com a demanda de eletricidade, custos de serviços públicos e outros impactos locais. Essa reação negativa representa um desafio político para os republicanos às vésperas das eleições de meio de mandato nos EUA, em 3 de novembro. A Amazon afirmou ter investido US$276 bilhões em data centers entre 2011 e 2025 e que tinha grandes projetos ou expansões em andamento em muitos estados, incluindo Indiana, Louisiana, Carolina do Norte, Virgínia e Mississippi. A Amazon Web Services afirmou que os planos de investimento comunitário anunciados nesta sexta-feira incluirão gastos com educação, treinamento profissional, acessibilidade à energia, preservação de água e energia e outras prioridades locais em partes dos EUA onde possui centros de dados. Em um longo comunicado, a empresa procurou refutar as críticas aos centros de dados relacionadas aos impactos ambientais, energéticos e econômicos, e observou que mais de 100 moratórias para data centers estavam sendo consideradas em todo o país. "Há urgência na expansão desses data centers porque não somos o único país que reconhece os benefícios da IA para a economia e a segurança nacional, e os países que lideram em IA irão moldá-la e tirar o máximo proveito dela", disse Matt Garman, presidente-executivo da AWS. A AWS também se comprometeu a ser positiva em relação à água em todos os seus data centers até 2030, devolvendo mais água às comunidades do que utiliza, e afirmou estar 75% perto de atingir essa meta.

artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Google suspende obras de data centers na Finlândia em meio a plano de US$ 15 bilhões Publicado 07/10/2026 • 11:30 | Atualizado há 20 horas KEY POINTS Foto: Unsplash Google suspende obras de dois data centers um mês após a empresa anunciar um investimento de US$ 15 bilhões em infraestrutura de IA. O Google foi obrigado a suspender as obras de dois data centers que desenvolve na Finlândia, um mês após a gigante de tecnologia anunciar um investimento de US$ 15 bilhões em infraestrutura de inteligência artificial no país. A Agência Finlandesa de Licenciamento e Supervisão (LVV, na sigla em finlandês) determinou na terça-feira (06) que a Tuike Finland Oy, subsidiária do Google, suspenda as obras dos projetos de data centers planejados para Muhos e Kajaani até que sejam concluídas as avaliações de impacto ambiental. Segundo uma tradução do comunicado da LVV feita pelo Google, a suspensão inclui, entre outras atividades, a remoção de árvores e de solo superficial, escavações, exploração de pedreiras, britagem, movimentação de terra, abertura de valas e construção de estradas e áreas de armazenamento. “Entendemos as preocupações e, neste caso, ficamos abaixo dos nossos próprios padrões elevados”, disse um porta-voz do Google à CNBC, acrescentando que a empresa seguirá as orientações da LVV. “Atuamos de boa-fé de acordo com a Lei Florestal, realizamos estudos ambientais e adotamos medidas para proteger áreas de alto valor”, afirmou o porta-voz. “Enquanto damos continuidade ao nosso trabalho de longo prazo na região, estamos avançando com nossos planos de paisagismo e biodiversidade, que incluem o plantio de árvores em uma área de 130 hectares em Muhos.” A LVV determinou que o Google interrompa as obras até, no máximo, 23 de outubro. A ordem não se aplica a atividades de planejamento, medições, estudos de solo ou outras medidas de baixo impacto que possam ser facilmente revertidas. “Em nossa avaliação, as medidas em questão vão alterar o meio ambiente e causar impactos cuja identificação e avaliação estão entre os principais objetivos do processo de avaliação de impacto ambiental”, afirmou Tommi Muilu, chefe do departamento ambiental da autoridade finlandesa de licenciamento e supervisão. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC Leia também: Google fecha acordo de 20 anos para garantir energia nuclear nos EUA A Finlândia se tornou um importante destino para data centers em meio ao avanço da inteligência artificial, atraindo grandes empresas de tecnologia e desenvolvedores interessados na disponibilidade de terrenos e energia no país — recursos escassos na maior parte da Europa. Vários projetos de data centers com capacidade potencial de centenas de megawatts foram anunciados recentemente na Finlândia. O aumento da demanda fez com que o país passasse a ser chamado de “Texas da Europa”. O estado americano se tornou um dos principais polos mundiais de data centers voltados à inteligência artificial, com diversos projetos de grande porte anunciados por grandes operadores de infraestrutura de nuvem e laboratórios de IA, incluindo Google, Meta, Microsoft e Anthropic. O plano de US$ 15 bilhões do Google para a Finlândia será o maior investimento da empresa na Europa.
