artigo.texto: We sat down with Norfolk-based artist Rhashida Bess to talk about jewelry making and upcoming programs. Who is Rhashida Bess? Rhashida is the owner and operator of Alodeuri (pronounced al – oh – durr – ee) Artisan Jewelry, an African-inspired, cold form metal smithing and jewelry-making business. A skill she first learned in high school and advanced through self-teaching, jewelry making launched Rhashida into the world of entrepreneurship when she was looking for a way to turn her hobby into a way to provide for her family. Rhashida’s adornments (the term she uses for her handmade, sustainable, intention-based jewelry pieces) incorporate materials such as copper, brass, cowrie shells, semi-precious stones and crystals. How did she get started with NPL? Rhashida started working with NPL after attending a program. While talking with another library patron about her personal business, she was approached by a staff member who asked if she, with her wealth of experience, might be interested in teaching a program at the branch. What does Rhashida love about working with NPL? Rhashida loves teaching library patrons about the history of traditional jewelry and supporting them on their jewelry-making journey. Rhashida believes in teaching people both new skills and how to use those skills to achieve future financial stability. While Rhashida’s true love is copper-based jewelry, particularly chains, she dabbles in a variety of types and techniques, including beading and paper rolling. Some of the many programs Rhashida has done with NPL include Weaved Words Bangles, Maasai-inspired earrings and Crystal Point Necklaces. Upcoming Programs This fall, Rhashida will be holding The ARTisan Academy at Jordan-Newby Anchor Branch. Join her select Thursdays from 5:30 – 7:30 p.m. to invest 24 hours in yourself to change the rest of your life! This vocational pathway to creative entrepreneurship will teach you how to create adorned jewelry and birth a microbusiness. Fun Fact: Alodeuri is a blend of her children’s names. Fun Fact 2: Her favorite material to work with is copper.

artigo.texto: Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) have recently been drawing growing attention in the battery industry. While solid-state batteries, noted as the ‘dream battery’ for their high energy density, have attracted interest for future industries such as robots and high-performance electric vehicles (EVs), ‘price competitiveness’ is becoming crucial for applications such as energy storage systems (ESS) and mass-market EVs. Sodium is the English name for natrium, and SIBs are also called ‘salt batteries’. They charge and discharge by sodium ions, rather than lithium ions, moving between the cathode and anode. Because sodium, the key raw material, is abundant and sourced from a relatively wide range of regions, it can reduce raw-material price volatility and supply-chain risk. They are safe and maintain performance at low temperatures, raising expectations for broad application from ESS and EVs to automotive auxiliary power and uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) for data centers. This is why SIBs do not hide their ambitions to be an ‘all-weather battery’. Batteries, is ‘performance above all’ not everything? Humanoid robots and the like are emerging as new future sources of battery demand, but the largest markets remain EVs and ESS. Market researcher TrendForce estimates annual demand for solid-state batteries for humanoids at 74 gigawatt-hours (GWh) in 2035. By contrast, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA) and BloombergNEF, EV battery demand in the same year is projected at 4,0005,000 GWh, with new ESS installations reaching 972 GWh. The issue is that the importance of the ‘price factor’ is growing in both markets. In EVs, high-energy-density batteries are drawing attention for large, long-range, high-performance vehicles, while cost-competitive batteries are in focus for compact, urban models. ESS, where weight and volume constraints are relatively modest, is no different in the importance of price. The overall leveling-up of batteries is also heightening the importance of price. According to the IEA, the latest SIBs reach up to 175 watt-hours (Wh) per ㎏, falling short of the latest lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries (205Wh/㎏), but they have risen to the range of typical LFP levels (150~200Wh/㎏). China is moving to preempt the SIB market. After unveiling its SIB brand ‘Naxtra’ last year, CATL this year revealed a passenger car equipped with SIBs together with Changan Automobile. For ESS-use SIBs, it is targeting cumulative shipments of 1 GWh by year-end. According to the IEA, more than 95% of SIB production capacity in 2030, combining existing and planned facilities, is expected to be concentrated in China. Three Korean battery makers say, “This time is different from LFP”…gearing up to target SIB Korean battery makers are also accelerating development of batteries such as SIBs. This is because global SIB production capacity is still just over 1% of that of lithium-ion batteries, making it an early-stage market. A battery-industry source said, “There was a case in which domestic response to LFP was delayed in the past, so there is a mood not to fall behind in the early leadership race for the SIB market.” According to an announcement by SNE Research on the 2nd, global EV battery usage reached 844.2 GWh in JanuaryAugust this year, up 19.7% from the same period last year, but the combined share of the three Korean firms fell from 16.6% to 12.7%, down 3.9 percentage points. Meanwhile, the share of LFP batteries, where Chinese companies are strong, rose from 52.2% to 57.3%. SIBs are therefore also a future strategy to gain a competitive edge in the mass-market battery segment centered on China. LG Energy Solution is testing 12V (volt) and 24V packs for automotive auxiliary power on customer vehicles. It has completed technology validation in the hundreds of ㎿h(megawatt-hours) range with long-cycle ESS customers, and from next year plans to ship trial volumes to global customers. SK On plans to develop an ESS-use SIB prototype next year and commercialize it in 2028, and is also reviewing SIBs for EVs. Samsung SDI is developing SIBs for UPS and power ESS. The Korean government has set a goal of securing an SIB energy density of 160Wh/㎏ by 2027 and raising it to 220Wh/㎏ by 2030 for commercialization. ‘Will it catch LFP, or remain a niche?’…diverging views However, opinions diverge on whether SIBs will grow enough to threaten the position of LFP. Those who view SIBs as a future growth engine are pinning hopes on price declines with future mass production. Because supplies are nt concentrated in specific countries as with lithium, raw-material supply instability is lower, and aluminum can replace copper for the anode current collector, reducing costs. If pack structures are simplified by leveraging SIB safety, system-level costs can also be reduced. Conversely, as LFP is also raising energy density and compensating for weaknesses through design improvements, there is analysis that it is uncertain whether SIBs will fully replace LFP. Because each battery type has different strengthssuch as low-temperature performance, energy density, output, and safetySIBs should be seen as just ‘one option’ to broaden the battery portfolio. Can Korea catch up with China, which is in the lead? For Korean companies, the key question is whether they can secure competitiveness that surpasses China. In particular, in the early SIB market, how quickly they can narrow the mass-production gap with China and, at the same time, secure non-China material supply chains and customers will likely determine future competitiveness. In this respect, the United States push to build a de-China battery ecosystem is a positive factor. However, it is a burden in practical terms that China is already ahead in industrialization. artigo.texto: Can AI navigate qualms about data centers, long-term debt? Q. When we speak about data centers, what exactly are we talking about? A data center is basically an industrial-scale computer farm. It's a large facility with a whole bunch of servers, storage and networking gear. The concept really predates AI. If you're storing your data in the cloud, you're basically a data center consumer in some sense. You're consuming storage and data retrieval services from a data center. The difference with AI is that AI dramatically increases the amount and consumption of these services. It's no longer just storing your data in the cloud and retrieving it when you want, but it's also actually doing computational work. For that reason, the scale of the infrastructure needed is enormously larger. For AI in particular, it needs really high-tech chips made by Nvidia and others. Also with large-scale computing, you need large-scale power and cooling infrastructure. All of that comes together in these data center projects. None of that is new, but the scale of it is new because of how much AI increases consumption. Q. How do data centers make money? It’s useful to think of the data center operator as an entity that finances the construction of all of that infrastructure and then monetizes it by leasing that computing capacity to a consumer. The consumer might be a large tech firm. Sometimes these data center operators are affiliated with one of the large tech firms. From our perspective, it's just useful to think of the data center operator as the part of the enterprise that builds out these data centers and leases out computing capacity. Q. The scale of data center construction appears to be unprecedented. Exactly how big is it? This is where you sort of forget the billions and you move into the trillions. There are many estimates of the cumulative CapEx (capital expenditures). If you look at the cumulative amount of CapEx that these firms will end up making over the remainder of this decade [roughly five years], the numbers are of the order of magnitude of $5 trillion. If you look at the cost of a data center, it seems to be in the ballpark of $30 billion to $40 billion per gigawatt used. So, a good way to measure the scale of these data centers is by the amount of power they consume. A gigawatt, by the way, is the equivalent electricity consumption of about 800,000 average homes. It seems that about half of that cost, maybe 60 percent, is the actual servers, chips and so on. The remainder is physical infrastructure, [providing electrical] power and the physical buildings. It's good to think of it as a [cumulative] run rate of $1 trillion a year, certainly not insignificant in the context of the overall economy, certainly not insignificant in the context of the amount of financing that needs to be raised. Q. Who has been funding the data center build-out? In the early stages of the build-out, it was mostly self-financed from the operating cash flow [of such firms as Meta, Microsoft and Amazon]. The numbers are now so large that you really have to tap into every available source of financing and then some. Wall Street research analysts have estimated where this money might come from. It's a combination of sources—20 percent of the overall CapEx might be operating cash flow and/or some sort of equity, maybe 30 percent will be in the form of unsecured debt in the high-grade debt markets. There will be some fraction coming from private lenders—private debt, potentially foreign investors. Then there's sort of a TBD [to be determined] fraction of it. Some of this is getting figured out as the build-out happens because this is a rapidly evolving landscape. If you just look at projections of debt supply in November [2025] versus now [September 2026], you know it keeps going up. This year, for instance, there's been about $200 billion in high-grade bond issuance to finance this. And about 70 percent of that is actually in the U.S. These borrowers are also tapping non-dollar currencies, the European bond markets, [the] yen and Swiss franc markets. A main takeaway is probably that the scale of this financing is large and, therefore, every possible avenue can and will be tapped. The positive side of that story is that tech firms have historically been very light on their debt footprint. Even though it's growing rapidly, at least in the initial stages, our contacts tell us that there's a lot of demand for this debt because a typical corporate bond investor is rather light on tech names. They're actually quite happy to take that issuance because in a sense, they're diversifying by buying debt from tech firms. Of course, there's a limit to that, and at some point, we'll get through that and the dynamic might change. But certainly, we seem to be in the relatively early stages, and there’s a willingness on the part of investors to buy tech company AI-related debt. Q. With so much AI debt going to market, what’s that doing to bond rates? Perhaps the best way to answer that is to look at what's happening among longer-term maturities [largely 10-year maturities]. The question of whether other borrowers are getting crowded out is difficult to answer at this stage of the game, but the impacts on long maturity sectors are becoming somewhat clearer. In general, there are a lot fewer issuers in the long end of the [yield] curve. Predominantly, the supplier of that debt is the [Department of the] Treasury—sovereign debt. Most firms tend to borrow shorter than that. Data center operators seem to prefer longer-term debt financing right now. Part of the reason could be the long-lived nature of the infrastructure. It could be issuers’ willingness or desire to just lock in financials for a longer period of time. It's hard to tell precisely why, but that's the observed dynamic. artigo.texto: A preliminary modeling study published in the Journal of Engineering Research suggests that underutilized geothermal reservoirs could support compressed air and CO2 energy storage. Geothermal heating improved round-trip efficiency by approximately five to six percentage points, although more realistic CO2 modeling revealed significant performance limitations that require further investigation. Can Underground Storage Solve Renewable Energy's Supply Challenge? Managing surplus electricity from fluctuations in wind and solar generation, and releasing it when demand surges, remains a key challenge. Thermal power plants can also generate surplus electricity when demand remains low. As a result, long-term energy storage has become crucial for balancing supply and demand in power systems. Subsurface energy storage is often discussed as a candidate for long-term storage because geological formations can offer far greater capacity than traditional surface systems. Studies have reported that underground energy storage is a feasible alternative for large-scale integration of renewable energy. Why Reservoir Integrity Matters for Energy Storage Subsurface alternatives are particularly attractive in nations with significant geothermal resources. For instance, in the United States, approximately three million abandoned wells have great potential for reuse. However, the presence of old wells alone does not confirm that a reservoir is suitable for subsurface storage. Based on compressed air energy storage (CAES), storage deliverability and integrity constantly play a crucial role within porous media. Studies have reported that seal quality, fluid recirculation, and gas bubble stability within the reservoir significantly affect utility-scale CAES in aquifers. Further developments emphasized the use of the reservoir as a heat source and a pressure reservoir. The selection of working fluids is another major problem. Studies have shown that, for compressed CO2 energy storage (CCES), the thermodynamic behavior of the storage fluid plays a critical role in the system's output within a saltwater aquifer. Against this backdrop, the magnitude of the realizable geothermal uplift, the adequacy of storage integrity, the acceptability of the pressure margin, and the justification of the added operational complexity by the advantage of CO2 require further investigation. Comparing Air and CO2 for Geothermal Energy Storage In this work, researchers assessed the preliminary feasibility of CO2 and air storage in inactive geothermal reservoirs using a low-order surface-well reservoir model. The model, developed using Python programming, allowed CO2 and air to be compared under equivalent pressure boundary, cycle scheduling, and geometric conditions. Using the fixed-property, ideal-gas-style screening model, the researchers compared CO2 and air across electrical performance (average net discharge power and round-trip efficiency), pressure margin, plume size (dispersion radius), mass retention, geothermal reheating, and storage integrity. Additionally, the authors combined field-based evaluation, geothermal reheating, well-reservoir response, and electrical performance approaches into one reduced-order model of the coupled well, surface, and reservoir system. Download a free copy of this page here! Modeling 18 Underground Energy Storage Scenarios The researchers conducted a preliminary modeling assessment informed by published geothermal field conditions. They considered inactive reservoir sectors with high temperatures and potentially reusable wells, while using assumed values for several reservoir properties that had not been verified through site-specific measurements. Based on three steps, including discharge, storage, and charging, the investigated system was developed. The primary architecture was dependent on one reversible access well for production and injection according to the conceptual model. Additionally, the location of the injection-production pathway, gas plume, and overburden described the energy sequence. Initially, geothermal reservoir sectors were screened depending on well integrity, pressure margin, caprock condition, and temperature. After defining the initial candidates, two working-fluid alternatives, along with three storage and temperature-integrity classes, were matched to each sector, yielding 18 scenarios under shared reservoir pressure and geometry limits. For every combination, the coupled surface–well–reservoir model was operated. Geothermal Heat Boosts Efficiency, but CO2 Faces Limitations The results demonstrated that high temperatures offered dual advantages: gas could be stored as pressure energy, while geothermal heat provided thermal uplift during storage and discharge. In the high-temperature geothermal case (553.15 K), air produced a geothermal temperature increase, average net discharge power, round-trip efficiency, energy density, and thermal assist fraction of 58.9 K, 6.20 MW, 27.18%, 5.634 kWh/m3, and 13.91%, respectively. Under matching conditions, CO2 produced 49.7 K, 6.90 MW, 29.46%, 7.615 kWh/m3, and 11.55%, respectively, with a 31.4 m plume radius, less than 34.5 m for air. Geothermal reheating increased round-trip efficiency by 6.08 and 5.48 percentage points and net power by 1.42 and 1.25 MW for CO2 and air, respectively, relative to non-geothermal conditions. However, the model indicated that only approximately 56% of the injected gas mass was recovered during the simulated cycles for both air and CO2. This relatively low recovery rate was a major contributor to the system's limited round-trip efficiency, as a substantial proportion of the energy used to compress the injected gas could not be recovered. The findings, therefore, highlight the importance of improving gas recovery when assessing the feasibility of underground compressed-gas energy storage. artigo.texto: EcoPro BM is strengthening its cooperation with Samsung SDI on materials development aimed at commercializing sulfide-based solid-state batteries. EcoPro BM said Oct. 6 that signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Samsung SDI to develop materials for solid-state batteries. The two companies will jointly develop battery cells and key materials, targeting commercialization in 2027. Their cooperation will span from early-stage research and development through quality evaluation and the establishment of mass-production systems. Samsung SDI will advance solid-state battery cell development and mass-production technology. EcoPro BM will develop key materials, including cathode materials for solid-state batteries, electrolytes for cathodes and electrolytes for separators. EcoPro BM operates a pilot plant with an annual capacity of 40 metric tons for producing sulfide-based solid electrolytes. The company is also developing cathode materials suited to solid-state batteries using its high-nickel cathode technology. EcoPro BM was selected in August for the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy's "Super Eul Project" for its sulfide-based solid-electrolyte technology. In July, the company identified 2027 as the earliest possible timing for mass production of solid-state battery materials.

artigo.texto: India is stepping up investment in battery energy storage systems (BESS) to stabilize its power grid. The government plans to invest 500 billion rupees to deploy 50 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of BESS by 2033. According to industry sources on Oct. 6, the Indian government approved the third phase of the Green Energy Corridor (GEC-III) on Sept. 30. The project will expand transmission networks and BESS in line with the country’s growing renewable energy capacity. India plans to build transmission infrastructure capable of accommodating up to 135 gigawatts (GW) of renewable energy by 2033. It will also install 50 GWh of BESS. The total project cost is 1.864 trillion rupees. Of that amount, 500 billion rupees has been allocated for BESS deployment. The government has not disclosed detailed conditions for the batteries to be used in the project, including battery chemistry, storage duration and procurement methods. The actual amount spent on batteries and systems could vary depending on those conditions. On a simple calculation, India will need more than 7 GWh of batteries annually for grid-scale energy storage systems (ESS) alone. But local battery production capacity is only about 2 GWh a year, meaning the country will have to rely heavily on imports. India has largely met demand through imports as it was late to establish a lithium-ion battery manufacturing base. Chinese-made batteries accounted for 75.2% of India’s lithium-ion battery imports in fiscal 2024-25. According to the India Energy Storage Alliance (IESA), India’s lithium-ion battery production capacity could reach 60 GWh to 70 GWh by 2030 if announced investment plans are implemented as scheduled. Over the same period, capacity for assembling battery packs and BESS using imported cells is expected to rise to 180 GWh to 220 GWh. Local cell production is therefore expected to lag well behind the expansion of BESS manufacturing capacity. Wood Mackenzie estimates that it will take India 10 to 15 years to build a self-sufficient battery industry with competitive pricing. It estimates that locally produced battery cells will cost 25% to 40% more than imported cells. High financing costs and an underdeveloped battery-materials supply chain are among the reasons. As India needs time to expand domestic battery production, it will have to rely on overseas technology and supply chains for the time being. That could create an opportunity for Korean companies to enter the market. Indian companies have traditionally worked mainly with Chinese battery makers because of their price competitiveness. But the business environment is changing as political tensions between India and China persist. Korean companies are also seeking opportunities to enter the Indian market. AI battery startup DeltaX signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Toptec in July to cooperate on targeting India’s ESS market. “India is expanding localization across its renewable energy industry, including requiring the use of domestically produced solar panels,” DeltaX Chief Executive Kim Soo-hoon said. “Local solar and renewable energy companies are also expanding into assembling and selling battery modules and packs for ESS, and are actively considering cooperation with companies outside China.” The growing adoption of Korean-made battery equipment in India is another positive factor. A key example is a battery plant with annual capacity of 40 GWh being built in India by Agratas, a Tata Group company. A number of Korean battery-equipment makers, including Yunsung F&C, PNT, Philenergy, Hana Technology, J's Robotics and Axvis, have been selected as suppliers for the project. Business by Korean battery manufacturers in India remains limited. LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI operate local sales subsidiaries, but their main business is supplying small batteries for smartphones and other information-technology devices. Their operations in India remain small in both scope and scale compared with major overseas markets such as North America and Europe. LG Energy Solution leads among companies in energy-related patents, having filed 2,225 patents in India. “Indian ESS companies have traditionally sourced battery cells mainly from Chinese companies,” an industry official said. “They also prefer lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, so opportunities for Korean battery companies to enter the Indian market could expand as they increase their LFP-related businesses.” India also built a large-scale power grid under previous phases of the Green Energy Corridor program. Phase I involved about 9,100 kilometers of transmission lines, while Phase II is adding about 7,900 kilometers across seven states. As transmission investment expands under Phase III, demand is also expected to rise for power equipment from HD Hyundai Electric, LS ELECTRIC and Hyosung Heavy Industries, alongside BESS.

artigo.texto: South Korea's power semiconductor industry has begun research aimed at improving the efficiency of power supply systems for data centers as electricity consumption from artificial intelligence (AI) data centers continues to rise. Park Sang-min, a Ph.D. researcher at the Korea Electronics Technology Institute (KETI), presented an overview of domestic power semiconductor research for AI data center power systems at the Power Semiconductor Industry-Academia-Research K-Forum, held at Hotel Nongshim in Dongnae, Busan, on Oct. 7. AI data centers require more power than conventional data centers because GPU performance requirements and the number of GPUs installed are increasing, driving up electricity consumption. While conventional data centers required about 10 to 20 megawatts (MW), data centers consuming more than 100MW have emerged. A 10MW load is roughly equivalent to the electricity used by 10,000 households at the same time, while 100MW corresponds to about 100,000 households. South Korean research institutions are focusing on improving server power-conversion efficiency. Electricity supplied from the external grid to a data center goes through six power-conversion stages before reaching the GPU. Power losses occur at each stage, reducing the amount of electricity ultimately available to the GPU. KETI is seeking to improve data center power efficiency with a focus on server power supply units (PSUs). A PSU converts electricity supplied to a data center into power that can be used by servers. KETI is also leading a government-funded project. The institute is demonstrating a 100MW-class data center power system compatible with the Open Compute Project's (OCP) Open Rack v3 (ORv3) specification. The project applies compound power semiconductors such as silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN), which offer faster switching speeds than silicon (Si). KETI is developing high-efficiency, high-power power supplies and building the system at the rack level. The resulting system will be validated by NAVER Cloud. KETI is also researching power supply architectures based on 800-volt direct current (DC). Racks currently use DC power at around 50 volts. As power consumption per rack increases, the existing distribution architecture is approaching its limits. The voltage supplied to racks can be increased to as much as 800V, reducing the current required to deliver the same amount of power. This can lower power losses during distribution. There are limitations to immediately applying 800V DC to data centers in South Korea. Converting existing power infrastructure to 800V DC would require changes to existing power equipment. One alternative is to generate 800V DC inside the data center while maintaining the existing external infrastructure. This approach would modify only part of the current architecture. In the longer term, the industry is considering the use of solid-state transformers (SSTs), which use power semiconductors to convert voltage. An 800V DC architecture distributes power inside a data center at 800V DC after converting the several-thousand- to tens-of-thousands-of-volt electricity entering from the external grid. Raising the voltage reduces the current required to deliver the same amount of power.

artigo.texto: At the end of 2024, Texas’ grid operator had 63 GW of large new customers in its queue. By this June, that figure reached 474 GW, more than five times record peak demand, about 90% of it data centers. Then Texas hit pause. What began as directions for data centers to pay for their own grid upgrades has since escalated to a freeze on all new permits. If you care about AI and American reindustrialization, this is important to understand. Why did it do this? The upcoming election is part of it, but the underlying issues are worth digging into. The first is the interconnection queue. This pause is just as much about how projects apply for approval as it is about the projects themselves. Developers routinely spam projects across several sites, and many are speculative builds with no customer yet. Often these new developers have never even plugged in a GPU, let alone a power plant, so dealing with low-quality submissions puts ERCOT, which runs most of the state’s grid, in a tough spot. Planners can’t tell which are real, and they don’t want ratepayers paying for upgrades built for projects that never show up. The second issue is community alignment. Noise, water, emissions, and power bills are top of mind for anyone who lives nearby. And regardless of the reality of these issues, people deserve straight answers when a data center comes to town, and they haven’t always gotten them (as of June, only 28 of 377 companies had answered a state survey on their resource use). In Hood County, commissioners were asked to support a tax waiver for “Project Patriot” without knowing who it was. To be fair, code names are common while companies shop for sites since a famous buyer can drive up prices, but that logic becomes tougher to defend once officials vote on tax breaks. The broader political backdrop is important, but I’ll be focusing on the energy side: why it’s so hard to power a data center, all the ways developers are trying to do it anyway, and where things are likely headed. What connecting to the grid actually means How Amazon purchases power helps illustrate what’s changed. For the last decade, they’d find a utility with network capacity, sign up as a large load, then enter long-term contracts to match their use on paper. These were often purely financial, meaning you didn’t always have to prove the power could reach you, and the grid connection was easy because utilities had spare network capacity. That’s no longer true. The grid is stretched thin, and almost any new large load or generator now requires an upgrade. Power flows across every connected path, so buying from one plant doesn’t reserve a route to your building (there are even markets for transmission congestion rights). So buyers went after firm power (available around the clock) they could claim more directly, typically by restarting retired plants or by building next to existing ones. Neither was a true escape, and some of the loudest fights are over “colocation,” which ERCOT describes as drawing power from a neighboring plant before it reaches the grid: - Susquehanna: Amazon bought a campus next to Talen’s nuclear plant, but FERC, the federal grid regulator, rejected Talen’s bid to send it more power directly. Utilities had argued it would let the campus dodge grid fees and push fixed transmission costs onto everyone else. After they restructured the deal, Amazon pays for delivery like any other customer. - Freestone: CyrusOne’s 760 MW campus beside Constellation’s gas plant needed approval from the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT), since it effectively takes much of the plant’s output from everyone else. The PUCT said yes in May, as long as the campus can cut its use or switch to backup power within 30 minutes of an ERCOT call. - Armstrong County: Two Crusoe data centers beside a wind farm got the same rule, and the second, approved in July, must also shed its entire load, so together they’d cut nearly twice what the wind farm can produce. Interconnection studies are how grid planners identify the wires and substations that need upgrades for any addition to the network. ERCOT used to review studies individually under rules built for 40 to 50 large loads at a time, but 2025 brought 225 new requests by mid-November. So this June, the PUCT approved a new batch approach. Under “Batch Zero,” ERCOT studies large loads of 75 MW or more together and allocates grid capacity among them. Primarily, the studies ask what happens when something breaks. NERC’s standard, the baseline for reliability across North America, covers a broad set of outage scenarios, with ERCOT adding its own requirements. Planners might simulate a transformer outage, then knock out a line or generator on top of that. Maintaining that reliability standard without shedding more load often means building additional infrastructure. A newer risk is load dropping off the grid all at once. Many data centers switch to backup power at the first voltage dip to protect their hardware, so one bad fault can pull an enormous load off the grid in seconds. This happened earlier this year in Virginia, but was fortunately handled well. Texas has even less room for error since ERCOT’s grid is largely isolated. Under some conditions, ERCOT can lose only about 3.2 GW of load at once before causing issues. A new voltage ride-through rule now requires new data centers to stay connected through routine faults, and I’ve even heard of labs running dummy jobs after a training run fails just to keep load from dropping abruptly. All of this can sound overly conservative, but the system was designed to put reliability ahead of cost. Put simply, the grid is built for the hot summer days and frigid winters when failure can mean life or death. That duty is what makes sizing the grid so hard; you build for a few peak hours but pay for it all year. So who does pay for all this resilience? artigo.texto: Novo regime tributário reduz custos para o setor e pode acelerar investimentos em data centers, enquanto a HostDime prepara em João Pessoa uma estrutura de R$ 250 milhões voltada a aplicações de inteligência artificial avançada O novo Redata pode provocar uma arrancada dos data centers no Brasil nos próximos anos. A avaliação é do CEO da Positivo Tecnologia, enquanto João Pessoa já aparece nesse movimento com um projeto de R$ 250 milhões voltado à inteligência artificial. Redata pode destravar uma fila de projetos no país A capacidade instalada de centros de processamento de dados no Brasil pode dobrar ou até triplicar nos próximos dois ou três anos. A projeção foi feita por Hélio Bruck Rotenberg, CEO da Positivo Tecnologia. Segundo o executivo, havia projetos aguardando uma definição sobre os incentivos tributários antes de avançar. Com o novo regime aprovado, a expectativa dele é de uma corrida por servidores, componentes e outros equipamentos necessários para colocar esses empreendimentos de pé. - Nova ponte de R$ 6,2 milhões vai sair do papel em Erechim e licitação já tem data marcada para começar - Multinacional alemã prepara investimento de R$ 712 milhões em Santa Catarina com construção de nova fábrica e expansão capaz de elevar produção em 130% - 40 mil pessoas a pé no meio dos caminhões: Via Dutra fecha 45 km de faixa com cones e leva à ANTT plano de calçada até Aparecida - De olho na indústria de rochas do ES, grupo italiano investe R$ 60 milhões para ampliar fábrica e elevar produção de 18 mil para 30 mil toneladas ao ano O Paraíba Business destacou que esse cenário já alcança o Nordeste e colocou a Paraíba no mapa dos novos investimentos, especialmente por causa da expansão da HostDime em João Pessoa. Rotenberg resumiu sua expectativa sobre o tamanho desse salto: “Acredito que deva duplicar ou triplicar nos próximos dois ou três anos”. A previsão é do executivo e, portanto, não representa uma projeção oficial do governo. Lei do Redata corta tributos e cria contrapartidas O Redata virou lei em 15 de setembro de 2026. A Lei nº 15.504 criou o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter e entrou em vigor na data de sua publicação. O programa prevê benefícios tributários para equipamentos e componentes destinados aos centros habilitados. Entre os tributos abrangidos estão Imposto de Importação, IPI e PIS/Cofins, incluindo cobranças incidentes sobre importações. Não é simplesmente uma liberação de imposto. Quem entrar no regime precisa cumprir contrapartidas, incluindo investimentos em pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação e regras relacionadas ao atendimento do mercado brasileiro. De acordo com o Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços, ao menos 10% da capacidade de processamento, armazenagem e tratamento deverá ser disponibilizada ao mercado nacional ou destinada, nas condições previstas, a instituições científicas, tecnológicas ou ao poder público. Para projetos localizados no Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste, a própria legislação prevê redução de 20% em determinadas contrapartidas. Esse ponto ajuda a colocar regiões fora do eixo tradicional do Sudeste na disputa pelos novos empreendimentos. Antes da aprovação, entidades empresariais apontavam uma diferença pesada no bolso. Segundo manifesto do setor produtivo, instalar um data center no Brasil custava 26% mais que nos Estados Unidos e 35% mais que no Chile. Data center de R$ 250 milhões coloca João Pessoa nessa corrida Na Paraíba, o projeto mais concreto é da HostDime Brasil. A empresa anunciou investimento de R$ 250 milhões para ampliar sua infraestrutura de data center em João Pessoa. A estrutura terá capacidade energética de até 15 megawatts e será preparada para cargas de inteligência artificial. A própria companhia também cita tecnologias de refrigeração líquida para lidar com servidores de alta densidade. A HostDime já mantém operação na capital paraibana. A nova estrutura representa uma expansão bem maior e mira aplicações que exigem muito poder computacional, justamente o tipo de demanda que cresceu com modelos de inteligência artificial. Há, porém, uma diferença importante nas datas divulgadas. A reportagem do Paraíba Business publicada em 5 de outubro informa que o novo centro deverá operar em 2027. Já comunicações da própria HostDime publicadas em setembro colocam o início da operação em 2028. Também há variação sobre o começo das obras: um conteúdo da companhia, de 8 de setembro, mencionava início ainda em 2026; outro, publicado em 16 de setembro, indicava construção a partir de 2027. O investimento de R$ 250 milhões e a capacidade projetada de 15 MW permanecem nos materiais da empresa. Expansão no Brasil também mexe com fabricantes O movimento não interessa apenas a quem constrói os galpões cheios de servidores. Para fabricantes de equipamentos, uma expansão rápida dos data centers pode abrir um mercado grande dentro do país. A Positivo Tecnologia já atua na fabricação de servidores e vê no Redata uma oportunidade de ampliar essa frente. Rotenberg também defendeu que a política permite trazer tecnologias ainda não produzidas localmente sem retirar espaço da indústria já instalada no Brasil. A lei diferencia ainda a tributação de bens importados. O regime suspende impostos dentro das condições previstas e estabelece regras específicas para estimular investimentos, ao mesmo tempo em que exige aportes em pesquisa e desenvolvimento. O tamanho real dessa expansão, no entanto, ainda será medido nos próximos anos. Dobrar ou triplicar a capacidade é uma projeção do CEO da Positivo, não uma meta legal do Redata. Por enquanto, o que já está definido é o novo regime tributário. E, na Paraíba, há um investimento anunciado de R$ 250 milhões que coloca João Pessoa entre as cidades que tentam ganhar espaço na nova infraestrutura digital brasileira. Fonte: Paraibabusiness.

artigo.texto: Novo projeto de infraestrutura em Dubai integra 2.000 MW de energia solar com um sistema BESS de 1.400 MW / 8.400 MWh para suprir a rede durante a noite. A transição energética no deserto de Seih Al-Dahal enfrenta o desafio de manter o suprimento elétrico estável quando o sol se põe. Para resolver essa intermitência em larga escala, a concessionária estipulou uma infraestrutura capaz de estocar gigawatts-hora diretamente na rede de transmissão. Por que um sistema gigante de baterias é necessário em um parque solar no deserto? Quando ligamos aparelhos elétricos à noite, a rede precisa entregar energia instantaneamente. O painel solar tradicional produz eletricidade apenas enquanto recebe radiação solar direta. Essa diferença entre o momento de geração e o pico de consumo é equacionada com sistemas BESS (Battery Energy Storage System). A nova etapa utiliza baterias com capacidade de injeção de 1.400 MW e armazenamento total de 8.400 MWh. Isso significa guardar seis horas seguidas de geração máxima em módulos estáticos. Assim, a energia captada sob o sol do deserto abastece as cidades durante o período noturno. Quais são os números e a capacidade técnica da 7ª fase do parque solar? A infraestrutura planejada pela Dubai Electricity and Water Authority (DEWA) combina painéis fotovoltaicos com um dos maiores conjuntos de baterias estáticas do planeta. Os dados estruturais demonstram a escala desse projeto de engenharia elétrica: Geração fotovoltaica instalada: adiciona 2.000 MW de potência através de módulos de silício monocristalino bifaciais montados em seguidores solares de eixo único. - Capacidade de potência do BESS: sistema de baterias dimensionado para injetar até 1.400 MW continuamente na rede elétrica. - Volume total de armazenamento: capacidade de 8.400 MWh para sustentação do fluxo elétrico por seis horas consecutivas. - Interconexão em alta tensão: integração direta em subestações de 400 kV e 132 kV para minimizar perdas de transmissão. - Química das células de armazenamento: baterias de lítio-ferro-fosfato (LiFePO4) escolhidas pela alta estabilidade térmica e vida útil prolongada. Como funciona o armazenamento e a entrega de energia na prática? Durante o dia, os inversores bidirecionais convertem a corrente contínua dos módulos e enviam parte dos 2.000 MW para carregar os contêineres de baterias. O sistema de controle monitora a frequência da rede e ajusta a carga em milissegundos para evitar variações de voltagem. Ao entardecer, quando a demanda por ar-condicionado atinge o topo, o sistema inverte a operação e descarrega até 1.400 MW nas linhas de transmissão. Dessa forma, a usina atua como uma geradora de base contínua, mantendo o sistema elétrico equilibrado sem falhas. Onde ver a estrutura do Parque Solar Mohammed bin Rashid em operação? O parque solar em Dubai ocupa uma área contínua no deserto de Seih Al-Dahal. A visualização das fases operacionais e do Hub de Inovação demonstra a organização espacial dos arranjos fotovoltaicos e das usinas de armazenamento. Acompanhar esses registros técnicos auxilia no entendimento da escala física necessária para instalar milhões de módulos e contêineres energizados sob altas temperaturas ambientais. Abaixo, um vídeo do canal oficial da DEWA Official que aprofunda o tema: Quais normas técnicas de engenharia garantem a segurança de grandes baterias? Sistemas de armazenamento em escala de gigawatts exigem conformidade com normas rígidas, como a IEC 62933 para integração de BESS e a NFPA 855 para proteção contra incêndios elétricos. Para testar a resistência contra fuga térmica em células, aplica-se o padrão UL 9540A. Os projetos incorporam barramentos isolados, paredes de contenção corta-fogo e resfriamento líquido acoplado aos contêineres. Seguir esses parâmetros impede o superaquecimento em climas secos com temperaturas superiores a 45 °C, garantindo a integridade dos equipamentos. Quando é necessário contratar um engenheiro eletricista especializado em energia solar? Projetos fotovoltaicos comerciais e industriais que incorporam armazenamento exigem a atuação de um engenheiro eletricista. Somente esse profissional pode calcular a capacidade dos inversores, realizar o estudo de curto-circuito e projetar a proteção contra surtos de tensão. A instalação sem dimensionamento adequado pode causar derretimento de cabos, disjunção incorreta e danos permanentes à rede do imóvel. Não é um trabalho que você faz sozinho porque envolve lidar com altas correntes contínuas e normas rigorosas da concessionária. Contexto importante: Este artigo é informativo. Para projetos estruturais e elétricos locais similares, recomenda-se avaliação de engenheiro eletricista, especialmente em contextos de risco de comprometimento elétrico, surtos de tensão e superaquecimento de baterias.

artigo.texto: IREN Dips Further After SemiAnalysis Flags Issues With Legacy British Columbia Data Centers: Retail Mood Drops - SemiAnalysis cited reports of power outages, network disruptions, and other failures at IREN’s Prince George and Mackenzie sites. - The research firm said IREN’s newer Texas facilities have stronger infrastructure. - Retail sentiment dipped further in the ‘bearish’ zone. IREN Ltd. (IREN) extended losses on Thursday after research firm SemiAnalysis raised concerns about the operational quality of the Bitcoin miner-turned-AI infrastructure provider’s legacy data centers in British Columbia. The stock fell more than 6% in Wednesday trading and was down another 1.2% in Thursday premarket trading, weighing on retail sentiment. SemiAnalysis Flags Legacy Site Issues In a series of posts on X on Wednesday, SemiAnalysis said IREN said it had heard reports from multiple customers and end users about IREN’s sites in Prince George and Mackenzie, describing them as the “#1 worst site in the industry” according to users. SemiAnalysis cited reports of multi-day power outages, network upgrades, storage failures and air-quality control problems that allegedly caused frequent network link flaps and system-level errors. SemiAnalysis, however, drew a distinction between IREN’s legacy infrastructure and its newer builds in Childress and Sweetwater, Texas. The semiconductor research outlet said the new sites “look much better,” highlighting their move away from N+0 configurations for power, cooling and internet service providers. N+0 generally indicates a setup without redundant capacity, leaving infrastructure more exposed to failures or maintenance disruptions. SemiAnalysis also pointed to Nvidia’s planned $2.1 billion investment in IREN, saying the funding should help the company avoid some of the technical compromises seen at its earlier facilities. Retail View On IREN On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment for IREN dipped further into the ‘bearish’ from a day earlier, although some traders were also hopeful for a rebound. “$IREN one upset customer and people want to jump ship… and for all we know, it could possibly be politically motivated. Nvidia is backing Iren. This company will continue to grow and thrive,” one said. IREN is the weakest performer in the neocloud group, which includes CoreWeave (CRWV) and Nebius (NBIS), with just a 2.4% year to date gain.

artigo.texto: São Paulo recebe, desde esta terça-feira e até esta quinta um dos maiores eventos globais de tecnologia voltada ao setor empresarial. O Data Center World Brasil, realizado no São Paulo Expo, é focado em soluções para companhias em áreas estratégicas, algumas das quais o Rio Grande do Sul tem sido um player cada vez mais competitivo, como a instalação de data centers, com oportunidades em negócios nas áreas de hardware, equipamentos e investimentos em geral. Prestes a completar 30 anos no Brasil, a Kingston, mais conhecida no mercado consumidor tradicional como fabricante de memórias e pendrives domésticos, busca acelerar sua atuação na infraestrutura corporativa no mercado latino-americano com outros produtos complementares, inclusive voltadas a relacionamentos, como parcerias com marketplaces. O Brasil, atualmente, concentra 58% da fatia de mercado da Kingston na América Latina e somente as vendas da linha enterprise cresceram 42% no primeiro semestre deste ano. “O Brasil hoje é o principal polo de data center na América Latina. A gente tem muita energia limpa no país e já possuímos vários cabos submarinos. Hoje um dos principais gargalos de construir data center no mundo é a questão da energia, e isso o Brasil tem bastante”, destacou o country manager da Kingston no Brasil, Paulo Vizaco. Para ele, a inteligência artificial está indo “para todos os lados”, em meio a uma “uma corrida gigante de players investindo até trilhões de dólares na criação de infraestrutura”. E o Rio Grande do Sul, como região que está recebendo projetos bilionários na área de data centers, como o da Parks, em Cachoeirinha, e o Scala AI City, em Eldorado do Sul, é um local onde há uma atenção concentrada, por meio de oportunidades de parcerias. “Obviamente que vemos monitorando todos esses projetos. Estamos em contato com a maioria deles conversando, vendo o que que a gente pode agregar”, comentou Vizaco. Para ele, a Kingston também acompanha de perto as discussões e iniciativas regulatórias e tributárias no Brasil, a exemplo do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), sancionado a nível no mês passado. Data Center World Brasil 2026 e participação da Kingston no evento Corrida global pela IA acelera Conforme o executivo, a consolidação de incentivos como este é fundamental para reduzir o custo de infraestrutura no Brasil e tornará o ecossistema nacional de data centers ainda mais competitivo frente ao mercado mundial. “Como uma empresa de capital privado, temos a facilidade de se mover muito mais rápido do que qualquer outra. Então nos adaptamos bem a estas condições, principalmente tributárias. Temos uma flexibilidade muito grande neste sentido”, disse ele. O gerente de Tecnologia da Kingston, Iuri Santos, comentou que as empresas de maneira geral têm visto inclusive ideias de voltar a viabilizar grandes projetos de infraestrutura tecnológica, ao verem na Kingston economia, suporte local e qualidade que, eventualmente, seja um gargalo em outros fornecedores. Na visão de Santos, “nunca se produziu tanto semicondutor na história da humanidade”, porque a corrida global pela IA gerou uma demanda sem precedentes por componentes de altíssima velocidade e capacidade. Para ele, os preços destes atingiram um novo patamar global, e é irrealista buscar comparar os orçamentos atuais com os de anos anteriores. “Não devemos olhar para os preços que tínhamos antes, porque aquilo é um mundo sem a IA. A gente mudou, a tecnologia mudou. As empresas que estão ficando para trás são as que ainda estão olhando para o passado em vez de olhar para o presente imaginando se preparar para o futuro. Virou uma questão de sobrevivência: eu preciso me digitalizar”, apontou ele.

artigo.texto: A major improvement for Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) and Carbon Usage Effectiveness (CUE), Valeo’s aluminum heat exchanger delivers a 38% increase in cooling capacity, a 25% reduction in electrical consumption, and over a decade of proven corrosion resistance. October 7, 2026 – SAN JOSE, Calif. — At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit 2026 (October 12–15), Valeo will present, with OVH Cloud, the validation status of its breakthrough aluminum heat exchanger technology for data center thermal management. This technology is applicable for the rear door cooling modules of rack or fan wall in the core space of data centers (white space). It represents a paradigm shift in the industry. With over two years of dedicated development in the sector, Valeo is demonstrating its industrial capability and readiness to scale production. Leveraging decades of automotive thermal management, heat exchangers and corrosion know-how, Valeo develops solutions aimed at supporting the AI industry’s exponential scaling needs. Pascale Herman, Data center & BESS Vice President at Valeo, said: “Presenting our ongoing work at OCP 2026 represents an important step in our journey within the data center ecosystem. Over the past two years, we have made significant progress in evaluating how aluminum liquid cooling can meet the rigorous reliability and performance standards required by modern high-density facilities. By combining these early testing metrics with our decades of automotive thermal management expertise, we are working to develop scalable thermal solutions to support the industry’s evolving infrastructure needs responsibly and effectively.” A validated breakthrough for data centers cooling As artificial intelligence (AI) workloads push rack densities to new heights, aluminum heat exchangers are being evaluated to provide a powerful, lightweight, more efficient, and scalable alternative to traditional copper hardware. Valeo’s aluminum solutions deliver a 38% increase in cooling capacity and 65% in power density versus traditional copper solutions, while simultaneously reducing fan electrical consumption by 25%. These validation results establish a clear technological breakthrough, directly optimizing Carbon Usage Effectiveness (CUE) and Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE), ideal for retrofitting existing or for new racks. Automotive-grade reliability: pushing the boundaries of endurance To evaluate long-term feasibility, and directly address industry concerns regarding aluminum corrosion, Valeo has implemented a comprehensive, accelerated long-run testing framework to simulate long-term reliability and OVH Cloud has been running real time and conditions tests for several months. Testing on Valeo’s specific coating has already successfully reached the equivalent of more than 10-years operating life, fully aligning with the standard infrastructure lifespan of the data center industry. Valeo is currently pushing tests up to 15 years ensuring the material unconditionally meets the stringent, long-term lifespan expectations of data center operators. This ongoing research aims to establish a clear pathway toward production-grade aluminum infrastructure for next-generation data centers. A comprehensive liquid cooling vision addressing the data center industry evolution While the aluminum exchanger takes center stage at OCP 2026, it is part of a broader liquid cooling ecosystem engineered to challenge traditional data center thermal limits and address the industry’s rapid evolution. Valeo’s technology portfolio also includes Direct-to-Chip (DLC) systems (both Single-Phase and Two-Phase) for high-density racks, as well as Zero-Water Immersion Units for Micro-Edge compute applications. By applying decades of automotive thermal expertise, stringent quality standards, and a vast global manufacturing footprint in all regions, Valeo brings a new industrial perspective to data center cooling. As accelerating AI demand reshapes digital infrastructure, Valeo combines high-volume production scale with cutting-edge innovation to power the digital transition. About Valeo Valeo is a leading global technology company creating innovative solutions and systems for automotive and technology partners worldwide. Valeo is structured around its POWER, BRAIN and LIGHT Divisions, and Valeo Service, the augmented service partner, for the aftermarket and new forms of mobility. Valeo is committed to making mobility safer, more sustainable and affordable to all. The Group is playing a vital role in shaping the Car of Tomorrow: which will be electrified, safer and software-defined. Valeo is leveraging its global industrial footprint and its technological leadership in electrification, advanced driver assistance systems, lighting and software to capture an increasing share of value per vehicle. Valeo is listed on the Paris Stock Exchange. artigo.texto: Growing up in Northern Virginia meant reaping the benefits of proximity to our nation’s capital. From field trips to the Smithsonian museums, walks across the National Mall and many hours spent on the Metro (objectively the best public transportation system on the East Coast), I was spoiled from an early age. People forget, however, that driving out of the city offers its own benefits. My favorite outside-of-DC stop was always Manassas, Virginia. Manassas is home to the historic Battle of Bull Run battlefields. My neighbor and I would drive through the battlefields on our way to summer camp at a farm in Manassas. I’d stare out the window at the cannons littered across open fields, the wooden fences leaning with time. Now? There’s a data center right next door. The farm my neighbor and I used to spend hot summer days at is being replaced by computer systems enclosed by sterile white buildings. Right next to where Robert E. Lee faced the Union Army. You can imagine my non-surprise when I found out about the proposed data center projects around South Bend. Because what goes better with tailgates and Touchdown Jesus than fiber-optic cables and AI systems? But on a serious note, the Northern Indiana data centers — and data centers in general — are more than just road trip eyesores. Sophomore Katherine Spiller spent her summer doing research and fieldwork in the St. Joseph County Kettle Lakes Corridor, just west of South Bend. The area is home to a sensitive sphagnum bog habitat, containing many endangered and rare species. A proposed data center project would pose huge environmental threats to such a rich habitat. Already, some of the lakes are drying up, and the massive amounts of water used to power data centers would cause even more drainage in the kettle lakes. Without water — or a home — the species that live in the lakes would cease to exist. “I believe hearing from those who see what the Corridor experiences ... is key to touching hearts and enacting positive change,” Spiller said. She asserted that over half of the people she interviewed brought up concerns about the effect of the data center on the local community, something that should compel tech companies and bystanders alike to step back and consider what they are supporting. We live in a next-step world where society is constantly coming up with ways to optimize and streamline our daily lives, and data centers fit into this future-focused mindset. But they’re almost counterproductive to the things that truly matter. In Virginia, a historical site backdropped by mass innovation provides a scary juxtaposition between past and future. In Indiana, a local ecosystem is slowly being sucked away by the hand of AI. Sure, ChatGPT is great and all, but is this really what we want? Is this really what it means to live in 2026?

artigo.texto: Zelestra and EDP strengthened their collaboration in Spain with two new hybrid PPAs that will incorporate 462 MWh of battery storage to 181 MWdc of solar capacity. The agreements pertain to the Pedroso project in Seville and the Valkyria project in Castilla-La Mancha. In both cases, additional measures will be added BESS systems to existing photovoltaic installations, which will allow part of the solar generation to be stored and its delivery shifted to other times of the day. Zelestra will own the projects while EDP will act as the energy buyer through new long-term power purchase agreements. The hybrid PPAs will incorporate four-hour batteries. In Pedroso, Zelestra will combine a 31 MWdc solar plant with a 25 MW BESS system and a 100 MWh battery storage capacity. Valkyria, meanwhile, will have 150 MWdc of photovoltaic generation and a 90.45 MW battery storage system with a 362 MWh capacity. The two systems will have approximately four hours of storage capacity. Together, they will provide the additional 462 MWh included in the new hybrid PPAs. This configuration allows the electricity produced during peak solar generation hours to be harnessed and stored for later use. In this way, batteries can increase the flexibility of power plants and reduce their reliance on production tied solely to hours of sunlight. Zelestra and EDP exceed 1 GWh of contracted storage The Pedroso and Valkyria agreements bring to four the number of solar energy and storage projects included in the collaboration between Zelestra and EDP in Spain. In 2025, the companies agreed a PPA for the Trujillo project in Extremadura, which combines 170 MWdc of solar capacity with 400 MWh of battery storage. Subsequently, in 2026, both companies expanded their collaboration through Pizarroso, a 50 MW solar plant in Cáceres where a 160 MWh BESS system will be incorporated. With Pedroso and Valkyria, the storage capacity linked to the four agreements reaches approximately 1,022 MWh. Unlike Trujillo, developed as a new solar project with storage, Pedroso, Valkyria and Pizarroso take advantage of photovoltaic plants existing ones to incorporate batteries. Batteries increase the flexibility of solar plants Hybridizing operational facilities allows for the addition of storage using existing infrastructure such as land, generation, and grid access. In addition, the model makes it easier for some of the renewable electricity produced during the day to be shifted to the late afternoon, evening, or other periods of higher demand. For independent power producers, this capacity opens up new commercial opportunities within PPAs. solar generation it is no longer strictly linked to the moment it occurs and can be better adapted to the buyer’s consumption profile. Zelestra has transferred to Europe some of the experience gained in markets such as Chile, where contracts combining renewable generation and storage have a longer track record. Likewise, the company is expanding this type of commercial structure in other European markets through hybrid PPAs and long-term storage contracts. Spain gains energy storage capacity The new operation also reinforces the role of BESS systems within Spanish renewable growth. Jaime Burguete, head of Zelestra in Spain, pointed out that the four joint projects demonstrate the viability of energy storage in the country and predicted that this segment will have a growing importance in the coming years. For its part, EDP seeks to use the combination of renewable generation and storage to provide a more flexible electricity supply and make better use of the energy produced by renewables solar installations. With the new agreements, Zelestra and EDP are expanding a strategy that links long-term supply contracts with large-scale batteries, a formula that can facilitate greater integration of solar energy within the Spanish electricity system. artigo.texto: 07/10/2026 - 13:34 Os FIIs de data centers abrem uma nova frente de financiamento para a infraestrutura digital no Brasil. A AZ Quest Panorama estruturou um fundo para adquirir ativos da Scala, enquanto a Alianza mantém em avaliação a criação de um veículo listado dedicado ao segmento. As estratégias buscam transformar imóveis e instalações de data centers em fontes de renda por meio de contratos de longo prazo. O avanço ocorre em paralelo ao Redata, regime tributário voltado à atração de investimentos para o setor. AZ Quest capta R$ 482 milhões para fundo de data centers O AZ Quest Panorama Data Centers (AZDC) captou R$ 482 milhões na primeira emissão e reuniu mais de 7 mil investidores, conforme as informações apresentadas pela gestora. O fundo adquire ativos da Scala e os aluga de volta à companhia. A estratégia inclui um data center em Fortaleza e três subestações, com contrato de dez anos e janelas específicas de recompra. Para Marcos Freitas, gestor de fundos imobiliários da AZ Quest Panorama, o modelo acrescenta uma alternativa às fontes de capital já utilizadas pelas empresas, como dívida corporativa e financiamento de projetos. “A gente traz uma nova fonte de capital, que é usar os ativos imobiliários que elas possuem como forma de financiamento do capital de giro e dos investimentos dessas companhias”, explicou ao InfoMoney. Remuneração depende do prazo e das condições de recompra O AZDC foi estruturado como fundo cetipado, com prazo determinado de dez anos. Segundo Freitas, a remuneração prevista parte de IPCA mais 9,5% ao ano, no cenário de permanência até o décimo ano. Em determinadas hipóteses de recompra antecipada, pode alcançar IPCA mais 10,5% ao ano. Os percentuais correspondem aos cenários descritos pela gestora e dependem do cumprimento das condições da operação. A proposta é oferecer exposição a ativos existentes, sem investir diretamente no desenvolvimento de um novo data center. “É um fundo que tem começo, meio e fim”, afirmou Freitas. A gestora informa que os rendimentos são isentos, enquanto ganhos de capital e amortizações têm tributação de 20%. A isenção dos rendimentos não se estende, portanto, a todos os valores recebidos pelo investidor. Alianza mantém plano de separar ativos do ALZR11 A Alianza considera transformar sua exposição a data centers em um fundo listado específico. O projeto de separação dos ativos, conhecido como spin-off, permanece condicionado à melhora das condições de mercado. Fabio Carvalho, sócio da gestora, aponta o nível dos juros e o tamanho crescente dos projetos como obstáculos. Segundo ele, empreendimentos que antes demandavam cerca de R$ 200 milhões passaram a alcançar R$ 700 milhões. Essa escala dificulta a compra integral por um único fundo. A Alianza avalia formas de participar de projetos maiores sem adquirir a totalidade dos ativos. O ALZR11, de estratégia multiestratégia, é citado pelo executivo como um veículo com flexibilidade para investir no segmento. Contratos longos sustentam a tese de renda Para Carvalho, a duração dos contratos é uma das características centrais dos data centers como ativos imobiliários. A carteira existente conta com contratos com mais de uma década restante. Novas operações poderiam ser estruturadas com prazos de 15 ou 20 anos, conforme o executivo. Essa duração favorece o planejamento das receitas, mas a criação de um fundo dedicado ainda depende da viabilidade das aquisições e das condições de financiamento. Redata amplia perspectiva de investimentos no Brasil O Redata foi sancionado em setembro de 2026 e prevê incentivos tributários para equipamentos utilizados em data centers. O acesso aos benefícios exige autorização do Ministério da Fazenda e contrapartidas das empresas. Freitas avalia que o regime, combinado às características energéticas e à posição geopolítica brasileira, pode favorecer projetos destinados ao mercado doméstico e a clientes de outros países. A Associação Brasileira de Data Centers estima R$ 500 bilhões em investimentos até 2030, com aumento da capacidade instalada de 730 MW para 3,2 GW. Para os FIIs, a expansão representa uma oportunidade de adquirir ativos com contratos longos. A concretização de novos veículos dependerá do custo de capital, da escala dos projetos e das condições negociadas com os operadores. artigo.texto: Nigeria is set to strengthen the integrity and credibility of its emerging carbon market through the deployment of robust Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) systems, as the Federal Government seeks to attract large-scale private investment into climate action. The Director-General of the National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), Mrs. Omotenioye Majekodunmi, disclosed this at a high-level roundtable on “Operationalising Nigeria’s Carbon Markets through Robust Measurement, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) Protocols,” convened under the European Union Climate Dialogues programme in Abuja, Nigeria’s capital. Represented by the Director, Energy, Transportation & Infrastructure of NCCC, Mr. Michael Ivenso, the Director-General said Nigeria was determined to ensure that carbon markets translate the country’s climate commitments into tangible economic opportunities while preventing greenwashing and protecting the interests of communities, investors and project developers. According to the Director-General, “carbon markets are only as strong as the integrity of the underlying credits,” stressing that Nigeria would not accommodate a carbon market that lacked transparency, credibility and environmental integrity. Mrs. Majekodunmi said the country’s objective was to ensure that carbon projects delivered real, additional and permanent mitigation outcomes, while contributing to community development, environmental protection and fair returns for project developers and investors. READ ALSO: Nigerian President Approves Carbon Market Framework The Director-General said carbon markets were not a panacea for Nigeria’s climate and development challenges, but argued that, when supported by transparency, credible MRV systems and effective stakeholder collaboration, they could become a major catalyst for sustainable development. The NCCC Boss, therefore, urged participants at the roundtable to move beyond discussion and develop an actionable and time-bound roadmap capable of positioning Nigeria as a leading destination for high-integrity carbon investment in Africa. “A major component of the new approach is the operationalisation of a unified and interoperable national carbon registry. “The registry is expected to provide a digital record of carbon credits generated, issued, transferred and retired in Nigeria, thereby helping to prevent double-counting and strengthening the integrity of carbon transactions.” She explained. The NCCC also plans to accelerate the adoption of digital Measurement, Reporting and Verification (dMRV) technologies, including remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, geospatial data and distributed ledger technologies. The technologies are expected to reduce the cost and time required to verify carbon projects while improving the accuracy and reliability of emissions data. The Director-General explained that without effective MRV systems, buyers would be unable to determine whether claimed emissions reductions were genuine, regulators would face difficulties tracking emissions and safeguarding against double-counting, while communities could struggle to monitor benefit-sharing arrangements. The NCCC called for stronger collaboration among federal ministries, state governments, private-sector operators, development partners, financial institutions, civil society organisations and academic institutions. Head of section, Green and Digital Economy, EU Delegation to Nigeria and ECOWAS, Ms. Yolanda San Jose, said carbon markets are playing an increasingly important role in supporting emissions reductions, mobilising finance, and encouraging investment. According to her, this is why Nigeria took a very important step last year by adopting its National Carbon Markets Framework. It established a structured legal and institutional system for domestic and international carbon trading under the Climate Change Act (2021) and Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The Framework is the foundation for confidence, trust, and effectiveness in Nigeria’s emerging carbon market system. Ms. Jose noted that, for Nigeria, the development of a strong national carbon market system is both imperative and a significant opportunity, and would help align climate targets with development priorities, support investment, and create an enabling environment for a low-carbon future. “Today’s event is intended to help shape that pathway. In particular, we aim to align stakeholder views around Nigeria’s National Carbon Markets Framework and to discuss a preliminary roadmap for its operationalisation. We will do so by emphasising the robustness of so-called Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) practices, to ensure that this market mechanism delivers credible results for both the Nigerian people and the environment.” She added that the European Union is pleased to support this process in partnership with Nigeria. Representing the Ministry of Environment, Mrs Halima Bawa-Buhari said the ministry is working towards a partnership that will lead to a robust Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) system and a high-integrity carbon market, contributing significantly to the Securing Nigeria’s Forest Future (SNFF) financing roadmap. One of the development partners, UKPACT Officer, Ms Folakemi Aletan, said a well-functioning carbon market in Nigeria represents more than a climate policy instrument. She said it provides an opportunity to mobilise investment, support sustainable development, strengthen competitiveness and ultimately mobilise climate finance. The representative of the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), Mrs Nifesimi Ogunkua, said; “the organisation is supporting the National Council on Climate Change through a partnership agreement to strengthen the operationalisation of Nigeria’s carbon market framework.” She said the support includes the design and deployment of a digital portal for managing the lifecycle of carbon credit projects. Please enter the email address you use for your account so we can send you a link to reset your password: Local opposition has exacted a much higher cost for developers than has been previously understood, according to new Heatmap Pro survey of public records and financial information. The country’s largest technology companies are expected to spend more than $800 billion this year investing in data centers and artificial intelligence. But new data suggests the local backlash to data centers may be taking a meaningful bite out of that boom. At least $260 billion of data center investments were canceled this year after sustained local opposition, according to new Heatmap Pro data. The pace and size of those cancellations is picking up. About $130 billion in data center investment — or about half of the total — was canceled in the three months ending on September 30. And in dollar terms, the size of canceled projects in the third quarter of 2026 exceeded the size of all data center projects canceled last year. Roughly $1 trillion in data center investment now faces some kind of sustained or meaningful local opposition, according to Heatmap Pro data. About half of all projects that have met local backlash this year were ultimately canceled, our data suggests. Our market intelligence service Heatmap Pro tracks local projects and regulations affecting clean energy, batteries, and data centers. We run a continuous survey of public officials, regulatory filings, and local media to monitor energy and data center cancellations nationwide. Our investment figures, which have not been previously published and are larger than other estimates, are likely an undercount. Only about 60% of data center projects disclose the size of their planned investment, especially during a proposal’s early stage when it is most likely to run aground. These figures also do not include every project currently stalled because of state-level data center moratoriums in Texas and New York. But the totals show that the surging backlash to data centers is beginning to kill a sizable share of large computing projects. In August, a Heatmap Pro and Embold Research poll found that 75% of Americans would oppose a data center getting built near where they live — a striking change from a year earlier, when Americans were roughly split over the projects. “The number of canceled data centers speaks to the vast and growing grassroots opposition to these projects in communities across the country. The fact that many of these projects were defeated in just the past few months speaks to the upward trajectory of this opposition movement,” Mitch Jones, a policy director at Food and Water Watch, an environmental group that opposes AI data centers, said in a statement. A spokesperson for the Data Center Coalition, which advocates for the industry, did not respond before press time. Most canceled data center projects in our database are terminated because they fail to secure a local permit or face a hostile local government action. Hundreds of U.S. counties and towns now maintain a ban or moratorium on data center construction, our data shows. The Senate’s bipartisan permitting reform proposal would not affect towns or counties’ ability to prohibit data center development under their jurisdiction.

artigo.texto: Côte d’Ivoire has shortlisted developers for two 100MW solar photovoltaic plants, each paired with 33MWh of battery storage, as the country moves to close the gap between its 45% renewables target by 2030 and a grid that currently runs on thermal power for roughly two thirds of its installed capacity. The two sites — Dabakala in the north east and Niakaramandougou in the centre of the country — will each be awarded as 25-year independent power producer (IPP) concessions covering design, financing, construction, operation, and maintenance. The concessions run through Ci-Energies, the state electricity utility, and the procurement was launched last year before advancing to shortlist stage, according to Africa Energy. The scale of the ambition is thrown into relief by the starting point. The International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) counted just 40MW of installed solar capacity in Côte d’Ivoire at the end of 2024. Thermal generation accounted for approximately 69% of the country’s 2,907MW of installed capacity as of 2023 — a grid profile that makes absorbing intermittent solar generation difficult without storage. The 33MWh of battery storage specified at each site addresses that integration problem directly. A predominantly thermal grid has limited tolerance for the midday surges that solar produces; battery systems capture that output and release it when demand rises after dark, smoothing the load curve and reducing curtailment risk that would otherwise undermine the economics of new solar investment. The procurement sits within the Pacte National Énergie, the government’s overarching framework for reaching 45% renewables — including hydropower — in the national electricity mix by 2030. The framework also encompasses Côte d’Ivoire’s ambition to position itself as a power exporter to neighbouring countries, giving the grid stability question a regional dimension: reliable, dispatchable renewable capacity is a prerequisite for cross-border supply agreements. West Africa’s power interconnection landscape makes that export ambition credible. Côte d’Ivoire already supplies electricity to several neighbours through the West African Power Pool (WAPP), the regional body coordinating grid integration across the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). Adding dispatchable solar-plus-storage capacity strengthens the country’s ability to honour export commitments regardless of time of day or weather conditions. For developers shortlisted on the two concessions, the 25-year contract horizon and the involvement of Ci-Energies as the offtake counterparty provide the long-term revenue visibility that project finance for utility-scale renewables typically requires. The move to award stage will be closely watched as a signal of how quickly Côte d’Ivoire can translate procurement ambition into contracted capacity.
