artigo.texto: harhar38/Shutterstock Save for later Print Download Share LinkedIn Twitter The essential role that battery energy storage systems (Bess) will play in the energy transition is widely recognized, and investment continues to flood into battery assets. But to make the best use of these, it is essential that operators have a clear picture of all aspects of operations. And the only way to ensure that picture is complete is to collect, assess and analyze data in detail. Battery technology continues to advance across a broad front, with cell density and cycle performance achieving new limits alongside developments in battery chemistry and improvements to degradation curves. In this context, it is unsurprising that the International Energy Agency should have reported that global battery storage deployment expanded “strongly” last year, with total capacity additions reaching 108 gigawatts, up around 40% from 2024. Indeed, batteries are now big business, but hardware doesn’t hold the keys alone: It is harmony between strong software and strong hardware that generates the best results. In recent years, there have been no technological breakthroughs significant enough that an operator would consider wholly replacing a fleet of batteries years before the end of their operational life. It is therefore all the more important that asset managers maximize the potential of hardware that is already in place — and software is key to this. Shifting Mindsets: Viewing Energy Assets as Data Generators There is a constant trade-off in the energy industry between “revenue today” and “revenue tomorrow.” For batteries, this is especially important, as every decision influences the wear and tear on the system: Push them too hard during the early years and you shorten their useable lifetime, but hold out for future revenue and you risk this never actually materializing. To help asset managers strike the best balance, every choice — across both commercial and technical asset management — needs to be as robust as possible. And data is the golden thread running through these twin tracks of decision-making. Modern batteries continuously generate vast amounts of operational intelligence and data on a sub-second basis, from state of charge and thermal metrics to state of health and electrical values. Collecting all this information is a vital first step. Then this needs to be put to work to help site operators improve an asset’s performance and “lifetime value” — i.e. the total revenue across an asset’s lifespan. This metric is the ultimate north star for an asset manager in Bess. For example, a leading Bess owner saw a $110,000 uplift per annum from a single existing 75 megawatt, 1-hour system on Ercot, the Texas power grid system, by realizing the benefits of a more accurate “state of energy” reading and embedding this into their operations. Data as the Money Maker An essential part of commercial asset management is ensuring that the highest-performing technical asset is transacting in the most suitable market at the right time to make the most money. There are three main markets when it comes to Bess assets. Firstly, there are the core energy arbitrage possibilities — charging when the price of energy is low and discharging when it is high. Then there are also capacity/reserve markets (when the battery is paid to be available for a given period) and grid stability services whereby system operators, such as the National Energy System Operator in the UK, procure batteries to help maintain system stability by having them respond in milliseconds to fluctuations in the frequency of the grid. Decisions around which market to monetize a battery in typically fall with third-party optimizers, who are in turn reliant on technical asset managers maximizing the availability of the portfolio. Each party can utilize data to inform and elevate their judgements at different stages of the process. The more visibility into metrics around availability, reliability and underlying performance which stakeholders can exploit, for instance, the more they will be able to position their strategy for targeting the best market at the best time — to make the best returns. Minimizing Downtime Dig deeper into the technical management of a battery asset and it again becomes clear how crucial data is in achieving the perennial aim of having a battery system perform at as close to 100%, as much of the time as possible. With this in mind, leveraging insights can enable asset managers to streamline their approach to maintenance. There are several key performance indicators that asset managers need to track constantly. These include the headline concerns around availability and degradation, as well as round trip efficiency (how much energy is lost between a charge and discharge cycle), cycles per day (how much energy has flowed through the battery for a given time period), and warranty compliance (is the system operating within the bounds of the manufacturer’s warranty). The recent heatwaves have also thrown a spotlight on the issue of temperature performance and the need to adjust cycles/market choices when it is extremely hot. Granular data can help asset managers spot more quickly when a system is falling short against one — or more — of these metrics, and to see not just the symptoms of a problem but the root cause. Asset managers can then look to harness data to target the most efficient window to take assets off line for maintenance, whether it be opting to accelerate a maintenance intervention to make an asset ready for a predicted high revenue period or deciding that the cost of a higher tier of service level agreement from a maintenance contractor is worth it to bring a battery and its income-making potential back on line faster following an issue. The cumulative effect of each optimized technical decision quickly builds to a meaningful difference in results and competitive standing. artigo.texto: BETHLEHEM, Pa. — Bethlehem City Council voted 7-0 Tuesday to give initial approval to the city’s first zoning rules for data centers, which face a final vote Oct. 20. Bethlehem’s zoning code currently treats a data center like any other industrial use, with no added limits, Planning and Zoning Director Cathy Fletcher told council. The new rules would add a public hearing, require studies on water, power, noise and heat, and keep data centers at least 1,000 feet from homes and schools. The rules will not cover the one data center already proposed in the city, a project on Industrial Drive that could not be built under them. During the nearly three-hour hearing, Councilwoman Jo Daniels said the rules fall short in the areas that matter most to residents. Other council members argued that passing them now is better than leaving data centers unregulated. Get the latest laws & regulations news and updates from across the Valley. By subscribing, you agree to our Privacy Policy and consent to receive updates. Most of the 24 people who spoke during public comment urged council to pass the rules and strengthen them over time. Daniels and Councilman Bryan Callahan both said during the hearing that they did not expect to vote for the rules. Both voted yes. The Industrial Drive project The proposed data center is a two-story building with a 65,000-square-foot footprint at 2184 Industrial Drive, replacing the former Crowder Service Center building along Route 22. Boyle Construction and Paxos, both of the Lehigh Valley, and Tensor IQ of Newark, Del., proposed the project. The site is in the city’s Planned Industrial district, where the ordinance would not allow data centers. City zoning and parcel maps also show every part of the 6.75-acre lot is within 1,000 feet of residentially zoned property. Because its application was filed before the amendment, it will be reviewed under the current code, Fletcher said. The project goes before the city Planning Commission at 5 p.m. Nov. 12 in the Town Hall Rotunda, where the public can comment, Council President Rachel Leon said. Get the latest laws & regulations news and updates from across the Valley. By subscribing, you agree to our Privacy Policy and consent to receive updates. That local review carries added weight under a state order. Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order on data centers on Aug. 18. Under it, the state Department of Environmental Protection will not issue a permit unless the project “has received all required local approvals.” The order also bans nondisclosure agreements, which keep project details secret, on data center projects. What the rules do State law requires every municipality’s zoning to allow every legitimate land use. That means Bethlehem cannot ban data centers or write rules so strict that one could never be built. Under the amendment, data centers would be allowed only in the city’s Industrial district, not its Planned Industrial district, and only by special exception. That means an applicant would need approval from the Zoning Hearing Board at a public hearing, in addition to the usual Planning Commission review. The city Planning Commission voted 4-0 on Aug. 25 to recommend the rules. In a review letter, the Lehigh Valley Planning Commission called them “a thoughtful and intentional response to a complex land use.” Applicants would have to submit several studies and plans with their application, including an environmental study, water and sewer approvals, an energy plan, an emergency plan, a decommissioning plan, a heat plan, a lighting study, and noise studies before and after construction. Noise would be measured at the property line. The post-construction noise study would be due one to 12 months after the city clears the building for use. Buildings would have to sit at least 80 feet from property lines, up from 20 feet for other industrial uses. The setback grows to 200 feet next to any non-industrial lot. It grows to 1,000 feet from a residential district or an existing home, school, day care, park, hospital, or recreation center. That is 50 times the current 20-foot minimum. Larger buildings would also require larger lots. Fletcher said a data center under 50,000 square feet could cover no more than 50% of its lot, down from 65% for other industrial buildings. The limit tightens as buildings grow, she said. Councilwoman Hillary Kwiatek later returned to the rule to walk the audience through it. The rule means “the bigger the building gets, the even huger the lot size has to be,” Kwiatek said. Under the ordinance, each square foot of building between 50,000 and 250,000 square feet needs 3 more square feet of land. Above 250,000 square feet, each added square foot needs 5 more. By that math, a 250,000-square-foot data center would need a lot of about 16 acres, and a 500,000-square-foot one would need about 45 acres. Where the rules stop Fletcher said the city cannot require yearly reports once a data center opens. Zoning Officer David Taylor said post-approval inspections would largely be driven by complaints. Councilman Justin Amann said a zoning fine of $500 a day “is not going to be an issue” for a data center operator. City Solicitor Jack Spirk said the city could also seek a court injunction to stop a violation. Jill Seitz, chief community and regional planner for the Lehigh Valley Planning Commission, said state law limits what zoning can cover. The state Department of Environmental Protection oversees air quality, and the Public Utility Commission oversees electric service, she said. A regional planning commission guide on the meeting’s materials table, “5 Questions for Legally Defensible Data Center Regulations,” makes the same point. It says local rules hold up best when they address measurable effects, such as noise, lighting, building height, and setbacks. artigo.texto: Google has been ordered to halt work on two data centers it's developing in Finland, a month after the tech giant committed to investing $15 billion in artificial intelligence infrastructure in the country. Finnish Licensing and Supervision Agency, or LVV, on Tuesday issued a notice to Google subsidiary, Tuike Finland Oy, to suspend building work for data center projects planned for Muhos and Kajaani until the environmental impact assessments have been completed. The suspension request applies, among other things, to the removal of trees, removal of topsoil, excavation, quarrying, crushing, transfer of soil masses, ditching, and the construction of roads and storage areas, according to a Google translation of an LVV press release. "We understand the concerns and have fallen short of our own high standards in this instance," a Google spokesperson told CNBC, adding that it would follow the LVV's guidance. "We acted in good faith under the Forestry Act, and ran nature surveys and put in place measures to protect high-value areas," the spokesperson said. "As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares [320 acres] at Muhos." The LVV ordered Google to halt work no later than Oct. 23. The request does not apply to planning, measurements, soil surveys, or other measures with minor impacts that can be easily restored. "In our opinion, the measures in question will change the environment and cause impacts, the identification and assessment of which are among the key objectives of the EIA procedure," Tommi Muilu, head of the environmental department at the Finnish licensing and supervision authority, said in the statement. 'Texas of Europe' Finland has emerged as a key location for data centers amid the AI boom, with hyperscalers and developers eyeing its available land and power, which is in short supply throughout most of Europe. Several data center projects with potential capacities of hundreds of megawatts have recently been announced in the country. The rise in demand has led to Finland being dubbed the "Texas of Europe." The U.S. state has become one of the leading locations for AI data centers globally, with a number of huge projects announced by hyperscalers and AI labs, including Google, Meta, Microsoft and Anthropic. Google's $15 billion plan for Finland will mark its largest investment in Europe. The capital will be deployed through 2028 into data centers and other supporting investments like energy projects, the company said in a statement at the time.

artigo.texto: LG Energy Solution Targets EV Commercialization on 2029, Focusing on Cost and Application-Specific Designs While Samsung SDI Pushes Faster Mass Production With Supply Chain Deals and Sulfide-Based Technology As the commercialization of solid-state batteries comes into sight, technological competition within the domestic battery industry is also beginning in earnest. While Samsung SDI is accelerating efforts up to establishing a material supply chain with the goal of mass production next year, LG Energy Solution puts more weight on securing technological differentiation and cost competitiveness rather than the timing of commercialization. According to the industry on Oct. 7, LG Energy Solution is aiming for the commercialization of graphite-based solid-state batteries for electric vehicles (EV) in 2029, and the commercialization of anode-free solid-state batteries for next-generation applications such as humanoid robots in 2030. A solid-state battery is a battery that changes the electrolyte, the pathway through which lithium ions move, from the existing liquid to a solid. It is also called a ‘dream battery’ as it does not use a flammable liquid electrolyte, thereby lowering the risk of fire and increasing energy density. However, complex manufacturing processes and high production costs are considered challenges that need to be solved for mass production. Rather than rushing commercialization, LG Energy Solution has chosen a strategy of subdividing its technology to fit actual applications. The plan is to secure competitiveness by varying the battery structure according to the required performance, rather than targeting all markets with a single solid-state technology. The company is also developing dry electrode technology to lower high manufacturing costs. This is interpreted as a strategy to lower equipment and process costs as well as production time by reducing the organic solvents and drying processes required in the existing wet process. This comes from the judgment that securing both mass producibility and economic feasibility is important for solid-state batteries to compete in price with existing lithium-ion batteries. In comparison, Samsung SDI is stepping up to establish a supply chain with the goal of commercializing sulfide-based solid-state batteries faster around next year. It recently signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with EcoPro BM and agreed to cooperate from the development of core materials such as sulfide-based solid electrolytes and cathode materials for solid-state batteries, to quality evaluation and the establishment of a mass production system. EcoPro BM is operating a sulfide-based solid electrolyte pilot plant with an annual capacity of 40 tons. The two companies, which had previously been cautious about disclosing their specific cooperative relationship, have formalized their collaboration for the commercialization of solid-state batteries through this MOU. An industry official said, “The solid-state battery is a market where technological prowess determines competitiveness,” and added, “Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution will engage in a competition for dominance with differentiated strategies that utilize their respective strengths.”

artigo.texto: LG Energy Solution, SK On and Samsung SDI See Combined Share Fall 11.1 Percentage Points Amid Weak North American Demand and LFP Shift South Korea’s three major battery makers are losing ground in the global electric vehicle battery market outside China. While the overall market grew by more than 20%, battery usage by Korean companies fell by double digits, sending their combined market share down more than 11 percentage points in a year. At the same time, Chinese battery makers continued to expand their presence, putting further pressure on Korean companies. SNE Research, an energy market research firm, said Oct. 7 that total EV battery usage in countries outside China reached 360.5 gigawatt-hours (GWh) from January through August this year. The figure was up 23.7% from the same period last year, exceeding the 19.7% growth of the global EV battery market as a whole. Despite the broader market expansion, combined battery usage by LG Energy Solution, SK On and Samsung SDI totaled 96.5 GWh, down 12.8% from a year earlier. Their combined market share consequently fell sharply to 26.8% from 37.9%, a decline of 11.1 percentage points. The primary factor behind the deterioration was weakening demand in North America. The three Korean companies’ combined battery usage in the region fell to 25.3 GWh from 47.4 GWh a year earlier, a 46.5% decline. The demand gap that emerged following the expiration of the U.S. EV tax credit has dealt a direct blow to Korean battery makers. By company, LG Energy Solution retained second place in non-China markets with battery usage of 58.1 GWh, but its market share fell 5.1 percentage points to 16.1%. SK On dropped from fourth to fifth place after its usage declined 14.4%, while Samsung SDI fell to seventh after recording the steepest decline among the top 10 companies, with usage down 32.0%. As Korean companies saw their market shares shrink, Chinese battery makers continued to gain ground. CATL ranked first in non-China markets with 121.3 GWh, up 43.3% from a year earlier, giving it a 33.7% market share. BYD, which ranked third, also increased its usage by 66.5%, raising its market share to 11.0%. Several smaller Chinese battery makers also posted triple-digit growth, further increasing competitive pressure on Korean companies. Gotion, SVOLT and EVE Energy recorded growth of 147.2%, 105.2% and 185.6%, respectively. The combined market share of six Chinese battery makers reached 56.2%, surpassing half of the non-China market for the first time. The shift in market share coincides with the rapid expansion of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries. LFP’s share of the non-China market rose 11.9 percentage points in a year, from 15.6% to 27.5%. The growing adoption of lower-cost LFP batteries in Europe and North America is creating a more favorable environment for Chinese battery makers, which have maintained a stronger position in the LFP segment. Korean battery makers are seeking to offset weaker utilization in North America by tapping demand for energy storage systems (ESS) and data centers. Battery usage in Europe increased 5.2%, maintaining modest growth, but the continued expansion of Chinese-branded EV sales in the region could make it more difficult for Korean companies to regain market share. An SNE Research official said local production capacity and price competitiveness, along with supply chain traceability capabilities needed to prepare for the battery passport taking effect next February, will determine companies’ market positions. The ability to respond to regional policy changes and diversify demand sources is expected to be critical to Korean battery makers’ efforts to recover market share.

artigo.texto: O Brasil se prepara para realizar, em dezembro de 2026, seus primeiros leilões de reserva de capacidade destinados especificamente a sistemas de armazenamento em baterias. Mais do que introduzir uma nova tecnologia no sistema elétrico, os certames podem criar uma classe de ativos de infraestrutura, com contratos de longo prazo e potencial para movimentar uma ampla cadeia de equipamentos, engenharia, software e serviços. Para aprofundar as reflexões sobre o assunto, a KPMG produziu a publicação Armazenamento de Energia: a nova indústria que o Brasil pode construir. O interesse do mercado já é expressivo. A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) recebeu 6.091 projetos, que somam 296.807 MW de potência. Trata-se do maior número de inscrições já registrado em certames do setor elétrico promovidos pelo governo federal. O volume cadastrado, entretanto, não corresponde à capacidade que será habilitada ou contratada. Os projetos ainda passarão por análise técnica, e o Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) estima contratar entre 5 GW e 6 GW nas duas modalidades previstas. Por que o Brasil precisa de sistemas de armazenamento? A expansão das fontes solar e eólica aumentou a disponibilidade de energia renovável, mas também tornou mais complexa a coordenação entre geração, consumo, transmissão e segurança operacional. Durante o dia, a produção solar reduz a demanda atendida pelas fontes controladas pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS). No fim da tarde, essa geração diminui rapidamente enquanto o consumo permanece elevado. O sistema precisa, então, disponibilizar um grande volume de potência em poucas horas. As baterias podem armazenar energia nos períodos de maior oferta e disponibilizá-la quando o sistema mais precisa. Sua resposta rápida também pode contribuir para a estabilidade da rede, reduzir parte do curtailment — o corte ou a limitação da geração disponível — e, em situações específicas, postergar investimentos em transmissão e distribuição. O armazenamento deve, portanto, ser entendido como uma infraestrutura que proporciona flexibilidade ao sistema elétrico. Seu valor não se limita à capacidade instalada, mas inclui a contribuição para a confiabilidade da rede, a integração das fontes renováveis e o melhor aproveitamento dos ativos existentes. Como funcionarão os primeiros leilões de armazenamento de energia? Os certames estão previstos para dezembro de 2026. O primeiro deles será destinado a sistemas que comprovem o uso de baterias com fabricação nacional, de acordo com critérios cuja verificação caberá ao Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES). Já o segundo será aberto aos demais projetos elegíveis, inclusive aqueles que utilizem equipamentos importados. Os contratos terão duração de 15 anos, com início do suprimento previsto para 1º de agosto de 2028. Requisitos anunciados: - Potência mínima de 30 MW. - Capacidade de descarga durante quatro horas. - Eficiência mínima prevista de 85%. - Despacho centralizado pelo ONS. - Possibilidade de até dois acionamentos diários. - Prazo máximo de seis horas para recomposição da carga. A remuneração será realizada por meio de uma receita fixa mensal vinculada à disponibilidade do ativo. Quais fatores determinarão a viabilidade dos projetos? A previsibilidade da receita cria uma condição importante para o financiamento dos projetos, mas não elimina a complexidade dos empreendimentos. A localização será um dos fatores decisivos. Como a bateria funciona como carga durante a recarga e como fonte durante a descarga, o ponto de conexão precisa suportar os fluxos nos dois sentidos. A capacidade remanescente da rede e os eventuais custos de reforço também poderão influenciar a competitividade do projeto. Outro aspecto central é a degradação. As baterias perdem gradualmente parte de sua capacidade à medida que são utilizadas. O modelo econômico-financeiro deve prever como o sistema continuará atendendo às obrigações contratuais durante os 15 anos, considerando sobredimensionamento inicial, reposição de módulos, manutenção, eficiência e exposição cambial. A escolha dos fornecedores também não pode ser orientada apenas pelo menor preço. Histórico de desempenho, capacidade produtiva e financeira, garantias, segurança contra incêndio, cibersegurança, assistência técnica e disponibilidade de peças são elementos essenciais para a sustentabilidade do ativo. Qual é o potencial para a indústria brasileira? Um sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (Battery Energy Storage System - BESS) envolve muito mais do que células e módulos. A cadeia inclui inversores, transformadores, sistemas de gerenciamento, proteção, climatização, combate a incêndio, automação, software, contêineres, obras civis, montagem, integração, operação e manutenção. O Brasil já possui competências em engenharia, equipamentos de potência, automação industrial, construção e montagem. Nos primeiros ciclos, o conteúdo nacional poderá se concentrar nessas atividades, enquanto a dependência externa tende a ser maior em células e determinados componentes eletrônicos. Para que os leilões gerem desenvolvimento industrial, será necessário combinar conteúdo local, competitividade, escala e previsibilidade. A continuidade das contratações poderá ser tão importante quanto o volume do primeiro certame para estimular investimentos produtivos e desenvolver conhecimento no País. Como transformar contratação em criação de valor? Os projetos mais sólidos não serão necessariamente aqueles que apresentarem apenas o menor custo dos equipamentos. A criação de valor dependerá da capacidade de integrar localização, conexão, tecnologia, financiamento, tributação, conteúdo nacional, contratos, execução e gestão do ciclo de vida. Os primeiros leilões podem representar uma nova etapa para a infraestrutura elétrica brasileira. O desafio será transformar o interesse do mercado em projetos seguros, financiáveis e capazes de gerar valor durante toda a vigência dos contratos.

artigo.texto: Chinese Battery Makers Grab 34% Share Outside China; South Korea's Big Three Slump to 27% Chinese battery manufacturers are rapidly expanding their market share in the global EV market outside China. From January through August this year, usage volumes for Chinese players including CATL and BYD surged sharply in non-China markets, while the combined share of South Korea's three major battery makers—heavily reliant on North America—fell below 30%. According to data released on October 7 by SNE Research, a specialized energy market research firm, total battery usage in battery electric vehicles (BEVs), plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), and hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) registered outside China from January through August reached approximately 360.5 GWh. That represents a 23.7% increase year over year, outpacing the global overall growth rate of 19.7% by 4.0 percentage points. However, the monthly growth rate for August alone slowed to 9%. SNE Research attributed this to the impact of the North American demand vacuum becoming more pronounced in monthly figures. Broad-Based Growth for Chinese Players CATL solidified its No. 1 position with 121.3 GWh of usage, up 43.3% year over year. Its market share climbed 4.7 percentage points from 29.0% to 33.7%. In Europe, usage rose 30.4% from 61.8 GWh to 80.6 GWh, while in Asia it more than doubled to 24.0 GWh. BYD maintained third place with 39.7 GWh, up 66.5%. Its share rose 2.8 percentage points from 8.2% to 11.0%. Usage grew broadly across Europe (14.5 GWh, +65.6%), Asia (13.2 GWh, +41.7%), and South America (6.2 GWh, +138.5%). Growth among later-entrant Chinese players was even steeper. Gotion High-tech surged 147.2% to 14.4 GWh, SVOLT jumped 105.2% to 11.4 GWh, and CALB rose 77.6% to 8.4 GWh. EVE posted the highest growth rate among the top 10 companies at 185.6%, reaching 7.5 GWh. South Korea's Big Three Fall Across the Board on North American Weakness The combined market share of South Korea's three major battery makers dropped 11.1 percentage points from 37.9% to 26.8%. The decline in usage was concentrated in North America. The trio's North American usage fell 46.5% from 47.4 GWh to 25.3 GWh, while Europe rose 5.2% from 49.9 GWh to 52.5 GWh and Asia increased 33.0% from 11.2 GWh to 14.8 GWh. LG Energy Solution posted 58.1 GWh, down 5.8% year over year, but held onto the No. 2 spot in non-China markets. European usage rose 9.8% to 31.3 GWh and Asia grew 44.4% to 9.2 GWh, but North American usage tumbled 42.3% from 25.2 GWh to 14.6 GWh, dragging down overall results. Its market share fell 5.1 percentage points from 21.2% to 16.1%. SK On remained in fifth place with 24.8 GWh, down 14.4%. Its share slipped 3.0 percentage points from 9.9% to 6.9%. North American usage fell 41.8%, and Europe also declined 1.5%. Samsung SDI posted the steepest decline among the top 10 companies, falling 32.0% to 13.6 GWh. Its share contracted 3.0 percentage points from 6.8% to 3.8%. European usage was roughly flat year over year at 8.3 GWh, but North American usage plummeted 62% from 10.4 GWh to 3.9 GWh. Japan's Panasonic ranked fourth with 29.7 GWh, up 1.8%. Tesla's North American volume underpinned its performance, but with growth well below the non-China market average, its share fell 1.7 percentage points from 10.0% to 8.3%. Non-China Market Usage and Share by Major Player Note: January–August 2026, excluding China market. Share change is versus the same period last year. Gotion High-tech's share was not disclosed. Policy and Supply Chain Capabilities Will Be Decisive SNE Research projected that regional policies and customer diversification will determine supplier competitiveness going forward. The research firm said, "Local production capacity, price competitiveness, and supply chain traceability capabilities in preparation for the battery passport regime taking effect next February will be the key variables determining market position." The rise of Chinese players reflects simultaneous penetration of the European market and expansion across Asia. South Korean manufacturers, by contrast, took a direct hit from slowing North American EV demand driven by policy shifts including the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). Given their heavy North American exposure, the shock of market contraction was proportionally severe. Investors and industry observers see the key question for South Korean battery makers as how quickly they can capture the timing of a North American demand recovery while sustaining growth in Europe and Asia. Given the pace of Chinese players' price competitiveness and production capacity expansion, securing next-generation battery technology and supply chain transparency—beyond simply defending market share—is expected to be the crux of long-term competitiveness. artigo.texto: For nine months, the Rev. Edward Moultrie of St. Paul CME Church and his congregation filled county meetings, urging officials to reject a proposal for a massive data center near their church and homes. They warned that the project near Walterboro, South Carolina, would threaten the waterways they rely on and bring pollution to their doorstep. On Monday, they won. In January, two weeks after Capital B first wrote about the proposal, residents sued Colleton County over its effort to change the zoning code to allow data centers in rural areas. This week, the Southern Environmental Law Center reached an agreement with the county to resolve that lawsuit. The fight in Colleton County underscored a pattern in where these facilities are proposed. Last year, after a majority-white county in Georgia blocked a data center, the data center developer, Eagle Rock Partners, proposed a similar project in Colleton County, where the share of Black residents is nearly twice as high. Analyses have found that communities closest to U.S. data centers regulated by the Environmental Protection Agency are “overwhelmingly” nonwhite. Moultrie said the settlement “is a relief.” “I can’t preach to my people that God is making a way for them and offering them hope, and then have something like this come into the community to take people’s hope away,” he said. “Black people here have worked hard all their lives to survive and thrive and protect their land. It gives us some kind of sense of pride knowing that we’re not going to go by the wayside or be destroyed or taken for granted — for now.” With the settlement, the county has agreed to establish a “Data Center Exclusion Area” that prohibits data centers across the majority of the ACE Basin in Colleton County, which is a rural area home to ecologically sensitive animals and some of the most important waterways in South Carolina. The exclusion area includes the land where the data center was proposed in December 2025. The data center would have been over 800 acres, making it one of the largest in the South, which has become the epicenter of data center development. “I have lived in the ACE Basin my entire life, right here in Colleton County. My family has been here for generations. The original data center complex that was proposed would have surrounded my property on three sides and completely changed the area,” said Miles Crosby, one of the residents who brought the lawsuit. “I’m thankful we could reach an outcome that not only prevents data centers from surrounding my home but also protects the majority of the ACE Basin in Colleton County from data center development.” In the first half of 2026, at least 115 data centers nationwide were blocked by local residents. The blocked projects’ price tags totaled roughly $200 billion, according to Data Center Watch, a group tracking data center development. At the same time, data center development continues to climb. August saw the most money ever spent on data center construction in the U.S., up more than 73% over the past 12 months. The struggle for local Black communities is not over. A new fossil fuel plant, partially proposed to keep this and other data centers running, is moving forward in a majority-Black area located in Colleton County. The methane gas power plant would result in more than $30 million in local health care costs as residents begin to struggle through respiratory illnesses, according to a pollution analysis by the Southern Environmental Law Center. The pollution from gas power plants — fine particulate matter known as PM2.5 — can penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, causing respiratory and cardiovascular disease. It is linked to asthma attacks, strokes, dementia, and cancer. Black Americans have the highest death rate from such pollution in the U.S. Chris DeScherer, the South Carolina office director for the Southern Environmental Law Center, said the group will continue to “help ensure that any data center projects in Colleton County and beyond are developed responsibly with respect to surrounding communities and natural resources.” Read More:

artigo.texto: Berlin-based ebike startup Lemmo has been shaking up the European market with a small selection of handsome mid-range models since 2022. It's now got something in the works for families and more adventurous riders with a versatile SUV ebike that promises to take you places while delivering an exceptionally comfortable ride. The Lemmo 3 is a long-tail ebike with room for cargo in the front and rear, plus pannier bags and up to two child seats. It sports a full suspension setup, a hydraulic seatpost, and all-terrain tires to soak up bumps and make it a breeze to cover all kinds of surfaces. The brand says this model is three years in the making, and includes plenty of tech for safety, performance, and convenience that you'd expect to see on the latest ebikes. It's also capable of covering longer distances than just your usual city commutes. Let's talk suspension first. A high-load spring for the rear suspension affords 80 mm of travel to ensure your little passenger is comfortable. Up front, you've got hydraulic forks that deliver 80 mm of travel too. Meanwhile, the seatpost offers 20 mm of travel as well. Closer to the asphalt, 65 mm wide all-terrain tires offer cushioning and stability while riding with heavier cargo. Lemmo's gone with a 960-Wh semi-solid state battery, which reportedly allows for up to 110 miles (180 km) of range and won't go up in flames from punctures or thermal runaway incidents. This pairs with a rear hub Bafang H720 motor that's rated for 750 W of continuous power in the US (500 W in Canada, and 250 W in Europe), and a three-speed automatic gearbox. This setup allows for a pedal assist up to 28 mph (45 km/h). With this kind of kit, the Lemmo 3 should be up to the task of tackling steep inclines and all manner of rough terrain. The brand says its direct steering makes it easier to maneuver than conventional cargo bikes, despite its long wheelbase. Riders ranging from 5ft1 (155 cm) to 6ft5 (195 cm) can enjoy a comfy upright riding position thanks to the adjustable stem and seat. If you plan to take this out on the trail on camping trips, it'll happily handle up to 176 lb (80 kg) of gear in the rear, and an additional 44 lb (20 kg) on the front rack. There's some neat tech on here too, including GPS tracking and a motion detection alarm for security, a 3.5-inch touchscreen displaying your riding metrics, a rear-approaching radar with automatic brake lights, and keyless start. That makes this a compelling option for people looking for a more versatile ebike than the vast range available for riding only around town. Lemmo is scheduled to crowdfund this model on Kickstarter later this month, during which the Essential model will be available at about US$2,155. That's discounted down from its expected MSRP of €3,390 ($3,890) – but it requires an early reservation on Lemmo's site with a refundable $45 deposit. You can add on a belt drive for an extra $193. There are also a couple of bike bundles which include accessories like a passenger guardrail, seat pads and foot boards, pannier bags, and a front rack. With that, Lemmo's set to go up against the Amflow TL Carbon we saw earlier this year. That's another capable SUV ebike, with a powerful motor and swappable add-on battery – at a slightly higher price above the $4,000 mark. Check out the Lemmo 3 on the company's site, and head here for the Kickstarter campaign that's yet to go live at the time of writing (you can sign up to be notified when it takes off). If all goes as expected, orders are estimated to begin shipping next April in the aforementioned regions. Source: Lemmo

artigo.texto: A moratorium on the facilities that enable artificial intelligence would last 45 days and could be extended to 22 months. The data centers powering artificial intelligence technology — and the accompanying public outcry — are officially something San Francisco city leaders can’t ignore. The San Francisco Board of Supervisors on Tuesday unanimously approved a 45-day moratorium on data centers that would pause city approvals of the facilities and task the Planning Department with studying their impacts and developing long-term controls. The moratorium now awaits action from the mayor. “During this period, we are looking at issues including energy, water, air quality, land use, and community impacts, while working toward stronger protections and meaningful community input, as well as a data center definition that is clear to everyone,” said Supervisor Shamann Walton, who authored the moratorium. Tuesday’s vote is a significant step as city leaders grapple with the wider land use and infrastructure impacts of one of the city’s biggest exports. By November, city leaders will convene a hearing about progress by the Planning Department and its findings on data centers. The moratorium could be extended to 22 months, but it’s unclear whether city leaders would entertain the idea. Walton represents District 10, which stretches from Visitacion Valley and Bayview Hunters-Point to Potrero Hill and Dogpatch. His district has two of the six data center sites in San Francisco, according to market intelligence firm Data Center Map (opens in new tab). His district may have been eyed for a third one. In August, a lobbyist for a private equity firm advertising a 1.6-acre data center (opens in new tab) met with two of Mayor Daniel Lurie’s policy chiefs about planning and building permits for a waterfront plot of land in Dogpatch. The cities of Oakley, Richmond, and Gilroy already have moratoriums on data centers, while Oakland and Hayward are considering it. The Land Use and Transportation Committee advanced Walton’s proposal to the full board. At the committee’s Monday meeting, more than a dozen people showed up in support of the moratorium on new data centers. Among them was Arieann Harrison, a Bayview resident and executive director of the Marie Harrison Community Foundation (opens in new tab). She said her community already deals with worse health outcomes than other parts of the city, triggered by the industrial facilities located in District 10. “We need for this committee right here to stand on business when it comes to the health outcomes of our districts,” Harrison said at the Monday meeting. Walton’s proposal is among his final priorities in office. He was first elected in 2018 and will term out in January. All three of the frontrunners in the race to replace him on the Board of Supervisors are supportive of a data center moratorium. “Transparency about water and energy demands enforceable community benefits and a real opportunity for residents to weigh in before projects are approved, not after,” Walton said at the Monday committee meeting. Correction: An earlier version of this story incorrectly stated the moratorium takes effect immediately. It awaits action from the mayor. More about the author Omar Rashad reports on San Francisco government and politics.

artigo.texto: Em Brasília, a CNA recebeu na terça-feira (6) integrantes da Nuffield, rede global de produtores e especialistas do agro voltada à formação de lideranças e ao intercâmbio de conhecimento. O grupo reuniu representantes de Brasil, Holanda, Irlanda, Malaui, Zimbábue e Austrália. Elena Castellani, responsável pela área internacional da CNA, destacou o perfil produtivo brasileiro e explicou frentes da CNA, do Senar e do Instituto CNA, como inteligência técnica, capacitação, defesa de interesses, representação e apoio gerencial e técnico a produtores. A comitiva passou ainda pelo Instituto CNA, onde viu tecnologias voltadas ao setor agrícola. A ferramenta de dados da CNA despertou dúvidas sobre como as informações são coletadas, analisadas e implementadas. PSA, sigla de pagamento por serviços ambientais, e mercado de carbono regulado foram apontados como desafios comuns a vários países. Para Jackie Morrison, da Nuffield Austrália, o encontro ampliou a leitura que o grupo fez do Brasil. Segundo ela, os participantes entenderam que o país pode ser concorrente e parceiro de cooperação. Criadora de mel em parceria com o marido, ela investiga desde 2023 o Manejo Integrado de Pragas (MIP) para apoiar a apicultura australiana diante do ácaro Varroa destructor. Luciana Kliemann, que integra a Nuffield Brasil e cultiva grãos em Mato Grosso do Sul, considerou relevante apresentar a CNA ao grupo após uma programação internacional voltada a soluções, inovação e contato com produtores. Além do Brasil, o roteiro passou por Austrália, França, Romênia, China e Cingapura, com atividades em setembro e outubro de 2026. No período, os participantes analisaram modelos de produção, políticas, inovações e desafios ambientais e comerciais do campo.

artigo.texto: New NCITE Research: Growing Security Risks to U.S. Data Centers As data centers become a growing part of American infrastructure, NCITE experts examine how evolving threats could put national security at risk. - published: 2026/10/08 - contact: Ben Battafarano - NCITE Communications - phone: 4025542972 - email: ncite@unomaha.edu - search keywords: - data centers - cyberattacks - critical infrastructure Data centers, once obscure on the urban skyline, are now at the forefront in society as they have multiplied in recent years, increased electricity costs and depleted water supplies. Such grievances combined with their integral role in data storage, transfer, and redundancy have made the sites an attractive target for terrorists and other bad actors looking to harm the United States. Read the paper: "Evaluating the Physical, Digital, and Sovereign Risks to U.S. Data Centers" explores methods of attacks and vulnerabilities, and makes recommendations for homeland security stakeholders. The paper’s authors are NCITE consortium experts Kevin Chen and Katrina McDermott, both master's of public policy candidates in the Yale Schmidt Program on AI, Emerging Technology, and National Power. Why it matters: Attacks on data centers put crucial American information at risk — in finance, energy, defense, and more. Safeguarding these facilities is necessary to protect everything from photos on social media to social security numbers. Key takeaways: - Attack methods differ by actor. Cyber espionage and cyberattacks on servers and their surrounding infrastructure — like cooling systems and business management software — are prioritized by nation states like Iran and China. Transnational criminal organizations and U.S.-based illicit actors engage in physical attacks to steal valuable machinery (sometimes for ransom) or disrupt and destroy data center operations. - Close physical concentration is a significant vulnerability. The U.S hosts over 38% of data centers globally and clusters them close together — for example, northern Virginia alone has over 250. This makes it easier to attack in bulk and threatens data redundancy efforts. This occurred in spring 2026 when Iran attacked multiple Amazon Web Services sites in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, resulting in the failure of that region's data redundancy plan. - Public opinion about the sites could be weaponized. Symbolism is key for actors when choosing targets, and as negative sentiment around data centers grows, they are increasingly likely to be chosen. Additionally, actors may attempt to directly manipulate public opinion and sow domestic unrest around the sites to serve their long-term goals for political change. The authors stress that "the great majority of ... opposition is lawful" and that conflating public opposition with terroristic or nation-state activities "is analytically unsound." - There is a public-private information sharing gap. Most data centers are privately owned and operated, and as such have commercial concerns when breaches happen — their reputation, shareholder liability, and regulatory penalties. Therefore, they're less likely to report incidents, which can delay investigation and prosecution. What they're saying: - Kevin Chen, author - "A modern data center has several layers an adversary can go after, and we found that different actors gravitate toward different ones depending on what they're capable of and what they want." - Katrina McDermott, author - “This white paper makes the case for treating data centers as critical infrastructure that must be secured.” What's next: This paper is the first in a series of expert insights on rapidly evolving, critical technology infrastructure emerging as threat risks.

artigo.texto: O Ministério das Comunicações (MCom) planeja avançar nas políticas para data centers, cabos submarinos, rodovias e inclusão digital ainda neste ano, afirmou nesta terça-feira, 6, o secretário de Telecomunicações, Hermano Tercius, durante o evento Futurecom, em São Paulo. Um passo importante nesse sentido deve ocorrer na quinta-feira, 8, quando o secretário vai apresentar a política nacional de data center e de cabos submarinos à Casa Civil. A expectativa é de que os planos saiam do papel ainda em 2026. Tercius deixou claro que "apenas o Redata não resolve" as demandas do setor de data center. O anseio do MCom é estimular a instalação de infraestruturas pelo território brasileiro, tanto data centers de borda como complexos para hyperscalers. No caso dos cabos submarinos, o secretário afirmou que a política setorial deve ampliar os pontos de ancoragem pela costa brasileira – atualmente, ainda estão bastante concentrados em Fortaleza, Rio de Janeiro, Salvador e litoral de São Paulo. Segundo exemplificou Tercius, a implantação do cabo Malbec em Porto Alegre já atraiu mais de R$ 4 bilhões em investimentos para a região Sul. Desse modo, a ideia é viabilizar pontos de ancoragem para cabos em outras localidades do País, como Belém e Recife. "Já mandamos para a Casa Civil a política pronta. Uma parte pode vir por portaria, outra tem que ser pelo Congresso", disse o secretário. "Com isso, a gente espera atrair para o Brasil mais data centers e fazer um cinturão digital nos próximos quatro anos", pontuou. Inclusão digital e rodovias O secretário ainda afirmou que a Política Nacional de Inclusão Digital (PNID) deve ser lançada em novembro – no mais tardar, no início de dezembro. A pasta ainda avalia se a política será implementada via portaria ou decreto. Em conversa com jornalistas, Tercius adiantou que o plano prevê um voucher para contratação de banda larga fixa ou móvel, de modo a subsidiar parte dos custos com o serviço, e medidas de letramento digital. Já a Política Nacional de Conectividade de Rodovias (PNCR) deve ser publicada ainda este mês, após alinhamento com o Ministério dos Transportes. Cada pasta deve publicar uma portaria, indicou o secretario. "A política vem sendo executada desde o início do ano. O que a gente vai fazer é uma portaria para dar um salto, levando em conta a questão do roaming, que queremos liberar e obrigar. [O ministério dos] Transportes vai pôr isso em concessões para ter cobertura nas rodovias federais", sinalizou.

artigo.texto: Silicon anodes can store around ten times more charge per gram than graphite and can support faster charging, but silicon swells by 300–400% as it charges, which has historically wrecked its cycle life. The silicon anodes now reaching EVs are silicon-graphite (or silicon-carbon) hybrids that deliver around 20% more range than graphite equivalents, with fewer charge cycles and a higher cost. Graphite remains the industry standard, but silicon is now in production cars. Lithium-ion batteries are the cornerstone of EV technology and most consumer electronics, and their basic architecture hasn't changed dramatically for decades. While cathode chemistries have evolved to give batteries different properties, the anode has almost always been graphite – sometimes with a few percent of silicon oxide blended in for a small capacity boost. Graphite became the staple anode material because it is stable and low cost, but there are other anode materials with a much higher specific capacity that could make EV batteries far more energy dense. The problem has been commercialising them. Related:Volkswagen and Gotion plan flexible LFP cell production across EV and energy storage applications Silicon is the best example of an anode material with huge potential that has been difficult to commercialise. It has around ten times the specific capacity of graphite and could enable faster-charging, more energy-dense EV batteries with a much longer driving range. However, silicon undergoes large volumetric expansion during charging that has historically degraded cells very quickly and made them unsuitable for commercial use. That is now changing. We're still not seeing pure silicon anodes in EVs, but hybrid anodes that combine silicon with graphite or other carbon materials have reached the market, and Mercedes-Benz has become the first carmaker to offer a high-silicon anode battery in a production vehicle. Silicon vs graphite anodes at a glance How do silicon and graphite anodes work? The silicon vs graphite anode debate has been running for a long time. The anode is a critical part of any battery: it stores lithium ions while the battery charges and releases them when it discharges, sending electrons through the external circuit that powers the EV. Silicon's theoretical specific capacity is roughly ten times that of graphite, which on paper makes it an ideal EV battery anode material. Depending on the material and form, silicon's theoretical specific capacity sits between 3,400 and 4,200 mAh/g, whereas the top end of battery-grade graphite is 372 mAh/g. In theory, a pure silicon anode could hold up to ten times more charge than a graphite anode of the same weight. That doesn't mean a battery with ten times the energy, though, because the cathode and the rest of the cell stay the same – and today's silicon hybrid anodes sit well below silicon's theoretical limit, somewhere between graphite and pure silicon. Related:Geely, NIO partner for Chinese battery swapping network However, specific capacity doesn't tell the whole story, and there's a reason graphite has been the industry standard since the 1990s. Graphite's inherent safety and stability have been key to its longevity, whereas silicon anodes have suffered from rapid degradation as they expand and contract during cycling. Battery safety is paramount to avoid EV fires. Graphite anodes also form a very stable solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer, while silicon's is less stable – one of the reasons current silicon anodes also contain carbon as a stabilising material. Even so, graphite is nearing its practical capacity ceiling, and as demand for longer-range EVs grows, new chemistries are needed to push further. Enter silicon, which offers higher energy density – translating into longer driving range – and the potential for faster charging. Silicon itself is a relatively cheap and abundant material, and there is already a large global silicon supply chain serving the electronics and solar sectors, even if a dedicated silicon anode supply chain is still small. However, making silicon anodes is currently more complex and expensive than making battery-grade graphite, which benefits from decades of high-volume production that have driven costs down. Silicon is already used safely in many high-power electronics, so the main barrier to battery safety and lifespan is the anode's expansion. Related:UK to invest over US$9 billion into EV batteries, but must make up 55GWh supply gap Energy density: How much better is silicon than graphite? Because silicon's theoretical specific capacity is so much higher (3,400–4,200 mAh/g against graphite's 372 mAh/g), its potential energy density is much higher too. But today's cells use silicon-graphite hybrids rather than pure silicon, so they don't come close to silicon's theoretical limits. Most practical hybrid anodes have a specific capacity of 600–1,500 mAh/g – still well above graphite, but the real-world gains are smaller than the headline figures suggest. At cell level, that currently means around 20% more energy density, with up to 40% expected as the technology matures. The gain comes from making the anode smaller. In a lithium-ion cell, the cathode supplies the lithium, and the anode has to be large enough to store it. Graphite's relatively low capacity means the anode takes up a large share of the cell. Silicon offers about ten times graphite's capacity by weight and roughly three times by volume, so a much thinner anode can store the same amount of lithium – freeing space for more cathode material, and therefore more energy, in the same cell. At the upper end, silicon alloys with lithium so that several lithium ions can be stored per silicon atom. The highest theoretical capacity (4,200 mAh/g) comes from the Li22Si5 phase, but the more practical figure demonstrated in studies (3,579 mAh/g) comes from the Li15Si4 phase. Artificial intelligence runs on electricity, and America’s appetite for it is climbing faster than the grid can comfortably follow. A DOE-backed Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory study released in June projects data centers could consume 9.5 percent to 15 percent of U.S. electricity by 2030, up from roughly 4.5 percent today, E&E News reported. For the Department of Energy, that curve has turned a utility-planning question into a matter of national security and industrial policy. Over the past 15 months, DOE has opened federal land to privately financed AI campuses, pressed grid regulators to speed hookups for power-hungry facilities and enlisted its 17 national laboratories in a push for AI-driven discovery. GovCon leaders who want to understand where DOE’s technology priorities are headed can hear from DOE Chief Information Officer Dawn Zimmer, a Wash100 Award winner, when she delivers a morning keynote at the Potomac Officers Club’s 2026 FedCiv Summit on Oct. 29. Make sure your GovCon company is represented at the event before tickets sell out! How Much Power Do Data Centers Need? The short answer: more than anyone planned for. The Berkeley Lab study found data centers are expected to drive more than 40 percent of U.S. electricity demand growth over the next five years, with efficiency gains in new chips swamped by the sheer volume of new computing. The climb is steep even by recent standards. Data center electricity use rose from 58 terawatt-hours in 2014 to 176 TWh in 2023, when it accounted for about 4.4 percent of national consumption. DOE has framed the gap between supply and demand as a reliability issue. Its July 2025 grid reliability report warned that plant retirements combined with projected load growth could raise the risk of power outages 100-fold by 2030. The report found 104 gigawatts of generation is slated to retire by 2030, to be replaced by 209 GW of new capacity, only 22 GW of which would come from firm baseload sources. How Is DOE Putting Federal Land to Work? DOE’s signature move has been to turn its own acreage into launch pads for privately funded AI campuses that bring their own power. The groundwork came from an executive order signed July 23, 2025, which directs DOE, Interior and the Department of War to authorize data center construction on appropriate federal lands. The next day, DOE selected four sites for AI data center and energy generation projects: Idaho National Laboratory, the Oak Ridge Reservation, the Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant and the Savannah River Site. Energy Secretary Chris Wright cast the effort in historic terms. “By leveraging DOE land assets for the deployment of AI and energy infrastructure, we are taking a bold step to accelerate the next Manhattan Project—ensuring U.S. AI and energy leadership,” Wright said. Two of the four sites now have named partners. Savannah River Site, South Carolina Amentum announced in July that the National Nuclear Security Administration selected it to negotiate a phased lease for a 1 GW AI data center backed by about 2 GW of on-site generation, starting with natural gas and bridging to advanced nuclear. NNSA said pairing the campus with dedicated generation is meant to keep its power costs off existing utility customers, the Aiken Standard reported. Mark Whitney, president of Amentum’s energy and environment business, tied the opportunity to the company’s long history at the site. “For generations, Amentum has helped solve some of the nation’s most complex engineering and nuclear challenges, including at the Savannah River Site,” Whitney said. Paducah, Kentucky On July 29, DOE tapped Brookfield to develop and operate a 1.8 GW AI campus at its Paducah site, with NextEra Energy building up to 2 GW of gas-fired generation and 2.6 GW of battery storage to power it, Reuters reported. The companies peg the privately funded investment at $100 billion, with operations scheduled to begin in 2028 and full development four years later. NextEra said the project fulfills the White House’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, meaning the campus brings and pays for its own power rather than passing energy costs to households. Idaho National Laboratory and Oak Ridge The remaining two sites are still in play. DOE’s Oak Ridge solicitation offers two parcels, one at the East Tennessee Technology Park and one next to Oak Ridge National Laboratory, for long-term leases funded entirely by the selected companies. Under Secretary for Science Darío Gil pitched the opportunity as a chance to build alongside the national labs. “This RFP represents more than a ground lease for AI data center development, it offers U.S. companies a potential chance to anchor their partnership with one of our nation’s greatest assets, our National Labs,” Gil said. Developer selections at Oak Ridge and Idaho National Laboratory rank among the most closely watched federal energy opportunities on the horizon. How Is DOE Speeding Up Grid Connections? Land is only half the equation. A data center can rise in a couple of years, but plugging it into the grid can take far longer, and DOE has leaned on regulators to close that gap. On Oct. 23, 2025, Wright used his Section 403 authority to direct the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to start a rulemaking on connecting large loads such as AI data centers to the transmission system, calling timely grid access for those facilities an urgent issue, according to Gibson Dunn. FERC answered on June 18 with show cause orders directing all six regional grid operators, including PJM, which serves Northern Virginia’s Data Center Alley, to justify or reform their rules for large and co-located loads, according to McGuireWoods. artigo.texto: The world of technology is full of myths and legends. That’s understandable when most of the technology we rely on operates completely behind the scenes. Recently, I’ve been hearing a lot of talk around data centers, and many of the “facts” I’m hearing aren’t quite as true as some people believe. Today, I want to address some of these myths, not to create division or try to win an argument, but instead to inform and clear up some misconceptions that are quite common within the conversation of technology and AI at the moment. Myth #1: Data Centers Use Too Much Water and Take it Away From the Public Water is a huge topic of discussion around data centers at the moment, but very few people actually know how data centers use water for cooling. I can’t speak for all data centers, but I can speak about the two types of Meta data centers that I have visited over the past few months. - A traditional air-cooled compute data center: These facilities use water for only a few months of the year to cool down air as it passes into the building. - An AI-optimized closed-loop liquid cooled data center: These facilities circulate a water and glycol mixture around a closed-loop system, meaning that the cooling loop is sealed, so water isn’t consumed as it circulates, passing the cold liquid over the server hardware until it gets warm, then sending it over to the heat rejection system. The heat rejection system cools the liquid and then sends it back to the servers in a continuous loop. I visited an infra lab to take a deeper look at liquid cooling and saw first-hand how this closed-loop system recirculates water in a sealed loop, using very little on an ongoing basis. So where does the water come from? The two sites I visited pulled from different places — one off the municipal system, one from a permitted on-site well. In both cases the withdrawal is permitted, metered, and counted in the local water plan, not carved out of it. The well case was the one that surprised me: the aquifer being tapped wasn’t suitable for drinking water in the first place. And in genuinely water-stressed regions, the closed-loop design I described above is the default, precisely because it barely consumes any water. As mentioned, I can’t speak for all data center operators, but these two efficient cooling methods and the associated water usage mean that many of Meta’s data center facilities use less water annually than an average US golf course will in the same amount of time. Myth #2: More Data Centers Mean Higher Energy Bills for Consumers It’s no secret that data centers do use a lot of energy, but the assumption that data center energy use automatically means higher energy bills is not true. Meta pays the full cost of their energy bills, just like any household would. But they go a step further by also directly paying for new and upgraded infrastructure needed to supply that additional energy to the data center. The important distinction here is that Meta doesn’t simply connect a huge data center to the grid and leave the local community to deal with the consequences. They work with the utility providers years before facilities come online to plan for demand, design new infrastructure, get it installed, and make sure it is able to meet their requirements before a facility goes online. In Louisiana, for example, Meta’s agreement with Entergy is structured so the data center pays for the new generation and transmission it requires, with protections written in so existing customers aren’t left holding the cost. Myth #3: Data Centers Don’t Create Jobs The important thing to remember here is that data centers don’t build themselves, and they definitely don’t run themselves. There are two stages in a data center’s lifecycle that create many jobs for local communities. Construction During construction, thousands of skilled trades are employed to help build the facility on site, with many thousands of jobs being supported through the purchasing of equipment through different suppliers during the construction process. These are also multi-year construction projects and often are extended when facilities are expanded or retrofitted. Operation As I mentioned earlier, data centers do not run themselves. They still need highly skilled engineers, technicians, IT professionals, security personnel, and more to keep the facilities maintained and operating smoothly. In many of the communities where Meta operates data centers, they are among the biggest local employers. Earlier this year, Meta also launched America’s Workforce Academy, a free program designed to train people for careers in the skilled trades with a guaranteed job at a Meta-partner site upon completion.

artigo.texto: Nigeria will not allow carbon markets that lack integrity or amount to greenwashing, the National Council on Climate Change (NCCC) has warned. The director-general of the NCCC, Omotenioye Majekodunmi, yesterday at the European Union Climate Dialogue programme organised by the NCCC in partnership with the EU Global Gateway and funded by the European Union. Majekodunmi, represented by the NCCC director of Energy, Transportation and Infrastructure, Michael Ivenso, said the country was determined to ensure that carbon projects delivered measurable environmental and economic benefits. He said global carbon markets offered a major opportunity to mobilise private capital for climate action, but warned that the market would collapse without credible systems for verifying carbon credits. “Global carbon markets present one of the most promising avenues to mobilise this private capital. “However, as I have repeatedly stated, carbon markets are only as strong as the integrity of the underlying credits. “A carbon market without rigour is merely an exercise in greenwashing—a scenario that Nigeria will not accommodate,” he said. Majekodunmi said Nigeria’s carbon projects must deliver “real, additional, and permanent mitigation outcomes” while benefiting communities, protecting ecosystems and ensuring fair returns for investors and project developers. She said climate finance was critical to powering clean energy transitions, restoring degraded lands, modernising agriculture, improving waste management and expanding access to clean technologies across the country. The NCCC boss said the operationalisation of Measurement, Reporting and Verification systems was central to building confidence in Nigeria’s emerging carbon market. “Frameworks on paper do not trade carbon—transparent and verifiable data does. This brings us to the core theme of today’s roundtable: Operationalising Measurement, Reporting, and Verification,” he said. “MRV is the backbone of market credibility.” He explained that without credible MRV systems, buyers could not determine whether carbon reductions were genuine, regulators could not properly track emissions, and communities could not ensure fair benefit-sharing. Majekodunmi disclosed that the government was operationalising a unified national carbon registry to prevent double-counting and ensure the integrity of carbon credits generated in Nigeria. “Every carbon credit generated, issued, transferred, or retired in Nigeria will carry a digital footprint to prevent double-counting and guarantee baseline integrity,” he said. He added that Nigeria was moving towards digital MRV using remote sensing, Internet of Things sensors, geospatial data and distributed ledger technologies to reduce verification costs and improve accuracy. The NCCC identified three immediate regulatory priorities, including finalising carbon market regulations, publishing sector-specific MRV guidelines and establishing local capacity-building hubs for Nigerian auditors and technical experts. Also speaking, the Director-General of the European Commission’s CLIMA Task Force on International Carbon Pricing and Markets, Jop Watering, said the European Union was prepared to deepen its engagement with Nigeria on high-integrity carbon markets. Watering said the EU had 20 years of experience with domestic carbon pricing and was now opening its climate strategy to high-quality international carbon credits. He warned that carbon markets would not succeed if issues surrounding integrity, transparency and accountability were not properly addressed. “If you don’t get the integrity right, the market will just not take off. It will just not be there,” he said. Watering said international carbon-crediting mechanisms had so far failed to fully realise their potential because of accounting loopholes and weak checks and balances. He said the EU wanted stringent methodologies, transparent registries, fair transactions and equitable benefit-sharing to underpin the international carbon market. The Head of Section, Green and Digital Economy, EU Delegation to Nigeria and ECOWAS, Ms Yolanda Josaid, credible systems were necessary to ensure transparency, accountability and environmental integrity. She said Nigeria’s National Carbon Market Framework, adopted last year, provided the foundation for domestic and international carbon trading under the Climate Change Act and Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The official said a credible carbon market could align Nigeria’s climate targets with development priorities, attract investment and support the country’s transition to a low-carbon economy. The Director of Forestry at the Federal Ministry of Environment, Halima Bawa Buhari, said Nigeria’s forests remained central to the country’s climate response. She said forests served as carbon sinks, temperature buffers and sources of livelihoods for millions of Nigerians, particularly rural and forest-dependent communities. Buhari warned that carbon market development must support forest conservation rather than create incentives for further exploitation. She called for stronger forest inventories, remote sensing, satellite monitoring and the use of appropriate artificial intelligence technologies to improve carbon measurement. “Forestry, I’d like to remind us all that the forest sector is central to Nigeria’s climate response because forests are both carbon sinks, temperature buffers, reducing natural disaster risk, livelihoods, humans’ primary food source, and famine, among several others,” she said. She also called for stronger coordination among institutions responsible for collecting, managing, validating and reporting forest carbon data. Meanwhile, the UK PACT Officer and Programme Manager at the British Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, Folakemi Aletan, said carbon markets could mobilise investment and strengthen Nigeria’s sustainable development. artigo.texto: Europe’s soil carbon market has reached a new milestone. The European Soil Revitalization Programme, covering farms in France and Belgium, has issued the first carbon credits worldwide under the Gold Standard Soil Organic Carbon (SOC) Framework Methodology. South Pole, agricultural technology company Gaïago, and Gold Standard announced the first issuance on October 6, 2026. The initial issuance covers 6,000 verified hectares. The wider program includes 727 farms and could expand to more than 39,282 hectares. At full enrollment, the project is forecast to remove 264,174 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent (tCO₂e) during its first crediting period. The milestone comes as Europe builds a stronger policy framework for soil health and carbon farming. The European Commission says 60% to 70% of EU soils are unhealthy, while new EU rules are creating a formal system for certifying carbon farming activities. That could create a growing role for high-quality soil carbon projects in Europe’s climate market. A First for Gold Standard Soil Credits The European Soil Revitalization Programme is the first project worldwide to issue credits under Gold Standard’s Soil Organic Carbon Framework Methodology. Gold Standard launched the framework to measure changes in soil carbon and greenhouse gas emissions when farmers adopt improved agricultural practices. The framework can cover both emissions reductions and carbon sequestration in soils. It also allows different approaches to measure soil carbon, including direct field measurements, scientific models, and approved default factors. Sarah Leugers, Chief Growth Officer at Gold Standard, said: “As the first project worldwide to issue credits under our Soil Organic Carbon Framework Methodology, the European Soil Revitalization Programme shows how rigorous standards can unlock vital finance for sustainable land management. We congratulate Gaïago and South Pole on this important milestone.” For the French and Belgian project, the specific activity module covers biostimulants for soil revitalization. The project combines this approach with other regenerative farming practices, including reduced or zero tillage and year-round cover crops. The program began in 2022 and has a planned 20-year operational horizon. South Pole has worked with Gaïago since launch as the carbon asset development partner. They help develop the project and complete the certification and verification process. The project uses the UN Food and Agriculture Organization’s GSOC monitoring, reporting, and verification protocol (MRV). It also aligns with the FAO’s RECSOIL initiative. 6,000 Hectares Mark the First Step The first issuance is based on the program’s initial 6,000 verified hectares. The full program is much larger. - Across its 727 participating farms, the project could eventually cover more than 39,282 hectares and remove an estimated 264,174 tCO₂e during its first crediting period. That works out to roughly 2.5 tCO₂e per hectare per year based on the project’s full enrollment forecast. The first group of participating farms has already produced measurable results. The project developers’ latest calculations from August 2026 show that the first cohort removed about 3.1 tCO₂e per hectare each year over the last three years. The developers have not publicly disclosed the exact number of carbon credits contained in the inaugural issuance in the announcement. That distinction matters. The 6,000-hectare figure is the verified area covered by the first issuance, not a statement that 6,000 credits were issued. As more farms join the program, the project could become a meaningful source of European soil-based carbon removals. Why Soil Carbon Matters to European Farmers The project arrives against a major soil-health problem. The European Commission says 60% to 70% of EU soils are in an unhealthy state. Soil degradation costs the EU more than €50 billion each year, according to the Commission. Loss of soil organic carbon is one of the main forms of degradation. Healthy soil does more than store carbon. It helps retain water, supports crops, protects biodiversity and improves the resilience of farmland. That gives soil carbon projects a different value proposition from credits focused only on carbon removal. Regenerative practices can potentially improve farm conditions while also creating carbon market revenue. For farmers, however, changing agricultural practices can involve upfront costs and uncertainty around yields. Carbon finance can help offset some of those costs by creating another source of income. That is a key part of the European Soil Revitalization Programme. The project aims to enhance soil structure, fertility, and water retention. It also boosts farm resilience and increases soil carbon stocks. Gold Standard Tightens the Rules for Soil Carbon Measuring soil carbon is not as simple as measuring emissions from a factory. Carbon levels can vary across fields and change with weather, farming practices and soil conditions. Carbon stored in soil can also be released later if management practices change. - Gold Standard has therefore placed strong requirements around additionality, permanence, uncertainty and measurement. Its SOC framework lets projects use various measurement and modeling methods. However, it requires that uncertainty be addressed in the calculations. In September 2025, Gold Standard also released specific guidelines for using soil organic carbon models. The guidelines set out a seven-step process covering model selection, data collection, calibration, validation, prediction, and verification. The goal is to make soil carbon estimates more consistent while still allowing models to reflect local soil and climate conditions. That could become increasingly important as more agricultural projects seek carbon market certification.
