artigo.texto: Panelists debated issues surrounding data centers at a panel sponsored by the O’Neill School of Public and Environmental Affairs on Tuesday. It was moderated by Ken Richards, an O’Neill professor of economics and sustainability. Nationally, just one in nine Americans support the construction of data centers in their communities. Opponents of data centers, which includes all four of the panelists, argue that downsides like noise and air pollution, strained infrastructure and higher utility bills outweigh the potential benefits, which the panelists described as unclear, for local communities. Panelist Justin Ross, a public finance, economics and policy analysis professor, noted the positive economic impacts of data centers. “If you take a look at, like, roads, they don’t directly employ anyone,” Ross said. “It is still crazy to think about their contribution to the economy.” Ross drew parallels between roads and data centers, which often employ few workers, but he argues they could still contribute to the local and national economy. Studies have found employment, wages and income all increase after the construction of a data center in a community. However, panelist Bryce Gustafson, an organizer for the Citizens Action Coalition, Indiana’s largest and oldest consumer and environmental advocacy organization, feels this is an oversimplification of the truth. “Not a lot of local jobs,” he said. “They are specialized jobs.” Gustafson explained that data center employees, who he said are often not local to the area, and the companies who own the centers benefit most from their construction. Gustafson also pointed to the 50-year tax breaks Indiana offers some data centers, which benefit the data center companies and deprive the local community of tax money. Panelist Saul Levin with the Global Center for Climate Justice criticized a frequent Meta talking point, which the company has often raised on what he described as a “press offensive around the country.” “Meta has been advertising all over the country that the Rayville, Louisiana, data centers are responsible for local teachers being granted $50,000 bonuses,” Levin said. “None of the marketing documents mentioned that this was already in local statute.” According to the New York Times, a local ordinance in Rayville mandates that 1% of local sales tax revenue goes to teachers; the huge bonuses for teachers in the town this year are partly due to sales taxes paid by construction workers working on the data center, who will leave after it is built. The panelists also discussed the power dynamics between local communities and data center companies. Levin explained this dynamic by asking guests a simple question. “Raise your hand if you’d be comfortable negotiating against a lawyer who makes $500,000 a year,” he said. No one raised a hand. Wu agreed, asking “(If this is a win-win,) how much win do they get and how much does the community?” The panel also discussed artificial Intelligence bubbles, which is the concern that more money is being poured into AI than the amount of revenue generated. Attendee Wade Catt raised concerns of noise pollution from data centers. He said the noise from data centers poses risks of cardiovascular disease and other negative health impacts. He pointed to Monrovia, a town in southwest Indiana where a data center was recently built. Catt said he knows people living by data centers in Monrovia and elsewhere who have struggled with noise pollution and said their homes have lost equity as a result. Catt also expressed his frustration with a lack of transparency in data center construction, noting that communities often aren’t adequately consulted before construction. “We don’t have the power to resist this,” Catt said to nods of agreement. “It is something that is happening to us.”

artigo.texto: U.S. District Court Judge Eli Richardson on Tuesday handed a significant win to Metro in the lawsuit filed by data center developer DC Blox in August. Richardson dismissed DC Blox’s claims. The company, which is seeking to build a data center at a site adjacent to the Nashville Zoo, had alleged that Metro’s “relentless efforts” to block the development illegally singled out the company. The lawsuit is focused on Metro’s implementation of new zoning regulations and a moratorium on new approvals of such projects, not on the city’s pending effort to seize the property using the condemnation process. “Plaintiff may believe, and is entitled to believe and contend, that it received a raw deal from (or was sandbagged by) the imposition of the Moratorium after it purchased the Property,” Richardson wrote in his opinion. “However, a raw deal or sandbagging — real or imagined, without more — does not a federal lawsuit make.” The legal battle is far from over, as Richardson gave DC Blox 21 days to amend some of the dismissed claims, and other avenues of relief remain outstanding. “I have said from the beginning that Metro has both the right and the responsibility to determine appropriate land uses through its legislative and zoning processes,” Metro Councilmember Courtney Johnston, who represents the zoo area, wrote on social media. “DC BLOX had every right to challenge those decisions in court. They did. This was the result.” A request for comment from the DC Blox legal team remains outstanding. “I am pleased with the ruling and remain confident that Metro has acted lawfully in its dealings with DC Blox and in the enactment of the moratorium on data center permitting,” Metro Legal Director Tyler Yarbro said.

artigo.texto: As the world's biggest technology companies race to build data centers across the country to power an AI boom, a yearlong Senate investigation argues that some firms are misleading the public about the true costs and benefits around those projects. The findings, first shared with TIME, are expected to be part of a broader effort in the coming year by members of Congress hoping to put more guardrails around the massive, power-intensive projects. “Congress must hold Big Tech accountable so these companies pay their fair share,” says Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat who has called for a national moratorium on new AI data centers until developers agree to cover the full costs. Warren's office led the investigation with fellow Democratic Senators Chris Van Hollen of Maryland and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, which focused on seven major data center developers—Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, CoreWeave, Digital Realty, and Equinix. The senators’ staff requested information from each company and interviewed employees. The findings, which largely match reporting from various news outlets over the past year, offer a detailed look at the increasingly contentious economics of the AI buildout. Data center companies routinely point to construction employment when making the case for incentives. But when the senators’ staff asked for comprehensive information about permanent employment, several of the companies refused to provide it, according to the report. Some companies told investigators that permanent staffing was roughly one worker for every megawatt of power demand. A 100-megawatt data center, by that measure, could consume roughly as much electricity as 100,000 homes while employing about 100 permanent workers after construction. “This report lays bare what we have long known: working Americans and local communities are footing the bill for Big Tech’s massive expansion of data centers, while these companies continue to operate without transparency,” Van Hollen says. Notably, the Senate investigators found that the most lucrative incentives for data center developers are not necessarily the attention-grabbing property-tax breaks, but sales-tax exemptions on computer equipment. AI facilities require vast quantities of specialized hardware, and GPUs account for an estimated 39% of the spending at an average 1-gigawatt AI data center, according to the report. All four of the major technology companies in the investigation—Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft—have routinely sought nondisclosure agreements during data center development, according to the report. Some acknowledged requesting them from government officials. While data center negotiations often deal with commercially sensitive information, the Senate report argues that NDAs have also restricted public scrutiny of deals involving tax dollars, utility rates, and public infrastructure. Microsoft told the investigators it would stop seeking NDAs with local governments, although it would continue using them with state agencies, public utility commissions and utilities. Amazon has announced a similar policy. Google and Meta declined to commit to ending the practice with local governments, according to the report. The report comes as data centers have become a hot-button issue on the campaign trail. About half of Americans say that data center construction is bad for the country, according to a recent Economist/YouGov poll. Both parties have been harnessing the issue, even as President Trump warns that opposition to data centers could push the AI buildout overseas. Who Pays for the AI Power Boom? A significant portion of the report explores whether tech companies are paying their fair share for data centers that are driving up the costs for nearby homeowners and businesses. State regulators and lawmakers are increasingly being asked to decide how much of that expansion should be paid for by the companies driving the demand, and how much should be borne by other customers and taxpayers. The Senate investigators found none of the seven companies would agree to a standard that would require them to pay for the building of new power infrastructure that would not have been needed if not for their data centers. The companies generally said they would pay the direct costs of serving their data centers, but argued that larger investments in the electric grid—like new power plants and transmission lines—can benefit other customers and should not automatically be assigned to the company that helped drive the need for them. The report points to a power plant in Richland Parish, Louisiana, that the local utility provider, Entergy, has sought to buy. Analysts argue the purchase was driven primarily by Meta’s planned $50 billion data center, which is expected to draw 4,500 megawatts of electricity—about four times the peak electricity demand of the entire city of New Orleans. Estimates indicate that the purchase could drive up electric bills for the average Entergy customer by $8-13 per month. Meta has disputed that its project is responsible for the costs. Congress Debates New Data Center Laws When Congress reconvenes after the midterm elections, data centers will be among the issues waiting for them. In September, the House overwhelmingly passed the bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act, 417-3, which would direct states to consider standards requiring large-load customers such as data centers to cover the incremental costs of the generation, transmission, and distribution infrastructure needed to serve them. But the measure stalled in the Senate, as Democrats argued it was toothless because it didn’t require states to push any costs to the companies. The Senate ultimately voted 57-43 against advancing the bill. Much of the authority over electricity rates remains with state regulators, which means the biggest fights will continue to play out in statehouses and public utility commissions. artigo.texto: Atmos Renewables, an Australian renewable energy company backed by Igneo Infrastructure Partners, has reached the Financial closing of the Teebar BESS project, of 400 MW and 1,600 MWh this development will take place in Queensland, Australia. This progress is part of a larger operation that also includes the 470 MW Parron Maam Marang wind farm, located in Western Australia. Both facilities are backed by Capacity Investment Scheme (CIS), an Australian Government program that seeks to facilitate investments in renewable generation and electricity storage, contributing to strengthening the capacity of the country’s energy system. Teebar BESS will store energy for four hours The Teebar BESS project will be located next to the Teebar Creek substation, operated by Powerlink, in the Fraser Coast region of Queensland. Its development will add new storage capacity to an area connected to the existing electricity transmission infrastructure. The facility will have a power output of 400 MW and an energy capacity of 1,600 MWh, which means it will be able to supply electricity for four consecutive hours when operating at its nominal power. This capacity will allow electricity to be stored during periods of high availability and returned to the grid when consumption increases or renewable generation decreases. In this way, Teebar BESS will help manage variations between supply and demand, providing greater flexibility to the operation of Australian electrical system it will also facilitate the use of energy from renewable sources, whose production depends on weather conditions. The financial close includes a 470 MW wind farm Together with Teebar BESS, Atmos Renewables confirmed the financial closing of Parron Maam Marang wind farm, which will have an installed capacity of 470 MW and will be located in the Wheatbelt region of Western Australia. The energy generated by this park will be sold through a long-term electricity purchase agreement (PPA) with Synergy, one of the leading electricity trading companies in the state. This agreement will allow the establishment of a commercial relationship for the sale of the planned electricity production, a relevant aspect to support the financial viability of renewable generation projects. Although both facilities will be developed in different regions of Australia, they are part of Atmos strategy to expand its participation in the energy market through generation assets and storage. The company will retain ownership of both projects during their construction and will be responsible for operating them once they begin providing service. Atmos Renewables reaches 970 MW of projects backed by the CIS With the financial closing of Teebar BESS and Parron Maam Marang, Atmos Renewables now has 970 MW of projects backed by the Capacity Investment Scheme that have completed this financial stage in the last 16 months. The total also includes Merredin BESS, a 100 MW and 400 MWh storage facility whose financial closure was finalized in June 2025. The three developments reflect the progress of the company’s portfolio, which combines different technologies to meet the needs of the Australian electricity system. Nigel Baker, CEO of Atmos Renewables, emphasized the importance of overcoming the necessary processes to transform these initiatives into viable projects. Among the key aspects he mentioned were access to financing, formalizing commercial agreements, and obtaining grid connections. These steps are especially relevant at a time when Australia needs to incorporate new energy infrastructure to meet the growth of the electricity demand and progressively compensate for the retirement of conventional power plants. Energy storage is gaining prominence in Australia Atmos Renewables currently has a national portfolio that exceeds 1.5 GW of wind, solar and energy storage projects, including facilities that are already operational and others that are under construction. The company is backed by Igneo Infrastructure Partners, an investment manager specializing in infrastructure whose investors include entities such as MLC and CBUS. Within this portfolio, Teebar BESS stands out for its ability to supply energy for four hours, a feature that will allow stored electricity to be moved from periods of lower demand to times when the system needs a greater supply. The development of these types of facilities is becoming increasingly important as the share of renewable energy in Australia’s electricity mix grows. Batteries allow for better use of available generation capacity and offer a more flexible response to fluctuations in consumption. With financing secured, Teebar BESS and Parron Maam Marang have passed a crucial milestone in their progress toward construction and future operation. Both projects are part of Atmos Renewables’ expansion and Australia’s efforts to add new clean energy generation and storage capacity to its electricity infrastructure. artigo.texto: Executivos da indústria de telecomunicações apontaram que o 5G RedCap, tecnologia que usa uma capacidade reduzida da quinta geração móvel para conectar dispositivos, ainda deve ser explorado no Brasil, especialmente em redes privativas e edge data centers. Em painel no Futurecom 2026, nesta quarta-feira, 7, em São Paulo, o diretor de Novos Negócios e B2B da TIM, Alexandre Dal Forno, afirmou que a operadora já tem condições de utilizar o RedCap em redes privativas, com base na tecnologia 5G standalone (SA). Contudo, disse que ainda não houve demanda e o custo dos dispositivos compatíveis ainda tem sido um impeditivo. "A grande dificuldade do RedCap é o custo dos dispositivos versus o 5G full", afirmou. "A tecnologia é bastante recente. Gosto de compará-la ao NB-IoT em 2017, quando ainda estava começando. Todo mundo ia para o 4G full", completou, em conversa com jornalistas. De todo modo, Dal Forno reforçou que vê espaço para adoção da tecnologia em redes privativas. Inclusive, apontou que, quando os módulos de RedCap forem incorporados a dispositivos, o custo da tecnologia deve cair. O executivo da TIM também indicou que a vertical deve ganhar tração com o desenvolvimento do parque de edge data centers pelo País. "O próximo passo da infraestrutura digital vai ser um aumento na quantidade de data centers distribuídos. Vejo o IoT e o RedCap ganhando uma oportunidade de fazer o upload para processamento no edge data center. Isso pode ser um motivo para investir na tecnologia", destacou. Massificação de dispositivos conectados Na avalição da Aisla Ezequiel, head de vendas da NLT Telecom, especializada em IoT e M2M, o RedCap vai encontrar mercado em operações com equipamentos que não precisam da velocidade oferecida pela rede 5G. Ela projeta que a tecnologia terá um custo menor e será menos complexa para operar. Já Sandro Tamman, diretor da Unidade de Negócios de IoT e Network Solutions da Allcom Telecom, vê o 5G RedCap avançando para conexão de dispositivos de gás, água, energia, iluminação pública e automóveis. No mesmo painel, Wilson Cardoso, assessor de Tecnologia do Senai-SP, indicou que o RedCap pode se tornar uma solução de redundância de conectividade. Como exemplo, ele citou maquininhas de cartão. Em determinados estabelecimentos, utilizam o Wi-Fi disponível no ambiente. No entanto, em caso de problema com a rede de fibra, os dispositivos poderiam continuar conectadas por meio da tecnologia baseada 5G de capacidade reduzida.

artigo.texto: Oakland has joined several other Bay Area cities in hitting pause on data centers. The City Council on Tuesday unanimously approved a 45-day moratorium on approvals for new data centers. The moratorium can be extended by the council. Councilmember Carroll Fife, who authored the moratorium, has said the goal is to give Oakland time to study the impacts of data centers and make any needed changes to the city’s planning and building codes to protect residents’ health, safety and welfare. People across the country have become skeptical of data centers as tech companies, especially those developing artificial intelligence, have moved fast in recent years to build massive computing warehouses in cities and rural areas. Because data centers consume large amounts of water and electricity, generate noise and take up huge swaths of land, many communities have opposed their construction. Oakland hasn’t seen a boom in data center construction, likely because land and electricity prices are high here. However, a developer has proposed building a data center in a downtown building that used to house a supercomputer. Many of the people who showed up to Tuesday’s council meeting said they’re not just worried about the potential effects on their utility bills or the neighborhood’s quality of life, but they have broader concerns about the AI industry’s vision for the future. “The luddites were onto something,” a District 2 resident named Charlotte told the council. “They understood that what matters about a technology is not just what it does but who controls it and what kind of power it has to concentrate power. We do not control this technology. I think it is a big mistake for us to gamble with the future of our city and trust that the oligarchs have a place for us in their vision at all.” Dohee Kim, an organizer with the Local Clean Energy Alliance, said Oakland’s moratorium is part of a nationwide pushback. “Moratoriums are temporary solutions, but our communities deserve the right tools and the proper avenues to determine meaningful accountability and oversight when AI Data Centers directly impact our energy, water and land usage during a worsening climate crisis,” Kim said in a statement released after the council meeting. According to the Stop AI Data Centers in Alameda County coalition, at least 26 cities in California are considering or have passed similar moratoriums. San Francisco also approved a 45-day moratorium on data center approvals at the Board of Supervisors’ meeting yesterday. Richmond approved a moratorium in September. Some Oakland residents are opposed to the moratorium. Mindy Pechenuk, who is running for mayor, showed up to Tuesday’s council meeting to urge city leaders to reject any pause on data center development. Pechenuk, who uses AI to generate campaign ads, likened the AI boom to the American space program of the early 1960s, which she said united the nation and led to significant scientific advances. “I oppose wasting taxpayers’ money on a moratorium,” Pechenuk said. Sharon Taylor, who described herself as a lifelong Oakland resident, said her family was able to flourish in the city decades ago because there was ready work. “Data centers will bring jobs, they will not take jobs away,” she told the council. Andrea Ingram said Oakland needs tech industry investment. “Oakland is good at driving those things out of the city, and then we turn around and say, ‘Why don’t we have enough money to give city workers?’” Moratorium supporters see the economic implications of the AI boom very differently. Arbaz, a District 2 resident who spoke at the council meeting, said many Oaklanders are worried about rising rents, food prices and utility bills. “We shouldn’t be siphoning off our resources and mortgaging our people’s future on an AI bubble that will likely be leaving us holding the bag at the end.” Fears that the hundreds of billions of dollars major corporations have poured into AI might lead to an economic crash are shared by some high-profile investors and top economists. Rene Coe, another moratorium supporter, said Oaklanders should be wary of the promises of the AI industry and data center developers. “The best-case scenario: AI will replace people,” Coe said. “If it doesn’t, the bubble will burst and cause a recession worse than 2008. Oaklanders know what happens when billionaires make bets on our homes and jobs.”

artigo.texto: Após dobrar a área de manufatura em fevereiro, a Adata prepara nova operação industrial em Manaus para montar e testar servidores de alta potência, enquanto avalia projetos para automação e setor automotivo em 2027 também A fábrica da Adata em Manaus vai ganhar uma nova frente industrial em dezembro de 2026, quando a companhia pretende iniciar a montagem e os testes de servidores, incluindo equipamentos de alta potência destinados a data centers. Fábrica da Adata em Manaus dobrou área de produção em 2026 A expansão faz parte de uma estratégia que vem sendo colocada em prática desde 2021, quando a Adata iniciou sua operação industrial na capital amazonense. Desde então, a unidade recebeu investimentos para ampliar capacidade, automatizar processos e aumentar o portfólio produzido localmente. Um dos movimentos mais recentes ocorreu em fevereiro de 2026. A empresa dobrou sua área de manufatura ao incorporar um segundo galpão industrial à planta de Manaus. - Gigante americana Sukup coloca Mato Grosso no radar e avalia instalar fábrica em Lucas do Rio Verde para produzir sistemas de armazenagem de grãos em um dos maiores polos do agronegócio brasileiro - Duas gigantes chinesas negociam novas fábricas de geladeiras e lavadoras no Brasil enquanto setor supera R$ 7 bilhões em investimentos e amplia corrida pela produção local de eletrodomésticos - Grupo Michelin amplia presença industrial no Brasil com nova fábrica da Fenner em Guarulhos e projeto prevê aumento de 40% na capacidade para atender mineração, cimento, siderurgia e outros setores pesados - Indústria da soja acelera no Brasil, capacidade cresce 13% em um ano e setor prepara R$ 7,65 bilhões em novas fábricas e expansões para adicionar 7,4 milhões de toneladas ao processamento nacional Segundo Nivaldo Gagliardo, vice-presidente de Operações da Adata Technology Brasil, essa nova estrutura começará a contribuir com o crescimento das operações locais ainda no último trimestre de 2026. A companhia não informou, na entrevista, o valor aplicado na ampliação nem divulgou a capacidade de produção que será acrescentada pelo segundo galpão. Unidade já monta módulos DRAM e SSDs Hoje, a operação de Manaus realiza a montagem eletrônica completa de módulos de memória DRAM e SSDs utilizando tecnologia SMT, além dos testes desses produtos. Os principais componentes utilizados, como circuitos integrados de memória DRAM e Flash destinados aos SSDs, são fornecidos pela fábrica da própria Adata localizada em Santo Antônio de Posse, no interior de São Paulo. A produção ocorre em ambiente com controle de temperatura e umidade. A planta também utiliza equipamentos automatizados para manipulação e inspeção de produtos e ferramentais. Parte dessas soluções emprega inteligência artificial e foi desenvolvida no Brasil em parceria com institutos de Manaus, dentro de projetos de pesquisa e desenvolvimento. Servidores para data centers entram na linha em dezembro O próximo salto será a entrada no mercado de servidores. A partir de dezembro de 2026, a Adata pretende começar, em Manaus, uma operação destinada à montagem e aos testes desses equipamentos. A fabricação será realizada em regime de manufatura sob contrato. Entre os produtos previstos estão servidores de alta potência voltados à utilização em data centers. Com isso, a planta amplia suas competências para além de memórias e unidades de armazenamento, entrando em uma área ligada diretamente à infraestrutura de processamento de dados. A expansão ocorre após a empresa ter um projeto de diversificação aprovado pelo Conselho de Desenvolvimento do Estado do Amazonas, o Codam. Automação e setor automotivo estão no radar para 2027 A Adata também avalia novos caminhos para sua estrutura industrial em Manaus. As equipes de engenharia da companhia estudam, junto às engenharias de clientes, oportunidades para produzir outros equipamentos eletrônicos. Entre os segmentos citados estão automação e indústria automotiva. Segundo a empresa, essas possibilidades estão sendo analisadas para produção a partir de 2027. Na avaliação da companhia, a Zona Franca de Manaus oferece previsibilidade para investimentos industriais devido à manutenção constitucional dos incentivos, além de contar com cadeia eletrônica consolidada e mão de obra especializada. A empresa afirma ainda que recebe apoio da Suframa, da Secretaria de Desenvolvimento Econômico, Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação do Amazonas e de institutos locais desde 2021. Para a Adata, a continuidade dessas políticas e a redução de gargalos operacionais são pontos considerados importantes para acelerar novos projetos e aumentar a eficiência das empresas instaladas no Polo Industrial de Manaus.

artigo.texto: San Francisco’s Board of Supervisors today passed a temporary, 45-day moratorium on data centers citywide, halting the construction of new centers including one proposed in Dogpatch. The move follows increased fears surrounding the potential environmental impacts of data centers, many of which are planned or already exist in District 10, the city’s industrial southeast. The measure, first proposed by District 10 supervisor Shamann Walton and co-sponsored by supervisors Connie Chan, Jackie Fielder and Cheyenne Chen, will take effect immediately. Sources close to Walton’s office say the supervisor hopes the moratorium will result in a permanent ban. The San Francisco Planning Commission will assess during the ensuing 45 days whether the several data centers throughout San Francisco, including larger facilities in District 10 and smaller, regional ones downtown, pose an environmental threat to nearby residents. During the moratorium, the planning department will study the data centers’ impact on water, energy, air quality, land use, and the surrounding community. In the legislation, data centers are broadly defined as any “facility, or part of a facility, that houses computing infrastructure, including graphics and central processing units, servers, storage devices, networking equipment, and associated power and cooling systems, for the primary purpose of processing, storing, or distributing electronic data.” If the data centers are found to have a significant environmental impact, the moratorium could be extended up to 22 months — or alternatively, result in permanent controls or restrictions. At the conclusion of the 45-day period, the planning department will hold a hearing to present its findings. The moratorium will pause the expansion of NOVVA, a 7.6-acre data center at 400 Paul Ave. in Bayview, which was slated to increase output from nine to 36 megawatts by 2028. Though permits have been filed for an additional, 160,000 square foot datacenter in the Dogpatch at 1215 Michigan St., no construction has yet taken place — though an extended moratorium could put plans to expand data centers in San Francisco on hold for an undetermined period. Walton’s term will end in January 2027, potentially before the end of a moratorium if it is extended beyond four months. But strong regulations on data centers — and potentially an all-out ban — has gained increasing support among the candidates racing to replace Walton. Each of the front-running candidates, Theo Ellington, J.R. Eppler, and Dion-Jay Brookter, have expressed support for a moratorium. Brookter was, at first, the only candidate to propose a permanent ban, but during a recent candidate forum, all the others said they would support one, too. District 10’s Bayview-Hunters Point, which has two of the city’s largest data centers, has experienced a disproportionate level of air pollution for decades, including from increased truck traffic and a since-shuttered PG&E power plant. “We need to know what these impacts are,” said Walton, at the time he announced his plans to introduce the moratorium. “Until we know what that is, it needs to stop.”

artigo.texto: Maryland nets 440 MW/1,760 MWh in first bulk energy storage procurement This story was originally published on Utility Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily Utility Dive newsletter. Dive Brief: - Two transmission-connected energy storage projects are slated to receive awards in the first round of the Maryland Next Generation Energy Act energy storage procurement, the state public service commission said on Thursday. - The finalists are Flatiron Energy's 400 MW/1,600 MWh Chalk Point Storage Project in south-central Maryland and REV Renewables's 40 MW/160 MWh Jade Meadow III Battery Storage Project in the far western part of the state. Both will receive flat pricing for 15-year terms at a combined cost of 6.98 cents/month for the average Maryland residential customer, the public service commission said. - The award will help address the PJM Interconnection's capacity woes, which Federal Energy Regulatory Commission chair Laura Swett last week called a "mess." The grid operator faces a capacity shortfall of 6.8 GW for the 2028-2029 delivery year, up 300 MW from the previous period, as capacity prices remain at the $325/MW-day cap. Dive Insight: Passed in 2025, the Next Generation Energy Act requires Maryland to conduct at least two solicitations for a combined 1.6 GW of energy storage capacity. Eligible projects must be designed to discharge at full power for at least four hours. The Maryland Public Service Commission announced the awards for the first solicitation round on Thursday, the statutory deadline. By law, it must open bidding for the second round by Jan. 1, 2027, and announce project awards by Oct. 1, 2027. Evan Vaughan, executive director of the regional clean energy group MAREC Action, said Thursday's selections will help mitigate the effects of PJM's high capacity prices. "These projects can help meet growing electricity demand while reducing exposure to volatile capacity prices that ultimately affect customers' bills," Vaughan said in a statement. Also known as the Mid-Atlantic Renewable Energy Coalition, MAREC Action consists of more than 50 developers and manufacturers serving the region's utility-scale solar, wind and battery storage industry. Flatiron Energy and REV Renewables are both members. Flatiron's project will be located at NRG's oil- and gas-fired Chalk Point power plant in the southeastern corner of Prince George's County, according to the Maryland Public Service Commission. REV will site its project on a portion of a reclaimed coal mine in mountainous Garrett County, near Maryland's border with West Virginia and Pennsylvania. The commission said it chose not to award the 500-MW/3,000-MWh Oystercatcher Energy Storage Project nor a 135-MW/540-MWh expansion Flatiron requested for the Chalk Point project in a revised filing after the first-round application window closed. The commission said Flatiron could reapply for the Chalk Point expansion and "invited [Oystercatcher] to consider participating" in round two, citing the "desirable electric grid location and characteristics" of the project's northeastern Maryland site while noting "the need for continued engagement with local stakeholders in Harford County if the project is pursued further." In addition to near-term cost pressures due to PJM's capacity crunch, Maryland has ambitious clean energy goals, including a statutory 2045 target for statewide net-zero emissions and a 2035 goal for 100% carbon-free electricity set by gubernatorial order. In a statement, Maryland Public Service Commission Chair Kumar Barve called the first-round award a milestone in the state's effort to meet its energy policy goals, while acknowledging its relatively modest contribution. "While we are disappointed that these awards are below our 800-MW target for Round 1, our Round 2 solicitation is expected to attract many more offers due to a pool of over 40 additional energy storage projects from PJM's Cycle 1 interconnection process," Barve said.

artigo.texto: Sistemas de armazenamento de energia elétrica, conhecidos pela sigla BESS, estão vendendo como nunca no País. Enquanto o leilão do Governo para contratar grandes projetos de baterias continua agendado para dezembro mas enfrenta incertezas, o mercado encontrou seu caminho no varejo. Instalações menores em indústrias, comércios, condomínios e residências, muitas vezes associadas a sistemas solares em telhados, têm movimentado a indústria num ritmo recorde. Em 2025, o volume vendido e contratado atingiu 730 MWh, mais do que o acumulado dos cinco anos anteriores. E só no primeiro semestre deste ano foram mais 504 MWh, a caminho de uma nova marca histórica para o setor, segundo um levantamento da consultoria Greener. “O leilão é importante, claro, mas o BESS de uma forma distribuída, vamos chamar assim, vai ser em minha visão uma das grandes fontes de flexibilidade para o sistema elétrico no País,” Marcio Takata, o CEO da Greener, disse ao Brazil Journal. Ele fez uma comparação com a indústria de energia solar, que começou a se movimentar com leilões do Governo para grandes projetos e nos anos seguintes teve uma disparada puxada pelo mercado de pequenas instalações em telhados e miniusinas. A capacidade em geração solar distribuída hoje soma mais de 53 gigawatts, contra 23,6 gigawatts em usinas de geração centralizada, segundo dados da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). No momento, o acumulado em sistemas de baterias no País representa 1,9 GWh, com empresas incluindo WEG e Grupo Moura apostando no setor. O leilão programado para dezembro deve contratar pelo menos 2 gigawatts para operação durante 4 horas diárias, segundo sinalizações de Brasília, o equivalente a 8 GWh – embora parte do mercado já espere volumes maiores. O Ministério de Minas e Energia também programou leilões anuais, até 2029, para contratação de reserva de capacidade, nos quais haverá espaço para sistemas de baterias. Esses certames, porém, vão promover uma disputa da tecnologia com termelétricas e hidrelétricas, incluindo as chamadas hidrelétricas reversíveis – que na prática funcionam como uma bateria, ao guardar água para produzir mais nos momentos em que o sistema precisa. A contratação dessa reserva de capacidade é vista como importante para que a rede elétrica possa lidar com a variação da geração eólica e solar, que por vezes resulta num excesso de energia, obrigando usinas a paradas forçadas, conhecidas como curtailment. “Hoje o tema mais quente no setor são as baterias. E as hidrelétricas reversíveis. Até por essa necessidade do sistema,” disse o diretor da consultoria Thymos Capital, André Millions. Apesar do intenso interesse de investidores, o leilão de dezembro está sob risco devido a discussões sobre quem vai pagar o custo dos projetos de armazenamento, segundo diversas fontes do setor. A legislação atual define o rateio dos custos entre todas empresas de geração, uma regra que gera ameaças de judicialização. No momento, empresas do setor se movimentam para convencer o Governo a trabalhar pela aprovação de um projeto do deputado Arnaldo Jardim que alteraria a lei para repassar a conta aos consumidores, como ocorre nos demais leilões do mercado de energia.

artigo.texto: Denver’s mayor and city council Wednesday announced a “working group” of 26 citizens and experts on data center growth that will make policy recommendations amid a city building moratorium, putting developers on notice the ban could be extended past May. “It will be Denver, not corporations, that decide if and how data centers may operate in our city,” Mayor Mike Johnston said, in a statement accompanying the working group appointments. City officials said more than 250 people expressed interest in joining the panel. “This group brings together people with different perspectives to help us get this right: setting clear rules, protecting Denver’s resources, and putting the interests of Denverites first,” Johnston said. City Council approved a one-year moratorium in May, amid rising controversy from residents in the Elyria-Swansea neighborhood of north Denver for opposing a 600,000-square-foot data center under construction by CoreSite. Globeville and Elyria-Swansea residents and advocates point out they have long been the victim of excess pollution from interstate traffic, the Suncor refinery, past Superfund polluters, the Purina plant and other industries. Denver’s pause also comes as communities up and down the Front Range launch their own intensive debates about whether and how to site other massive data center proposals. Brighton’s City Council on Tuesday night approved a one-year ban on data centers, as neighborhood groups protest a 2.5 million square foot proposal in the northern part of the city that extends into Weld County. A city council member said that application had been withdrawn. Date Center opponents in Weld County are now circulating petitions for a public vote on a ban there, after commissioners rezoned for a large Global AI data center in an unincorporated part of the county near Windsor. Aurora, Colorado Springs and a handful of other cities are also debating data center rezonings and potential moratoriums. Denver data centers permitted before May were not impacted by the City Council moratorium. Denver officials who jointly announced the new working group emphasized it includes representation from the neighborhoods most impacted by potential data centers, as well as “union, utility, and industry representatives,” nonprofits, healthcare and air quality experts. The meetings will begin Oct. 9 and will be streamed. The group “will put community voices and community solutions at the center of Denver’s data center debate because the people who live closest to these projects should shape the rules that govern them,” said Council Member Darrell Watson, who represents many of the affected neighborhoods in District 9. Working group members listed as community representatives include Solicia E. Lope, Erin Overturf, Andrea Nemer, Precious Lawrence, V. Quintana, Dr. Brandon Scott, Alfonso Espino, Rebecca Trujillo, Jessica N., Gilbert Herrera, Rev. Terrance D. Carroll and Marcus Weaver. Union representatives include IBEW Local 68 representative Julian Aguilar and Cecil Courtney from Pipefitters Local Union 208. Appointed from utility interests are Melissa Almond, corporate economic development manager, Xcel Energy; and Andrew Hill, government affairs manager, Denver Water. From industries related to data centers, members include Steve Jackson, CEO, Empowercom; and Matt Gallagher, senior manaer of strategic partnerships, Satoshi Energy. Nonprofits in related fields will be represented by Courtney Fieldman, director of utility programs, Southwest Energy Efficiency Project; Ean Thomas Tafoya, vice president of State Programs, GreenLatinos; and Jim Garcia, CEO and founder of Tepeyac Community Health Center. Air quality and healthcare members include Priyanka deSouza, assistant professor, Department of Urban and Regional Planning, University of Colorado Denver; Dr. Kate Jennings; and Abi Balajee. voices from academia include Mark Orrs, teaching associate professor in the Department of Engineering, Design, and Society at Colorado School of Mines; and Benjamin Xie, assistant professor of computer science, University of Denver.

artigo.texto: TERI Awards 115 MWh Battery Storage Tender in Delhi ⚡ Quick Read - What happened: The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) has officially announced the winner of its auction for 57.5 MW/115 MWh of BESS capacity located at four 66/11 kV grid stations in Delhi. - Why it matters: This project represents a critical step in integrating large-scale energy storage into urban distribution networks, serving as a blueprint for future grid-balancing infrastructure. - Watch: Further details on the winning developer and the project commissioning timeline as the grid integration phase commences. Background and Context The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) has successfully concluded its competitive auction process for the deployment of 57.5 MW/115 MWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS) in the National Capital Territory of Delhi. This initiative, which was originally floated in July 2026, is aimed at enhancing grid stability and managing peak demand fluctuations within the city’s power distribution infrastructure. By targeting 66/11 kV grid stations, the project focuses on decentralized storage solutions that can provide immediate support to the local grid. Key Details The awarded capacity totals 115 MWh of storage, supported by a 57.5 MW power rating. The project is strategically distributed across four specific 66/11 kV grid stations, ensuring that the storage assets are positioned to mitigate localized congestion and improve power quality. This auction is part of a broader push to integrate advanced energy storage technologies into India’s urban electricity grids, moving beyond traditional generation-centric models to more flexible, demand-responsive architectures. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and developers, the TERI auction serves as a significant indicator of the growing demand for BESS projects in urban settings. As distribution companies (DISCOMs) look to manage the intermittency of renewable energy and the rising demand for electric vehicle charging, the requirement for localized, medium-scale storage is expected to surge. EPC firms with expertise in grid-connected battery systems, safety compliance, and power electronics will find lucrative opportunities in similar upcoming tenders across other metropolitan areas in India. What Happens Next Following the announcement of the winning bidder, the project will move into the detailed engineering and procurement phase. Stakeholders will be closely monitoring the execution timelines and the integration of these systems with the existing Delhi grid infrastructure. As India continues to scale its renewable energy sector, the successful deployment of this 115 MWh capacity will provide vital operational data, influencing future policy frameworks and tender designs for energy storage projects nationwide. The integration of such storage assets is essential for the long-term reliability of India’s evolving energy landscape. 📊 Key Data The following table summarizes the key parameters of the TERI battery storage auction.

artigo.texto: Volunteers Scott Foreman and Irene Purcell, right, encourage fellow Raton resident Betty Poe to sign a petition against a data center on June 20 in front of a grocery store. The Raton City Commission has voted down a proposed one-year moratorium on new data centers. Raton resident Pat Walsh, who has helped lead the charge against a data center in Raton, says she is disappointed by the City Commission's recent decision to vote down a proposed one-year moratorium on such projects. An attempt to pump the brakes on data center development in Raton went down in defeat last month after members of the City Commission voted 3-2 against a proposed ordinance that would have put a one-year moratorium against such projects. The Sept. 22 vote came after commissioners were presented with a petition signed by nearly 500 Raton residents expressing opposition to data centers in the Colfax County community of about 6,000 residents just south of the Colorado border. The City Commission’s decision stands in contrast to an August vote by the Colfax County Commission to adopt a one-year moratorium on data centers in unincorporated parts of the county. That made Colfax the fourth county in New Mexico to adopt such a restriction, joining Santa Fe, Sierra and Socorro counties. Raton Mayor Lori Chatterley and City Commissioners Daniel Campbell and Mark Honeyfield voted against the moratorium, while Commissioners Linde Schuster and Sally Hoger, who proposed the measure, voted for it. Campbell, who did not respond to a request for comment from The New Mexican, said at the meeting last month he saw no point in adopting the measure. “I can’t see that it gains us anything to be the first municipality in New Mexico that does this,” he said. Campbell noted Raton lacks the electrical power and water necessary to operate a data center, and the city’s ownership of the utilities that control those commodities serves as an adequate hedge against any potential development. “The data center issue was never going to happen to the degree that that’s been discussed because we don’t have the power to do that,” Campbell said. Hoger, however, described it as a commonsense measure and dismissed the idea the city already has adequate safeguards in place. “I don’t agree with that,” she reiterated in a recent interview. How it got started The issue arose in Raton earlier this year after leaders of Atterix LLC, a Denver-based company incorporated in late 2025, signed a memorandum of understanding with Raton officials to conduct a feasibility study for a data center project. That agreement, signed in February, gave the company six months to conduct the study; during that time, the city was prohibited from soliciting a similar project from another company. Atterix officials had floated the idea of creating a three-phase project in Raton that would have been constructed over several years, vastly increasing the city’s consumption of electricity. The company has not submitted the results of the feasibility study to the city, Hoger said. Chatterley said at the Sept. 22 commission meeting there was no project for the city to consider. She did not respond to The New Mexican‘s request for additional information. Kimberle Burke, owner and operator of a local ice cream shop, presented a petition to the commission Sept. 22 opposing a data center, warning against negative impacts a project might bring to the city when it comes to water, noise, the economy and “long-term repercussions that we may not know about right now.” Burke said people who signed the petition are anxious to understand what value a data center would provide to the community and who would benefit from it. “We want a moratorium so the community’s concerns can be addressed and we can all be aware of what’s going on, when and why,” she said. “Something of this magnitude should be decided by the community by the majority, not just a few.” Another resident who spoke in favor of the moratorium, Max Holland, reminded commissioners the adoption of a one-year moratorium would not permanently ban data centers from Raton. “A moratorium is not a no,” he said. “A moratorium is a timeout. Let’s utilize that time to inform ourselves and make sure we are doing the right thing.” Raton resident Pat Walsh, who co-founded Protect Our Resources, residents who oppose a data center in the city, said last week she was disappointed but not surprised by the commission’s action. She believes the issue is a long way from being dead in Raton. “We are going to keep an eye on various parts of city government to stay vigilant to see if any applications come through for power, utilities or water, or planning and zoning so we don’t get blindsided,” Walsh said. “I don’t want to take a chance on it being done,” Walsh said. “Nothing I can see would prevent someone else from coming in.” Hoping for a remedy Walsh and Hoger said they are more optimistic an ordinance regulating data center operators will get the commission’s approval, especially after the mayor has spoken in favor of such a measure. “I’m still very much in support of an ordinance of having strong guardrails,” Chatterley said Sept. 22. Hoger said she is part of a committee that has drafted an ordinance, which has been submitted to the city’s legal staff for review. She said it includes provisions that would require data center operators to work with local utilities to determine how much water and power they could use, establish minimum distances between such facilities and the nearest residence, and set limits on the amount of noise they could generate. She said the measure is based on similar ordinances adopted in other communities across the country. Hoger said she isn’t sure how to assess the data center battle in Raton with the defeat of the moratorium and the regulatory measure awaiting legal approval. artigo.texto: Azul Conecta fecha acordo com Auren para compensação de emissões de todos os voos de 2026 Parceria com a Auren Energia prevê compensar cerca de 10 mil toneladas de CO₂ equivalente com créditos de carbono de projetos eólicos no Piauí e em Pernambuco A Azul Conecta anunciou uma parceria com a Auren Energia para compensar as emissões de carbono associadas ao consumo de combustível de todos os seus voos realizados ao longo de 2026. A iniciativa, batizada de Conecta NetZero, prevê a utilização de créditos de carbono certificados e não terá custo adicional para os passageiros. A Azul Conecta é a operação regional da Azul voltada à ligação de cidades de menor porte aos principais centros urbanos da companhia. Com aeronaves menores, principalmente do modelo Cessna Grand Caravan, a empresa atende mercados que não comportam os aviões utilizados nas rotas comerciais de maior demanda. O anúncio, portanto, vale apenas para os voos desta divisão regional da companhia e não para os voos feitos em outras linhas e aeronaves menores. A estimativa é que sejam compensadas cerca de 10 mil toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente (tCO₂e) ao longo do ano. Os créditos utilizados são provenientes dos complexos eólicos Ventos do Piauí I e Ventos do Araripe III, integrantes do portfólio de geração renovável da Auren. Segundo as empresas, os créditos seguem o Verified Carbon Standard (VCS), programa administrado pela organização Verra, e passaram por processos independentes de validação e verificação. Eles também tiveram sua elegibilidade reconhecida para a fase piloto do CORSIA, mecanismo criado pela Organização da Aviação Civil Internacional (ICAO) para lidar com as emissões da aviação internacional. Depois de utilizados na compensação, os créditos serão aposentados no registro da Verra em nome da Azul Conecta. A aposentadoria significa que as unidades deixam definitivamente de circular e não podem ser revendidas ou utilizadas novamente para compensar emissões. A medida busca dar rastreabilidade à compensação e evitar a dupla contagem dos créditos — uma das questões centrais nas discussões sobre a credibilidade do mercado voluntário de carbono. O programa, no entanto, é parte de uma estratégia mais ampla de redução de emissões da companhia aérea. A compensação não elimina as emissões produzidas pela queima de combustível das aeronaves, mas procura neutralizar, por meio de créditos certificados, uma quantidade equivalente de emissões contabilizadas pela companhia. A Azul afirma que sua estratégia de descarbonização também inclui renovação e modernização da frota e medidas de eficiência operacional. Entre 2019 e 2025, segundo a empresa, a intensidade de carbono de sua operação caiu cerca de 20%. Para César Grandolfo, diretor de Relações Institucionais, Tributárias e de Sustentabilidade da Azul, o programa representa mais uma etapa da estratégia climática da companhia. “Ao compensar integralmente as emissões associadas ao consumo de combustível dos voos da Azul Conecta por meio de créditos certificados, reforçamos nosso compromisso de combinar eficiência operacional, inovação e responsabilidade ambiental”, afirmou. A Auren afirma que já comercializou mais de 7 milhões de créditos de carbono para clientes em mais de 20 países. A empresa também informa possuir um portfólio de créditos associado a projetos de geração renovável e conservação de florestas nativas. “A parceria mostra como a geração de energia renovável pode contribuir também para a descarbonização de outros setores da economia”, disse João Guillaumon, vice-presidente de Clientes e Comercialização da Auren Energia. Compensação não substitui redução das emissões A iniciativa ocorre em um momento em que empresas aéreas enfrentam o desafio de reduzir sua pegada climática em um setor particularmente dependente de combustíveis fósseis. Mesmo com ganhos de eficiência, as emissões totais continuam crescendo à medida que aumenta a demanda por voos. Em 2024, as companhias aéreas emitiram globalmente cerca de 942 milhões de toneladas de CO₂, segundo a Associação Internacional de Transporte Aéreo (IATA), alta em relação aos 882 milhões de toneladas registrados em 2023. No mesmo período, porém, a intensidade de carbono da operação — medida pelas emissões por tonelada-quilômetro transportada — caiu 3,7%, sinal de que as aeronaves e operações estão ficando mais eficientes, mas que esses ganhos ainda não são suficientes para compensar o crescimento do tráfego. Embora avanços tecnológicos, eficiência operacional e renovação de frota possam reduzir o consumo de combustível por passageiro, a aviação ainda depende majoritariamente de combustíveis líquidos. Com isso, sozinha, a aviação responde por cerca de 2,5% das emissões globais de CO₂, de acordo com análise baseada em dados do Global Carbon Project. Contudo, seu impacto climático é maior quando considerados outros efeitos além do CO₂, como a formação de contrails ( aquelas linhas brancas que aparecem atrás dos aviões no céu) e alterações na química atmosférica. Para o setor aéreo, o desafio permanece maior do que compensar emissões: trata-se de reduzir, de forma estrutural, a quantidade de carbono emitida por cada voo. Nesse processo, tecnologias mais eficientes, combustíveis sustentáveis e mudanças operacionais deverão ter papel central — enquanto os créditos de carbono aparecem como uma ferramenta complementar na transição. A lógica é que uma tonelada de CO₂ equivalente emitida pela atividade seja compensada por uma unidade certificada correspondente a uma tonelada de emissões evitadas ou removidas em outro projeto. A efetividade climática desse mecanismo, porém, depende da qualidade, adicionalidade, rastreabilidade e integridade dos créditos utilizados. A certificação e a aposentadoria das unidades são, portanto, elementos importantes para demonstrar que os créditos empregados não serão utilizados por mais de uma empresa. artigo.texto: How AI is Reshaping Data Center Financing The race to build computing capacity for artificial intelligence is reshaping data center financing in the United States. As projects become larger, more capital-intensive and increasingly developed in phases, sponsors need financing that can adapt to changing capital requirements while still providing certainty of execution on increasingly compressed timelines. Some of the largest developments now represent multi-billion-dollar investment programs encompassing multiple buildings and years of construction. Rather than financing a single asset with a defined completion date, sponsors may be funding a campus that grows in stages as new capacity is added. The result is a financing model that increasingly needs to evolve alongside the project itself. Financing a project built in phases A large data center campus is rarely developed all at once. Sponsors may begin with land and site infrastructure before moving into the first buildings, then add capacity over time as customer demand develops. Each phase can bring different capital requirements, construction milestones and operating considerations. That makes flexibility increasingly important. “Five years ago, you were looking at a very different type of data center project,” says Michael Lardieri, Managing Director, Institutional Client & Financial Sponsors at BBVA USA. “Today we're talking about campuses that can require billions of dollars of investment and are being developed in multiple phases. That changes how sponsors think about capital and what they need from their banks.” Financing can therefore become part of a longer development strategy rather than a single transaction. Sponsors and lenders need to consider when capital will be required, how later phases relate to earlier ones and how the financing may need to evolve as a project moves from construction into operation. Speed is changing the equation At the same time, the expansion of AI infrastructure is putting greater pressure on development timelines. Suitable land, power capacity, equipment and construction resources are all in demand. Once those elements have been secured, delays elsewhere in the development process can become costly. Financing is no exception. For sponsors, having access to capital is essential, but so is knowing that financing can be executed within the project's timetable. Large transactions may require substantial underwriting commitments and coordination among multiple institutions, often while other parts of the development are moving simultaneously. “Clients don't only want to know whether the capital is available,” Lardieri says. “They want confidence that it can be delivered on the timeline the project requires. As the market has accelerated, that certainty has become increasingly important.” The asset cannot be viewed in isolation The infrastructure surrounding a data center is also becoming more relevant to financing decisions. Power is the most visible example. Large AI-oriented facilities require significant electricity capacity, and the timing of that capacity can influence when a project is built and when capital needs to be deployed. "The challenge is not simply the amount of capital required." But the same principle extends to other parts of a development, from connectivity and construction to customer commitments and the timing of future expansion. For lenders, that means understanding the financing increasingly requires understanding how the project itself will develop. Financing the next phase of growth AI is expected to continue driving significant investment in digital infrastructure. As it does, the financing supporting that expansion will have to keep pace with a sector that is changing quickly. The challenge is not simply the amount of capital required. It is matching that capital to projects that are being developed at greater scale, in multiple phases and under increasingly demanding timelines. For sponsors and financial institutions alike, that is making data center financing a more dynamic part of the infrastructure landscape.

artigo.texto: Northfield council moves away from data center ban, toward tiered regulation After more than two hours of public comment and council discussion, the Northfield City Council voted 7-0 Tuesday night to reduce the required setback between data-processing facilities and parks or trails from roughly three-quarters of a mile to 200 feet. But the setback change was only part of the story. In a separate motion, the council also directed staff to explore a tiered regulatory framework for data-processing facilities as part of the upcoming Land Development Code update, looking beyond just power consumption to include water use and other emerging concerns. The change to the setback had been in the works since 2024, when the city passed an ordinance regulating data-processing facilities. That ordinance required a 3,950-foot setback from any existing or planned park, trail, or recreational feature. It also required a 200-foot setback from residential structures. Community Development Director Scott Wopata acknowledged the moment was about more than one number. “This one's going to be hard,” he said. “In any example I look at around Minnesota or the Midwest or nationally, there aren't a lot of examples where communities have figured out a way to have this conversation and learn from each other and to empathetically see things from different perspectives. There's a lot of negative examples of how elected officials and staff members in different cities have signed NDAs, dismissed the public, not listened to public concerns.” Wopata framed the night as an effort to rebuild public trust after a year of conversations that started long before any application existed. "In 2024, we put a moratorium on all data-center development so that we could develop policies before we had a project application," Wopata said. "That is what we did. We have been following those best practices." The city's regulations include 17 performance standards covering noise, water use, glare, vibrations and more. They also require a conditional use permit triggered by any water use. “If we read anywhere anything about data centers, [there] is a very well documented track of negative externalities,” Wopata said. “There are water quality issues. There's water quantity issues. There are stories of communities losing water pressure. There's stories of communities where residents have seen significant spikes in their utility bills because the data centers moved in and this corporate development has happened.” But he also drew a distinction between prohibition and regulation. "Regulating is often a more strategic and sophisticated and just successful approach than prohibition," Wopata said, listing alcohol and cannabis prohibition as negative examples from history. "Bringing something into the light and regulating it can often help ameliorate some of the biggest harmful negative externalities." City Planner Mathias Hughey explained the rationale for the change. The 3,950-foot setback made every industrial parcel in the city undevelopable, and it was originally drafted without a clear rationale. "This is still much more restrictive than other industrial uses," Hughey said. Hughey said the planning commission had separately recommended that data-processing facilities be prohibited outright and that staff research a tiered regulatory framework. Because that recommendation was not part of the published public hearing notice, the council had to proceed with the setback item as written. Competing priorities More than a dozen residents spoke during public comment, most urging the council to keep the moratorium or reject the setback change. One Northfielder, Trisha Brunk, even led the room through a song. Councilor Kathleen Holmes acknowledged the volume of opposition in the room but said the council has to weigh competing priorities. “While there is a high number of people who have spoken out against data centers, we, those of us decision makers, policymakers up here, have to hold many priorities,” she said. “And while we have heard the thoughts, the feedback, the opinions on data centers, I would say probably all of us here more often and more frequently hear 'Lower our taxes.’ … I take this as the belief that the path forward is through regulation and not prohibition.” Councilor Jessica Peterson White said she saw parallels to hog feedlot debates from the early 2000s. "But when we were talking about hog feedlots, the scale was a really important part of the conversation," she said. "I don't have a clear sense myself of what scale of data center or other types of development is where we should set a regulation, but I believe that the regulations that we have make it vanishingly unlikely that we will get a hyperscale data center, and that seems good." She also addressed the equity dimension. "There is a history in this country of affluent white communities sort of offshoring their industrial needs to communities that don't have the same resources, don't have the same organizing power, and those industrial uses are then underregulated and create issues for poorer and less white communities," she said. "And I hope we don't play a role in that." No one is saying ‘Let’s build a huge data center’ Councilor Davin Sokup said he was voting yes despite his own uncertainty. "But I just really want to highlight that what we're considering here tonight, I think, in my opinion, does show an openness to having a data center in Northfield," he said. "I'm not willing to say that it couldn't possibly be that in the future." Councilor Chad Beumer said he understood the distrust but believed the city's regulations were already strong. “I don't think there's a single person sitting up here that is saying, ‘Let's build a huge data center out there that's going to burn up all kinds of energy and waste a whole bunch of water,’” he said. “I think our ordinance 1098 clearly dictates that that's not going to happen.” Mayor Erica Zweifel closed the discussion by noting the s

artigo.texto: Climate experts and other stakeholders yesterday gathered in Abuja for the European Union Climate Dialogues programme ( EUCDs2) for Nigeria’s carbon market roadmap. The event, which focuses on “Operationalising Nigeria’s Carbon Markets Through Robust Monitoring, Reporting And Verification (MRV) Protocols,” brought together government officials, development partners, private-sector operators, investors, civil society organisations and other stakeholders. The Director-General of the National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), Mrs Omotenioye Majekodunmi said Nigeria’s carbon market must be built on integrity, transparency and credible data, warning that the country would not tolerate practices capable of undermining confidence in carbon credits generated in Nigeria. Represented by the Director, Energy , Transportation and Infrastructure, Mr Michael Ivenso, l she said that the council had issued about 26 million carbon credits so far from projects previously executed in Nigeria, describing the development as evidence of the country’s capacity to participate in international carbon markets. According to her, Nigeria’s objective is to ensure that carbon projects deliver “real, additional and permanent mitigation outcomes” while protecting communities, ecosystems and the interests of investors and project developers. The Director-General said the operationalisation of the National Carbon Markets Framework would provide the institutional foundation for a credible carbon market capable of mobilising private capital for clean energy, agriculture, forestry, waste management and other climate interventions. The NCCC boss said a key component of the strategy was the establishment of a unified and interoperable national carbon registry through which every carbon credit generated, issued, transferred or retired in Nigeria would have a digital record. “This will help prevent double-counting and strengthen the integrity of carbon transactions,” she said. She added that Nigeria was also moving towards digital MRV, leveraging remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, geospatial data and distributed ledger technologies to improve the accuracy of carbon measurement while reducing the cost and time required for verification. Majekodunmi said effective MRV would also enable regulators to track emissions trajectories, assure buyers that claimed emission reductions were genuine and help communities monitor benefit-sharing arrangements. She called for stronger coordination among federal ministries, state governments, project developers, development partners, financial institutions, civil society organisations and academic institutions. She said the Council was working with relevant stakeholders to ensure that future carbon credit transfers under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement were supported by credible national systems. The Director, Federal Department of Forestry at the Federal Ministry of Environment, Halima Bawa-Bwari, said the forestry sector remained central to Nigeria’s climate response and could become one of the country’s biggest opportunities in the carbon market. She said forests served as carbon sinks and temperature buffers while providing biodiversity, soil protection, water regulation and livelihoods for millions of Nigerians, particularly rural and forest-dependent communities. “We must therefore ensure that carbon-market development supports forest conservation rather than creating pressure for further forest exploitation,” she said. Bawa-Bwari stressed that credible carbon markets could not be built without credible data, particularly in the forestry sector. She said Nigeria needed reliable information on forest cover, degradation, deforestation, biomass and carbon stocks to determine how much carbon was being stored or removed and how those changes occurred over time. She called for continued strengthening of the National Forest Inventory and forest monitoring systems, as well as increased use of satellite imagery, remote sensing and artificial intelligence. However, she cautioned that satellite information must be complemented with ground-based measurements and field verification. The director also called for increased capacity among federal and state forestry institutions to collect and manage forest data. “MRV should not be developed as a stand-alone carbon-market activity. It should build on existing national systems for forest monitoring, greenhouse-gas accounting, REDD+ data, land-use planning and climate reporting,” she said. Bawa-Bwari urged relevant agencies to avoid establishing parallel systems that collect similar information, calling instead for clear institutional responsibilities for the collection, management, validation and reporting of forest-carbon data. On it part, the European Union said Nigeria’s efforts to develop a credible carbon market could help attract much-needed finance for climate action while supporting sustainable economic growth. Mr Jop Weterings, a member of the Task Force on International Carbon Pricing And Marketing Diplomacy at the EU said the bloc had stepped up cooperation with Nigeria on carbon markets over the past year, describing the roundtable as an important milestone in the partnership. The EU said its shared interest with Nigeria was to scale up high-integrity carbon markets capable of strengthening global climate action, channeling resources into Nigerian initiatives and driving sustainable economic growth. It noted that Nigeria’s adoption of the National Carbon Markets Framework had provided an important foundation for building confidence and trust among investors, buyers and other market participants. The EU representative said the focus should now be on operationalising the framework, particularly through strong MRV systems that would ensure carbon credits generated in Nigeria represented credible climate outcomes. artigo.texto: The Public Utility Commission of Texas is asking a Travis County judge to block the release of information showing where data centers and virtual currency mines operate, saying those details could aid terrorists. The lawsuit filed Monday pits the state agency responsible for regulating utilities against Attorney General Ken Paxton’s office over the scope of Texas’ public-records law and the state’s protections for critical infrastructure. At the center of the dispute are two seemingly basic geographic details: the county where a facility is located and the regional water planning area in which it sits. The PUC argues that those details are “privileged information” and become sensitive when combined with other information collected through its survey of the industry, including electricity demand, actual electricity consumption, projected peak demand, water consumption, water sources, cooling technology and the utilities and infrastructure serving a facility. The commission is not asking the court to declare the entire survey confidential. Instead, it wants the court to rule that the two geographic fields are exempt from disclosure under the Texas Homeland Security Act, which is meant to “protect against homeland security threats and hazards . . . and prevent significant criminal and terrorist attacks.” The lawsuit does not represent a final ruling on whether the information ultimately must be released. But it does come as Texas officials are seeking more information about the state’s data center industry. Gov. Greg Abbott has ordered state agencies to conduct additional reviews of data centers seeking to connect to the state’s electric grid, including reviews of electricity and water use, cooling systems and other information. He has also directed the Texas Water Development Board to take enforcement action against data centers that fail to comply with required water use reporting. What’s in the PUC water and energy use survey? In 2025, Texas lawmakers directed the PUC to collect information about water and energy consumption at data centers and virtual-currency-mining facilities to better understand the growth of the industry. The effort reflects a growing concern among state officials and Texans about the resources required by large computing facilities. Data centers can consume enormous amounts of electricity because of the thousands of servers operating inside them. Depending on their cooling systems, they can also require substantial quantities of water to help keep their servers cool during operation. The PUC developed its survey in cooperation with the Texas Water Development Board, the state agency tasked with overseeing the state’s water planning process. The information was intended to help state officials better understand the relationship between electricity demand and water consumption and to inform future planning. The Legislature also directed the PUC to share information with other state agencies and produce a report on its findings. The survey was sent to 377 facilities and sought information including a facility’s location, county and regional water-planning area, electricity load and consumption, projected future peak demand, cooling technology, water consumption and sources and information about the facility’s connection to the electric grid. The response was limited and called “pathetic” by one state representative during a June legislative hearing where PUC officials said 28 companies representing 92 facilities had responded to the survey. Lawmakers questioned whether the resulting data would be sufficient to support long-term policy decisions. The PUC later reopened the voluntary survey for an additional 10 days in July. As of August, 13 virtual currency mining and 77 data center facilities had filled out the survey, according to an email from a PUC spokesperson. The PUC lawsuit The PUC dispute with the attorney general’s office began after a resident from McLennan County and four journalists, including a reporter at The Texas Tribune, sought the survey responses through open records requests. The PUC denied those requests, saying that the information should be protected from disclosure in its entirety. Those requestors have an opportunity to participate in the open records dispute if they choose. Under Texas law, when a governmental agency believes requested records aren’t open to the public, it can ask the Attorney General’s Open Records Division for a ruling. That is what the PUC did. The commission argued that at least some of the survey information was protected under the Texas Homeland Security Act, which makes certain information concerning vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure confidential. But the PUC, the government entity seeking to withhold records, must establish that the statutory exception applies. That distinction is at the heart of the dispute. The Attorney General’s office issued two rulings concluding that the PUC had not sufficiently established that the disputed information identified the kind of technical vulnerabilities covered by the Homeland Security Act. The PUC is now challenging those rulings by asking a court to reach a different conclusion. The agency argues that the individual pieces of information in the survey cannot be considered in isolation. A county name, for example, ordinarily would not reveal much about a facility’s security. But the commission argues that the county and regional water planning area can be combined with information about a facility’s electricity consumption, water use and the infrastructure that supplies those resources. In the PUC’s view, identifying the facility allows otherwise general operational information to be connected to a particular physical site and potentially reveal vulnerabilities that could be exploited in a physical or cyberattack, which could then affect the reliability of the state’s power grid and drinking water systems. “This combined disclosure would give a person intending an act of
