artigo.texto: Empresário transforma negócio de manutenção de maquininhas de cartão em serviços de integração de data centers Com a reestruturação, RGL Solutions passou de uma receita inferior a R$ 500 mil, em 2023, para R$ 18 milhões no ano passado Atualizado Com uma estrutura de 15 colaboradores, que atuam na sede em Barueri (SP), a RGL Solutions experimentou uma virada operacional e financeira expressiva no setor de infraestrutura crítica de tecnologia da informação nos últimos três anos. A empresa, que faturou R$ 465 mil em 2023 durante seu processo de reestruturação, deu um salto significativo ao atingir R$ 17,4 milhões em receita em 2024. No ano passado, registrou R$ 18 milhões em faturamento, movimentando cerca de R$ 40 milhões em transações. Agora, a empresa está estruturando planos de expansão focados em desenvolvimento e sustentação de sistemas baseados em IA. Essa nova frente de soluções é apontada como a alavanca estratégica para atingir uma meta de crescimento de 80% em 2027. Especializada em integração de data centers, redes corporativas e conectividade crítica, a RGL tornou-se parceira estratégica da fabricante chinesa Huawei e assumiu o retrofit completo do data center da fábrica de caminhões e ônibus do Grupo Volkswagen, em Resende (RJ). A projeção para 2026 é alcançar R$ 23 milhões em faturamento. Por trás dessa transformação de modelo de negócio está a trajetória do fundador e diretor-executivo William Cavalcanti. Nascido e criado em Itaquera, bairro humilde da Zona Leste de São Paulo, o empresário iniciou sua caminhada profissional do zero. Formado como tecnólogo em engenharia de automação industrial, ele ingressou no mercado de tecnologia. "Comecei como estagiário numa empresa de meios de pagamento. Honestamente eu nem a conhecia, ainda estava procurando estágio. Então, por acaso, eu consegui emprego nessa empresa. Começamos com um laboratório com quatro pessoas, cinco pessoas, e mirando o que dava para fazer naquela realidade", relembra o executivo. Dificuldade inspirou o empreendedor Cavalcanti ingressou em outra empresa de logística como funcionário, desta vez para montar um centro de reparos dentro da companhia. Lá, ele identificou um gargalo crítico na cadeia de manutenção de terminais de pagamento (máquinas POS) das credenciadoras (empresas responsáveis por credenciar estabelecimentos comerciais para aceitarem pagamentos por cartão e por processar e liquidar essas transações financeiras). Enquanto as devoluções de equipamentos levavam cerca de 45 dias para serem concluídas pelos fabricantes, William idealizou, entre 2007 e 2008, o primeiro laboratório instalado diretamente dentro de um operador logístico. "Nós fomos o primeiro laboratório técnico a ter um centro de reparo dentro do operador logístico. Adotamos uma estratégia e conseguimos reduzir a devolução do equipamento para três dias, diz o empreendedor. Em 26 de agosto de 2010, William fundou, ao lado de um sócio, a empresa batizada originalmente de TOP. A operação iniciou focada na manutenção e logística reversa de terminais POS para gigantes como Cielo e Rede. Em 2012, a companhia fechou um contrato de grande porte com o grupo América Móvil (Claro, Net e Embratel), expandindo sua presença industrial para duas plantas em São Paulo (Cotia e Campinas) e uma no Amazonas, em Manaus. No auge desse modelo, a empresa empregava quase 300 funcionários e recuperava de 150 mil a 200 mil equipamentos por mês. Em 2018, William decidiu vender sua participação de 50% no negócio para o seu sócio. O empreendedor estava em busca de novos desafios. "Vendi as minhas cotas para o meu antigo sócio e segui a vida. Fui fazer outras coisas", conta. Durante esse afastamento, ele fundou um provedor de internet (ISP), implementando mais de 200 quilômetros de rede de fibra óptica e alcançando cerca de 8 mil clientes até vender o negócio, em 2022. Enquanto Cavalcanti conduzia seu novo empreendimento, a antiga empresa enfrentou sérias dificuldades de mercado. Retorno do fundador Com a entrada de concorrentes agressivos e a perda progressiva dos contratos com o grupo América Móvil, a operação original entrou em crise financeira. Procurado para reestruturar a empresa, o empresário selou seu retorno em 28 de outubro de 2022. A repactuação societária envolveu a divisão da operação em dois CNPJs; William assumiu de forma isolada e com 100% do capital o CNPJ original que havia fundado em 2010. "Fui ajustando o que dava para ajustar e assumi os clientes que foram possíveis de recuperar", explica. Com o controle total em mãos, o executivo promoveu uma reestruturação profunda. Transferiu a sede de Campinas para Alphaville, em Barueri, e alterou o nome corporativo para RGL Solutions. Mais do que uma mudança de marca, ocorreu uma pivotagem completa do modelo de negócios. A RGL encerrou as atividades com equipamentos remanufaturados e passou a focar exclusivamente em serviços de TI de alto valor agregado, como redes Wi-Fi 7 corporativas, engenharia de data centers e migração de infraestruturas legadas (com projetos de substituição de tecnologia Cisco para Huawei). "O meu foco foi me dedicar à TI, não mais em equipamento remanufaturado. Nosso forte não é venda de equipamento, nosso forte é prestação de serviço, que é mais rentável", detalha o fundador. Aliada às certificações de qualidade ISO 9001 (e em fase final para a obtenção da ISO/IEC 27001), a RGL mantém uma filosofia de células de trabalho enxutas e de alta produtividade. "Eu sempre procurei ter a quantidade de pessoas suficiente para determinada atividade. Então, geralmente a gente estrutura uma célula para um determinado segmento, amadurece ela, deixa ela redonda antes de expandir. Se eu fosse falar o que é o segredo de sucesso, seria isso", diz o empreendedor.

artigo.texto: Next Upcoming Canary Live Bay Area By Canary Media Households and the power grid run on alternating current. Batteries — including those in electric vehicles — run on direct current. That AC-DC divide has complicated the prospect of EVs as home backup batteries. Today, almost every commercially available vehicle-to-home (V2H) backup power system in the U.S. requires a pricey DC bidirectional charger: a device that converts direct current from the vehicle to home-ready alternating current. The only exception is Tesla’s. Over the past few years, the major EV and home battery manufacturer has been working out how to get its vehicles to do the job of sending AC power to homes and the grid. Tesla’s Cybertruck has had this ability for more than a year, and on Tuesday, the firm announced it is expanding the capability to its new Model 3 and Model Y EVs — as long as your home has a Powerwall 3 battery, that is. “This is us bringing the whole ecosystem together and allowing our products to complement each other,” said Colby Hastings, head of Tesla Energy’s residential energy business. Instead of relying on a DC bidirectional charger to do the power conversion, AC bidirectional charging does the job with hardware in the vehicles themselves. The Powerwall 3 retails for $8,200 and costs several thousand dollars more to install, but it’s a complete home backup system. The only additional equipment Tesla requires to add between two and three days of additional V2H backup power from an EV battery is its standard Wall Connector charger, which retails for $595. It’s cheaper to set up a Cybertruck for home backup power, since those vehicles don’t require homes to have a Powerwall. Customers simply need to pay for a V2H hardware package that retails for $1,990, plus about $1,800 to $2,200 for installation. Either way, these prices are a good deal compared to the $6,500 to $10,000 and up it typically costs to buy a DC bidirectional charger — a price that doesn’t include a home battery. That’s largely because it’s a lot cheaper to convert DC to AC power within an EV — which already has to convert incoming AC to DC for its battery — than to buy a separate power conversion system that attaches to your house, Hastings said. “We’ve been very focused on what we think is the more long-term scalable pathway,” she said. “That’s what led us to this architecture.” To be clear, Tesla EVs and Powerwall batteries still cost a lot of money. And arguably, Tesla could be seen as something of a latecomer to the V2H game, which other automakers have offered for years with DC V2H backup systems. But in terms of establishing a means for lower-cost AC hardware to turn EVs into home batteries, Tesla’s latest development is a big deal, said Zach Woogen, executive director of the Vehicle-Grid Integration Council. “Many in the industry expect AC bidirectional charging equipment will be economical for customers and manufacturers alike at a lower price point,” he said. “This is an exciting proposition for a technology space that’s been limited by relatively high up-front costs.” Woogen’s group represents EV and charging manufacturers working with utilities and regulators across the country to streamline the use of EVs as backup batteries and as grid assets. The cumulative impact of millions of EVs could be huge. A recent study found that California could get one-third of its grid energy storage needs from tapping just 10% of the 9.7 million EVs it expects to have by the mid-2030s. Automakers have been touting the potential of EVs to back up homes during power outages for years, from the first Nissan Leaf EVs to the discontinued Ford F-150 Lightning. General Motors’ GM Energy business offers home battery and EV charger-power conversion systems that currently retail for just under $12,000 to more than $20,000. Kia markets its EV9 with V2H charging, and electric truck maker Rivian is working on similar capabilities. But beyond Tesla, automakers selling EVs in the U.S. haven’t publicly announced that they have embedded the technology so that the cars can provide AC backup power on their own. That’s partly because adding such tech tacks on complexity and cost to the vehicle manufacturing process. Things get even more complicated when you start talking about sending EV battery power back into utility grids. That’s called vehicle-to-grid, or V2G. Utilities have been running V2G pilot projects for decades, and a handful have started to expand into standard programs that pay customers who let the utility tap their EV batteries. But right now, only California and Maryland have established utility regulations that allow for AC bidirectional charging outside of pilot projects, although other states are working on it. Pacific Gas & Electric, California’s largest utility, has been running V2G pilots for years now and is now testing V2H capabilities with EVs from GM, Kia, Nissan, Polestar, and Volvo using bidirectional DC chargers. But the cost of the gear required for households to sign up has been daunting, said Eli Darby, part of PG&E’s clean energy transportation team. “We’ve had decent participation from DC systems,” Darby said. “But we’ve seen there’s a ceiling to the amount of money customers are willing to spend. The $10,000 to $15,000 it takes to pay for equipment and also installation and interconnection is a barrier.” That’s why PG&E has been working to certify the technology combos that can supply AC power directly from EVs to home chargers, and from there to the grid. artigo.texto: ESS, an opportunity for K-batteries Summary The global energy storage system market is rapidly expanding, driven by AI data centers and renewable energy growth. In the first half of 2026, lithium-ion battery shipments for ESS reached 461 GWh, up 71 percent year on year, while the Korean government introduced technology, tax and deployment measures to support the industry. Korean battery companies face strong Chinese competition and intensified price pressure but can pursue opportunities in Europe and North America through local production, supply-chain diversification and compliance advantages. Key Facts - The global ESS market is forecast to reach 1,870 GWh in annual shipments by 2035, roughly twice this year’s level. - The Korean government plans to invest more than 250 billion won in next-generation battery technology, while the industry is expected to invest approximately 8 trillion won through 2030 in manufacturing-process innovation and material localization. - The third ESS Central Contract Market will select project developers for a record-high total capacity of 1,180 megawatts, with successful bidders entering 15-year contracts through the Korea Power Exchange. - Chinese companies accounted for nearly 55 percent of the global ESS market in the first half of 2026, and global ESS supply capacity exceeded actual demand by 288 GWh at the end of 2025. - Europe’s combined renewable-energy and battery facility capacity is expected to rise from 6.3 GW in 2025 to around 35 GW in 2030. A new current is reshaping the global battery market. In the first half of 2026, global shipments of lithium-ion batteries for energy storage systems (ESS) reached 461 gigawatt-hour (GWh), up 71 percent from 270 GWh in the same period a year earlier, according to SNE Research. This represents a remarkable leap for the ESS market, especially compared with the 20 percent year-on-year growth in global battery demand for electric vehicles (EVs), which reached 609 GWh over the same period. Key drivers include rising energy demand from artificial intelligence (AI) data centers, where speed and reliability are critical, and growth in renewable power generation, which requires solutions to address its intermittency. The expansion of AI data centers and the transition to renewable energy are powerful trends unlikely to reverse in the short term. As a result, the global ESS market is forecast to reach 1,870 GWh in annual shipments by 2035, roughly twice this year’s level. The Korean government is also stepping up efforts to develop the domestic ESS industry through a range of policy measures. On the technology front, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources announced its Battery Industry Technology Roadmap on Sept. 22. The road map’s main elements are to position sodium-ion and solid-state batteries as new growth engines: The government will invest more than 250 billion won in next-generation battery technology development; the country’s three cell manufacturers will collaborate on research and standardization in noncompetitive areas; and the industry as a whole will invest approximately 8 trillion won ($5.97 billion) through 2030 in manufacturing-process innovation and the localization of materials. On the production front, the government has pledged tax support. On Aug. 3, the Ministry of Finance and Economy announced its 2026 Tax Reform Proposal, which introduced a domestic production tax credit to expand local manufacturing capacity in industries of strategic importance to the green transition and economic security. Rechargeable batteries are among the eligible products. On the deployment front, the government is expanding the market through auctions under the Central Contract Market. On Sept. 23, the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment announced the third ESS Central Contract Market in which it would select ESS project developers with a record-high total capacity of 1,180 megawatts. By the auction, the Korea Power Exchange competitively tenders the ESS capacity needed to stabilize the grid and enters into 15-year contracts with successful bidders. This is an encouraging development, as it creates substantial new demand for a battery market that has slowed amid moderating growth in EV demand. For K-batteries to build on these policies and strengthen their position, however, they must increase their share of the rapidly expanding global ESS market. This presents both significant challenges and important opportunities. The fact that China has already established a strong lead in the ESS market is a challenge for Korea. The top four companies in the global ESS market in the first half of this year were all Chinese, and together, they accounted for nearly 55 percent of the market. Korean companies have also recorded strong year-on-year growth, but the gap in absolute volume with China remains substantial. Moreover, with global ESS supply capacity exceeding demand — 900 GWh against the actual demand of 612 GWh at the end of 2025 — price competition is intensifying. Competing with Chinese companies, which have maintained operating margins through economies of scale, can seem like an uphill battle. At the same time, several factors create opportunities. First, regional imbalances between battery supply and demand mean that key export markets for Korean companies are likely to face shortages. For example, battery supply in China is expected to exceed demand by about 90 percent in 2030, while Europe is projected to face a supply shortfall of 40 percent. North America is also expected to face a shortage from 2035. This presents an opportunity for Korean companies, which have established production bases in Europe and North America, to increase their market share. Second, in Europe, capacity for facilities combining renewable energy and batteries is expected to rise by more than 450 percent, from 6.3 GW in 2025 to around 35 GW in 2030. In parallel, the region is working to reduce its reliance on battery supply

artigo.texto: Climate experts and other stakeholders yesterday gathered in Abuja for the European Union Climate Dialogues programme ( EUCDs2) for Nigeria’s carbon market roadmap. The event, which focuses on “Operationalising Nigeria’s Carbon Markets Through Robust Monitoring, Reporting And Verification (MRV) Protocols,” brought together government officials, development partners, private-sector operators, investors, civil society organisations and other stakeholders. The Director-General of the National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), Mrs Omotenioye Majekodunmi said Nigeria’s carbon market must be built on integrity, transparency and credible data, warning that the country would not tolerate practices capable of undermining confidence in carbon credits generated in Nigeria. Represented by the Director, Energy , Transportation and Infrastructure, Mr Michael Ivenso, l she said that the council had issued about 26 million carbon credits so far from projects previously executed in Nigeria, describing the development as evidence of the country’s capacity to participate in international carbon markets. According to her, Nigeria’s objective is to ensure that carbon projects deliver “real, additional and permanent mitigation outcomes” while protecting communities, ecosystems and the interests of investors and project developers. The Director-General said the operationalisation of the National Carbon Markets Framework would provide the institutional foundation for a credible carbon market capable of mobilising private capital for clean energy, agriculture, forestry, waste management and other climate interventions. The NCCC boss said a key component of the strategy was the establishment of a unified and interoperable national carbon registry through which every carbon credit generated, issued, transferred or retired in Nigeria would have a digital record. “This will help prevent double-counting and strengthen the integrity of carbon transactions,” she said. She added that Nigeria was also moving towards digital MRV, leveraging remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, geospatial data and distributed ledger technologies to improve the accuracy of carbon measurement while reducing the cost and time required for verification. Majekodunmi said effective MRV would also enable regulators to track emissions trajectories, assure buyers that claimed emission reductions were genuine and help communities monitor benefit-sharing arrangements. She called for stronger coordination among federal ministries, state governments, project developers, development partners, financial institutions, civil society organisations and academic institutions. She said the Council was working with relevant stakeholders to ensure that future carbon credit transfers under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement were supported by credible national systems. The Director, Federal Department of Forestry at the Federal Ministry of Environment, Halima Bawa-Bwari, said the forestry sector remained central to Nigeria’s climate response and could become one of the country’s biggest opportunities in the carbon market. She said forests served as carbon sinks and temperature buffers while providing biodiversity, soil protection, water regulation and livelihoods for millions of Nigerians, particularly rural and forest-dependent communities. “We must therefore ensure that carbon-market development supports forest conservation rather than creating pressure for further forest exploitation,” she said. Bawa-Bwari stressed that credible carbon markets could not be built without credible data, particularly in the forestry sector. She said Nigeria needed reliable information on forest cover, degradation, deforestation, biomass and carbon stocks to determine how much carbon was being stored or removed and how those changes occurred over time. She called for continued strengthening of the National Forest Inventory and forest monitoring systems, as well as increased use of satellite imagery, remote sensing and artificial intelligence. However, she cautioned that satellite information must be complemented with ground-based measurements and field verification. The director also called for increased capacity among federal and state forestry institutions to collect and manage forest data. “MRV should not be developed as a stand-alone carbon-market activity. It should build on existing national systems for forest monitoring, greenhouse-gas accounting, REDD+ data, land-use planning and climate reporting,” she said. Bawa-Bwari urged relevant agencies to avoid establishing parallel systems that collect similar information, calling instead for clear institutional responsibilities for the collection, management, validation and reporting of forest-carbon data. On it part, the European Union said Nigeria’s efforts to develop a credible carbon market could help attract much-needed finance for climate action while supporting sustainable economic growth. Mr Jop Weterings, a member of the Task Force on International Carbon Pricing And Marketing Diplomacy at the EU said the bloc had stepped up cooperation with Nigeria on carbon markets over the past year, describing the roundtable as an important milestone in the partnership. The EU said its shared interest with Nigeria was to scale up high-integrity carbon markets capable of strengthening global climate action, channeling resources into Nigerian initiatives and driving sustainable economic growth. It noted that Nigeria’s adoption of the National Carbon Markets Framework had provided an important foundation for building confidence and trust among investors, buyers and other market participants. The EU representative said the focus should now be on operationalising the framework, particularly through strong MRV systems that would ensure carbon credits generated in Nigeria represented credible climate outcomes. artigo.texto: Nigeria is moving to strengthen the credibility and integrity of its emerging carbon market by improving carbon verification and measurement, reporting and verification systems. The National Council on Climate Change is working with the European Union and other stakeholders to operationalise a unified national carbon registry, develop digital MRV systems and establish stronger standards for carbon projects. Key Overview - Focus: Carbon market integrity and verification - Key system: National carbon registry - Technology: Digital MRV, remote sensing, IoT, geospatial data and distributed ledgers - International partner: European Union - Market framework: National Carbon Markets Framework - Priority: High-integrity carbon investments - Key areas: Article 6 cooperation and voluntary carbon markets Nigeria Targets Higher-Integrity Carbon Market Nigeria is seeking to strengthen the credibility of its emerging carbon market as the government looks to attract more private investment into climate action. The National Council on Climate Change (NCCC) has called for stronger carbon verification to ensure that carbon projects generate credible and measurable climate outcomes. The push was discussed during a high-level roundtable on carbon markets in Abuja organised under the European Union Climate Dialogues programme. Government officials, development partners and other stakeholders used the meeting to discuss how Nigeria can operationalise its carbon-market framework and improve the systems used to measure and verify emissions reductions. NCCC Director-General Omotenioye Majekodunmi said Nigeria needs to translate its climate ambitions into tangible, bankable and verifiable actions that can support sustainable economic growth and attract climate finance. Stronger Measurement, Reporting and Verification A central part of Nigeria’s strategy is the development of stronger Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) systems. The NCCC is promoting digital MRV technologies, including remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, geospatial data and distributed ledger technologies. These technologies are expected to improve the accuracy and reliability of emissions data while reducing some of the costs and time associated with verifying carbon projects. The NCCC says effective MRV is necessary for buyers to establish whether claimed emissions reductions are genuine. It can also help regulators track emissions, prevent double-counting and give communities greater visibility over benefit-sharing arrangements. National Carbon Registry Planned Nigeria is also working to operationalise a unified national carbon registry. The registry is expected to create a digital record of carbon credits generated, issued, transferred and retired in Nigeria. This would provide greater visibility over the lifecycle of credits and help reduce the risk of the same emissions reduction being counted more than once. The system is part of the broader effort to create a transparent infrastructure for Nigeria’s carbon market as activity increases. The NCCC also wants to finalise carbon-market regulations, publish sector-specific MRV guidelines and establish local capacity-building hubs to strengthen verification expertise within the country. EU Supports Nigeria’s Carbon Market Development The European Union is supporting Nigeria’s efforts through the EU Climate Dialogues programme. The Abuja roundtable formed part of the second phase of the EU Climate Dialogues, which is focused on supporting Nigeria’s climate and carbon-market development. EU representatives said credible carbon markets require robust systems for transparency, accountability and environmental integrity. The partnership is also intended to help stakeholders align around Nigeria’s National Carbon Markets Framework and develop a roadmap for putting the framework into operation. The EU sees stronger carbon-market systems as a way to support emissions reductions while mobilising investment and encouraging the development of low-carbon economic activities. Nigeria’s National Carbon Markets Framework Nigeria’s National Carbon Markets Framework provides the institutional and regulatory architecture for carbon-market activities in the country. The framework covers domestic and international carbon trading, including Article 6 cooperation, and voluntary markets. It is intended to provide greater clarity for project developers, investors, buyers and regulators while supporting Nigeria’s participation in international carbon markets. The NCCC says the framework can help position Nigeria as a destination for high-integrity carbon investment, provided the country strengthens the systems needed to verify and monitor carbon projects. artigo.texto: Clock ticking for Illinois data center regulation Lawmakers, advocates believe regulations must be approved as soon as possible SPRINGFIELD, Ill. (WAND) – Advocates and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are committed to getting data center regulations across the finish line during veto session. Many believe the POWER Act needs to pass as soon as possible. Illinois has provided millions of dollars in tax credits to data centers since 2019, but Gov. JB Pritzker said AI data centers didn’t exist back then. “What we now see is these hyper-scale massive data centers where they want to take an entire nuclear power plant offline and apply it to a data center that might be many millions of square feet,” Pritzker said. More IL Statehouse Coverage Pritzker said big tech companies need to bring their own clean energy, pay their fair share for power and use closed-loop water systems. The POWER Act could also establish consumer protection and pollution control policies. Some believe local governments should decide where facilities can be located and prevent data centers from being approved within three miles of residential communities. “They’re still on our grid,” said House Minority Leader Tony McCombie (R-Savanna). “They’re still using our energy, and they’re reaping the benefits that are coming to communities. There again, it has to be the community’s decision of whether or not they want them.” The Illinois Environmental Council said communities have been trying to make major decisions about data centers on their own without proper resources. IEC CEO Jen Walling said the POWER Act would ban NDAs for data centers and require full and transparent access to any agreements signed. “I think that this has more political power and urgency behind it in getting things done than anything that I’ve ever seen in Springfield,” Walling said. “I think that people all over the state, bipartisan basis, are pushing legislators to act.” Walling and McCombie note that Illinois will continue to learn new information about data centers, so it is likely multiple plans will need to be passed to address issues that pop up over the next decade. State lawmakers return to Springfield Nov. 17 and only have six days of veto session. They could finalize data center regulations during lameduck session in early January if they fail to pass a bill this fall. Copyright 2026 WAND. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: POSCO Future M signs KRW 1,1 trillion LFP Cathode Material Supply Contract with SK On POSCO Future M (CEO EOM Gi Chen) has signed a large-scale supply contract with SK On for LFP (lithium iron phosphate) cathode materials. Hard on the heels of last month’s long-term agreement to supply 190,000 tons of LFP cathode materials to a Korean battery maker, the company has now secured another major contract as it moves into the LFP market in earnest. POSCO Future M has been working with SK On as a supplier of anode materials and plans to strengthen the partnership further through this contract, its first to supply SK On with cathode materials. The contract also means POSCO Future M now supplies cathode and anode materials to all three Korean battery makers, broadening its customer portfolio and putting its mid- to long-term growth on an even firmer foundation. The contract, signed on the 22nd, is worth approximately KRW 1.1 trillion over three years, from 2027 through 2029, and can be extended by an additional two years upon agreement between the two companies. While LFP batteries have lower power output than ternary batteries such as NCM (nickel-cobalt-manganese) and NCA (nickel-cobalt-aluminum), their strengths lie in competitive pricing and a long lifespan. With power demand recently surging due to the build-out of AI data centers, among other factors, demand for LFP batteries used in ESS is growing to ensure a stable power supply. LFP batteries are also increasingly being adopted in the electric vehicle market, particularly in entry-level models. POSCO Future M is actively responding to customer demand by adding LFP cathode materials to its existing portfolio centered on ternary (NCM and NCA) materials. The company recently completed converting part of its high-nickel cathode material production lines at the Pohang plant to LFP cathode material production, and is set to begin mass-production supply from the end of this year. POSCO Future M plans to continue expanding production capacity by converting more lines as further orders come in. Going forward, the company also plans to produce and supply LFP cathode materials with further improved cost competitiveness and quality by applying a new process that uses lithium from salt lakes in Argentina, drawing on raw material supply chain cooperation across POSCO group. POSCO Future M continues to hold discussions with major battery makers and automakers on supplying cathode and anode materials, backed by a diverse product portfolio and by a supply chain and technological capabilities that can navigate global trade regulations. The company is also stepping up the expansion of its production capacity. Its moves include a KRW 1 trillion long-term supply contract for synthetic graphite anode materials, signed with a global automaker in March this year, and plans to invest approximately KRW 357 billion in a new synthetic graphite anode material plant in Vietnam. A plant to process spherical graphite, an intermediate material for natural graphite anode materials, is under construction at the Saemangeum National Industrial Complex in Jeonbuk and is scheduled to begin trial operation in early 2027, with completion and full-scale mass production planned for the second half of the year. In July, POSCO group announced its future growth strategy, outlining a vision to build a Triple-Core system and become a “national supplier of critical resources.” The system spans industrial resources (steel), strategic resources (such as lithium, cathode and anode materials, and rare earths), and energy resources (LNG and renewable energy). In line with this strategy, POSCO Future M aims to build on its unrivaled technology to strengthen its business competitiveness and expand its markets, and to emerge as a global leader in the cathode and anode materials business, one of the pillars of the group’s strategic resources. artigo.texto: India's battery storage demand to hit 236.22 GWh by FY32, require Rs 3.49 trillion investment: Report Synopsis India's battery energy storage system market is expected to reach 236.22 GWh by FY2031-32. The country will require Rs 3.49 trillion in investments for this growth. Significant advancements in BESS deployment were noted between early and mid-2026. The government is providing extensive support through various initiatives and schemes. These measures aim to enhance project viability and stimulate private-sector participation in the energy storage sector. Furthermore, as of August 2026, 9.08 GWh of BESS capacity was operational, while 79.92 GWh was under construction, with 79.92 GWh under construction, 24.13 GWh awarded, and 63.53 GWh under tendering, taking the total operational and identified project capacity to 176.66 GWh, with the current CEA project pipeline scheduled for commissioning till FY2029-30. In capacity terms, the report noted, this represents approximately "75% of the NEP's projected FY2031-32 requirements, although the identified capacity is at different stages of development and is not yet fully operational." "The share of BESS in India's total energy storage requirement is expected to increase from ~42% in FY2026-27 to ~57% in FY2031-32," it said. The report estimated that India will require around Rs 3.49 trillion in investment in the sector by FY2031-32. Separately, the broader energy storage sector is expected to attract about Rs 4.79 trillion in investments by 2032. The report expects India's BESS market to expand strongly, supported by investments in domestic battery manufacturing, a sizeable project pipeline and government initiatives. Measures including Viability Gap Funding (VGF), the National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) Battery Storage and interstate transmission system (ISTS) charge waivers are expected to improve project viability and encourage private-sector participation. The government is also stepping up support for the sector. The Union Cabinet has approved the Rs 1.86 trillion PM-DHARA (PM-Developing Harmonized and Accelerated Renewable-energy Access) Scheme, which includes Rs 500 billion for the deployment of 50 GWh of BESS capacity by FY2032-33, it noted. artigo.texto: Note to readers • This story is made possible through a partnership between The Salt Lake Tribune and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization. As the number of planned data center projects seemingly explodes across Utah, most residents aren’t happy with how their elected leaders have handled them, according to a new survey. A vast majority of Utahns – 86% – also don’t feel the cost of data centers, including their water and energy demands, outweigh their touted economic benefits, according to results from Utah State University’s Community and Natural Resources Institute’s survey. And nearly 76% of residents oppose or strongly oppose building more data centers in Utah. The findings offer clues as to why the developments are facing intense backlash across the state, from Box Elder County to Spanish Fork to Utah’s coal country. “We thought it would be nice to have a representative sample of voices from across the state to see what people are thinking about this emergent issue so people can’t say that what they’re necessarily hearing is just the loudest voices,” said Jessica Schad, director of the institute and administrator of the survey. Researchers surveyed nearly 900 Utah residents about data centers in August. But they began preparing their study in the spring, before plans emerged for the massive Stratos hyperscale data campus in Box Elder County. That project, led by celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary, drew large crowds of protestors and factored heavily into Box Elder County commissioners and Senate President Stuart Adams losing their primaries. Schad had time to include a few questions about Stratos in the survey. Nearly 95% of respondents had heard about the project, and 78% either opposed or strongly opposed the project. “The thing that was most surprising to me,” Schad said, “was just how much people voiced a desire to be heard more in the process of data center development.” Eighty-five percent said it was “very important” to have a public process for locals to participate in decision-making about data centers, according to the survey results. Another 10% called it “somewhat important.” And 89% want the state to ensure the public and local residents can influence decisions about data centers. Details about other large data centers have emerged in the months since Stratos grabbed national headlines, including two sprawling data and energy sites planned for Millard County that will collectively consume more than 1.5 times energy than Stratos. More than 1,000 Tooele Valley residents signed a letter protesting a 500-megawatt data center and natural gas in their county near the Great Salt Lake. And details recently became public about a 9,000-acre computing, manufacturing and small modular nuclear reactor campus on Bureau of Land Management lands near Price. About 30% of residents said using nuclear energy sources would make them “slightly” or “much” more likely to support data centers, but 41% said it would increase their opposition. More than half — about 51% — said they would be more likely to support data centers if they relied on renewable energy. Only 18% said renewables would increase their opposition. Another 54% said using recycled water or non-drinking water would increase their support for data centers. Nearly 78% also want the state to enact environmental regulations for data centers, and 87% want regulations that restrict local water uses by the computing complexes. Another 79% want the state to restrict the volume of energy data centers consume. More than half of respondents — 56% — want the state to leave decisions about data centers to the local residents who will live near them. Only 19% want the state to leave those decisions to local governments. But an overwhelming majority of Utahns are also disappointed with how governments have handled data center development in the state so far. About 52% are “very dissatisfied” or “dissatisfied” with their local or city government, 58% feel that way about their county government, 76% feel that way about state lawmakers and 74% feel that way about Gov. Spencer Cox. Cox previously responded sharply when critics of the Stratos project voiced concerns that the project was moving too fast. “It’s the dumbest thing ever,” Cox said in April. “We think that taking time makes things better or safer. It absolutely does not.” The governor also said Utah had an “obligation” to build hyperscale data centers. But following statewide backlash, Cox has since walked back his stance. Still, 84% of survey respondents said the data center development process in Utah is moving too fast. And despite state and federal leaders touting national security and global competitiveness as a rationale for building data centers, only 35% of Utahns “agree” or “strongly agree” with those justifications. Even fewer, at 29%, agree or strongly agree that data centers are important for economic prosperity, while 31% feel they are important for scientific leadership. Tabitha Benney, a professor in the University of Utah’s School of Public Affairs, was not involved in the survey but reviewed its findings. She said the response rate was surprisingly small — the USU researchers mailed 20,000 randomly selected Utahns, but only 4.8% completed the survey online. Utahns who don’t understand data centers or aren’t following data center news may have been among those who opted not to respond, Benney said. “Overall, it seems like a decent survey,” Benney said. She added that the results aren’t surprising, particularly the overwhelmingly negative attitudes toward data centers and frustrations with lawmakers. “Decisions are being made behind closed doors in a way they weren’t before,” Benney said. “It’s a shame, in my opinion.” Slightly more men responded to the survey than women, and the average age of respondents was 51, with respondents ranging from 18 to 92 years old. artigo.texto: Charleston City Council introduced a slew of bills Monday night, including rules for data centers, a renewal plan for the East End and the reallocation of $300,000 in federal grant money. Data center regulations Bill 8097, written by Councilman Emmett Pepper and co-sponsored by council members Joe Solomon and Frank Annie, would require any data center plan to: Gain Planning Commission and council approval Face a public hearing Sign a community benefits agreement No data center has been proposed in Charleston, but Pepper said the bill is a needed precaution. “The goal is to make sure that if there are going to be data centers that come to the city, they’re developed in a responsible way that is good for the community and will benefit the community,” Pepper said. The bill would require data centers to be built at certain distances from homes and schools, with larger facilities pushed farther away. It covers facilities using up to 89 megawatts. State law bars cities from regulating larger ones. “As we’ve seen around the country, as data centers have gone in places, they are greatly increasing the cost for electric customers,” Pepper said. The bill also caps noise — with $5,000/day fines for noise violations — and requires the data center to have a plan in place to mitigate rising electricity costs and bring jobs into the city. The bill was referred to the Ordinance and Rules committee and the Planning, Streets and Traffic committee. Bill 8096, sponsored by Councilwoman Mary Beth Hoover, would adopt the East End renewal plan that council authorized the Charleston Urban Renewal Authority to draft. The plan would run through 2046. Most of the proposed work is on the streetscape: fixing sidewalks, adding public art and making intersections safer. The plan names no properties for purchase or demolition. It bars taking owner-occupied homes by eminent domain but allows eminent domain on rental properties only as a last resort after public input. The plan sets no price, pointing to tax credits and private investment to cover costs. It has been referred to council’s Urban Renewal and Economic Development Committee. Other bills The council also discussed a few other bills. Resolution 26-112, sponsored by Councilman Joseph Jenkins, would move $300,000 in federal Community Development Block Grant money to demolish a building at 915 Main St. The money would come from completed or canceled projects, including $122,809 from a 2025 ADA curb-cut project and $92,740 from a roof replacement at Sojourner’s homeless shelter, plus leftover contingency money. It has been referred to the Finance Committee. Resolution 26-114, also from Jenkins, would hand a stalled federal pandemic-relief project to Mountaineer Food Bank. In 2022, the city awarded the Partnership of African American Churches $440,000 in American Rescue Plan money to buy and redevelop the former Save a Lot on 748 Virginia St. W. PAAC and the city has not “satisfactorily performed the original project,” according to the resolution. The property has already been turned over to the city, which would then transfer it to Mountaineer Food Bank as a volunteer center where they store and distribute food. The resolution has been referred to the Finance Committee Bill 8099, from council members Solomon and Becky Ceperley, would expand public notice before the city permanently closes a street, alley or other public right of way. People who own property or live within 350 feet would be notified at least 15 days before the Planning Commission’s hearing. Petitioners would also have to name a council member willing to sponsor the closure, and nonprofits could ask the city attorney whether they qualify to receive the land as a donation. artigo.texto: Suzuki’s newly launched e-Sky relies on BYD’s LFP battery technology while targeting the most affordable position in Japan’s Kei EV market. Suzuki’s newly launched e-Sky has drawn attention for an important detail behind its competitive pricing: the electric Kei car uses battery technology supplied by Chinese automaker BYD. The collaboration has helped Suzuki position the e-Sky as Japan’s most affordable Kei-class electric vehicle. The e-Sky represents Suzuki’s first passenger Kei EV and has been developed specifically for Japan’s compact-car market. Rather than relying entirely on in-house battery development, Suzuki has partnered with BYD to keep production costs under control while offering practical electric range. 26 kWh BYD LFP Battery The Suzuki e-Sky is equipped with a 26 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery supplied through the BYD collaboration. Suzuki claims the battery enables a WLTP driving range of up to 310 km. The electric vehicle uses a dedicated EV platform and Suzuki’s own e-Axle drive system. Its compact dimensions measure 3,395 mm in length, 1,475 mm in width and 1,625 mm in height, while the wheelbase stretches to 2,460 mm. BYD Battery Helps Keep Costs Low Battery technology is a key part of the e-Sky’s pricing strategy. The model starts at 2.12 million yen, making it cheaper than several competing Kei EVs before government incentives are applied. Japan’s EV subsidy of 568,000 yen can reduce the effective consumer price to around 1.55 million yen. This puts the Suzuki e-Sky below the subsidised prices of rivals such as the BYD Racco and Nissan Sakura. The e-Sky also weighs approximately 1,030 kg, which is significantly lighter than the BYD Racco. Suzuki’s lower vehicle weight contributes to the model’s claimed driving range despite its relatively compact battery. Suzuki Targets 1,000 Monthly Sales Suzuki is offering the e-Sky in three variants. The entry-level version is primarily aimed at corporate customers and excludes certain equipment, including fast-charging capability, as part of the effort to maintain a lower price. Suzuki is targeting combined monthly sales of around 1,000 units for the three versions. The company’s strong position in Japan’s Kei-car segment gives the e-Sky an established customer base as it expands into electric mobility.

artigo.texto: O mercado brasileiro de sistemas de baterias para armazenar energia elétrica, conhecidos no setor como BESS, vive um boom de vendas puxado por instalações de menor porte em comércios, indústrias, condomínios e residências, segundo reportagem de Luciano Costa no Brazil Journal. Enquanto o leilão federal para grandes projetos segue previsto para dezembro sob incertezas, o segmento encontrou no varejo a via para crescer em ritmo recorde. Conforme levantamento da consultoria Greener citado na reportagem, as vendas e contratações de BESS somaram 730 MWh em 2025, mais do que a soma dos cinco anos anteriores. Nos seis primeiros meses de 2026, foram outros 504 MWh, caminho de um novo recorde histórico. Muitos desses projetos vêm acompanhados de painéis solares em telhados. O CEO da Greener, Marcio Takata, afirmou ao Brazil Journal que o leilão é relevante, mas que o BESS distribuído deve se firmar como um dos principais vetores de flexibilidade da rede elétrica. A trajetória lembra a da geração solar, que decolou com grandes usinas contratadas pelo governo e depois com telhados e miniusinas. Segundo a Aneel, a geração solar distribuída já soma mais de 53 GW no País, contra 23,6 GW das usinas centralizadas. O armazenamento acumulado no Brasil chega a 1,9 GWh, com companhias como WEG e Grupo Moura apostando no segmento. O leilão de dezembro deve contratar pelo menos 2 GW para operar quatro horas por dia, o equivalente a 8 GWh, segundo sinalizações de Brasília, ainda que parte do mercado espere volumes maiores. O Ministério de Minas e Energia também programou certames anuais até 2029 para reserva de capacidade, nos quais as baterias disputarão espaço com termelétricas e hidrelétricas reversíveis. Para André Millions, diretor da Thymos Capital, baterias e hidrelétricas reversíveis são hoje os temas mais quentes do setor. A reserva é considerada importante para a rede absorver a oscilação da geração eólica e solar, mas o certame está sob risco por causa do impasse sobre quem paga a conta dos projetos, conforme fontes do setor ouvidas pelo Brazil Journal. A regra atual divide o rateio entre todas as empresas de geração, o que ameaça levar o tema à Justiça, e o setor pressiona o governo a aprovar um projeto do deputado Arnaldo Jardim que transfere o custo aos consumidores.

artigo.texto: Cindy O’Neil understands the boom-and-bust cycles of industry. Her husband spent years working in Carbon County’s namesake coal mines. In this pocket of central Utah, energy and the economy have long been intrinsically linked, at great sacrifice to county residents. “We’ve had the coal. We’ve dealt, the whole community, with black lung,” O’Neil said. “The explosions, the fires and all the things that came along with it.” But a new industry and type of energy production is about to move near her rural home. And she says it has her and her neighbors even more worried than they were about the dangers that came from their long history with coal. “It’s all descending, these data centers,” said O’Neil, who tracks mysterious new projects in the works and shares updates on Facebook community pages. “They’re setting these things within a couple of miles of homes.” Her latest updates involve a lot of chatter about Valar Atomics, a nuclear startup. The company plans to build a mega-complex of 456 small modular reactors — a still largely untested and unproven technology in the United States — on the vast tracts of Bureau of Land Management land in the county. The project will store radioactive waste, according to a report from National Public Radio, and power an array of industrial activities, including data centers. “Project Beehive” has support from the state of Utah, and will include a square mile of state-owned trust lands. Another data center complex planned for the county, Altigen Energy’s “Jurassic Spark,” will cover hundreds of acres and include a massive natural gas plant. It’s an abrupt shift. Carbon County’s coal mines produced nearly 10 million tons of coal in 2006. But a shift to cheaper energy sources, like renewables and natural gas, along with depleted supplies in the coal seams, sank the region’s main economic engine in just a few decades. Since 2023, not a single pound of coal has been mined in Carbon County. “They say everything’s left us, and if we don’t grab these table scraps we’re not going to get anything,” said O’Neil. “I don’t think our county has to take the table scraps.” None of Carbon County’s new data center plans call for coal. The Utah Trust Lands Administration recently agreed to lease a square mile of its state-owned land for up to 100 years to Valar Atomics. The nuclear startup intends to use that lease to run some of its SMRs, process its uranium TRISO-fuel to feed the reactors, build water desalination, manufacture steel, refine critical minerals — and support data centers. The Valar site is expected to generate $35 million in lease rents over 50 years, according to information the Trust Lands Administration staff presented to its board last month. Revenue collected from the project benefits Utah schools. (The state agency declined to comment on the Valar project.) During that September board meeting, three Carbon County residents who are employed or expected to be employed by Valar spoke in favor of the project. All three of the Carbon County Commissioners also voiced their support. “[We] realize that this topic is a hot button now, along with data centers,” said Larry Jensen, one of the commissioners. “It’s important that you understand that the Carbon County Commissioners are committed to allowing these things to move forward. Even with the pushback — we realize that there are a few in our community who will push back — but the silent majority are the ones that we really represent.” Cheryl Lupo, a longtime resident of the county, balked at that assertion. She is running for a seat on the county commission this year. As an unaffiliated candidate, she had to collect 300 signatures to land on the ballot. She said the opinions she heard during that process were overwhelmingly opposed to data centers and nuclear plants. “People are up in arms,” Lupo said. “Torches and pitchforks. Because they’re not being heard.” Governor Spencer Cox, U.S. Senator John Curtis and other high-ranking Utah officials welcomed Valar to the state earlier this year, allowing it to test its “Ward250” microreactor at the San Rafael Energy Lab in neighboring Emery County. Valar announced it had achieved “self-sustaining criticality” in June – a process where atoms split and maintain a steady fission chain reaction without being fed more neutrons. The company has plans to power a 30-megawatt nuclear-powered AI data center in Emery County, too, in partnership with the computer-chip giant Nvidia. Small modular reactors have yet to be deployed for commercial use in the United States. During last week’s Trust Lands Administration meeting, Mike Nelson, the board’s chair, seemed to acknowledge that the deal with Valar came with some unknowns. “We weren’t always sure what to ask about,” Nelson said, while offering praise for the nuclear startup, “and probably still aren’t sure of everything to ask about because this is a first, right?” Utah has a troubled history with nuclear testing. Lupo’s mother was 38 years old when she died, and Lupo believes the cause was downwind effects from radioactive weapons testing in nearby Nevada during the 1950s. Her mother lived in Carbon County at the time. She believes the fallout caused her grandfather’s death, too. “I will never, ever be a proponent of nuclear,” Lupo said. Even before the proposal to build Valar’s complex started causing a stir, rumors swirled about the possibility of another data center campus in Carbon County. Altigen, a company that builds natural gas-power plants for data centers, has selected an area east of Wellington for its 1,200-acre “Jurassic Spark” project — nearly double the size of the Valar campus, according to meeting minutes from the local Community Economic Development Board. Plans call for building a 250-megawatt gas plant to power the complex initially, but it could eventually produce 3 gigawatts of electricity, according to Jensen. artigo.texto: South Texas to get $22B power project tied to data center The United States and South Korean governments are working together on a plan that would bring a large gas power plant to La Salle County, Texas, to directly power data centers. Project Star is a $22 billion power project According to the U.S. Department of Commerce, the 6.47 gigawatt combined-cycle gas power plant will be built in Encinal, Texas. The plant will be operated by Related Companies and NextEra Energy Resources, with the first stage expected to come online in 2029 and operate at full capacity in 2032. According to Related Digital, the power plant will be used to power a 5GW data center on an adjacent site, with the remaining power going to the Texas power grid. Related's project page states that the data center project will use a closed loop water cooling system that will use around the same amount of water daily as an office building. The power project is looking for ways to use produced water, water that is a byproduct of oil and natural gas extraction, for cooling. Power plant to bring 170 jobs to the area NextEra said construction on the project is expected to bring 8,400 jobs to the area. Once construction is complete, the power campus is expected to have 170 permanent jobs and the data center will create "hundreds of good-paying permanent jobs." What they're saying: "Project Star demonstrates how energy infrastructure and economic growth can advance together," said John Ketchum, chairman and CEO of NextEra Energy. "By bringing new generation online to serve new demand, we're helping strengthen reliability, support investment and jobs and protect electricity customers." The project comes as part of the implementation of the trade deal between Korea and the United States, announced on July 30, 2025, and the Strategic Investment MOU signed on Nov. 14 of that year. Those efforts aim to enhance cooperation between Korea and the United States in strategic industrial sectors such as energy and artificial intelligence. "I am excited to be working with two world class companies in Related Digital and NextEra Energy to develop Project Star," said Rod Lewis, Founder and CEO of Lewis Energy Group. "This project will bring much needed jobs to South Texas, add new power generation to be available to the state of Texas, and ensure the natural gas produced in the South Texas region provides direct economic benefits to our local communities. As a long-time ranching family and resident of La Salle and Webb Counties, we look forward to working with local communities to create a meaningful and environmentally responsible addition to the local economy." The Source: Information in this article comes from a release from NextEra Energy, the U.S. Dept. of Commerce and Related Digital.

artigo.texto: Telcomp cobra agilidade nas licenças para data centers Entidade relata demora superior à construção de empreendimentos e aponta impasses na regulamentação do Redata como entrave. A demora na emissão de licenças e as pendências na regulamentação do Redata estão entre os obstáculos à implantação de data centers no Brasil, segundo o presidente da Telcomp, Luiz Henrique Barbosa. Durante a abertura do Data Center World, nesta terça-feira, 6 de outubro, o dirigente defendeu maior previsibilidade para atrair investimentos e integrar o país às cadeias internacionais de infraestrutura digital. Barbosa relatou o caso de uma associada que aguardou dois anos por uma licença para atravessar uma rodovia no interior de São Paulo. Segundo ele, o prazo foi superior ao necessário para construir o próprio data center. Para o dirigente, situações desse tipo comprometem a segurança jurídica dos projetos. Ele afirmou que investidores estrangeiros comparam as condições brasileiras com as de outros mercados e que o país precisa considerar essa concorrência ao definir regras, tributos e procedimentos de licenciamento. A Telcomp reúne aproximadamente 60 empresas de diferentes segmentos, incluindo operadores de cabos submarinos, satélites, data centers e redes de transmissão de longa distância e metropolitanas. Impasse sobre equipamentos Barbosa também cobrou a conclusão da regulamentação do Redata. Segundo o presidente da Telcomp, há divergências com fabricantes nacionais de equipamentos, preocupados com o alcance dos benefícios para importações. Na avaliação do dirigente, a indefinição mantém investimentos parados. Ele defendeu que o regime seja entendido como uma forma de aproximar a tributação brasileira das condições oferecidas em outros países. No mesmo painel, Walter Wolff, diretor de projetos da Brasscom, afirmou que a regulamentação envolve discussões sobre os equipamentos contemplados e sobre o fornecimento de energia aos empreendimentos. Já o presidente da Equinix, Victor Arnaud, alertou que o detalhamento das regras pode comprometer os resultados do incentivo caso imponha burocracia excessiva aos projetos. Cabos submarinos e segurança jurídica Para exemplificar os efeitos internacionais de decisões sobre infraestrutura, Barbosa citou a proposta de instalação de uma usina de dessalinização na Praia do Futuro, em Fortaleza, nas proximidades de cabos submarinos. Segundo ele, a discussão gerou preocupação entre agentes de outros países porque as conexões que passam por Fortaleza também atendem ao tráfego internacional. O dirigente citou as ligações com a África, a Europa, os Estados Unidos e a Argentina para defender que decisões locais considerem o papel dessas redes. A relação entre data centers e telecomunicações também foi destacada pelo diretor jurídico da Conexis, Bruno Cavalcanti. Ele afirmou que a atração de investimentos em processamento depende de redes de fibra, backbones e conectividade de alta capacidade. Cavalcanti defendeu uma regulação responsiva, com espaço para atuação do mercado, e segurança jurídica para os investidores. Na avaliação do representante da Conexis, regras antecipadas que burocratizem a implantação dos empreendimentos podem prejudicar o crescimento do setor e a competitividade brasileira.

artigo.texto: Coordinating Minister for Food Zulkifli Hasan outlined three primary sectors open to green investment, including sustainable agriculture through low-emission rice cultivation, waste-to-energy processing, and marine conservation through blue carbon development. Jakarta (VNA) - Indonesia is offering carbon market incentive schemes to global business leaders investing in green projects across the archipelago, said Coordinating Minister for Food Zulkifli Hasan. artigo.texto: An industrial park in Irvine, California, may seem an odd spot to show off technology that wouldn’t be out of place in Dune, but that’s what’s happening on a sweltering September morning. The temperature is already over 80 degrees Fahrenheit as the sun rises on a 20-foot-tall, metal-clad machine in the parking lot of Atoco, an Irvine, California-based startup. Engineers open panels to check systems and an iPad that shows a steadily ascending line that reveals the device’s purpose: harvesting water from thin air using special materials known as metal organic frameworks, or MOFs. The materials won Omar Yaghi, the company’s founder, the Nobel Prize for chemistry in 2025, and Atoco has shown they work in prototypes capable of producing gallons of water per day. What’s unique about this iteration of Atoco’s technology is what it doesn’t require. No grid connection or even electricity is needed to grab water from the air at the microscopic level, nor is it required to in turn wring the water out of the materials in a form useful for humans. Instead, all that’s needed is low-level industrial heat. That, Atoco says, makes them a perfect candidate to hook up with AI data centers, which throw off loads of waste heat as servers churn out everything from math proofs to virtual editors while also often requiring massive amounts of water. “We were not really thinking of AI data centers,” four or five years ago, says Atoco CEO Samer Taha. But the massive buildout has created an opportunity for the startup that could allow it to get a step closer to its larger goal of ensuring people living in water-stressed regions have control over an increasingly precious resource. When Yaghi was a PhD student, he says, creating something like MOFs was “every chemist’s dream.” Part of his Nobel-winning work over the past 20 years has been taking theoretical research into the real world, creating a stable molecular structure that links organic material with metal ions. The structure of a MOF looks somewhat “like a jungle gym on a playground,” says Seth Cohen, the dean of the School of Physical Sciences at UC Irvine. MOFs are essentially “molecular sponges—they’re a solid material that’s very, very good at absorbing other molecules,” says Cohen, who is not involved with Atoco. Like a sponge, the materials can also be wrung out using methods including heat to release whatever they’re holding onto. These jungle-gym-like frameworks create open spaces on the microscopic level that can hold an unbelievable amount of material, and small tweaks can yield even more interior space. “The footage of a gram of MOF could cover two football fields,” Yaghi explains. “They can store hydrogen in there to make clean energy, or you could store CO2 in there to make clean air. Or, in this case, you can store water.” Atoco has developed what Taha calls “precision materials” with a specific objective of being able to harvest water, release it, and then do it over again and again. He quips that, as vice president of R&D Benjie Limketkai puts it, the material has to like water but not love it. To succeed commercially, it also has to use as little energy as possible. “The scientists reach a level of precision [where] we really know even the angle of the atom,” in a given material, Taha says. In Atoco’s technology, air passes through the MOF, which has been specially tailored to attract water molecules. Those molecules adhere to the pores. But the material feels completely dry to the touch even when saturated, and squeezing it doesn’t release a single drop. (Taha was kind enough to let WIRED try our hand at it.) Instead, the company relies on heat to release the captured molecules. There are other means of harvesting water. Cohen notes that silica, a popular desiccant, can also pull water out of air, but it doesn’t hold as much moisture and requires you to “heat the heck out of it to get the water back out,” he says. The monolith in the parking lot of the company’s Irvine facility is the culmination of decades of precision development. Atoco’s materials and approach allow its off-grid system to work even when relative humidity is in the teens. The MOFs in the device can harvest and release water with heat as low as 100 degrees Fahrenheit, Taha says. With no data center nearby, Atoco’s team simulated it by piping heat from a source that was around 150 degrees Fahrenheit. A solar panel powers various systems but not the water-harvesting operation itself, making the metal-clad machine eerily quiet. Cars pulling into the adjacent businesses create more of a sonic disruption, but Taha is ready to show the device has been working hard. It’s a little after 9 am, and the temperature is over 90 degrees Fahrenheit when he pushes a button on the side and turns a spigot. Out tumbles a clear stream of water that looks good enough to drink. Unfortunately it’s not on offer for legal liability reasons, though Taha notes it’s the equivalent of distilled water, because Atoco’s MOFs aren’t built to gather air pollution. Tossing it in the bushes, Taha retreats to an air-conditioned conference room where he lays out the company’s vision for its new machine. “Roughly 70 percent of the industrial waste heat is low-grade, unutilized, thrown into oceans or into the air,” he says. “If you convert that waste heat to clean water using our technology, you're talking about trillions of liters of clean water.” Data centers are an increasingly big source of that waste heat, with a single facility capable of pumping out as much heat as tens of thousands of homes. Operators are forced to disperse that heat into the surrounding environment, creating heat islands, while also paying for various types of cooling systems. Many of those cooling systems also rely on water, and some can consume millions of gallons per day. Atoco’s technology would thus address two of data centers’ biggest problems. artigo.texto: The Yankton County Commission is split on whether to enact a moratorium, or pause, on electronic energy storage facilities in the county. Commissioners Ryan Heine and Dan Klimisch are taking different approaches. Heine has drafted a resolution calling for a moratorium until new ordinances are written, while Klimisch believes the county can tighten up zoning definitions or use conditional-use permits. In the end, Heine’s resolution for a moratorium will be published and placed on the next agenda. The Planning and Zoning (P&Z) Commission will also review ordinance definitions at its next meeting. Heine said an electronic energy storage company had shown interest in Yankton County. He was concerned about the storage of large batteries, particularly lithium ones that could become flammable and pose a public health and safety risk. Last month, Heine said he drafted a resolution that he wanted published for public review, so it was ready for discussion and action. At this week’s meeting, Heine expressed frustration at what he saw as a lack of movement. He showed anger that his resolution hadn’t been published since the last meeting and wasn’t ready for action. “That’s the point of a moratorium – when you know that there is something that is not well defined – and the pressure is right there on our front door now,” he said. Auditor Patty Hojem replied that he hadn’t provided her with a copy of the resolution for publishing or distribution. Heine responded that he would email her a copy yet that evening. NEW DISCUSSION In response to the previous discussion, Klimisch added an agenda item to this week’s meeting calling for “discussion on utility facilities and service establishments.” Klimisch informed the commission that he and Deputy Zoning Administrator Bill Conkling discussed how the county zoning ordinances would treat an electronic energy storage facility. Klimisch believes the current ordinances can be revised to meet future needs. He recommended that the P&Z change ordinances to move certain facilities from permitted to conditional use. Klimisch acknowledged that more work and discussion may be needed down the line. However, he felt the tools were in place for addressing the storage facilities. Currently, companies that meet requirements for a service establishment or utility permitted use are issued a building permit. With a CUP, the process would require P&Z oversight, public hearing and final county commission action. Klimisch believes the change would provide an immediate answer, at least for now. “It’s kind of a stop-gap measure,” he added. THE RESPONSE Heine feared that relying on conditional-use permits could create uncertainty. “How do you do business in a county where the rules are not consistent for everyone?” he asked. “What I’m saying is, we should avoid trying to legislate on the fly with conditions and hoping the CUP process can do big things,” Heine added. The county officials talked about current definitions of a service establishment. They also discussed the impact of placing every service establishment under a conditional-use permit. The commissioners talked about striking a balance between protecting the public and overburdening businesses and the P&Z with too many definitions and regulations. Conkling said he saw merits in both approaches. “I don’t want to see everything have to go under a microscope,” he said, but he also agreed that definitions may need tweaking for greater clarification. Klimisch said he didn’t want to declare frequent moratoriums for every new development or situation that arises. Heine countered that the moratoriums can be done only for specific matters, such as the possible electronic energy storage facility and aren’t needed for things that don’t exist. OTHER VOICES Commissioner Wanda Howey-Fox pointed to the provisions in the current zoning ordinances. She used the example of the public input on a controversial project. In that case, nearby residents would be notified of such an application, public notices would be published, the P&Z would hold hearings and public comments would be received both for and against such establishments. “Isn’t that the purpose of the Planning and Zoning Commission?” she asked. County Commission Chairman John Marquardt noted the application fees would raise revenue for the county, while others spoke about the process’ transparency. Commissioner Don Kettering asked about any impact on the county’s budget and financial situation. At that point, Heine raised his concerns about the county’s past use of conditional-use permits and what he considered widely ranging decisions. “I am very concerned about how we use CUPs and try to put conditions on businesses and projects, and they are not the same across the board,” he said. “I feel using that method to regulate is really dangerous for our county.” Yankton County is moving toward making everything CUPs, Heine said. “Anything that has any ambiguity in there, it’s going to be a CUP,” he said. “And then we can make up rules on the fly and hope that we’re consistent through the various changes in our board – and hope no on sues us for being inconsistent.” WHAT’S AHEAD In the end, the commissioners agreed to publish Heine’s moratorium resolution and place it on the Oct. 20 agenda. Conkling asked if the commissioners also wanted P&Z to review ordinance definitions and make recommendations at its next meeting. “When these (definitions) were written, the landscape was different, development was different,” he said. “We’ve got new things coming in, and so it’s not a bad idea to review those.” The commission agreed to the P&Z review and recommendations as part of the process.

artigo.texto: A U.K. homeowner says a new 10-kilowatt-hour battery setup sharply reduced peak-time grid use in its first week, offering an early example of how pairing battery storage with rooftop solar can cut electricity costs on a time-of-use tariff. For households dealing with high utility rates and unpredictable weather, that kind of system can provide more control. Here's what to know According to a Reddit post, the setup uses two hardwired Anker Solarbank 4 Pro units stacked for a total of 10 kWh, along with four 410-watt solar panels feeding the MPPT inputs. The household is on Octopus Go, with electricity priced at 8.5p overnight and 30.1p during the day, and the poster said daytime grid imports dropped from roughly 80 kWh before installation to around 15 kWh. Based on those numbers, the poster said the first week delivered a net saving of about £16.50 (~$21.90 USD). They estimated that roughly 65 kWh of electricity that otherwise would have been bought at peak rates was avoided. The panels generated about 40 kWh in total, with around 30 kWh stored in the battery while the household was at work and 10 kWh used directly in the home as it was produced. That meant only about 35 kWh had to be added during the overnight charging window, at a cost of around £3 (~$4). Adding battery storage is one of the best ways to protect your home during outages, save money on energy, and keep more of your solar power available when you actually need it. If you want to explore your options, EnergySage can help you compare home battery storage choices and get competitive installation estimates. More background The post also highlighted the limitations of a modest-sized battery during colder weather. The original poster said, "Two evenings we had the heating on and the stack ran out before 00:30, so those last couple of hours came straight off the grid." They also cautioned that the system could be under more pressure in winter, when solar production is likely to fall. Still, other commenters described similarly strong solar performance. "I generated 174kWh since I had my system installed on September 10th," a commenter wrote. "8 x 495 panels spread 4 east and 4 west. Cannot wait for next summer." Battery storage can also help households rely less on the grid by shifting cheap overnight electricity into the more expensive part of the day and by storing solar power that would otherwise be exported or go unused. What can be done? "40kWh is very good for 4x 410W panels at the end of September," a commenter reacted. "Must have been much more sunny than average back home. It will be interesting to see your data longer term. It's definitely the way to go though." If you're thinking along those lines, EnergySage has teamed up with the electrification brand Qmerit to guarantee you get the best price on home battery storage solutions. Another option is Pila, which offers excellent battery backup choices. Its plug-and-play batteries cost a fraction of a whole-home backup system. Where can I learn more? Home batteries and solar are reshaping how communities manage electricity costs. • In the U.K., a proposal says neighborhood-scale batteries could cut bills by storing cheap power. • In England, residents raised £440,000 for the U.K.'s first community-owned battery to capture excess solar.
