artigo.texto: Russian internet giant Yandex suspended operations at one of its key data centers on Thursday after a drone strike as Ukraine continues to target the country's infrastructure. The attack caused a fire at the company's data center in Sasovo, Ryazan, in western Russia, and affected part of its infrastructure, Yandex said in a statement to CNBC. The data center has stopped operating entirely, and some Yandex services may be unavailable to users, it added. "There are no casualties, and emergency services are on site dealing with the aftermath," Yandex said. Moscow-headquartered Yandex, known as the Google of Russia, provides the country's most widely used search engine. It also developed the region's leading generative AI model, YandexGPT. Although Ukraine has not claimed responsibility for the Yandex attack, it has been stepping up its attacks on Russian infrastructure, including energy, over recent months, such as targeting Russian oil refineries, which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said are used to "finance the war and the killing of Ukrainians." Ukraine also increased attacks on Russian retail giant Wildberries, a critical part of the consumer infrastructure. Last week, Zelenskyy said the country will double down on its attacks on Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of airstrikes from Moscow designed to force people to leave Kyiv and other cities. Kyiv's power issues Emergency power cuts were enforced in Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, on Thursday due to ongoing Russian air strikes on the country's power grid. Last week, Russia hit key facilities in Kyiv and other major cities across the country, as it looks to destabilize Ukraine's energy foundation ahead of the winter season, threatening heating and other essential services for civilians. In response, Ukraine has been attacking Russia's fuel and energy facilities, with Zelenskyy warning Russian President Vladimir Putin at the United Nations General Assembly in September that Kyiv would make winter painful for Russia if the two sides were unable to come to an energy truce. "Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us. But in response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too," Zelenskyy said on Sept. 23.

artigo.texto: Delray Beach, FL, Oct. 07, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- The global Data Center Energy Storage Systems Market is projected to grow from USD 5.17 billion in 2026 to USD 10.48 billion by 2032, registering a CAGR of 12.5% during 2026–2032. Growth is driven by rising AI and hyperscale workloads, increasing data center power demand, renewable energy integration, and the need for resilient and flexible power infrastructure. Key Players: Tesla, Panasonic Holdings, Samsung SDI, LG Energy Solution, CATL, BYD, Schneider Electric, Vertiv, Eaton, ABB, Siemens Energy, Delta Electronics, Hitachi Energy, Fluence, and Saft. Why This Market Matters Data centers are facing rapidly increasing electricity requirements as AI, cloud computing, and high-performance workloads increase computing density. Energy storage systems provide backup power while also supporting peak-load management, power quality, renewable integration, and grid services. Market Overview The market covers Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), Flywheel Energy Storage Systems (FESS), Supercapacitors, and other technologies, including hydrogen-based storage. ESS applications are expanding beyond conventional backup power toward energy optimization, peak-load management, renewable integration, and grid support. Analyst Perspective The transition toward AI-driven data centers is increasing both power density and power fluctuations. This is creating demand for storage technologies that can provide rapid response, reliable backup, and greater flexibility in managing electricity demand. The emergence of hybrid and multi-technology ESS architectures is also creating opportunities to combine different storage technologies according to specific data center requirements. By Energy Storage Technology — Supercapacitors Grow Fastest Supercapacitor energy storage systems are projected to register the highest CAGR of 16.5% during 2026–2032. Their rapid power delivery and ability to withstand frequent charge-discharge cycles make them suitable for managing short-duration power fluctuations, power quality, and peak-shaving requirements in AI-intensive facilities. By Data Center Type — Cloud & Hyperscale Leads Growth Cloud & hyperscale data centers are expected to record the fastest growth, with a 14.8% CAGR. Increasing AI workloads, cloud adoption, and expansion of large-scale digital infrastructure are increasing requirements for reliable and flexible power systems. By Application — Renewable Integration & Grid Services Renewable integration & grid services is expected to register the highest CAGR of 18.3%. Energy storage enables data centers to manage renewable-energy intermittency, balance electricity supply and demand, and improve overall energy flexibility. Regional Analysis North America — Largest Market North America is expected to account for the largest share of the global market, supported by its established data center infrastructure and strong investments in cloud computing, AI, and digital services. The region's large hyperscale, enterprise, and colocation ecosystem is creating significant demand for reliable power and energy management solutions. Asia Pacific — Fastest-Growing Region Asia Pacific is projected to register the highest CAGR during 2026–2032. Rapid digitalization, expanding cloud and AI infrastructure, and increasing data center construction are driving demand for energy storage solutions across the region. Key Industry Trends AI-driven power demand: Higher computing density is increasing data center electricity requirements. Renewable Integration: ESS is increasingly used to manage intermittent renewable power. Hybrid ESS Architectures: Multiple storage technologies are being combined for different power requirements. Peak-load Management: Energy storage can help manage periods of high electricity demand. Smart Energy Management: AI-enabled monitoring and predictive management are emerging opportunities. Market Dynamics Key Drivers Accelerating investments in AI-driven and hyperscale data centers Expanding ESS adoption across backup, energy optimization, and grid-support applications Key Restraint High upfront capital requirements for ESS deployment Key Opportunities Growing retrofit demand for higher power density and resilience Hybrid and multi-technology ESS architectures Key Challenges Complex ESS integration with existing data center power infrastructure Safety and thermal management across different ESS technologies. Competitive Landscape The market includes major battery, energy-storage, power-management, and data center infrastructure companies. Key Players Tesla Panasonic Holdings Corporation Samsung SDI LG Energy Solution Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. (CATL) BYD Schneider Electric Vertiv Eaton ABB Siemens Energy Delta Electronics Hitachi Energy Fluence Saft Recent Industry Developments June 2026: Schneider Electric launched the ASCO 300 SERIES Multi-Voltage Transfer Switch for backup power architectures. artigo.texto: O projeto em Abu Dhabi combina painéis fotovoltaicos e armazenamento em baterias de escala gigante para superar a intermitência do sol e alimentar data centers de inteligência artificial sem parar. Como a luz do sol consegue gerar eletricidade durante a noite inteira? Você já percebeu como uma luminária solar de jardim se apaga poucas horas após o anoitecer? Em uma rede elétrica industrial, essa oscilação causaria apagões imediatos em fábricas e servidores de computadores. Para evitar falhas, o sistema usa uma técnica de superdimensionamento de captação combinada com armazenamento imediato, chamada de geração ininterrupta Round-the-Clock (RTC). A usina gera 5,2 GW em horário de pico, volume mais de cinco vezes superior à capacidade de entrega contínua. Esse excedente diurno carrega um sistema de armazenamento em baterias BESS (Battery Energy Storage System) de 19 GWh, quantidade suficiente para abastecer centenas de milhares de casas por uma noite inteira. Assim, a energia flui de forma estável para a rede sem depender de usinas a gás. Qual é o tamanho e a capacidade do maior complexo solar e de baterias do mundo? Projetado pela estatal Masdar e pela concessionária EWEC com investimento de US$ 6,1 bilhões, o complexo reúne números inéditos na engenharia de energia global. Capacidade fotovoltaica total: 5,2 GW em corrente contínua instalados em painéis de alta eficiência no deserto de Abu Dhabi. - Armazenamento em baterias: capacidade nominal de 19 GWh em módulos de íon de lítio acoplados à rede. - Fornecimento contínuo garantido: entrega firme de 1 GW de potência limpa sem interrupção 24 horas por dia. - Aporte financeiro: orçamento fechado de US$ 6,1 bilhões com consórcio bancário internacional. - Previsão de operação: início de funcionamento comercial programado para o ano de 2027. Como o sistema gerencia a oscilação entre o dia e a noite na prática? Durante as horas de sol forte no deserto, os 5,2 GW de painéis solares produzem energia máxima. Os inversores centrais direcionam 1 GW direto para a rede elétrica e enviam os 4,2 GW restantes para carregar os bancos de baterias em contêineres climatizados. Quando o sol se põe, o sistema de controle inteligente chaveia a fonte em milissegundos sem deixar a voltagem cair. As baterias assumem a descarga e mantêm a transmissão de 1 GW até o alvorecer seguinte, garantindo fornecimento ininterrupto para infraestruturas críticas. Onde assistir aos detalhes do projeto gigawatt de energia solar e baterias? Engenheiros da empresa estatal Masdar e da parceira construtora PowerChina detalharam os desafios de erguer uma infraestrutura desse porte no clima desértico. A instalação exige milhares de rastreadores solares e estruturas de climatização para evitar o superaquecimento dos módulos de bateria. O vídeo oficial de apresentação mostra a maquete técnica, o canteiro de obras e a arquitetura do sistema elétrico que vai abastecer os novos data centers de inteligência artificial da região. Abaixo, um vídeo do canal oficial da Masdar que aprofunda o tema: Quais normas internacionais garantem a segurança de baterias em escala de gigawatt? Projetos de armazenamento em baterias deste porte precisam cumprir rigorosos padrões globais de segurança contra incêndios e gerenciamento térmico, como as normas IEC 62933 para sistemas BESS e a NFPA 855 para prevenção de riscos em baterias de íon de lítio. Além disso, a conexão com a rede de alta tensão segue a norma IEEE 2800, garantindo que as baterias consigam estabilizar a frequência e a voltagem do sistema elétrico sem causar oscilações no grid nacional. Quando é necessário contratar um engenheiro eletricista especializado em energia renovável? Seja para projetar um parque solar comercial ou instalar um sistema de baterias industrial, é fundamental contar com um engenheiro eletricista ou um especialista em sistemas de energia para dimensionar a carga e a proteção contra surtos. Projetos de armazenamento envolvem alta densidade energética e riscos térmicos que não permitem improvisos. Uma avaliação técnica incorreta pode resultar em curtos-circuitos, perda de eficiência das células de bateria ou desaprovação junto à distribuidora de energia local. Contexto importante: Este artigo é informativo. Para projetos estruturais e elétricos locais similares, recomenda-se avaliação de engenheiro eletricista ou especialista em engenharia de energia, especialmente em contextos de risco de sobrecarga, aquecimento térmico ou integração com a rede elétrica.

artigo.texto: Vishay Battery Show North America 2026 – Vishay Intertechnology, Inc. (NYSE: VSH) announced that the company will showcase its latest passive component technologies, semiconductors, and reference designs at The Battery Show North America 2026, taking place October 12–15 in Detroit (Booth 4807). At the event, Vishay will highlight solutions that address key design challenges in battery management, protection, and high voltage power conversion for electric vehicles and energy storage systems. At The Battery Show North America 2026, Vishay will present: - Passives: - AEC-Q200 qualified NTC thermistor solutions that enable fast, accurate, and stable temperature monitoring in battery cells, modules, and packs, supporting thermal runaway mitigation, charging optimization, and extended battery life - UL-recognized resettable overcurrent protection solutions that help safeguard battery packs, charging circuits, and auxiliary power networks from fault conditions for increased system safety and reliability - Semiconductors: - Gen 5 TrenchFET® MOSFET technology engineered to reduce figure of merit (FOM) for increased efficiency in power conversion applications - P-channel MOSFET solutions and Gen 3 MaxSiC silicon carbide (SiC) trench MOSFETs for high voltage power conversion - Latest-generation SiC Schottky diodes, FRED Hyperfast rectifiers, and TMBS® technologies designed to reduce power losses and provide high efficiency switching and rectification - Automotive qualified optoelectronic solutions for battery systems, including isolated MOSFET drivers, optical cell to cell balancing, and photo relays for leakage detection at load voltages up to 1500 V. The portfolio also includes a wide body phototransistor optocoupler with 11 mm creepage and a high speed optocoupler supporting CAN, LIN, SPI, and I2C communication up to 1 MBd. - Reference Designs: - Active discharge circuit reference designs providing reliable solutions for discharging stored energy in 400 V and 800 V DC-Link capacitors, helping automotive systems reach safe voltage levels within required timeframes - An intelligent battery shunt sensor reference design that enables high bandwidth, accurate current and voltage measurements across a wide temperature range without temperature compensation At Booth 4807, Vishay experts will also be available to discuss customer design challenges across battery management systems, onboard chargers, DC/DC converters, traction inverters, and high voltage power architectures. Attendees are invited to bring their questions, schematics, requirements, and design goals to explore system-level solutions and design tradeoffs with Vishay’s technical experts. Further information, including a meeting request form, is available here. For more information visit: www.Vishay.com.

Continue reading On Tuesday morning, Zsolt Tárkányi, a member of the National Assembly from TISZA, published seven pages of documents on social media regarding the agreement signed for the Chinese battery factory in Debrecen (eastern Hungary), Világgazdaság reported. The tone of the post suggests that this politician strongly disapproves of what the Orbán government promised the world’s largest battery manufacturer to persuade it to build its next plant in Hungary. However, upon reviewing the letter of intent, no glaringly unusual promises can be found in it; rather, it can be concluded that the previous FIDESZ-KDNP-led cabinet sought to make a good offer to the Chinese side. This is, of course, no coincidence, since when this agreement was reached, CATL was considering a massive investment totaling 7.3 billion euros to build a battery manufacturing plant with an annual capacity of 100 GWh. The Hungarian government, for its part, expressed its intention to support the implementation of the planned investment in Hungary at the priority site in Debrecen that CATL was considering. This is because the Chinese side had previously considered Hungary as a potential investment location after deciding to expand its manufacturing presence outside of China. The fact that CATL ultimately chose Debrecen was by no means a foregone conclusion, as several European countries—including Western ones—were competing for the project. In other words, the Orbán government’s proposal deserves to be evaluated from this perspective: it fought hard to win the Chinese company’s favor in a highly competitive situation, securing a commitment to invest more than 2,600 billion forints here. Hungary may have caught the attention of the Chinese because, by that time, it had already become one of the most attractive destinations for direct foreign investment (FDI) by major battery manufacturers. According to the Orbán government’s view, the related large-scale investment projects contribute significantly to the country’s economic development. In addition, they have a substantial impact on long-term employment, technology transfer, and cluster effects, as well as stimulating industrial and technological development. It is a fact that, thanks to FDI, Hungary’s innovation performance has improved rapidly and significantly in recent years. Zsolt Tárkányi, however, focuses not on this but on the fact that the Chinese investment was granted VIP status. In reality, though, this simply refers to a completely standard category. The point is that with the establishment of the Debrecen Southern Industrial Park in 2015, Debrecen committed itself to attracting future industrial investments to boost economic growth in the region and in Hungary. To support the development of the Industrial Park, the Orbán government designated existing and future investments in the Industrial Park as projects of priority importance to the Hungarian economy. This is what the “VIP Status” referred to in the recently published cooperation agreement signifies. The Orbán government was aware that CATL’s potential investment and other industrial developments in the priority region would pose infrastructure challenges. Therefore, as a prerequisite, it ensured that adequate public utilities would be developed and made available to all investments in the region. It decided to provide funding for the existing utility infrastructure and the utility development program in the area where CATL plans to carry out its project. The Chinese side had already indicated its potential utility needs—including water, gas, wastewater, and electricity—in this document, but Zsolt Tárkányi redacted these details. It was also put in writing that the Hungarian government would do everything in its power to ensure that airlines establish regular flights between Debrecen and China, either directly or with layovers in Türkiye or the United Arab Emirates. As is the case with many other major investment projects, the government at the time would also provide other (including non-financial) support in connection with the CATL plant, such as Tárkányi took particular issue with the fact that CATL had been promised tax breaks on several counts. Specifically, the development tax credit would have entailed a reduction of up to 80% of the corporate income tax (CIT) liability for a maximum of 13 tax years, subject to European Union approval once the national threshold was exceeded. However, based on the document, cash grants for innovation would also be available for innovation projects, covering up to 25% of the costs. At the same time, it is important to emphasize that the published letter of intent cannot be considered legally binding. It also states that any transaction between the parties remains subject to the conclusion of a final, written, and signed agreement(s), as well as approval by CATL’s general meeting, the relevant Chinese government authorities, the Hungarian government, and the European Commission. artigo.texto: Next Upcoming Virtual Hold onto Your Tax Credits: How to Get Ahead of the 2027 Deadline By Canary Media This article is part of the series “Power Struggle: Building Clean Energy in Rural America.” Read more. The soil in northwest Iowa is so fertile it’s referred to as “black gold.” “It’s incredibly rich, wonderful topsoil from thousands of years of silty deposits from the Missouri River,” said Luke Seaberg, a researcher at Iowa State University’s extension program. So rich that some counties restrict development on land that scores especially high on the state’s official Corn Suitability Rating. The Smith family has been farming that soil for six generations in Cherokee County, population 11,000. But the corn market has been depressed lately, prompting the three Smith brothers to consider other uses for a 160-acre parcel, 10% of their farmland. Looking at rising beef prices and the region’s ballooning energy demand, they landed on an idea: Graze cows amid rows of solar panels. “We’re trying to diversify into another revenue stream. The cattle business is really good right now, and grain has been not as good,” Mark Smith told me over the phone, as he drove across the state for his son’s high school football game. “With solar, we can put cornfields back to pasture. Solar revenue plus cattle revenue makes it work.” But to loft the solar panels up above the butting heads of grazing cattle costs more than a regular solar installation; indeed, this type of agrivoltaics only recently entered commercial-scale use, at a 40-acre, 3-megawatt site in Tennessee developed by Silicon Ranch. To mitigate the extra cost, the Smiths want to pair 30 megawatts of cattle-friendly solar capacity with a 25-megawatt/100-megawatt-hour battery composed of modular containerized units covering about an acre and a half. The Smith brothers’ desire to install batteries on their land, though, set them on a collision course with local authorities. When the county supervisors heard of the plan, they approved an indefinite moratorium on March 24, blocking any battery projects in the county. Similar bans are popping up around the country as communities grapple with the real and perceived risks of lithium-ion batteries, which rose from obscurity over the last decade and now constitute the largest source of on-demand power getting built in the U.S. In many counties, this story ends with the battery moratorium, stymieing new emissions-free power capacity at a time when everyone from climate advocates to AI giants to the Trump administration wants to see more batteries get built. But the Smiths found an ally in Supervisor Shane Bellefy, the lone vote against the moratorium. Together, they set out to flip the county back to a place that lets landowners decide what to do on their acreage. Within just five months, they succeeded. Iowa subscribes to the “home rule” philosophy, whereby the state constitution leaves many decisions up to city or county governments, Seaberg said. But even those local authorities typically take a hands-off approach. The state’s “right to farm” law blocks local governments from regulating what landowners choose to grow or raise on their farmland. Some rural counties don’t even have a zoning code. “Your nearest neighbor might be 5 or 10 miles down the road,” Seaberg explained. “The general policy of county supervisors was, folks can do what they want to do with their land.” That attitude started to shift after the onshore wind boom came to Iowa in the early 2000s. The state has since added 13 gigawatts and remains the nation’s top state for share of wind energy produced. But in some rural counties, the nonexistent zoning code enabled a frenzy of development that “left a bad taste in their mouths,” Seaberg said. Now some counties have added land use regulations — but only for wind and solar. In Cherokee County, an earlier proposed 900-acre solar project prompted the supervisors to throw up a solar moratorium last year. But they subsequently worked through their concerns with the technology and adopted an ordinance allowing large-scale solar, with some restrictions. The March 2026 battery moratorium, though, would block the Smiths’ project, jeopardizing tens of millions of dollars in financing that the developers had lined up from investment banks. The Smiths might have had a case to challenge the moratorium on procedural grounds, since it passed without the usual multiple readings and lacked a specified time frame. But instead, they opted for persuasion. After the moratorium was approved, it fell to the county zoning board to compose a long-term ordinance to govern battery development. That body held a public meeting in May where the Smiths testified about their plans. The family also invited Seaberg to answer the community’s questions about battery technology based on Iowa State University’s independent research. The Smiths explained what they wanted to build on their land in partnership with energy developer Nomad Infrastructure. The Indiana-based firm has considerable experience constructing solar and battery projects, and one brother, Thomas Smith, works there as an engineer. They had gotten permission from the local rural electric cooperative, Mark Smith noted, to transmit the generation over the wires and sell it in the broader regional grid, run by the Midcontinent Independent System Operator. The MISO grid has very high rates of wind and solar production, but batteries are just starting to proliferate there. Meanwhile, data center expansion is driving up electricity demand in the region to never-before-seen heights, making for auspicious conditions to sell on-demand power from a battery. Bellefy, who works as a banker, pitched his fellow supervisors on the economic potential of allowing the project to move forward. The Smith installation would involve investing upwards of $80 million, which could generate $60,000 to $80,000 in new county tax revenue annually, Bellefy estimated. “Land in Iowa is our

artigo.texto: O data center da Omnia no Ceará, com investimento total estimado em R$ 200 bilhões, está sendo construído no Complexo do Pecém para atender à ByteDance, empresa chinesa responsável pelo TikTok. A infraestrutura permitirá exportar serviços de processamento de dados, incluindo aplicações de inteligência artificial, para operações globais. A destinação comercial ganha relevância diante da dimensão apresentada nessa quarta-feira (07/10), durante o Siará Tech Summit 2026. Segundo Bruno Patrocínio, engenheiro-chefe da Omnia Data Centers, a primeira fase terá 200 megawatts (MW) de capacidade de tecnologia da informação (TI), o equivalente a 28,5% dos aproximadamente 700 MW atualmente instalados nos demais centros de dados brasileiros. Essa expansão, entretanto, não representa necessariamente uma nova oferta de processamento disponível para contratação por empresas nacionais. A capacidade inicial já está vinculada à ByteDance, conforme informações confirmadas anteriormente pela companhia e divulgadas pela Reuters. Data center da Omnia no Ceará terá operação voltada à exportação O empreendimento no Pecém foi estruturado para fornecer serviços digitais a operações globais, incluindo treinamento de inteligência artificial, armazenamento em nuvem e processamento de alto desempenho. Em novembro de 2025, a ByteDance confirmou ao Reset, veículo especializado em negócios, que seria a única cliente do empreendimento. Com isso, o data center da Omnia no Ceará poderá manter a infraestrutura física no Brasil enquanto presta serviços de processamento para demandas de outros mercados. Isso não significa que todos os dados processados serão estrangeiros. As informações disponíveis não detalham qual parcela da capacidade atenderá atividades relacionadas ao mercado brasileiro, o que impede tratar a operação como exclusivamente destinada ao exterior. Investimento bilionário também envolve geração de energia A escala do empreendimento exige uma estrutura energética própria. Em maio, a Omnia e a Casa dos Ventos firmaram um contrato de aproximadamente US$ 2 bilhões, por 20 anos, para abastecer o complexo. O acordo prevê até 300 MW médios de energia renovável, provenientes de projetos eólicos no Ceará e no Piauí. A Omnia também participará de ativos de geração, em um modelo de autoprodução que dará suporte ao data center da Omnia no Ceará e busca maior previsibilidade de custos. Os valores têm naturezas diferentes: os R$ 200 bilhões correspondem ao investimento total estimado no projeto, enquanto os US$ 2 bilhões se referem ao contrato de fornecimento de energia ao longo de duas décadas. Expansão não garante redução da dependência externa Durante o Siará Tech Summit, Bruno Patrocínio afirmou que 60% dos dados das redes sociais brasileiras são processados fora do país. O executivo considera que a ampliação da infraestrutura nacional com o data center da Omnia no Ceará poderá contribuir para alterar esse cenário. Entretanto, não há informação pública que permita calcular quanto da capacidade contratada pela ByteDance será destinada ao processamento de dados brasileiros. Segundo o cronograma divulgado anteriormente pela Omnia, a operação comercial está prevista para começar no terceiro trimestre de 2027, com ampliação gradual até 2029. Assim, o data center da Omnia no Ceará poderá ampliar a participação brasileira na oferta internacional de processamento de dados. O efeito sobre a dependência nacional de servidores no exterior, porém, permanece sem quantificação pública e dependerá da utilização efetiva da infraestrutura.

artigo.texto: Em uma manhã ensolarada de agosto, Bob Clark visita o novo Obama Presidential Center, no Jackson Park, zona sul de Chicago. Fundador da gigante da construção Clayco, ele ajudou a erguer o complexo, avaliado em US$ 850 milhões (R$ 4,23 bilhões). Clark faz uma rápida inspeção no “Obamalisk”. É assim que chama, carinhosamente, a torre central de oito andares, feita de granito, vidro e concreto. Depois, cumprimenta Valerie Jarrett, ex-assessora sênior da Casa Branca e atual CEO da Obama Foundation. A visita é rápida. Clark entra no banco traseiro de um Escalade branco e segue pela Lake Shore Drive. O destino é outro de seus projetos, que pode ter uma importância ainda maior para Chicago e para o mundo. Às margens do Lago Michigan, o “Quantum Shore” ocupa uma área onde funcionava uma fábrica da U.S. Steel. Quando for inaugurado, no fim de 2027, será um dos maiores campi de computação quântica dos Estados Unidos. Entre os ocupantes estarão a IBM e a PsiQuantum, empresa de Palo Alto, na Califórnia. A companhia pretende construir no local um computador quântico de 1 milhão de qubits. Uma máquina desse porte teria uma capacidade difícil de imaginar. Poderia quebrar os tipos tradicionais de criptografia que protegem grande parte dos computadores — e das contas bancárias — do mundo. No futuro, também poderia acelerar o aprendizado de sistemas de inteligência artificial. Isso ocorreria por meio da redução do tempo de treinamento de determinadas arquiteturas complexas de aprendizagem profunda. O Quantum Shore é um empreendimento complexo — e caro. A primeira fase está sendo desenvolvida pela CRG, subsidiária imobiliária de Clark, em parceria com o escritório do Meio-Oeste da gigante imobiliária Related Companies. O projeto custará US$ 12 bilhões (R$ 59,76 bilhões). Desse total, US$ 500 milhões (R$ 2,49 bilhões) serão aportados pelo estado de Illinois. Os bits quânticos, conhecidos como “qubits”, são extremamente sensíveis às condições ambientais. Por isso, a estrutura terá uma instalação criogênica. Ela fornecerá hélio e nitrogênio líquidos super-resfriados aos computadores. “A única maneira de estabilizar o chip é mantê-lo mais frio do que o espaço sideral”, diz Clark, enquanto guindastes de 550 toneladas passam pelo local. A complexidade da obra impressiona até mesmo o empresário. Ele se lembra de quando o CEO da PsiQuantum lhe disse que projetaria um edifício que iria “mudar tudo”. O negócio Clark, de 67 anos, parece adequado para comandar um projeto dessa dimensão. Ele constrói data centers desde a década de 1980. Somente no ano passado, concluiu 16. Outros 77 estão em andamento em 13 estados americanos. Os centros de dados devem responder por 75% da receita de quase US$ 12 bilhões (R$ 59,76 bilhões) da Clayco em 2026. A expansão do segmento deve ajudar a companhia a elevar o faturamento em 43% na comparação com 2025. “Trabalho no setor de data centers durante a maior parte da minha carreira, mas nunca teria imaginado o que está acontecendo hoje”, afirma. Quando Clark começou, há quatro décadas, um data center era algo bem mais simples. Eram apenas algumas salas de computadores instaladas nos fundos de um banco. Hoje, o cenário mudou. Sediada em Chicago, a Clayco ergue estruturas que equivalem a cidades autossuficientes de bilhões de dólares. Elas praticamente não têm presença humana e podem abrigar 100 mil ou mais das GPUs mais avançadas do mundo. Entre os clientes estão Amazon, Microsoft e Oracle. Para construir esses complexos com eficiência e em grande escala, a Clayco controla suas próprias empresas de arquitetura, concreto, compras e logística. É uma máquina criada para alimentar as máquinas insaciáveis da inteligência artificial. Corrida dos data centers Os gastos dos Estados Unidos com a construção de data centers mais do que triplicaram desde 2023. Neste ano, devem chegar a US$ 75 bilhões (R$ 373,5 bilhões), segundo dados do Census Bureau. O montante nem sequer inclui a compra dos computadores. Esses equipamentos podem representar 40% do custo total de um projeto. Jeff Blau é CEO da Related e parceiro de Clark no Quantum Shore. Os dois também trabalham em um data center de US$ 1,2 bilhão (R$ 5,98 bilhões) para a CoreWeave, em Cheyenne, no Wyoming. Segundo Blau, a forte demanda por centros de dados, somada aos juros elevados, tirou espaço de muitos outros grandes projetos de construção. “Isso não tem precedentes. Nunca tivemos algo com uma demanda tão forte e, ao mesmo tempo, em uma escala tão grande”, afirma. A Related Digital, comandada por Blau, tem US$ 55 bilhões (R$ 273,9 bilhões) em projetos de data centers em desenvolvimento. Para as construtoras, é uma ótima notícia. Quase 1.300 data centers já estão em funcionamento nos Estados Unidos. Essas colmeias de concreto e aço consomem aproximadamente 70 milhões de galões de água por dia. Também precisam de um fornecimento constante de 62 gigawatts de energia. Para efeito de comparação, a cidade de Nova York utiliza, em média, seis gigawatts. E a expansão está longe de terminar. Outros 2.142 centros estão planejados ou em construção, segundo a empresa de inteligência em infraestrutura Cleanview. Sem medo de uma bolha O boom da IA também tornou Clark muito mais rico. Seu patrimônio líquido quadruplicou nos últimos três anos e chegou a US$ 7 bilhões (R$ 34,86 bilhões). A fortuna garantiu ao empresário uma estreia na lista Forbes 400 deste ano. Ele aparece na 245ª posição. Mas a expansão dos data centers também trouxe outro efeito: uma oposição cada vez maior. Uma pesquisa recente do Annenberg Public Policy Center mostrou que 61% dos americanos são contrários à construção dessas instalações em suas comunidades. Quatro meses antes, eram 49%. Segundo o Data Center Watch, projetos avaliados em US$ 18 bilhões (R$ 89,64 bilhões) foram bloqueados. Outros US$ 46 bilhões (R$ 229,08 bilhões) em construções sofreram atrasos. Clark não se intimida com a reação. Prefere manter o foco nos resultados. “Não vemos nenhum sinal de alerta no horizonte”, afirm

artigo.texto: ESS, an opportunity for K-batteries A new current is reshaping the global battery market. In the first half of 2026, global shipments of lithium-ion batteries for energy storage systems (ESS) reached 461 gigawatt-hour (GWh), up 71 percent from 270 GWh in the same period a year earlier, according to SNE Research. This represents a remarkable leap for the ESS market, especially compared with the 20 percent year-on-year growth in global battery demand for electric vehicles (EVs), which reached 609 GWh over the same period. Key drivers include rising energy demand from artificial intelligence (AI) data centers, where speed and reliability are critical, and growth in renewable power generation, which requires solutions to address its intermittency. The expansion of AI data centers and the transition to renewable energy are powerful trends unlikely to reverse in the short term. As a result, the global ESS market is forecast to reach 1,870 GWh in annual shipments by 2035, roughly twice this year’s level. The Korean government is also stepping up efforts to develop the domestic ESS industry through a range of policy measures. On the technology front, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources announced its Battery Industry Technology Roadmap on Sept. 22. The road map’s main elements are to position sodium-ion and solid-state batteries as new growth engines: The government will invest more than 250 billion won in next-generation battery technology development; the country’s three cell manufacturers will collaborate on research and standardization in noncompetitive areas; and the industry as a whole will invest approximately 8 trillion won ($5.97 billion) through 2030 in manufacturing-process innovation and the localization of materials. On the production front, the government has pledged tax support. On Aug. 3, the Ministry of Finance and Economy announced its 2026 Tax Reform Proposal, which introduced a domestic production tax credit to expand local manufacturing capacity in industries of strategic importance to the green transition and economic security. Rechargeable batteries are among the eligible products. On the deployment front, the government is expanding the market through auctions under the Central Contract Market. On Sept. 23, the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment announced the third ESS Central Contract Market in which it would select ESS project developers with a record-high total capacity of 1,180 megawatts. By the auction, the Korea Power Exchange competitively tenders the ESS capacity needed to stabilize the grid and enters into 15-year contracts with successful bidders. This is an encouraging development, as it creates substantial new demand for a battery market that has slowed amid moderating growth in EV demand. For K-batteries to build on these policies and strengthen their position, however, they must increase their share of the rapidly expanding global ESS market. This presents both significant challenges and important opportunities. The fact that China has already established a strong lead in the ESS market is a challenge for Korea. The top four companies in the global ESS market in the first half of this year were all Chinese, and together, they accounted for nearly 55 percent of the market. Korean companies have also recorded strong year-on-year growth, but the gap in absolute volume with China remains substantial. Moreover, with global ESS supply capacity exceeding demand — 900 GWh against the actual demand of 612 GWh at the end of 2025 — price competition is intensifying. Competing with Chinese companies, which have maintained operating margins through economies of scale, can seem like an uphill battle. At the same time, several factors create opportunities. First, regional imbalances between battery supply and demand mean that key export markets for Korean companies are likely to face shortages. For example, battery supply in China is expected to exceed demand by about 90 percent in 2030, while Europe is projected to face a supply shortfall of 40 percent. North America is also expected to face a shortage from 2035. This presents an opportunity for Korean companies, which have established production bases in Europe and North America, to increase their market share. Second, in Europe, capacity for facilities combining renewable energy and batteries is expected to rise by more than 450 percent, from 6.3 GW in 2025 to around 35 GW in 2030. In parallel, the region is working to reduce its reliance on battery supply chains from any one country. For example, it is preparing an Industrial Accelerator Act that would encourage greater use of components and batteries manufactured within Europe when awarding public procurement contracts and subsidies. Korean battery companies are well positioned to benefit, as they already have a substantial manufacturing footprint in Europe. Third, the U.S. market is also opening up significant opportunities for Korean companies. ESS demand is growing rapidly as AI data centers proliferate, while U.S. policies to reduce reliance on Chinese supply chains are being strengthened. The ESS market is expected to grow by an average of 16 percent annually to reach 320 GWh by 2035, while the uninterruptible power supply market for AI data centers is projected to expand at an average annual rate of 47 percent to 135 GWh. Meanwhile, tariffs on Chinese ESS products are rising under measures such as Washington's Section 301 of the Trade Act and forced labor standards under the environmental, social and governance (ESG) pillars. The Advanced Manufacturing Production Credit and restrictions concerning prohibited foreign entities are also creating additional opportunities for K-battery companies with U.S.-based manufacturing operations. artigo.texto: In a new analysis, Wood Mackenzie claims that the LCOE of four-hour battery storage is now cheaper than open-cycle gas turbines across 43 markets assessed Analysts expect battery storage costs in the Middle East and Africa to fall 33%, from $120/MWh in 2026 to $80/MWh by 2035 The analysis also finds that solar PV remains a cost-competitive power generation technology, while falling battery storage costs strengthen the economic case for renewables Four-hour battery energy storage systems (BESS) are now cheaper than open-cycle gas turbines (OCGTs) on a levelized cost basis in all 43 markets where both technologies were assessed, says Wood Mackenzie. Expanding battery manufacturing capacity is helping lower storage costs, while gas turbine shortages and fuel price volatility are increasing the cost of gas-fired peak power generation. The global benchmark cost for a 4-hour battery project dropped 27% YoY to $78/MWh in 2025, according to a BloombergNEF report from February 2026 (see Battery Storage Project Costs In 2025 Dropped To Record Lows Since 2009). “The economic shift is decisive and widening,” said Ahmed Jameel Abdullah, Principal Analyst at Wood Mackenzie. The findings are part of the research firm’s latest levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) analysis, covering Europe, North America, Latin America, Asia Pacific, and the Middle East and Africa. In the Middle East and Africa region, analysts project the cost of four-hour battery storage to fall 33% from $120/MWh in 2026 to $80/MWh by 2035. Utility-scale solar is already the region’s lowest-cost power generation technology, with an LCOE of $37/MWh for projects using single-axis trackers. Wood Mackenzie expects solar costs in Saudi Arabia and the UAE to fall below $20/MWh by 2033. As storage ‘cements’ its role as the enabling technology for solar and wind integration, Wood Mackenzie analysts said, “This shift means storage is displacing open-cycle gas turbines on cost in every gas market across the region, marking a significant structural turning point for power system planning across both the Gulf and Africa.” In North America, analysts see near-term solar costs to increase due to tariffs and import restrictions, with distributed solar projects facing greatest pressure. Utility-scale solar remains partially protected by 168 GW of safe-harbored capacity. However, module prices are expected to rise around 5% annually through 2030. Battery storage continues to benefit from investment tax credits (ITC), which partly offset the effects of foreign entity of concern (FEOC) restrictions and supply chain constraints. Once the tax credits expire in 2038, costs may spike, but storage LCOE will drop 10% by 2060, driven by long-term new battery chemistries, hardware commoditization, and domestic supply chain expansion. Growing electricity demand from data centers is further strengthening the long-term case for renewables and battery storage in North America, they highlight. Across Latin America, solar PV with single-axis trackers remains the lowest-cost generation technology in 2026. Wood Mackenzie expects average costs for solar to decline by 38% by 2060, and for storage to drop by 42% driven by storage requirements for renewable energy projects, standalone procurement and maturing regulatory frameworks. Solar PV remains Europe’s cheapest power generation technology, with fixed-tilt costs projected to fall 22% by 2060 despite a near-term increase in capital expenditure. Onshore wind costs are also expected to decline, reaching $60/MWh by 2060 as turbine performance improves. Battery storage capital costs in Europe rose 2% in 2026 due to higher battery cell prices and lithium costs but are forecast to fall 12% by 2031. Meanwhile, Europe’s fossil-fuel generation costs are expected to rise, with carbon costs projected to exceed fuel costs by 2030, according to Wood Mackenzie. Utility-scale solar PV remains the cheapest power generation source in Asia Pacific, although costs vary significantly across markets. China has the region’s lowest grid-scale battery storage costs – a benchmark LCOE that’s 55% lower than the rest of Asia Pacific average of $134/MWh – supported by domestic supply chains and large-scale manufacturing. Analysts project average storage costs across the rest of Asia Pacific to fall to $92/MWh by 2036, though Japan, Australia, and the Philippines are expected to remain more expensive.

artigo.texto: Poll: Voters hold negative view of data centers Published 12:00 am Friday, October 9, 2026 Majority say they are considering issue in elections Ohio’s voters hold a negative view of data centers, according to results of a Bowling Green University poll. Voters were first asked how much they had heard about the issue, and results showed it has been front and center in their media consumption. Among respondents, 50 percent said they have heard a lot about data centers, 47 percent said a little and 3 percent said not at all. Voters were then asked about the impact of data centers on several aspects: • On the environment, 70 percent of respondents said data centers had a mostly bad impact, while 24 percent said neither good nor bad and 6 percent said mostly good. • On home energy costs, 69 percent said that effects were mostly bad, 24 percent said neither good nor bad and 6 percent said mostly good. • On the quality of life of people near data centers, 65 percent said mostly bad, 27 percent said neither good nor bad and 8 percent said mostly good. • On local jobs, 30 percent said mostly bad, 36 percent said neither good nor bad and 34 percent said mostly good. • On local tax revenue, 35 percent said mostly bad, 36 percent said neither good nor bad and 29 percent said mostly good. Respondents were then asked if they supported data center construction in various locations, and results showed opposition grew when the construction was closer to home: • In their local community, 45 percent of respondents said they strongly opposed construction, 30 percent opposed, 19 favored construction and 6 percent strongly favored construction. • Elsewhere in Ohio, 28 percent of respondents said they strongly opposed construction, 35 percent opposed, 29 favored construction and 8 percent strongly favored construction. • In the U.S. overall, 24 percent of respondents said they strongly opposed construction, 31 percent opposed, 32 favored construction and 13 percent strongly favored construction. Voters were then asked whether they favored or opposed a ban of construction of new data center until more information can be gathered about their effects. 50 percent of voters strongly favored such a ban, while 28 percent favored one. 6 percent said they strongly opposed a ban, while 15 percent opposed. Regarding the election, voters were asked how much a candidate’s stance on data centers affected their vote. The results showed that an overwhelming majority are considering the issue going into the elections. 19 percent said it was extremely important, while 28 percent said very important, and 35 percent said somewhat important. 13 percent said not very important and 5 percent said not important at all. The Bowling Green University poll was conducted among 1,000 likely voters from Sept. 1-10 and has a margin of error of +/- 3.96 percent.

artigo.texto: Frederico prevê regulamentação do Redata até o fim do ano Ministro das Comunicações diz que pendência está concentrada na questão energética e diverge da estimativa de seis meses apresentada pelo governo paulista O ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho, afirmou nesta terça-feira, 6, que o governo trabalha para concluir até o fim de 2026 a regulamentação do Redata, regime tributário destinado aos investimentos em data centers. A declaração foi dada a jornalistas durante a Futurecom 2026, em São Paulo, após o vice-governador paulista estimar que o processo poderia levar aproximadamente seis meses. Segundo Frederico, a etapa considerada mais difícil — a aprovação do regime pelo Congresso — já foi superada. Agora, disse, restam questões de regulamentação. “A questão da regulamentação agora são ajustes finos”, afirmou. Segundo ele, “com relação à infraestrutura digital está resolvido” e permanece em discussão a questão energética. “A expectativa é que sim, a gente consiga resolver até o final do ano.” A declaração estabelece uma diferença de expectativa entre o governo federal e o paulista sobre o calendário necessário para que o regime possa produzir efeitos sobre novos investimentos. São Paulo trabalha com prazo maior Pouco antes, o vice-governador de São Paulo havia afirmado que a regulamentação poderia levar cerca de seis meses e associado a conclusão desse processo ao avanço da discussão estadual sobre ICMS. No discurso de abertura, ele disse que São Paulo pretende acompanhar a regulamentação federal para posteriormente adequar a legislação estadual, “principalmente em tópicos do ICMS”. Questionado pelos jornalistas sobre essa diferença de calendário, Frederico sustentou a possibilidade de concluir o processo ainda em 2026. O ministro não anunciou, entretanto, uma data para publicação dos atos nem detalhou quais instrumentos normativos ainda serão necessários. Também questionado sobre a possibilidade de os efeitos do Redata perderem relevância diante da entrada em vigor de etapas da reforma tributária, Frederico afirmou que o governo está concentrado no efeito econômico final para os investidores. “O que vale no final do dia é qual é o benefício que toda essa solução vai trazer ao investidor. Se vai ser o Redata ou se vai ser reforma tributária, o importante é a gente discutir o benefício”, disse. Governo discute regulamentação entre ministérios Frederico afirmou que o Ministério das Comunicações mantém discussões com outras áreas do governo, citando Minas e Energia, Casa Civil e outros ministérios envolvidos no tema. Questionado se algum projeto poderia utilizar os benefícios ainda em 2026, respondeu que o governo trabalha para acelerar as definições no período posterior às eleições. A regulamentação também apareceu no discurso oficial do ministro na abertura da Futurecom. Na ocasião, Frederico afirmou que o governo trabalha para dar previsibilidade ao setor produtivo e evitar a perda de investimentos. O Redata também foi citado pelo vice-governador paulista e pelo deputado federal e ex-ministro das Comunicações Juscelino Filho durante o evento, indicando convergência entre União, governo estadual e Congresso quanto à utilização do regime como instrumento de atração de data centers. A diferença está, neste momento, no calendário e nas etapas complementares necessárias para que os incentivos sejam operacionalizados. ICMS será próxima frente O ICMS aparece como uma dessas etapas. Como o tributo é estadual, sua eventual redução depende de decisões dos estados e das regras aplicáveis à tributação estadual. O governo paulista afirmou que pretende atuar nessa frente, mas depois de conhecer a regulamentação federal. Além da tributação, autoridades presentes à Futurecom relacionaram a expansão dos data centers à disponibilidade de energia, redes de fibra óptica, cabos submarinos e infraestrutura de conectividade. Frederico afirmou que data centers dependem de uma rede capaz de transportar os dados processados e armazenados. Essa combinação entre incentivos tributários, energia e telecomunicações deverá determinar a capacidade do Redata de efetivamente destravar novos projetos.

artigo.texto: Just outside Toledo, Ohio, Meta is building an $800 million data center campus. Annually, the data center will use only as much water as two full-service restaurants using a technology known as a closed-loop system. The Great Lakes region offers an unmatched set of resources ripe for data center development, including an abundance of fresh water for cooling; longer, colder winters than the South or Sunbelt; and former industrial lands ready for redevelopment. But in Illinois, a polarizing data center debate has heated up in recent weeks. I agree with Gov. JB Pritzker’s recent statement at New York’s America is All in Conference. When asked whether we should be welcoming data centers into Illinois, he said that we need to ensure that data centers are bringing their own energy, and they are using their own closed-loop water systems. There are still very valid public concerns about letting these data centers develop projects untethered to government accountability. I hear them weekly on the campaign trail from Chicagoans who voice concern that we could damage Lake Michigan by exploiting its resources too heavily and that our electricity bills could skyrocket. I have two solutions for those main two concerns. Regarding the first concern — water usage — many Chicagoans I speak with hear “data center” and picture a server farm drinking up the lake. My vision is to build a massive geothermal heat sink coil system in Lake Michigan. This system is closed loop and filled with liquid coolant. This loop would be miles, perhaps tens or hundreds of miles, long and coiled far offshore at or near the bottom of the lake (the deeper, the better, as it’s colder). This system would consume water over time, thus taking a data center’s water consumption to virtually zero. The second concern I have heard is that with this new architecture, we would cook the lake. But Lake Michigan holds about a quadrillion gallons of water, so adding data centers is like setting a sealed coffee thermos in a swimming pool — it wouldn’t change. From a thermodynamics perspective, even with miles of coils and loops constantly cooling themselves in Lake Michigan, we likely could not even marginally increase the temperature or create an environmentally noticeable impact. But “it’s fine, trust me” is not good enough for a lake this city drinks from, so I propose a water and environmental study before a single pipe goes in, with the results and data published where anyone can read it. On top of closed-loop infrastructure at the bottom of the lake, data centers should have windows. It may sound basic, but right now, data center construction typically creates hard cases of primarily concrete with no ability to leverage the outside cold air. They are basically heat-trapping boxes, and, as we now know, they produce a massive amount of heat. When a house is hot, open the windows. When a data center is hot, open the windows. Chicago’s cooler fall, chilling winter and brisk spring climates all lend themselves to a basic idea of circulating cold air into the data center itself and hot air out. With windows open, they essentially have natural air conditioning three-quarters of the year. The marginal cost to put in windows and natural cooling systems in northern and colder climates such as Chicago far outweighs the risk of continuing to use billions of gallons of water and energy to sustain these operations. The potential savings are not marginal; they are massive. Cornell University has cooled its campus from a Finger Lake for 25 years and reports saving roughly 85% of the energy conventional refrigeration would burn. Toronto has cooled more than a hundred downtown buildings with Lake Ontario since 2004, saving about 90,000 megawatt hours a year, enough to power a town of 25,000 people. Its system is nearly full, and it is spending $100 million to expand it. A massive, closed-loop coil system in Lake Michigan could cool much more than data centers; it could provide air conditioning and cooling for hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of households and buildings across the city as climate change increases the overall temperature throughout the year. None of this is theoretical anymore because the demand is already here. Chicago’s data center vacancy rate is under 2%. There is not a single block of 5 megawatts or more available to lease anywhere in this market, and developers asking ComEd to connect new projects are being told 2032 and beyond, which is why they are now buying land based on where the power is rather than where they want to be. The real question is whether we shape our response or let it shape us. We are constantly told we have to pick. Jobs or the lake. Investment or affordable power bills. The artificial intelligence economy or the environment. I have never accepted that framing, and my entire plan for Chicago when I am mayor argues against it. This is not a “this or that.” It is both creating more jobs while protecting the lake and environment. Chicago has an answer, and it is sitting a few miles off Michigan Avenue at the bottom of the lake. Joe Holberg is a Chicago mayoral candidate. He was a math teacher on the West Side, then a small business owner and entrepreneur helping Chicagoans work toward financial goals. Adding battery storage is one of the best ways to protect your home during outages, save on energy costs, and move closer to going off-grid. artigo.texto: Grupo Leste entra em data center de US$ 1,75 bilhão nos EUA Gestora participa do empreendimento com a Harrison Street e oferecerá a investidores brasileiros acesso à operação, que já tem contrato de locação por 15 anos Pedro Gil Editor do Exame INSIGHT Publicado em 8 de outubro de 2026 às 09:00. RESUMO ＋ O Grupo Leste, gestora brasileira de investimentos alternativos, participa como coinvestidor de um projeto de data centers de US$ 1,75 bilhão em Ohio, nos Estados Unidos, apurou a publicação EXAME Insight. Desenvolvido com a gestora americana Harrison Street, o campus terá quatro edifícios, capacidade de 324 MW e contrato de locação de 15 anos. A conclusão é prevista em quatro anos. O Grupo Leste, gestora brasileira de investimentos alternativos com mais de US$ 4,5 bilhões no portfólio, participa como coinvestidor de um projeto de data centers de US$ 1,75 bilhão em Ohio, nos Estados Unidos, apurou o EXAME Insight. Desenvolvido em parceria com a gestora americana Harrison Street, o campus terá quatro edifícios e capacidade total de 324 megawatts (MW). Toda a área já está locada para uma das maiores empresas de tecnologia do mundo, em um contrato de 15 anos. A operação prevê US$ 400 milhões em capital próprio, majoritariamente de investidores institucionais americanos. Uma parcela será oferecida à base de investidores brasileiros do Leste por meio de um fundo dedicado ao projeto, com aporte mínimo de US$ 2,5 milhões. O horizonte estimado do investimento é de quatro anos, período previsto para a construção do campus. A estratégia é vender o empreendimento a um investidor institucional americano depois de concluído e em operação, já gerando receita de aluguel. Contrato assinado A empresa que ocupará o complexo não teve o nome revelado. No mercado, a estimativa é que a locatária seja a Nvidia, fabricante de chips que vem ampliando sua atuação no financiamento e na viabilização de infraestrutura para inteligência artificial. Em agosto, a Nvidia concordou em destinar até US$ 105 bilhões para viabilizar outro complexo de data centers em Ohio, que será alugado pela OpenAI. Localizado no condado de Pike, o projeto prevê até 8 gigawatts de capacidade, com os primeiros 800 MW programados para entrar em operação até 2028. A instalação será construída e operada pela SB Energy, empresa apoiada pelo SoftBank. A incorporação ficará a cargo da Panattoni, empresa especializada no desenvolvimento de imóveis industriais e de infraestrutura. A companhia já entregou mais de 90 projetos para a mesma empresa de tecnologia que ocupará o campus, segundo interlocutores. Os quatro edifícios somarão aproximadamente 81 mil metros quadrados e seguirão o modelo powered shell, no qual as estruturas são preparadas para receber os equipamentos e a infraestrutura tecnológica do ocupante. Tese do negócio A tese do investimento combina a demanda por capacidade computacional, impulsionada pela inteligência artificial e pela computação em nuvem, com um contrato de locação de longo prazo. A disponibilidade de energia e a baixa vacância de imóveis desse tipo na região também estão entre os fundamentos considerados pelos investidores. Para o Leste, a operação amplia o acesso de sua base brasileira ao mercado imobiliário ligado à infraestrutura digital americana. A participação se concentra no desenvolvimento do imóvel que abrigará o data center, com a receita de aluguel contratada e a venda do ativo como estratégia de saída. artigo.texto: Scale Microgrids, the corporation behind Nodaway County’s proposed data center project, is partnering with another company to operate the facility, though that end user is not yet known. While the Nodaway County Commission said the company is close to announcing the details of the partnership, not everyone is so sure this is true. Missouri allows data center developers in the state to receive tax exemptions on their facilities. Scott Wilson is an independent candidate running for Nodaway County presiding commissioner this November. He said he feels like Scale Microgrids is waiting for the commission to give the company a tax abatement before the public receives more information. Last week, Wilson took these concerns to a Nodaway Says No informational meeting in Graham, Missouri, which saw around 100 attendees. He said he feels apprehensive about how a hyperscale data center could affect environmental safety and the local ecosystem. “There’s a lot of different ways that people talk about it, and a lot of the people, the citizens, have had to try to prove to the commissioners that the things that are being said are actually true, and I don’t know that that’s a 100% fair way to do it,” Wilson said. “It would seem more like that data center developer and the commissioners would have to prove to the citizens that it is safe, not the citizens having to prove to them that it’s not safe.” He said he has heard many people talk about the impact data centers have on livestock due to the sound pollution it causes. Particularly, he heard it can reduce reproduction and increase stillbirths in cattle populations. Cows are not the only animals at risk. Horses, sheep — and even insects — are sensitive to sound. “They’ve talked about the bees, and they communicate with sound, and they can’t hear this,” Wilson said. “Someone mentioned just the other day, it’s like being at a loud party, and they can’t figure out what’s going on, so they can’t even get back to their hives, and it could drive the wildlife out of that area,” Wilson said. Nodaway County, he said, has a lot of land that is tilled up and farmed. He said adding a data center into such an agriculture region feels invasive — both to people and animals. “They talk about a heat dome…I think someone said it could raise the temperature within six miles of 16 degrees, like, average four to 16 degrees, just because of the massive amounts of concrete and all the cooling systems,” Wilson said. Another major concern for many residents is water. Scale Microgrids will need at least 1.5 million gallons of water to operate its facility, but not all residents see how it is feasible. “Of course, the river, if they suck too much water, they’re going to run the river lower than it already is at times,” Wilson said. The water Scale Microgrids uses would routinely filter through the 102 River every three years. However, many data centers add synthetic compounds — known as forever chemicals — into their water supplies. These can take hundreds or thousands of years to break down, and they are harmful to the ecosystem, according to the World Economic Forum. The Missourian reached out to the Nodaway County Public Water Supply District No. 1, which would supply water to the data center, and received a message in response. “When the project particulars are agreed to by all entities public and private maybe we could give a story with background on the whole thing,” the message said. “However since the district is in the middle of contract negotiations with suppliers and customers, we really say can’t speak to much.” Along with water stress and rising temperatures, emitted light from the facility can also be an issue, as it can disturb humans and confuse animals. People living within a half-mile of Scale Microgrids’ project, called White Cloud Acres, may be most heavily affected by the light. “They say that the critters need to have time at night to where they know it’s night and day, and if the lights are on all the time, it bothers them, but some of this can be mitigated,” Wilson said. “They can have different dimming type of lights or different ways to help all these problems along the way, but again, all that costs more for the developer, and it makes the return on investment less, but that really shouldn’t be our problem.” He said officials at hand should strive to make the best decision possible regardless of money. “I believe that the commissioners should strive to make this as safe as possible, and it doesn’t really matter what the developer’s return on investment is,” Wilson said. “If it doesn’t work out for them, it just doesn’t work out.”

artigo.texto: Stryten Energy has completed the acquisition of C&D Technologies and Trojan Battery Silver Point Capital is supporting these acquisitions through a $650 million term loan Stryten said it plans to expand US battery manufacturing and advanced energy storage technologies US-based battery manufacturer and energy storage company Stryten Energy has completed the acquisition of C&D Technologies and Trojan Battery Company. This expands its battery manufacturing footprint to 18 facilities across the US, Mexico, and China. The deal brings together businesses serving stationary power, industrial, and mobility markets, with Stryten planning further investment in domestic manufacturing capacity and energy storage technologies. The acquisition brings together complementary businesses with different end markets under Stryten’s ownership. C&D Technologies supplies stationary batteries for applications including data centers, telecommunications networks, utilities, and other critical infrastructure. These batteries support backup power and reliability requirements where interruptions can affect essential operations. Trojan Battery specializes in deep-cycle batteries used in golf carts, low-speed electric vehicles, marine applications, and industrial equipment. Global private equity firm KPS-owned C&D acquired Trojan Battery in 2018 to expand its energy storage solutions portfolio. Both these businesses broaden Stryten’s reach across stationary power, industrial equipment, transportation, and critical infrastructure. The combined business operates 15 manufacturing plants in the US, alongside facilities in Mexico and China. It also has offices across Europe and Asia. Stryten Energy plans to increase investment in US battery manufacturing, advanced energy storage technologies and military production. CEO and President Mike Judd said the company aims to expand its capabilities to serve demand across transportation, data centers, telecommunications, industrial equipment, and other markets. The combined company employs approximately 4,800 people worldwide and will continue to operate under the Stryten Energy name, retaining the C&D Technologies and Trojan Battery brands. Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed. Stryten, a portfolio company of Atlas Holdings, said it plans to accelerate investment in domestic battery manufacturing, advanced energy storage technologies, and military production capabilities. However, the company has not disclosed the amount or timeline of its planned manufacturing investments. The acquisition is supported by a $650 million term loan led by the direct-lending business of Silver Point Capital. The company led the syndication to existing and new lenders. Silver Point previously financed Stryten, leading a $400 million financing for the company in 2024.

artigo.texto: Battery Energy Storage Trends: Shorter PPAs and Market Growth ⚡ Quick Read - What happened: Battery energy storage developers are pushing for shorter PPA tenures, while the MNRE updated ALMM List-II to 37,394 MW and Chhattisgarh approved a ₹2.98/kWh tariff for a 125 MW/500 MWh BESS project. - Why it matters: Shorter, more flexible PPAs are essential for the bankability of BESS projects, which currently face rigid 20-25 year contract structures similar to solar and wind. - Watch: Further regulatory shifts regarding transmission charges for open access customers and the progress of upcoming pumped hydro and solar tenders. Background and Context The Indian energy storage market is undergoing a significant evolution as stakeholders call for more flexible contractual frameworks. While solar and wind projects have traditionally relied on 20-25-year Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs), battery energy storage developers are increasingly advocating for shorter tenures to better align with the operational lifecycle of battery technology. This shift is critical as the country integrates larger volumes of variable renewable energy into the grid. Key Details Regulatory activity remains high across the sector. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) has revised its standardized nomenclature for solar cells under the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) List-II. The 11th revision has expanded the total enlisted capacity to 37,394 MW, mandating that module model numbers clearly identify the country of origin for both cells and modules. In the storage segment, the Chhattisgarh State Electricity Regulatory Commission (CSERC) has set a benchmark by adopting a tariff of ₹2.98 (~$0.031)/kWh for a 125 MW/500 MWh standalone battery energy storage system. Meanwhile, in Karnataka, Sumitomo Corporation has committed to investing in a 500 MW solar and wind project with a co-located 200 MWh BESS, being developed by Hero Future Energies in Bidar. Other notable developments include the rejection of MP Power Transmission Company’s petition on transmission charges by the Madhya Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission, and NTPC Renewable Energy’s call for bids for interstate transmission system-connected pumped hydro projects. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and developers, the push for flexible PPAs signals a maturing market where risk-sharing is becoming more sophisticated. The standardization of ALMM nomenclature provides greater transparency in the supply chain, which is vital for procurement planning. Furthermore, the adoption of competitive tariffs for BESS projects suggests that storage is becoming increasingly cost-competitive, opening new avenues for large-scale infrastructure projects. What Happens Next The industry is closely watching the outcome of the NTPC Renewable Energy pumped hydro tender, with bids due by November 3, 2026. As the India renewable energy sector continues to scale, the interplay between regulatory policy, such as the ALMM updates, and commercial innovations in PPA structures will define the next phase of growth for developers and EPC firms alike.

artigo.texto: Director-General, National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), Mrs Omotenioye Majekodunmi, has called for a stronger carb on verification to enhance the credibility and integrity of Nigeria’s carbon market. Majekodunmi, who was represented by Mr Michael Ivenso, Director, Energy, Transportation and Infrastructure, NCCC, made the call at an NCCC/European Union Climate Dialogues High-Level Roundtable on carbon markets in Abuja on Tuesday. Majekodunmi said Nigeria must turn its climate ambition into tangible, bankable and verifiable action to support sustainable economic growth and attract climate finance. She said Nigeria’s National Carbon Markets Framework had established the institutional and regulatory architecture required to govern carbon activities, including Article 6 cooperation, voluntary markets and national oversight. She said the NCCC was operationalising a unified national carbon registry while promoting digital Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) through remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, geospatial data and distributed ledger technologies to enhance accuracy. The director-general called for stronger collaboration among government agencies, private developers, financial institutions, development partners, civil society and academia to establish bankable projects and strengthen local verification capacity. Majekodunmi said priorities included finalising carbon market regulations, publishing sector-specific MRV guidelines and establishing local capacity-building hubs to position Nigeria as a destination for high-integrity carbon investments. Jop Weterings, Policy Professional and Team member at the DG CLIMA’s Task Force on International Carbon Pricing and Markets, European Commission, said the EU adopted legally binding target to cut emissions 40 per cent by 2040. Weterings said the target includes at least 85 per cent domestic reductions and up to five per cent high-quality international carbon credits under Article 6, from 2036. He said quality, transparency and robust accounting were essential to scaling carbon markets, and urged stronger methodologies, fair transactions, equitable benefit-sharing and national strategies protecting domestic climate priorities. Weterings said that EU support for carbon pricing and international markets was increasing, while cooperation with Nigeria offered opportunities to operationalise its framework and strengthen high-integrity markets. Mrs Halima Bawa-Bwari, Director of Forestry, Ministry of Environment, urged Nigeria to strengthen forest inventories, monitoring systems, remote sensing, satellite technology and artificial intelligence for carbon monitoring. Bawa-Bwari said satellite information should complement ground measurements and field verification, while forestry institutions require stronger capacity to collect, manage and utilise reliable data for carbon markets. She called for coordinated, transparent and independently verifiable forest-carbon data, warning against parallel systems and stressing clear responsibilities, accountability, technical credibility and stakeholder partnership for high-integrity markets. Ms Yolanda Jose, Head, Green and Digital Economy, EU Delegation to Nigeria and ECOWAS, said that credible carbon markets require robust systems ensuring transparency, accountability and environmental integrity. Jose said Nigeria’s adoption of its National Carbon Markets Framework established a structured legal and institutional sytem for domestic and international carbon trading under relevant climate agreements. She said the EU Climate Dialogues roundtable would align on operationalising Nigeria’s framework, strengthen MRV practices, mobilise investment and support Nigeria’s low-carbon development pathway. Mr Huzi Mshelia, Country Facilitator, Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) partnership said robust MRV systems were essential for building trust and investor confidence, welcoming the dialogue’s convergence of stakeholders to establish common national standards and understanding. He stressed partnership among NCCC, Finance, Budget and National Planning institutions, ensuring climate actions align with development priorities, while technical support strengthens Nigeria’s MRV system globally.

artigo.texto: The e SKY, Suzuki’s first electric kei car, is expected to undercut BYD’s Racco as Japan’s cheapest mini EV, starting at around $13,500. Suzuki launches its first mini EV using BYD batteries Suzuki is entering Japan’s competitive electric mini car segment with the e SKY set to launch on November 16. The e SKY will start at around 2.12 million yen, or about $13,500, according to Nikkei, making it the lowest-priced EV in its class. BYD currently holds the title with the Racco EV priced from 2.145 million yen ($13,600). Suzuki said the e SKY offers a WLTC driving range of up to 310 km (192 miles) and a “class-leading” AC energy consumption rating of 97 Wh/km. Suzuki developed a dedicated kei EV platform and electric drive system for the e SKY to optimize efficiency. Interestingly, Suzuki’s mini EV uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries supplied by BYD’s battery unit to cut costs. Government subsidies have yet to be announced, but if it qualifies for the same 568,000 yen subsidy as its commercial kei EV, the e-Every, the e SKY would cost about the same as the Spacia. The Spacia is Suzuki’s most popular gas-powered kei car. It starts at 1.53 million yen, or slightly under $10,000 in Japan. BYD’s cheapest Racco 200 model uses a 22.4 kWh LFP battery, providing a WLTC driving range of 210 km (130 miles). High-priced trims, including the Racco 300 Plus and Premium models, use a larger 35.84 kWh battery with a range of up to 320 km (199 miles). BYD said it was the first kei EV to offer over 300 km range. BYD’s Racco and the Suzuki e SKY will be more affordable and offer a longer driving range than the Nissan Sakura, which starts at ¥2,448,600 ($15,000). BYD aims to sell 10,000 Racco models by the end of 2026. In its first two weeks on the market, BYD’s mini EV secured 1,000 orders. On Monday, BYD Japan also celebrated reaching 10,000 domestic cumulative registrations.

The ability of Perry and Dare Wayne to connect with voters on hot-button issues like data centers and shipments of radioactive waste to Wayne Disposal could be critical in a district that Miller won by a slim margin in 2024. Environmental advocates say DTE is proposing new natural gas plants to fulfill data center demand, and DTE says the facilities are replacing the outgoing, coal-fired Monroe Power Plant. Miller endorsed Dare Wayne in the race, which Hall said reflects well on the candidate. “But I haven’t seen anything on Shannon’s page that speaks specifically to the hyperscale data center,” Hall said.
