artigo.texto: Dear editor, “No Data Center” signs proliferate in Monticello and Wright County, and for good reason. Americans oppose the construction of data centers in their local areas due to noise, impacts on ecosystems, massive electricity consumption, strain on local water supplies and concerns about who benefits financially. A recent Economist/YouGov poll found that more than half of those polled oppose building a data center in their community; a Gallup survey found that seven in 10 oppose building AI data centers locally. On Monday, Aug. 31, President Donald Trump wrote in a post: “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want data centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor.” As reported in MinnPost, our congressional representative, Tom Emmer, endorsed Trump’s message supporting data centers by saying, “President Trump is absolutely spot on.” Before you cast your vote in this year’s general election, ask yourself: What does Emmer’s response to the data center debate tell you about whose concerns he listens to? That is worth considering alongside the legitimate questions Minnesotans are raising about data centers. When you vote, consider whether Emmer’s position on data centers reflects your priorities and concerns. Emmer’s opponent, Doug Chapin, confirmed that he is not taking crypto or data center lobby money. By the end of this election cycle, Chapin’s campaign says he will have held 20 or more in-person town halls. Emmer’s last documented in-person town hall was in August 2023. Chapin is visible in his district and listening to the people he hopes to represent. Tom Grue Monticello

artigo.texto: ROX Capital Launches Gulf Energy Storage Platform ROX Capital has launched a platform to develop utility-scale and commercial energy storage projects in Gulf. October 06, 2026. By EI News Network ROX Capital Group has launched the ROX Gulf Energy Storage Platform to develop utility-scale and commercial energy storage projects in the UAE and Oman, as the Gulf region expands its large-scale solar capacity. The UAE-based real assets investor and developer said that the platform will assess multiple energy storage technologies, including vanadium redox flow batteries, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and sodium-ion batteries. It will also evaluate long-duration energy storage technologies such as CO₂ batteries, gravity-based storage, compressed-air energy storage and thermal storage. ROX said that it will partner with selected technology providers based on their track record in deploying large-scale storage projects, expertise in long-duration energy storage, financial and operational capabilities, and ownership or control of core technology intellectual property. The platform will prioritise technology providers offering bankable systems, established manufacturing capabilities, long-term technical support, performance guarantees and warranties, according to the company. ROX and its technology partners will participate in upcoming energy storage tenders in the UAE and Oman. The platform will also examine opportunities for local assembly and manufacturing in the region where commercially viable. Robin Antony, Founder of ROX Capital Group, said the Gulf’s growing deployment of large-scale solar projects was increasing the need for energy storage to make renewable power available after sunset and during periods of peak electricity demand. Antony said that no single storage technology would be able to address all energy storage requirements in the region. The platform will therefore seek to match different technologies with the specific requirements of individual projects while also exploring opportunities for local manufacturing. ROX said that lithium-ion batteries will remain an important part of the Gulf’s energy storage mix, but regional conditions could create demand for a wider range of technologies. High summer temperatures in the Gulf can increase cooling requirements for battery systems, while power systems with a high share of solar generation require longer-duration storage to supply electricity after sunset. Against this backdrop, ROX said that technologies including vanadium flow batteries, CO₂ batteries, gravity-based storage and thermal storage could complement lithium-ion systems in the Gulf market. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: Canadian Solar Inc. (NASDAQ:CSIQ) said its energy storage subsidiary, e-STORAGE, has signed an agreement to supply and commission a 100 MW/200 MWh battery energy storage system for OX2's Muswellbrook Solar Farm and Battery project in New South Wales, Australia. The system will use e-STORAGE's SolBank 3.0 battery containers alongside Power Conversion Systems, plant controls and the company's EQ-S Energy Management System. e-STORAGE will also provide a hybrid power plant controller to coordinate the battery storage system with the co-located solar farm. The company will be responsible for overall system integration and commissioning. Shipments Scheduled to Begin in Third Quarter of 2027 Shipments for the project are scheduled to start in the third quarter of 2027, with commercial operations targeted for the third quarter of 2028. Canadian Solar said the battery cells and SolBank system will be manufactured at its own facilities. The agreement also includes a 20-year long-term service arrangement covering hardware, software and system performance. Project Located at Former Coal Mine Site The Muswellbrook project is located approximately 2.5 kilometres east of Muswellbrook on land at a former coal mine within the Hunter-Central Coast Renewable Energy Zone. Once operational, the battery system will support a long-term hybrid power purchase agreement that OX2 has signed for the project. "Australia's energy transition is being decided in regions like the Hunter, where storage now has to carry the load that retiring coal once did. We control this project from the cell through to our own energy management software and 20 years of service, which means OX2 has one partner accountable for how the system performs over its full life," said Jeff Roy, President of e-STORAGE. artigo.texto: This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here. No one wants to be “Data Center Dave” Voters on both sides of the aisle despise hate data centers. But do they hate them enough to influence the midterms? As far as political slurs go, this one is pretty tepid: “Meet Data Center Dave Crowley,” intones the stern-voiced narrator of a recent Tom Tiffany campaign ad. Tiffany, a Republican, and Crowley, a Democrat, are both running for governor of Wisconsin. And in this very tight race, as in dozens of midterm contests across the country, voters’ growing animus toward AI could potentially make a real difference. In less than four weeks, Americans will head to the polls to decide which party controls Congress, along with a slew of state and local offices. The stakes are arguably, unusually high: Voters will choose whether to check the power of a president who has bulldozed over historical limits and launched an unpopular war that has worsened a cost-of-living crisis. As we count down to that momentous and potentially messy day, I’m partnering with my colleague Astead Herndon and Vox’s The Midterms, Actually team for weekly editions on the biggest issues shaping the midterms. We’re breaking down one issue each week and suggesting further reading and races to watch in November. Last week, we tackled the dual identity crises that both parties have suffered since 2024. And this week, we’re digging into the dramatic bipartisan backlash to AI and data centers. One analyst recently told NPR the issue “upended politics as we know it.” But it’s less clear how that’ll play out in November’s contests. Go a little deeper There was a time not so long ago when “Data Center Dave” might be a neutral nickname for the well-meaning IT guy at work. Then Americans soured on AI and the hulking, cavernous warehouses that supply its computing power. The hostility crosses geography and party lines. At first, opponents focused on noise, water use, and energy costs — quality-of-life concerns for nearby residents. But increasingly, even voters far from these projects grew leery of them. Too often, the public got little say in where data centers were built and on what terms. And as Vox’s Marina Bolotnikova reported over the summer, the construction boom gradually became a stand-in for broader fears about artificial intelligence. Would AI cause mass unemployment (…or worse, mass extinction)? Would it widen the gap between rich and poor? And do politicians cater to business interests over the needs of ordinary people? Without clear answers to those questions — let alone a rigorous plan to address AI’s fallout — many voters channeled their unease into stopping, or slowing, data center development. Candidates have reacted by “falling over themselves to sound tough on data centers,” Washington Post data reporter Jeremy Merrill recently told Vox’s Noel King. He analyzed thousands of social media posts and newsletters to see how elected officials are talking about data centers, and the answer is: not positively! Some candidates in high-profile midterm races have backed policies that would keep data centers from raising household energy bills. Others have called for ending the facilities’ tax breaks and subsidies or requiring public notice before new construction. Strikingly, both Republicans and Democrats have supported these types of proposals … and both Republicans and Democrats have sought to tar their opponents as “Data Center Daves” of one kind or another. I asked my colleague Andrew Prokop, who covers politics, if many races will actually turn on this. “Data centers have been a major theme in several races, particularly governor’s races where one of the candidates has taken past pro-data center positions,” he said. But even when voters say they oppose data centers, very few list the issue among the most important concerns determining how they cast their ballots. In Ohio, for instance — a hub for both data-center development and the grassroots movement opposing it — only 3 percent of voters named data centers as the top issue driving their vote. And that’s the highest share in the entire nation. Andrew points to the Democratic gubernatorial primary in Wisconsin, where “Data Center Dave” triumphed over Francesca Hong, an outspoken data center critic. “That just goes to show that data centers don’t necessarily crowd out everything else,” Andrew said. Still...that’s just one race. And voters’ hatred of data centers has only grown since. ➨ Races to watch: - Wisconsin governor’s race, where both candidates have attempted to distance themselves from data centers without embracing an actual ban; - Texas governor’s race, where Republican Governor Greg Abbott has hastily retreated from his previous, pro-data-center position; - Ohio Senate race, where Democrat Sherrod Brown has hammered incumbent Republican Jon Husted over his past votes for data center development. ➨ More from Vox: One link for later ➨ Get better at being alone with your thoughts. According to one oft-cited study from 2014, many people would rather give themselves electric shocks than spend a few minutes alone with nothing to do. But being alone with your thoughts is good for you! You can practice by making a list of topics to ponder and parking your phone in another room. Then see what kind of cogitation surfaces for you. Before you go… - Did you know…that there are more than 96 bags of human waste on the moon? Astronauts with the Apollo missions left them there more than 50 years ago. - Today’s trivia: Which fruit kills more people than sharks each year, according to urban legend? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword. Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) - Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you the word for a baby eagle. That would be eaglet, and they are adorable.

artigo.texto: HELLENiQ Renewables, a member of HELLENiQ ENERGY, has completed construction of the group’s first battery energy storage system (BESS) at its industrial facilities in Thessaloniki. With installed capacity of 100 MW and storage capacity of 200 MWh, the project is one of the largest electricity storage facilities to have been developed in Greece and southeastern Europe. The investment, with a total value of approximately 50 million euros, marks an important milestone for HELLENiQ ENERGY as it expands its portfolio beyond renewable power generation into critical infrastructure designed to enable more efficient use of renewable energy. The project will also provide flexibility and balancing services to Greece’s national electricity transmission system, strengthening its reliability and resilience while contributing to the country’s energy security. HELLENiQ ENERGY has been expanding its renewable energy portfolio in recent years as part of a broader strategy to diversify and modernize its energy business. The group has also been pursuing investments in energy storage alongside renewable generation, while seeking to strengthen its position in the wider Southeast European energy market. Better use of green energy A significant share of renewable electricity generation is lost when instantaneous demand is lower than output. Projects such as the HELLENiQ Renewables facility allow more renewable energy to be utilized by storing it in batteries for use when demand is higher. This improves the efficiency of the electricity system, reduces renewable-energy curtailment and creates the necessary grid capacity to accommodate additional renewable energy units in the national system. The development also comes as HELLENiQ ENERGY positions renewable generation and storage as complementary components of its broader energy strategy, with the company identifying storage as an important element in improving flexibility and supporting Greece’s transition toward a more diversified and resilient energy system.

artigo.texto: Following major purchases in recent months by tech billionaires, Oakland is putting a pause on data center development in the city. The Oakland City Council on Tuesday unanimously approved a 45-day moratorium on building the controversial facilities, giving leaders more time to create a regulatory framework for appropriate uses that protect workers, the power grid and environmental resources. As author of the legislation, Councilmember Carroll Fife said the moratorium is “prudent and critical” at the local level. “Given advancements in technology, the City reasonably anticipates that absent this moratorium, applications for data centers will be submitted under existing regulations before the City can complete the necessary study and adopt regulations,” a policy analysis from Fife’s office states. With the number of data centers growing nationally, so have concerns about the resources they generally require for operation. In 2023, data centers used about 176 terawatt-hours of electricity, about 4% of total U.S. consumption that year, according to a 2024 Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report. Data centers are expected to consume up to 12% of all available electricity in the country by 2028, the report stated. Because data center servers require a cooling system, some of the larger facilities can use as much as 5 million gallons of water per day – equivalent to more than seven Olympic-sized swimming pools, according to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute. In response, hundreds of municipalities across the U.S. have announced moratoriums – sometimes even outright bans – on data centers until they can properly regulate them. In the Bay Area, Richmond and San Francisco each recently approved a pause on data center developments. “It’s a real testament to the power of the people organizing and what we can achieve against these big tech companies,” said Adi Varshneya, an organizer for the Party for Socialism and Liberation, one of the key groups against data centers in Oakland. “Thousands have signed petitions, hundreds have been volunteering and sharing online with their community network.” Oakland’s pause comes as major companies this summer announced plans to invest in the city, sparking public outcry for increased action at City Hall. The Behring Company is seeking to create a 20,000-square-foot data center at the former Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory supercomputer site at 415 20th St. Jeff Bezos’ artificial intelligence startup Prometheus leased a 100,000-square-foot space in West Oakland. Tesla leased a 40,000-square-foot facility in West Oakland for potential robotics and manufacturing work. Many residents who spoke during public comment on Tuesday urged the council to go further than the moratorium. “What we’d like to see is a ban on data centers,” said Quanah Parker Brightman, executive director of United Native Americans, an Indigenous civil right organization promoting decolonization. “We have an opportunity here today to start that process.” Some residents, however, did not view data centers as a negative for the city. Oakland resident Andrea Ingram said AI data centers are simply the next major innovation, much like electricity. She said the city should consider the tax revenue benefits the facilities could provide as Oakland faces a structural deficit exceeding $100 million. “We need the data centers. We need every form of modern science and technology and industry that we can get” Ingram said. “Oakland is good at driving those things out of the city, and then we turn around and ask why we can’t give a raise to city workers.”

artigo.texto: Armazenamento de energia com usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis entra na pauta do setor elétrico e será debatido na Coniben 2026 Brasil se volta para o potencial de seu parque hidrelétrico com dezenas de barragens que poderão funcionar como caixa d'água de energia armazenada Clique aqui e escute a matéria As projeções da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), no Plano Decenal de Energia (PDE 2035), indicando que o Brasil pode incorporar cerca de 7 gigawatts (GW) em armazenamento de energia e outros 3 GW em mecanismos de resposta da demanda, abrem uma nova perspectiva de que tecnologias como além de baterias usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis possam ter protagonismo, enquanto fontes despacháveis passam a exercer papel cada vez mais voltado à garantia de capacidade. Tema do painel sobre usinas reversíveis no painel de armazenamento de energia na Conferência Ibero-Brasileira de Energia Coniben, o assunto desperta forte interesse no setor elétrico, dado o fato de que o Brasil, um país com enorme parque hidráulico, ainda se utiliza dessa tecnologia que pode redefinir o tamanho da nossa capacidade de armazenamento de energia. A Coniben é reconhecida como um fórum que, ao longo dos anos, vem debatendo o planejamento da segurança energética no Brasil, em Portugal e na Espanha. A Conferência Ibero-Brasileira de Energia deste ano vai debater as mudanças globais na geopolítica e na geoeconomia. O encontro de 150 líderes e executivos do setor reunidos nos dias 12 e 13 de novembro em Lisboa. Segundo o coordenador técnico do Coniben, Reive Barros, isso é natural porque o Brasil sempre foi um país de grande potencial hidroenergético que nos fez ancorar toda nossa capacidade de produção em barragens de grande porte. Nesse contexto, essa abundância de energia não fazia necessário pensar em usinas reversíveis, embora os projetos sempre vissem essa possibilidade. Faz sentido. Até a chegada das novas matrizes renováveis, como eólica e solar, de fato, não era urgente pensar que uma hidrelétrica acomodasse sistemas de reversão. Mas o mercado brasileiro cresceu e, com o desenvolvimento proporcionado pelos projetos de energia limpa, porém intermitentes, a questão do armazenamento se tornou uma necessidade em que o país agora começa a trabalhar com o tema. Sistemas como o BESS, usinas termelétricas a gás e usinas renováveis estão disponíveis e juntos, esses recursos serão fundamentais para atender às necessidades de potência do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), mas sua viabilização depende de um marco legal estável e de avanços regulatórios. Reive Barros chama a atenção para o fato de o próprio Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade (LRCAP - Armazenamento) de 2026, que poderá contratar novos sistemas de armazenamento que naturalmente incluem as usinas reversíveis. Ele destaca que essa tecnologia, perfeitamente possível em diversos projetos brasileiros, é conhecida dos engenheiros brasileiros e que, pela abundância do potencial hidrelétrico em novos empreendimentos, não foi prioridade. “Mas esse momento chegou", diz o coordenador técnico do Coniben, e o Brasil vai poder agregar essa tecnologia com caixa d'água de energia acoplada às barragens já em funcionamento. Entidades como a Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (ABSOLAR) veem essa possibilidade como um fator estratégico para fechar o ciclo de produção de energia renovável. O armazenamento, nesse cenário, também surge como alternativa competitiva às térmicas a combustíveis fósseis, segundo análises da consultoria da CELA (Clean Energy Latin America). De acordo com o estudo, o uso de baterias pode reduzir em até 48% os custos totais de capacidade e em até 66% as emissões de carbono, além de contribuir para maior eficiência operacional. O que torna o armazenamento com energia oriunda de usinas reversíveis um elemento estratégico. O Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade (LRCAP - Armazenamento) de 2026, promovido pelo Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME), prevê a realização de um Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade (LRCap) na forma de potência por ano entre 2027 e 2029, com possibilidade de participação de baterias e sistemas de armazenamento hidráulico (também conhecidos como usinas reversíveis). A expansão da contratação dessas hidrelétricas foi incluída pelo Congresso durante a tramitação do marco legal das eólicas offshore, em um conjunto de dispositivos que tratam de fontes de geração que não eram o objeto original do projeto. Parte desses dispositivos foi inicialmente vetada e depois promulgada após a derrubada dos vetos pelo Congresso. Reive Barros chama a atenção para o fato de a mudança ser proporcionada pela Lei 15.269/2025. A legislação passou a prever a contratação de 4,9 GW de centrais hidrelétricas de até 50 MW por meio de reserva de capacidade, com período de suprimento de 25 anos. Isso fez com que o assunto entrasse na programação da Coniben, cuja marca tem sido antecipar debates sobre soluções que serão adotadas no setor elétrico. Segundo ele, com isso, o Ministério de Minas e Energia abriu a possibilidade de incluir usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis e termelétricas movidas a biometano, biogás, biocombustíveis e resíduos nos leilões de reserva de capacidade, com previsão de realização a partir do segundo semestre de 2027. E essa sinalização aparece no novo calendário estimado de contratações do setor elétrico para o período de 2027 a 2029. A novidade está na indicação expressa de sistemas de armazenamento hidráulico (as hidrelétricas reversíveis) e das térmicas que utilizam esses combustíveis entre as alternativas para os certames de contratação de potência. A relação também inclui baterias eletroquímicas, hidrelétricas e outras termelétricas. O novo calendário também cita baterias eletroquímicas, hidrelétricas e termelétricas, inclusive unidades abastecidas por biometano, biogás, biocombustíveis e resíduos, entre as tecnologias que poderão ser consideradas nas futuras contratações de potência. artigo.texto: UMBC poll finds more than 75% of Maryland voters oppose new data centers A new poll from the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, finds that more than three-quarters of Maryland voters oppose building new data centers in the state and in their own communities. Those surveyed cited concerns about potential negative impacts, including rising energy costs and water quality. The findings come as Maryland Gov. Wes Moore moves to establish new statewide guidelines for data centers. Last month, Moore signed an executive order outlining a standardized review process for data center projects requiring 25 megawatts or more of power. The order also establishes a Maryland Data Center Task Force and a public data center dashboard. Moore said large data centers will be subject to "one standard, one review process and one public record" when seeking state action, including permits, incentives or letters of support. The governor has also said he supports repealing Maryland's tax exemption for data centers, which was established in 2020. "While federal inaction and Donald Trump's aggressive rollback of safety regulations have granted Big Tech free reign to write their own rules – raising electricity bills and polluting our air and water – our administration is taking action to put control in the hands of Marylanders," Moore said in a statement. "By signing this executive order, we are establishing clear safeguards to ensure Marylanders do not foot the bill, our people benefit, community voices are heard, and our environment is protected — all while centering transparency and accountability throughout the process." The executive order stops short of imposing a statewide ban or moratorium on data centers, as some Maryland counties have done. Poll finds concerns about Maryland's economy The UMBC poll also found widespread pessimism about the state's economic conditions. Nearly all respondents rated Maryland's current economic conditions as either poor or fair, and just 12% said they expect conditions to improve over the next year. The poll examined voters' views on several economic factors, including the cost of everyday goods and services, personal finances, housing costs, state taxes and fees, interest rates, unemployment and the stock market. Additionally, 49% of Maryland likely voters said the state is headed in the wrong direction, while 37% said it is moving in the right direction. The UMBC Poll surveyed 776 likely voters in Maryland from Sept. 22 through Sept. 27, 2026.

artigo.texto: A Motorola anunciou nesta terça-feira (6) o lançamento do novo Moto G37 para o mercado brasileiro, focado em apresentar características mais básicas ao mercado de entrada. O novo aparelho da companhia traz um conjunto de câmeras suficiente, com principal de 50 MP, e bateria para 43 horas, mas pouca memória RAM. Com características mais básicas, o Moto G37 aposta em uma tela HD+ e tamanho de 6,7 polegadas. O painel é simples, de LCD, com taxa de atualização de 120 Hz e brilho máximo de 1.050 nits, mas sem grandes funcionalidades além da profundidade de cores em 8-bits. Em termos de bateria, a fabricante explica que a capacidade do componente é de 5.200 mAh, proporcionando uma autonomia de 43 horas. Vale notar que no site estrangeiro da companhia esse número vai para 63 horas. Já o carregador é padrão de 20W. Câmera de 50 MP e chip MediaTek Por ser um produto bem inclinado ao mercado de dispositivos de entrada, o Moto G37 possui um conjunto traseiro de câmeras bem básico, mas aparentemente suficiente. Esse sensor principal trabalha com resolução de 50 megapixels, mas acompanha um sensor de ambiente dois em um. - Quando o assunto são as especificações internas desse celular, o chip escolhido pela Motorola é o Dimensity 6300, da MediaTek; - A plataforma foi lançada no fim de 2024, fabricada em um processo de 6 nanômetros e compatível com a rede 5G; - A parte mais complicada é o fato de esse aparelho ter somente 4 GB de memória RAM, embora a marca cite os 8 GB de memória virtual; - Além disso, há opções de 64 GB ou 128 GB para o armazenamento interno, mas há compatibilidade com cartão microSD para expansão de até 1 TB; - O modelo possui certificação militar MIL-STD 810H e proteção IP64 contra respingos d’água e poeira; - As possibilidades de gravação incluem resolução 2K a 30 fps na frontal e traseira; - Por ser um modelo de entrada, a conexão de 3,5 mm para fone de ouvido está disponível; - Tecnologias como o Gemini e o Circule Para Pesquisar são integradas ao aparelho. O novo Motorola Moto G37 já pode ser oficialmente adquirido no mercado brasileiro, através do site da fabricante, pelo preço de R$ 899 na versão de 64 GB e R$ 1.079 na variante de 128 GB. É possível adquirir o produto nas cores grafite, azul turquesa, azul náutico e rosa com certificação Pantone. Ficha técnica - Tela: LCD de 6,67 polegadas, resolução HD+ (1604 x 720), taxa de atualização de 120 Hz e brilho de até 1.050 nits - Processador: MediaTek Dimensity 6300 (octa-core de até 2,4 GHz, 6 nm) - Memória RAM: 4 GB LPDDR4X (expansível via RAM Boost) - Armazenamento interno: 128 GB (expansível via cartão microSD de até 1 TB) - Câmeras traseiras: 50 MP (f/1.8, PDAF, Quad Pixel) e sensor 2 em 1 de luz ambiente e detecção de cintilação - Câmera frontal: 8 MP (f/2.0) - Gravação de vídeo: até 2K a 30 fps (frontal e traseira) - Bateria: 5.200 mAh com carregamento TurboPower de 20 W e recarga reversa com fio de 6 W - Sistema operacional: Android 16 - Construção e durabilidade: vidro frontal Gorilla Glass 7i, proteção IP64 contra poeira e respingos d’água, e certificação militar MIL-STD-810H - Áudio: alto-falantes estéreo com Dolby Atmos e entrada P2 (3,5 mm) para fone de ouvido - Conectividade: 5G, Wi-Fi dual-band (2,4 GHz e 5 GHz), Bluetooth 5.4, NFC e porta USB-C 2.0 - Segurança: leitor de digitais na lateral e reconhecimento facial - Dimensões e peso: 166,23 x 76,50 x 7,85 mm; 191 g Compre o Moto G37 - Moto G37 de 128GB por R$ 1.079,10 no site da Motorola - Moto G37 de 64GB por R$ 899,10 no Magazine Luiza - Moto G37 de 64GB por R$ 999,00 na Amazon - Moto G37 de 64GB por R$ 999,00 no Mercado Livre Por falar em produtos, a Motorola lançou os novos Moto Watch Ultra recentemente no Brasil com especificações bem robustas. artigo.texto: (The Center Square) – Cost of living, immigration, water and data centers were among the issues debated Wednesday night by candidates for Arizona’s Congressional District 1. Presented in partnership with Clean Elections, the Citizens’ Clean Elections Commission and the Arizona Media Association, the event offered a stark contrast between the two major party candidates: the Republican, Thomas “Jay” Feely IV, and the Democrat, Dr. Amish Shah. The race for the open seat is widely regarded as one of the competitive contests that will help determine which party takes control of the U.S. House in the Nov. 3 midterm election. "On my side, I believe in limited government, in lower taxes, in individual liberties," Feely said during the debate, which streamed live from Sneaky Big Studios in Scottsdale, Ariz. "Shah and Democrats believe in bigger government, government solutions, more government intrusion and higher taxes." Shah, an emergency room physician and former state legislator, emphasized his hands-on experience treating patients and working across the aisle. Shah said that will be needed to help Arizonans. "Gas is high. Diesel is even higher," said Shah. "We're talking about groceries, people looking at a box of cereal and having to put it back." Shah added that the increased cost of energy from the conflict in Iran is a big reason for today’s prices. "What we say in the Emergency Department is, 'Let's stop the hemorrhage,' " said Shah. "Let's stop making this worse so we can end the war." Feely, a former NFL player, broadcaster and financial adviser, countered by pointing to historical inflation rates, arguing that excessive federal spending fueled the current economic climate. He suggested actions to help people earn more money. "When you put more money into people's pockets, it helps them to deal with inflation," said Feely. "No. 2, stop printing money." When it comes to healthcare access and the cost of treatment, Shah expressed deep concern over hospital financial strains and patient debt. "I have to treat those people because Ronald Reagan signed EMTALA [Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act] in 1986, which I happen to agree with, which says that everybody who comes to an Emergency Department has to get seen and has to get treated," said Shah. "It's the moral thing to do. And I agree with it. But that care isn't free. Somebody has to pay that." Feely criticized past healthcare reform laws for empowering large insurance companies at the expense of individual consumers. Advocating for transparent, market-driven changes, Feely pushed for things such as price transparency. “It’s the only industry where you do not know what something costs before you go in there and then you take advantage of it,” said Feely. “You have to have that.” Border policy and national security formed another critical point in the debate, particularly regarding how immigration intersects with federal safety nets and public resources. Focusing heavily on enforcement, Feely argued past policy changes wrongfully extended government benefits to noncitizens. While agreeing on core limitations regarding public assistance, Shah emphasized practical enforcement and criticized blanket administrative maneuvers. “I don’t think illegal immigrants should be on Medicaid.” Still, Shah disagreed with methods such as rigid work requirements, arguing that states that tried this created administrative waste rather than practical solutions. The candidates agreed on Arizona's need for an adequate water supply. They discussed the Colorado River - a key source for water supplies, irrigation for agriculture and recreation in the Southwest - and a federal plan requiring Arizona, Nevada and California - the lower basin states - to make cuts in their usage. The plan, developed by the Bureau of Reclamation, doesn't require cuts of the upper basin states of Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming. If federal cuts need to be made, upper basin states and the lower basin states should make those cuts equally, Feeley argued. "Water impacts everything,” the Republican candidate noted. “It impacts our ability to have more housing. It impacts our ability to bring industry here." Feely then pushed for innovative solutions and regional cooperation. "When you talk about desalination, when you talk about new farming practices, Arizona has done a really good job of conservation,” he said. “We should have a desalination plant. We should look at all the measures that we can do to make sure that we are water-independent.” Shah, whose first vote in the Legislature was for a drought contingency plan, said Arizonans should “fight like hell for every drop” of water. "Thinking outside the box while I was in the state Legislature again, a lot of the Republicans were talking about desalination,” the Democratic candidate said. “So I'm glad we agree also that this is something that can be done. We're talking about a study committee right now to look at that and buying up water rights while we help build desal plants elsewhere." Near the end of the debate, the candidates were asked about data centers. It was a timely question, with many states and cities expressing concern about data centers using too much water and electricity. Supporters downplay the concerns. Shah said the U.S. is going to need data centers because artificial intelligence is coming. "I just don't want them in CD1, our district here,” he said. “The reason I say that is because, again, I'm fighting for the voters and making sure that their wishes are what is paramount here." In contrast, Feely has framed data center development as vital for technological competitiveness against China. He added that data centers benefit Arizona’s economy. “Right now in the state of Arizona, data centers bring in $27 billion to our GDP. artigo.texto: BYD unveils interior of its third-generation Tang EV BYD has officially unveiled the interior of its third-generation Tang. Lu Tian, General Manager of BYD’s Dynasty Series Sales Division, released the official images today with two new interior colour schemes: Dune Beige and Amber Brown. The interior design features a “Star Ring” display and a panoramic glass roof. BYD has utilised fine leather upholstery with diamond-quilted stitching. The cabin has integrated ambient lighting that runs throughout the dashboard and door panels. The third-generation Tang is also known as the 8 Series Tang, and joins the Tang L and the larger 9 Series Da Tang (Great Tang) in BYD’s domestic SUV family, while overseas markets have used the Atto 8 and Sealion 8 names for related models. Exterior and Dimensions The third-generation Tang continues the evolution of BYD’s “Dynasty” design language. The front fascia is dominated by a full-width LED light bar and air intakes. The side profile features a floating roof design and semi-concealed door handles. Customers can choose between 20-inch and 21-inch wheels. Vehicle Dimensions: - Length: 5,045 mm - Width: 1,980 mm - Height: 1,760 mm - Wheelbase: 2,950 mm Performance and Technology Under the hood, the new Tang is powered by a TZ205QYD electric motor, delivering a maximum power output of 300 kW (402 hp). The vehicle is equipped with BYD’s second-generation Blade Battery, available in two capacities: 88.682 kWh and 105.792 kWh. Depending on the configuration, the model offers CLTC-rated pure electric ranges of 730 km (591 km WLTP), 830 km (672 km WLTP), and 850 km (689 km WLTP). The vehicle also supports BYD’s flash-charging technology. The third-generation Tang features the DiSus-A intelligent air body control system, which includes dual-chamber air suspension and intelligent road-surface preview technology, allowing the vehicle to adapt rapidly to changing road conditions. Additionally, the SUV is equipped with the “God’s Eye B” intelligent driving assistance system.

artigo.texto: Veja o resumo da notícia - Pastores no Quênia processam organização local por redesenhar rotas de pastoreio para gerar créditos de carbono. - A medida, que visa sequestrar carbono, restringe o acesso dos rebanhos a pastagens tradicionais e afeta o modo de vida local. - Netflix, Meta, British Airways e Beiersdorf estão entre as empresas que compram esses créditos de carbono. - A ação judicial questiona a legitimidade do consentimento das comunidades e a distribuição dos valores arrecadados. - O caso levanta debate sobre a qualidade dos offsets climáticos e o impacto social em territórios tradicionais. - No Brasil, dilemas semelhantes surgem em projetos de crédito de carbono na Amazônia, com comunidades cobrando participação. - A disputa expõe a assimetria de poder entre o mercado global de carbono e as comunidades que habitam as áreas afetadas. Os pastores que há gerações conduzem o gado pelas mesmas rotas no norte do Quênia afirmam que perderam o controle prático sobre a terra quando uma organização local passou a redesenhar o pastoreio para gerar créditos de carbono vendidos a empresas ocidentais, entre elas a Netflix e a Meta. A revolta virou processo judicial em torno da área do reservatório natural de Biliqo Bulesa, uma reserva a algumas centenas de quilômetros a nordeste de Nairobi, a capital queniana, território usado por comunidades de pecuaristas desde tempos imemoriais. Segundo os autores da ação, o Northern Rangelands Trust, conhecido pela sigla NRT, teria começado a transformar o manejo do solo sem o consentimento pleno das famílias que dependem daquelas pastagens, e o resultado imediato é a restrição de caminhos por onde o rebanho sempre circulou. A reportagem do NOS descreve o mal-estar como consequência direta de um esquema em que companhias pagam para, no papel, reduzir a própria pegada de dióxido de carbono enquanto a organização queniana “fabrica” os créditos ao impedir que o gado paste em trechos determinados, permitindo que a vegetação cresça mais e armazene mais carbono. Os pastores cobram transparência sobre os valores exatos arrecadados e dizem que a entidade passou a exercer poder excessivo sobre o modo de vida que sustenta suas famílias. O mecanismo em disputa é o crédito de carbono, instrumento pelo qual cada tonelada de dióxido de carbono que deixa de ir para a atmosfera ou que é capturada pode ser convertida em um comprovante negociável. Países e empresas usam esses comprovantes para cumprir metas climáticas ou para compensar emissões difíceis de cortar na própria operação. O vendedor, seja governo ou organização, não pode mais contabilizar aquele volume para as próprias metas depois de repassar o crédito, mas recebe dinheiro pela transação. No projeto queniano, um dos maiores do mundo nesse formato de pastagens, a lógica central é ajustar rotas tradicionais de pastoreio para que plantas voltem a crescer com menos pressão do gado, produzindo biomassa maior e, com ela, mais sequestro de carbono. Netflix, Meta, British Airways e Beiersdorf figuram entre os compradores que repassam recursos à organização local e, em troca, contabilizam uma emissão menor em seus balanços climáticos. Para os pastores, o que aparece como solução climática no exterior se traduz em perda de acesso a áreas de pasto, incerteza sobre renda e a sensação de que a terra ancestral foi convertida em ativo financeiro sem que as comunidades tivessem voz decisória sobre o desenho do projeto. Como o crédito de carbono transforma pastagem em ativo negociável para big tech Na prática cotidiana, o rebanho precisa se deslocar conforme a chuva, a seca e a regeneração do capim, e qualquer redesign de rotas que feche corredores históricos obriga os pastores a alongar jornadas, concentrar animais em faixas menores ou aceitar pastos de pior qualidade. O NRT argumenta, no desenho do programa, que a regeneração controlada aumenta a capacidade de armazenamento de carbono das pastagens e, portanto, gera créditos legítimos. Os herdeiros da tradição pastoril respondem que a transformação ocorreu sem autorização clara e que a organização lucrou milhões com a venda desses créditos enquanto as famílias ficaram sem informação detalhada sobre valores, contratos e distribuição de benefícios. A exigência judicial de abertura dos números não é apenas contábil: trata-se de saber se a compensação financeira chega de fato a quem perdeu flexibilidade de manejo e se o preço pago pelas empresas cobre o custo social de alterar um sistema de subsistência construído ao longo de gerações. A tensão cresce porque o mesmo solo que alimenta o gado passa a ser lido, nos relatórios corporativos de tecnologia e aviação, como sumidouro de carbono capaz de limpar parte da imagem climática de plataformas de streaming, redes sociais e companhias aéreas. Empresas de tecnologia e de entretenimento digital operam cadeias globais de data centers, deslocamentos de equipes e produção audiovisual com pegada energética elevada, e a compra de créditos aparece como atalho para metas de neutralidade anunciadas em relatórios anuais. No caso queniano, o atalho passa por uma paisagem semiárida onde a sobrevivência depende da mobilidade do rebanho. Quando a organização gestora limita o pastejo para maximizar o crescimento vegetal mensurável, o indicador de carbono sobe e o crédito se valoriza, mas o pastor vê encolher a margem de manobra que sempre usou para enfrentar secas. A ação judicial em torno de Biliqo Bulesa coloca em xeque não só a legitimidade do consentimento, mas o próprio modelo de governança em que uma entidade intermediária concentra poder de redesenhar o território e negociar com compradores internacionais. Os pastores afirmam que essa concentração altera regras de uso da terra e de convivência entre clãs e famílias, porque quem controla o mapa do pastoreio controla, em última instância, o calendário da sobrevivência. artigo.texto: Startup de ganhador do prêmio Nobel de Química quer produzir água do ar usando calor residual de data centers Tecnologia aproveita o calor que hoje é descartado por data centers para extrair água da umidade do ar Uma startup americana quer transformar o calor residual de data centers em água extraída do ar. A Atoco desenvolveu uma tecnologia que usa materiais capazes de capturar moléculas de água da atmosfera e liberá-las com a ajuda de calor industrial, sem precisar de eletricidade para realizar o processo. A empresa vê na expansão dos data centers de inteligência artificial uma forma de ampliar o uso da tecnologia. Segundo a Wired, a empresa já demonstrou o funcionamento do sistema em um protótipo em sua sede, na Califórnia. O equipamento pode produzir até 300 litros de água por dia e utiliza estruturas metal-orgânicas, conhecidas pela sigla em inglês MOFs, que funcionam como esponjas microscópicas capazes de reter moléculas. O material captura a umidade do ar e, quando aquecido, libera a água armazenada. A tecnologia foi desenvolvida a partir das pesquisas de Omar Yaghi, fundador da Atoco e vencedor do Prêmio Nobel de Química de 2025. O diferencial desta versão da tecnologia é justamente que não é necessário conexão à rede elétrica, nem mesmo eletricidade, para capturar água do ar em escala microscópica. E também não é preciso usar eletricidade para retirar a água dos materiais e transformá-la em algo útil para as pessoas. Em vez disso, basta calor industrial de baixa temperatura. Segundo a Atoco, isso torna a tecnologia uma candidata ideal para ser conectada a data centers de IA, que geram grandes quantidades de calor residual enquanto seus servidores processam desde provas matemáticas até editores virtuais — ao mesmo tempo em que frequentemente exigem enormes volumes de água. “Quatro ou cinco anos atrás, não estávamos realmente pensando em data centers de IA”, disse Samer Taha, CEO da Atoco, à Wired. Mas a expansão gigantesca desse setor criou uma oportunidade para a startup, que pode avançar em direção a um objetivo maior: garantir que pessoas que vivem em regiões com escassez de água tenham controle sobre esse recurso cada vez mais precioso. Quando Yaghi era estudante de doutorado, ele diz que criar algo como os MOFs era “o sonho de todo químico”. Parte de seu trabalho, que lhe rendeu o Nobel, nos últimos 20 anos foi levar pesquisas teóricas para o mundo real, criando uma estrutura molecular estável que conecta material orgânico a íons metálicos. Como funciona as estruturas metal-orgânicas A estrutura de um MOF se parece um pouco “com um brinquedo de trepa-trepa em um parquinho”, diz Seth Cohen, diretor da Escola de Ciências Físicas da Universidade da Califórnia em Irvine (UC Irvine). Os MOFs são essencialmente “esponjas moleculares — são um material sólido muito, muito bom em absorver outras moléculas”, afirma Cohen, que não tem envolvimento com a Atoco. Assim como uma esponja, os materiais também podem ser espremidos por meio de métodos que incluem o uso de calor para liberar aquilo que retiveram. Essas estruturas semelhantes a trepa-trepas criam espaços abertos em escala microscópica capazes de armazenar uma quantidade impressionante de material, e pequenas alterações podem gerar ainda mais espaço interno. “Um grama de MOF pode cobrir uma área equivalente a dois campos de futebol”, explica Yaghi. “Você pode armazenar hidrogênio ali para produzir energia limpa, ou CO₂ para produzir ar limpo. Ou, neste caso, pode armazenar água.” Como o equipamento gera água? Como não havia um data center nas proximidades da sede da empresa, a equipe da Atoco simulou a situação conduzindo calor de uma fonte a cerca de 65,5 °C. Um painel solar alimenta os diversos sistemas, mas não a operação de captura de água em si, o que deixa a máquina revestida de metal, que fica no estacionamento da empresa, quase silenciosa. Taha demonstrou à Wired como o equipamento funciona. Eram pouco depois das 9h, com a temperatura acima dos 32 °C, quando ele apertou um botão na lateral e abriu uma torneira. Um fluxo de água transparente começa a sair, com aparência boa o suficiente para beber. Ela não é oferecida para consumo por questões de responsabilidade legal, embora Taha observe que equivale a água destilada, porque os MOFs da Atoco não foram projetados para capturar poluentes presentes no ar. “Cerca de 70% do calor residual industrial é de baixa temperatura, não é utilizado e acaba sendo lançado nos oceanos ou no ar”, afirma. “Se você transformar esse calor residual em água limpa usando nossa tecnologia, estamos falando de trilhões de litros de água limpa.” Data centers no centro da discussão Os data centers são uma fonte cada vez maior desse calor residual. Uma única instalação pode liberar uma quantidade de calor equivalente à produzida por dezenas de milhares de casas. Os operadores precisam dissipar esse calor no ambiente, criando ilhas de calor, e ainda pagam por diferentes tipos de sistemas de resfriamento. Muitos desses sistemas também dependem de água, e alguns podem consumir milhões de galões por dia. A tecnologia da Atoco, portanto, poderia atacar dois dos maiores problemas dos data centers. Os data centers estão investindo muito dinheiro para se livrar do calor residual, diz Taha. “Nós, na verdade, queremos esse calor; precisamos dele. Devolvemos água, o mesmo produto que está causando o problema.” Ele afirma que a empresa também quer ajudar a levar água a comunidades rurais, onde concessionárias às vezes precisam transportar água em caminhões por falta de infraestrutura. Para fazer isso, será necessário um grande salto de escala. A Atoco imagina data centers usando várias unidades dispostas em uma espécie de grade para produzir água e trabalha em uma versão comercial capaz de gerar até 1.000 litros por dia, segundo a Wired. artigo.texto: Battery energy storage is moving from a supporting role in the energy transition to one of its central pillars. IDTechEx puts figures on that shift in its newly updated report Batteries for Stationary Energy Storage 2027–2037, forecasting that the global lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS) market will reach $135 billion by 2037, with cumulative installations exceeding 10.5 TWh worldwide. It traces this growth to the rising share of renewables in electricity grids, new demand from data centre build-out and a shift in policy from headline storage targets towards bankable revenue frameworks and more sophisticated routes to market. A rapid shift in battery demand Lithium-ion remains the dominant chemistry for stationary storage, supported by broad availability, falling costs and steady performance gains. Total lithium-ion battery demand continues to climb, but the application mix is changing quickly. Electric vehicles still account for the largest share of global demand, although their portion fell from 84 percent in 2023 to 78 percent in 2025, while the BESS share rose from 10 to 19 percent over the same period. Policy shifts in the EV market have contributed to this change, but the main driver is the faster growth of stationary storage as grids integrate more variable renewable generation and require greater flexibility. AI turns storage into a multi-revenue asset for industry Within lithium-ion, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) continues to extend its lead over nickel manganese cobalt (NMC), reflecting lower cost, longer cycle life and better thermal stability. Sodium-ion is also gaining ground as developers improve performance and cut production costs, but LFP is expected to remain the chemistry of choice for most BESS applications over the forecast period. Deployments triple in two years IDTechEx estimates that annual global Li-ion BESS deployments across grid-scale, commercial and industrial, and residential segments rose from 92 GWh in 2023 to 318 GWh in 2025, an increase of more than threefold. China accounted for 58 percent of 2025 deployments at 183 GWh, with the United States contributing 57 GWh, or 18 percent. China is likely to retain its lead over the coming decade, supported by intense domestic competition, growing grid flexibility requirements and expanding LFP cell and BESS manufacturing capacity. The US market, by contrast, is being reshaped by industrial policy aimed at reducing reliance on Chinese cells and systems. That policy is accelerating the localisation of the domestic supply chain, with several players expanding LFP cell and BESS manufacturing capacity in the country, while most Chinese suppliers have scaled back or exited the market. Beyond the two leaders, countries previously absent from the global top tier are now entering it at scale. Saudi Arabia emerged as the third-largest market in 2025, boosted by several gigawatt-hour-scale projects, and Chile also broke into the top ten. IDTechEx expects more countries to follow, with leading suppliers already securing projects of several hundred megawatt-hours up to gigawatt-hour scale in markets where deployment had previously been limited. Europe scales up through policy and procurement Europe is emerging as one of the most dynamic regions in the global BESS market, with the report covering Germany, Italy, the United Kingdom, Bulgaria, Spain and Poland in detail. Two policy schemes stand out. The UK’s cap-and-floor framework for long-duration energy storage is designed to unlock projects that struggle to secure financing on merchant revenues alone, while Italy’s MACSE auction establishes a central procurement route for large-scale storage. Europe hits 100 GWh as utility-scale takes over the storage market Beyond these schemes, Germany continues to anchor Europe’s residential and commercial storage segments, and markets such as Bulgaria, Spain and Poland are moving quickly from early projects to structured pipelines. Together, these developments are shaping Europe into a region where storage deployment is increasingly underpinned by predictable revenue mechanisms rather than merchant exposure alone. Procurement, revenue models and bankability The same shift is under way well beyond Europe. Governments and system operators are moving beyond headline targets towards mechanisms that can carry large waves of BESS projects through tendering and commissioning. Examples include Australia’s Capacity Investment Scheme and the New South Wales Long-Term Energy Service Agreements, as well as state-backed tenders in the Middle East. Overstated battery availability puts investor returns at risk Project financing is also becoming more sophisticated. Revenue floors, capacity contracts, tolling agreements and stacked revenue models combining arbitrage, ancillary services and capacity payments are improving bankability and enabling a broader pipeline of projects to secure investment. In the residential segment, subsidies continue to play a decisive role, as shown by the strong uptake under Australia’s Cheaper Home Batteries Program. When such schemes are phased out, however, activity can drop quickly. Technology trends: larger cells, denser systems At the technology level, developers are increasingly launching containerised grid-scale systems built around higher-capacity cells, with a growing number of units rated at 6.5 MWh or more. Larger cells can improve system-level energy density by reducing the number of cells, interconnections and casings per megawatt-hour, allowing a greater share of the container to be occupied by active battery material. The approach also simplifies manufacturing and can lower project-level costs, as fewer units are needed for a given site capacity. Although energy density has traditionally mattered less for stationary storage than for EVs, it is becoming a point of differentiation. artigo.texto: Where does the proposed data center next to Nashville Zoo stand? NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WZTV) — The fight over a proposed data center next to the Nashville Zoo is heading to Nashville’s Board of Zoning Appeals, where a dispute over which zoning rules apply could determine whether the project moves forward. PREVIOUS COVERAGE | Judge dismisses DC BLOX lawsuit for now A federal judge dismissed DC BLOX’s claims against Metro, but that ruling did not settle the future of the proposed facility on Grassmere Park Drive. We’re not out of the woods yet,” Councilmember Rollin Horton said. Its proposed location immediately beside the zoo has drawn opposition, with the zoo reporting that its petition has reached more than 600,000 signatures. The next question is whether the project has vested rights, meaning it can proceed under older zoning rules rather than restrictions Nashville adopted in July. If they’re subject to old rules, the data centers by the Zoo will likely move forward,” Horton said. If the new rules apply, Horton said, the project would not be able to proceed as proposed. Those restrictions require at least a half-mile separation between this type of data center development and the zoo, he said. “The property that they’ve selected on Grassmere is immediately adjacent to it,” Horton said. According to Horton, the zoo is challenging the project’s permits, arguing that the development does not comply with the new rules. That challenge is expected to go before the Board of Zoning Appeals in December. Horton encouraged residents concerned about the proposal to participate in the hearing. JULY COVERAGE | Metro Council member points to Board of Zoning appeals to stop data center near zoo It’s important that we win this case that the zoo has brought before the Nashville Board of Zoning Appeals in December,” he said. The new regulations also prohibit data centers larger than 500,000 square feet and restrict where other large facilities can be located and how they are approved, according to Horton. He said the rules include protections for homes, schools, churches and the zoo. In a social media update following the federal ruling, the Nashville Zoo said it was continuing to monitor the proposed development. The zoo reported that its petition had reached 600,404 signatures. We’re still keeping an eye on the proposed data center,” the zoo wrote. In an earlier interview, Kirk Offel, founder and CEO of Overwatch Mission Critical, said communities should have a say in where data centers are built while recognizing their role in supporting digital infrastructure. I don’t wanna see the environment erode because of the demand of technology, but there has to be a way to be able to let those two both coexist,” Offel said. Offel, who said he had not worked with DC BLOX, also acknowledged that a technically sound project could be proposed in the wrong location. The data centers don’t belong everywhere, right?” he said. The federal litigation could also continue. DC BLOX has 21 days to try to amend three of its dismissed claims. Horton said Metro’s temporary moratorium on new data centers would be nearly expired by the end of that amendment window. He said the lasting issue for the zoo project is whether Nashville’s permanent zoning restrictions apply. FOX 17 News reached out to DC BLOX for comment on the ruling and its next steps; they did not immediately respond.

artigo.texto: MONTGOMERY, Ala. – The Alabama Public Service Commission unanimously adopted a procedure Tuesday allowing automatic approval of Alabama Power’s contracts with large load data centers if the commission fails to take a vote within 90 days of submission. Chief Administrative Law Judge Luke Bentley had recommended that the PSC adopt a policy requiring a vote on every large load data center contract but did not include a time window for a vote, which is standard for PSC procedures. Following legislation, the PSC defines large load data centers as facilities that require 150 megawatts or more of electricity and operate on one piece of land. Commissioners Chris Beeker and Jeremy Oden expressed concerns about contracts potentially falling through because of the PSC not acting in a timely manner. Oden called the automatic approval procedure a “consequence” for the PSC not voting. “I want the commission to vote, but then again, I understand if they do not vote, then it’s not on the company and it’s not on the data center. It’s really and truthfully back on the commission …” Oden said. “Saying, ‘Well, since we just didn’t bring it up and vote, it’s gone,’ I don’t think that’s a good move, I don’t think it’s a good economic presentation for the state if we do that.” Though she ultimately introduced an amendment setting up an automatic approval in the case of the PSC’s inaction, PSC President Cynthia Almond said she felt strongly that the commission should take a public vote on data centers because of the public’s concern about the massive facilities that power artificial intelligence. She included the 90-day window for voting in her amendment. “We should not follow the ‘deemed approved’ process that we’ve been following for a number of years,” Almond said. “The current (rate) FCR deals with industry that is one megawatt or greater, and we’re talking about industry now that is at least 150 megawatts, and those are some of our smaller data centers. So these are just to me different animals, and it should be a very public process that we go through.” Data centers previously fell under the general rate flexible contract rate docket – rate FCR – like all commercial and industrial customers with accounts of at least one megawatt. The rate FCR for data centers temporarily had a turnaround time of 45 days, up from the standard 10, while the commission established new procedures. Under Almond’s amendment, the commission is supposed to vote on the contracts within 90 days. If it doesn’t, the contract will automatically be approved. The new procedure does not mandate a public hearing about proposed data center contracts. Tuesday’s vote came after a monthslong general proceeding seeking input from members of the public about how the commission should evaluate Alabama Power’s contracts with data centers. Legislation requiring data centers to pay for the additional electricity they need and refining the longstanding public interest standard sparked the proceeding. Nineteen people and organizations submitted initial comments in the proceeding, while 10 offered reply comments, Bentley said. The newly approved procedure for evaluating contracts also establishes specific reporting requirements for Alabama Power and its data center customers, including a public petition naming the entities behind the facility, its maximum electric capacity and the municipality or county where the center will be. Alabama Power, the state’s largest utility, will now also be required to submit a full copy of its contracts to the PSC and the attorney general’s office. This submission will be confidential. The company must also include in the confidential submission an estimate of impacts on other customers’ costs, how much revenue the project would generate for the company and the cost of the incremental capacity required. It also has to provide a detailed explanation of how the contract meets the public interest standard expanded in Senate Bill 270. That legislation, which established that data centers are in the public’s interest only if they “promote positive benefits” to other customers, went into effect Oct. 1. Lowering the cost for other customers, increasing the efficiency of the power system and contributing to economic growth in the community where a data center is located are examples of positive benefits the bill lays out. The new procedure also forbids the utility from informally submitting information to the PSC or attorney general’s office before filing the public petition. Alabama Power told Alabama Daily News that it is committed to complying with all applicable regulatory requirements, including the one approved Tuesday. “Alabama Power will continue to require large load data center customers to pay the full cost to serve their energy needs, so costs are not shifted to existing customers,” the company said in a statement. “Alabama state law affirms that same standard and the Alabama Public Service Commission approves contracts that meet that standard while promoting positive benefits for other customers.” Though Energy Alabama and the Southern Environmental Law Center celebrated some of the new transparency requirements created by the PSC on Tuesday, the advocacy groups said in statements that they wished the commission had done more to loop the public into its future decision-making. Daniel Tait, executive director of Energy Alabama, said that customers should be able to participate in the process fully since they “are the ones who pay if one of these deals is priced wrong.” In addition to requesting a public vote every time, Energy Alabama had asked in its general proceeding comments that Alabamians be able to see a redacted version of the data center contracts. “For three decades, rules built for manufacturers let contracts take effect without a vote of the Commission. BESS Business Continues to Grow: LION Smart Wins Three Additional Storage Projects With a Total Capacity of 30 MWh in Germany NewMediaWire Thu, October 8, 2026 at 1:37 PM PDT 3 min read LMIA.DE 0.00% ZUG, SWITZERLAND - October 8, 2026 (NEWMEDIAWIRE) - LION Smart Production GmbH, part of LION E-Mobility AG, announces further project wins in its BESS business. In the third quarter of 2026, the company secured three additional projects for stationary battery energy storage systems (BESS), each with a storage capacity of 10 MWh. With a total volume of 30 MWh, LION Smart is continuing its previous success in the stationary energy storage sector. At the same time, the company is currently planning to expand its offering to include "BESS as a Service" for operators of photovoltaic and wind farms. Three Projects with Different Application Concepts The newly secured projects comprise three different storage applications. One battery storage system with a capacity of 10 MWh is planned for co-location with an existing photovoltaic system. Another green power storage project, also with 10 MWh, combines the battery storage system with a new photovoltaic system. In addition, LION Smart has secured a standalone storage project with a capacity of 10 MWh. The new BESS projects are scheduled to be completed and connected to the grid in Q1 2027. The projects underline the diverse potential applications of stationary battery storage systems, both in combination with renewable generation assets and as standalone storage solutions. LION Smart as System Integrator: Tailor-Made Storage Solutions In the BESS business, LION Smart acts as a system integrator and implements tailor-made storage solutions for its customers, designed to meet the specific requirements of each project. Its service portfolio covers the entire lifecycle of a storage project: from consulting and system design to engineering, integration and commissioning, as well as service and maintenance. Before delivery, each container is approved by an in-house engineering team in accordance with European quality standards. In addition, LION Smart safeguards the performance of its storage systems through performance guarantees. LION Smart is seeing strong customer interest in these solutions. Interested parties include independent power producers and operators of solar and wind power plants, as well as traditional utilities and municipal utilities. BESS as a Service: Battery Storage Without Own Storage Investment With "BESS as a Service", LION Smart is opening up another route to stationary battery storage for operators of photovoltaic and wind farms. The model enables the use of a storage system without requiring operators to make their own investment in the storage asset and creates the opportunity to generate additional storage revenues alongside income from photovoltaic and wind energy. LION Smart also assumes the technical risk and provides service for the storage system. The focus is on a one-stop solution: one partner for the storage project and a concept tailored to the specific application. The concrete structure and economic potential are assessed on a project-specific basis. artigo.texto: Oakland City Council approves 45-day moratorium on new data centers OAKLAND, Calif. - The Oakland City Council voted unanimously Tuesday night to place a 45-day temporary moratorium on all new data center development across the city. Oakland Enacts Temporary Moratorium on Data Center Construction The urgency measure, sponsored by Councilmember Carroll Fife, pauses new approvals to allow city leaders time to study the potential environmental and operational impacts of data centers on local water supplies, electrical grids, and air quality. Before the vote, protesters rallied outside Oakland City Hall to demand a pause on data center developments, expressing concerns over natural resource consumption. Inside council chambers, community members and activists offered mixed testimony on the proposal. Opponents of data centers highlighted the massive water demands required for cooling systems. "My concern about it being in Oakland is that we have limited water from the Mokelumne River, and that’s in the Sierra Nevada, and we’re already taking up to 60 to 70 percent of that river out of the river," said Dr. Elizabeth Dougherty. "If we increase water use here, that would take more and more out, so what would be impacting not just our ecosystem, but also up river in the Sierra Nevada." Other residents voiced fears regarding daily utility volume, with one speaker noting that "a large data center can use up to 5 billion gallons of water a day," while another called on the council to implement a permanent ban. Conversely, supporters urged the council to reject the moratorium, emphasizing the economic potential and job creation tied to technology infrastructure. "I oppose the moratorium on data centers," one resident told council members. "Data centers will bring jobs. They will not take jobs away," another resident added. Concerns Over Non-Disclosure Agreements and Downtown Proposal Councilmember Fife, who proposed the moratorium, has criticized developers for using non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) to shield specific project details from city officials and the public. The vote followed growing scrutiny over plans announced by Behring Companies to convert the ground floor of a building near 20th and Franklin streets in downtown Oakland into a data center. The developer stated that the other floors of the facility would serve as office space for artificial intelligence research. Mayor Barbara Lee noted that the pause would provide necessary time for public engagement. "This is a moment to have the public weigh in, and the public will be able to weigh in during this 45-day moratorium to see exactly what people here in Oakland want," Mayor Lee said. Next Steps and Public Forum The 45-day moratorium takes effect immediately. City officials will use the interim period to analyze policy options and development standards for future data center projects. Councilmember Fife has scheduled a community conversation for Oct. 24 at 10 a.m. at the Beth Eden Baptist Church at 1183 10th Street in West Oakland to allow residents to further discuss the future of data centers in the city.

artigo.texto: EASTHAMPTON — Easthampton is the latest Valley community to temporarily ban new data centers, as the facilities face growing scrutiny across the country and municipalities grapple with how to regulate them. The City Council on Wednesday night passed the moratorium, barring new data center construction for 18 months while the city develops permanent regulations. The measure amends the city’s Zoning Ordinance to add the temporary moratorium. “I think that we’re all aware of the national energy and climate around data centers and this really strong push to get these built, and then the impacts that they’re having on communities,” said City Councilor At-Large Kiam Jamrog-McQuaid. The moratorium moved swiftly to approval, even though no data centers are currently proposed in the city. The Planning Board unanimously approved the measure last month, with members praising it, as did the council’s ordinance subcommittee, which Jamrog-McQuaid chairs. Moratoriums like Easthampton’s have been spreading quickly across the state. Other Valley communities that have passed one include Holyoke and Shutesbury, while Northampton, Greenfield, Westfield and Ludlow are considering similar measures. Northampton recently formed a 10-member committee to study the impacts of data centers. Last month, Gov. Maura Healey signed an executive order giving municipalities the power to reject data centers, and in June, paused new applications for such facilities. During Easthampton’s 18-month ban, the moratorium calls on the ordinance subcommittee and the Planning Board to study permanent regulations on data centers. A number of factors would be considered such as permitting criteria, and regulations surrounding water use, noise, energy demand and more. “That (work) would be incumbent on us after this passes,” Jamrog-McQuaid said. The moratorium broadly defines data centers as a building or group of buildings used primarily to run technology such as computer systems, servers, cryptocurrency mining equipment and artificial intelligence infrastructure. The measure includes several protections for smaller data equipment used for businesses or government buildings. It does not ban accessory equipment smaller than 2,500 square feet, and it allows replacement, repair and limited expansion of existing equipment. Jamrog-McQuaid said a resident reached out to him with concerns that the 2,500-square-foot limit may be too small, but the councilor said he was comfortable moving forward with that size. Responding to a question from Councilor Jonathan Schmidt, Jamrog-McQuaid said he was not aware of businesses or entities that would be impacted by this limit. The moratorium was a collaboration of several municipal bodies and was originally drafted by Planning Director Allyson Manuel with City Council President Koni Denham. Denham thanked Manuel and others for moving it forward. Mayor Salem Derby lauded the council’s work at the meeting. Derby, a member of the national Climate Mayors group, said data center regulations are being discussed at length among its members. “One of the things that is front and center for all of the mayors that are in the climate mayor’s group is data centers,” Derby said. “I think moratoriums are where a lot of people are starting and trying to create some smart regulations.” Data centers began garnering national attention in late 2022 when the debut of OpenAI’s ChatGPT ignited worldwide demand for chatbots and other generative AI products that typically require large amounts of computing power to train and operate. Now, Oracle, Meta, Google, Amazon and Microsoft expect to plunge more than $700 billion into data centers in the U.S. this year alone, according to the Associated Press. Tech giants and developers need huge tracts of land to accommodate mammoth computing warehouses, so they’ve been exploring deeper into rural America. The push has united conservative ranching and farming communities with left-leaning environmental advocacy groups, who share a combined concern about drought-stricken waterways, pollution in food-growing areas and shrinking farmland. Governors who once pursued data center projects for their states are shifting their stances or taking steps to toughen regulations on data centers. In some states, governors have halted their state’s sales tax exemption for new data center projects. Other states are trying to force data centers to pay for their own electricity supply, limit their water use, disclose more about their operations and win community support before they get a state permit or tax exemption. Material from the Associated Press was used in this report.

artigo.texto: da Agência iNFRA O MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) projeta uma capacidade de 7,2 GW (gigawatts) de baterias no sistema elétrico até 2036. O dado está no relatório do PDE 2036 (Plano Decenal de Expansão da Energia 2036) colocado em consulta pública aberta nesta quinta-feira (8). O primeiro leilão visando a contratação da tecnologia está previsto para o início de dezembro. Agentes do segmento estimam uma demanda entre 4 GW e 10 GW. Ao todo, até 2036, a capacidade de armazenamento deve somar 9,2 GW, contando com 2 GW de hidrelétricas reversíveis – que funcionam como “baterias” de água, usando dois reservatórios para armazenar água e gerar energia. É a primeira vez que a tecnologia aparece na indicação de expansão do PDE. Geração A geração de energia elétrica deve crescer 110 GW no horizonte estudado, sendo puxada pela expansão das fontes eólica e solar, que serão 32,9% da matriz nacional em 2036. Boa parte desse aumento se deve à MMGD (Micro e Minigeração Distribuída), que deve alcançar 92 GW de capacidade ao fim do horizonte do PDE. Hoje, a capacidade instalada é de 50 GW. O PDE também projeta crescimento de 14 GW de termelétricas não renováveis (gás natural, diesel e carvão). Consumo O documento estima ainda um aumento da eletrificação e a entrada de grandes cargas, como os data centers, no sistema elétrico. A projeção é de que haja um aumento de carga dos data centers de 3 TWh (terawatts-hora) em 2026 para 30 TWh em 2036.

artigo.texto: Três carros para comprar com valor do novo BYD Sealion 7 O BYD Sealion 7 tem 531 cv de potência, 70,3 kgfm de torque e roda 360 km de autonomia com uma carga completa A BYD lançou um novo modelo elétrico para o mercado brasileiro chamado de Sealion 7. O SUV 100% elétrico tem mais de 4,80 metros de comprimento e desempenho de esportivo. Com preço de R$ 339.990, a reportagem da CNN Brasil separou algumas opções de carros para comprar com esse valor. O BYD Sealion 7 tem 531 cv de potência, 70,3 kgfm de torque e pode rodar 360 km com uma carga completa. Com essa mecânica, o SUV atinge os 100 km/h em 4,5 segundos e a velocidade máxima é de 215 km/h. Com esse valor do SUV, uma opção semelhante é o Volvo EC40. O modelo da marca sueca parte de R$ 334.950. A configuração perde na potência, que conta com 238 cv e acelera de 0 a 100 km/h em 7,3 segundos. A vantagem fica por conta da autonomia. Segundo o Inmetro, o Volvo EC40 pode rodar 385 km com uma carga completa, superando o número do BYD Sealion 7. Em termos de tamanho, contudo, a vantagem fica para o modelo chinês. Um outro SUV chinês que é posicionado no mesmo patamar do Sealion 7 é o GAC Hyptec HT. Com preço de R$ 314.990, o modelo entrega mais autonomia elétrica. Na versão Elite, de entrada, são 431 km de autonomia elétrica com uma única carga. O SUV da GAC também é superior em algumas dimensões. Tem 4,93 metros de comprimento (+10 cm), 1,92 de largura e 2,93 metros na distância entre os eixos. O porta-malas tem 670 litros — O BYD tem 500 L. Com R$ 10 mil a mais no bolso, uma outra alternativa é o Chevrolet Equinox EV. O SUV elétrico tem 304 cv de potência (menos que o Sealion 7), mas ganha com grande vantagem no alcance elétrico. Segundo dados do Inmetro, o Equinox EV consegue rodar 443 km com uma única carga de bateria completa. Com os 443 quilômetros de autonomia, a velocidade de recarga é de até 22 kW (AC) e 150 kW (DC). Em apenas 10 minutos nesta última, o motorista pode somar 130 km de autonomia. No porte, o Equinox é bem semelhante ao Sealion 7. São 4.840 mm de comprimento, 1.954 mm de largura, 1,64 metro de altura e 2.336 kg. O entre-eixos tem 2,95 metros.
