artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia Os créditos de carbono classificados como de alta qualidade pela MSCI tiveram valorização de 75% em 12 meses e chegaram a US$ 14 por tonelada, enquanto os de menor qualidade são negociados abaixo de US$ 2. Os dados foram apresentados por Guy Turner, diretor-geral da área de mercados de carbono […] 7 de outubro de 2026, às 14:57 Os créditos de carbono classificados como de alta qualidade pela MSCI tiveram valorização de 75% em 12 meses e chegaram a US$ 14 por tonelada, enquanto os de menor qualidade são negociados abaixo de US$ 2. Os dados foram apresentados por Guy Turner, diretor-geral da área de mercados de carbono da companhia, durante a Climate Week NYC, realizada em Nova York em setembro de 2026, e indicam avanços em três frentes: ampliação dos sistemas regulados, diferenciação de preços por qualidade e mobilização de capital. Segundo a apresentação, foram registrados US$ 5,5 bilhões em investimentos em contratos futuros e projetos, distribuídos em mais de 200 transações, com um quarto dos recursos destinado a iniciativas de remoção de carbono. Os contratos de compra antecipada de créditos de restauração da natureza monitorados pela MSCI, com entrega prevista para 2035, alcançaram US$ 45 por tonelada, alta de 10% em relação ao primeiro semestre de 2025. Sistemas regulados ganham escala No período analisado, a União Europeia passou a incluir integralmente as emissões do transporte marítimo no comércio de emissões do bloco, o EU ETS. A Indonésia avançou em normas para dar clareza e amplitude às negociações de carbono, e o México se comprometeu a lançar um sistema nacional em 2027, com cobertura de 40% de suas emissões. Na Ásia, a Índia colocou em operação um portal para administrar registros e transações do período de conformidade de 2025 a 2027, que abrange 740 entidades e mais de 700 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO₂e). O Vietnã contabilizou as primeiras operações de seu sistema, referentes ao ciclo 2025 a 2026, e o Japão tornou obrigatório o GX-ETS, que cobre 40% das emissões nacionais de gases de efeito estufa e reúne entre 300 e 400 empresas. Para Laura Albuquerque, co-CEO da Future Climate e membra do Comitê da Ambição Net Zero da Rede Brasileira do Pacto Global da ONU, durante cerca de duas décadas a defesa desses mercados se apoiou em estudos sobre seu potencial para reduzir o custo de cumprimento das metas climáticas. “A lógica econômica permanece: direcionar recursos para oportunidades de redução e remoção de emissões que permitam alcançar essas metas com maior eficiência. A diferença é que, hoje, a experiência acumulada oferece dados concretos para orientar decisões de política pública e investimento”, afirma. Demanda corporativa e integridade No segmento de créditos, os números da MSCI mostram atividade consistente. Cerca de 4 mil empresas definiram metas pela Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi), o equivalente a 4 bilhões de toneladas de emissões, e um quarto delas assumiu compromissos de emissões líquidas zero (net zero). Em 12 meses, mil novos projetos foram registrados, outros 1.150 entraram na carteira em preparação e empresas aposentaram créditos provenientes de 2.850 projetos. A projeção da MSCI indica que as aposentadorias globais de 2026 devem ficar próximas do volume de 2025, em torno de 200 milhões de toneladas. Na leitura da co-CEO, o sinal mais relevante está na distância de valor entre projetos, que torna a avaliação de qualidade parte central da decisão de alocação de recursos para compradores e investidores. A executiva observa ainda que a convergência em torno dos Core Carbon Principles, definidos pelo Conselho de Integridade para o Mercado Voluntário de Carbono (ICVCM, na sigla em inglês), cria uma linguagem comum sobre integridade, mas exige que preços e financiamento reconheçam os custos de desenvolvimento. Capital antes da receita Para as desenvolvedoras, o cenário evidencia a necessidade de recursos antes da geração de receita. “Projetos exigem recursos para estruturação, implantação, monitoramento, ratings para a verificação ao longo de anos. A valorização dos créditos de qualidade precisa se traduzir em condições de financiamento que permitam produzir essa oferta”, diz Laura. Segundo ela, os contratos futuros podem contribuir nesse processo ao conectar a demanda dos compradores ao ciclo de investimento dos projetos. O Brasil tem diferentes vias de demanda em construção: o mercado voluntário; o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), instituído pela Lei nº 15.042, de 11 de dezembro de 2024, com os Certificados de Redução ou Remoção Verificada de Emissões (CRVEs); os mecanismos do Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris; o programa de combustível sustentável de aviação (SAF, na sigla em inglês) previsto na Lei nº 14.993; e o Esquema de Compensação e Redução de Carbono para a Aviação Internacional (Corsia). Na avaliação da executiva, são caminhos com regras e escalas distintas, que precisam ser considerados na estruturação dos investimentos. Laura pondera que preços, investimentos e aposentadorias não substituem a mensuração dos resultados climáticos, embora demonstrem uma base observável de atividade econômica, demanda e alocação de capital. “Para o país, a oportunidade está em usar essa experiência para desenvolver um mercado capaz de financiar projetos de qualidade, e o próximo avanço dependerá de transformar os sinais de demanda em capital disponível para quem entrega reduções e remoções verificáveis”, conclui a executiva. artigo.texto: Manatee County approves one-year moratorium on data centers MANATEE COUNTY, Fla. (WWSB) - Manatee County commissioners unanimously approved a one-year moratorium Thursday on new data center projects. This gives the county time to consider rules and regulations before any proposals come forward. The moratorium pauses the acceptance, processing and approval of new data center projects in the county. Commissioners plan to study potential effects on energy, water, infrastructure and local communities. There are no data center projects currently planned in Manatee County, according to commissioners. The moratorium is intended to give the county time to prepare in case a proposal is submitted. Martin Hyde, a local resident, said data centers should be built on uninhabited land. “To me, if you take a satellite picture of the United States, there’s plenty of uninhabited land, and that’s where these things should go,” Hyde said. The decision follows North Port’s approval of an 18-month moratorium on data centers. Copyright 2026 WWSB. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Texas regulators have signed off on a long-debated move away from one of West Texas' thirstiest coal plants. The decision tests whether wind, solar, and battery storage can replace aging fuel-burning infrastructure without sacrificing grid reliability. It carries particular weight in a drought-prone region, where the Tolk plant has depended on the shrinking Ogallala Aquifer and where customers in Texas and New Mexico still rely on steady power. Here's what to know For Southwestern Public Service Company, the ruling means the Tolk coal plant near Lubbock can be retired and replaced with a new resource package: 1,100 megawatts of wind, 189 megawatts of solar, and 322 megawatts of battery storage, as CleanTechnica reported. Across Texas and New Mexico, the company says that combination should produce enough power for roughly 375,000 households. Texas regulators didn't rely on renewables alone. They also signed off on two gas peaker plants in Texas, but only under strict cost caps, allowing the utility to add limited gas backup instead of keeping the older coal plant in service. Josh Smith, a Sierra Club Environmental Law Program attorney who has spent years working on the Tolk plant, said the ruling shows there's "a common-sense path in Texas to transition away from expensive, dirty, thirsty coal. Texas doesn't need coal anymore, even as it prepares for increased demand, and today's decision clearly shows that." He added, "When Tolk closes, it will save abundant water in a drought-prone region, millions of ratepayer dollars, and eliminate millions of tons of harmful pollution every year, making rural West Texas a healthier place to live." The plant's retirement schedule had already been moving forward. SPS, which is owned by Xcel Energy, had previously said Tolk would close by 2032 under a 2020 Sierra Club agreement, then later proposed a December 2028 shutdown, as CleanTechnica reported. Rulings from the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission and Texas regulators set the closure for early 2029. More background Tolk's water demand is enormous. Sierra Club's analysis, Watts Wasting Texas Water, cited by CleanTechnica, said Tolk drew 1.2 billion gallons of groundwater in 2024. In 2015, its water use reached 3.3 billion gallons. Renewable energy uses very little water during operation. Closing the plant could ease pressure on the Ogallala Aquifer, a crucial groundwater source that has been under strain for years, while also reducing pollution tied to coal combustion and transport. The pollution concerns are significant as well. In 2025, Sierra Club figures cited by CleanTechnica said Tolk emitted 3.2 million tons of carbon pollution, along with 5.4 million pounds of nitrogen oxide pollution and 15.5 million pounds of sulfur dioxide. A 2026 Sierra Club health analysis linked the plant to 10 premature deaths each year, mostly in surrounding rural counties. Sierra Club said the closure should also mean fewer open-air rail shipments of coal from Wyoming, reducing coal dust and particle pollution along the route. What's being done? Texas regulators capped costs on the gas peaker plants, while the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission allowed the renewable and gas construction to move forward but, as CleanTechnica reported, didn't rule on the utility's request to classify the new gas-fired power plants as zero-carbon resources. Cyrus Reed, the Legislative and Conservation Director of the Lone Star Chapter of Sierra Club, said the approved replacement mix is the most practical option available. "These solar, wind, and battery storage projects are clearly the most cost-effective and efficient means of replacing the aging and increasingly expensive Tolk coal plant while also maintaining system reliability, saving scarce groundwater resources, utilizing existing transmission rights, and reducing harmful pollution," Reed said. Where can I learn more? These stories follow the same change for Tolk, with utilities leaning on solar and battery storage to replace older plants across the country. • Near Dallas, developers launched a major solar-and-storage buildout to help meet Texas demand. • In Texas, a massive solar farm entered service with 80 MWh of batteries. • In San Antonio, CPS Energy added a massive new battery to back up peak demand. • Duke Energy is turning a massive coal plant overhaul into solar-and-battery capacity. • In Kentucky, regulators approved an unprecedented solar expansion after retiring seven fossil plants. artigo.texto: BYD continues to develop its technological potential in the field of electric vehicles and energy storage, filing a patent for an innovative two-chamber battery case, which marks the beginning of the transition to a more efficient cooling solution. The patent reveals a serious engineering advance in addressing one of the biggest challenges facing lithium-ion batteries - managing extreme thermal loads during ultra-fast charging. The new architecture relies on dividing the battery into two isolated sections. The lower compartment is designed to be filled with a dielectric coolant, in which the battery modules themselves are directly immersed, while the upper chamber remains completely dry and contains the sensitive electrical equipment and control units. The main innovation in the design lies in the precise routing of the signal and power cables upwards through the top of the wet compartment, thus avoiding passage through the floor or side walls of the lower chamber and ensuring long-term tightness. Although standard industrial solutions usually rely on indirect plate cooling, full immersion in a dielectric liquid ensures significantly faster heat dissipation and perfect thermal uniformity between individual cells. This allows the system to maintain high charging capacities without the risk of cell degradation or activation of current-limiting protection mechanisms.

artigo.texto: MAHOMET – Mahomet officials have ended talks with a data center developer after facing backlash from the community, Village President Jason Tompkins announced Monday. Officials had been in talks with Clean Cloud Energy, a data center developer based on the east coast, about a proposal to build a data center in the village as early as January. “I have publicly opposed this project,” Trustee Bruce Colravy said in a statement. “I am proud of those in the community and surrounding area who spent time and energy standing in opposition to it. They have made a difference.” In a press release, officials said questions and concerns from residents played a “significant role” in making this decision. “Our responsibility is to carefully evaluate potential developments and determine whether there is a path forward that serves Mahomet’s interests,” Tompkins said. “Listening to our residents is an essential part of that responsibility.” The press release states officials are still committed to attracting commercial development and expanding the village’s commercial tax base, but they will focus on opportunities that align with the community’s priorities and long-term interests, which does not include data centers. Champaign County currently has a one-year pause on data center development, but it does not apply to development within Mahomet. The data center moratorium ends next spring and was put in place to allow a task force to develop new guidelines for future large-scale projects in the county. Many residents have called for the county to outright ban data centers, but some county officials say they lack the authority to do so without home rule. An effort to put home rule on the November ballot was thwarted in August by a bipartisan group of board members, saying they lacked information to make an informed decision on the issue. State lawmakers have not enacted data center regulations thus far, but Gov. JB Pritzker has called on legislators to take up the issue in the November legislative veto session. In the meantime, he paused the state’s data center tax incentive and released a framework to regulate data centers.

artigo.texto: This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Joseph LeGare, a 24-year-old project engineer based in Frederick County, Maryland, who works at Rowan Digital Infrastructure, a hyperscale data center developer. It has been edited for length and clarity. I studied philosophy for two years at The Catholic University of America before dropping out and working as an assistant superintendent at a construction company. After about a year, I moved into residential and did administrative work, including daily reports, county inspection scheduling, quality verification, and weekly safety meetings with foremen. I even worked as a materials management specialist at a residential home manufacturer. At the same time, I was taking night classes in construction management at Frederick Community College. I assumed I'd go into residential construction, but my classes made me realize I really wanted to pursue commercial construction. I wanted to get out of office work and back into the field. My professor said that if I wanted field experience, getting into the data center industry would be a game changer. The data center industry caught my eye because it's so fast-paced Rowan Digital Infrastructure, which builds data centers, ran an internship program with my school, and one of my professors recommended I apply. They hired me full-time after six months. The data center industry uses the most up-to-date technologies to build projects — whether those technologies are related to safety equipment, heavy equipment, or tools — and it's fascinating to see. I enjoy working in the data center industry, as there is a massive need for it, and I want to help build the infrastructure that keeps the world running. As an intern, my mornings started with reviewing data center drawings I learned to read construction drawings and specifications while gaining hands-on field experience. These are data center-specific, but they share many similarities with general commercial construction drawings. The only real difference is that when we follow our drawings, we build a data center. It could just as easily be for a warehouse or apartment building. Most mornings, my mentor and I reviewed the drawings and specs. Then we'd head out with an iPad or printed drawings to watch the crews work, whether they were installing or lifting a wall. In data center construction project management, you don't need specialized skills beyond those required for any other construction project. However, data center construction is extremely fast-paced work. You'll need to adapt to constant changes, whether that's new details being released, deliveries being delayed, or a schedule being pulled in. I got to be in the field, and the pay was generous My main focus was on being in the field and learning. I was also learning how requests for information, or RFIs, work and how to move between the architects, designers, engineers, general contractors, and subcontractors. The internship pay was generous, in the high five figures. I thought I might be taking a pay cut going into commercial construction. Instead, Rowan offered me a full-time job with a six-figure salary after my internship. I'm making more than I was earning at my last job. My full-time data center role focuses on getting answers One of the biggest responsibilities after being hired was overseeing the RFI and submittal process with the general contractor. I went from observer to main point of contact. Now the GC comes to me practically daily with a problem or an RFI, and I assemble the right people to get an answer. Basically, I keep all the documentation moving. Much of my job is closing the gap between what's on the drawings and what's happening in the field. When something doesn't line up, I track down the answer. That means going back through the specs, talking to the trades, and getting questions to the design team. I'm constantly coordinating to make sure everything lines up. The specific problem is different almost every day. However, probably the most common issue is that field conditions differ from the construction documents. Sometimes the issue is easy to fix, and we can make a call right then and there. Other times, we have to reach out to the design team for guidance. We also focus heavily on testing and commissioning before turnover because everything has to work reliably. Additionally, our project is a brownfield site, which means the soil contains higher amounts of regulated materials than is typical. This is because the site used to be an aluminum smeltery, so we have to work hand in hand with the Maryland Department of the Environment to ensure we avoid adding to that regulated soil and remediate it. There are pros and cons, but overall, I'm happy working in the data center industry The biggest pro is how fast my career has advanced. The opportunities I've been given are crazy, and so is the knowledge and skill I've been able to build. I thought it would take five to 10 years to get here, but the company gave me the opportunity right off the bat. The biggest con is the stress, which I didn't fully expect. Every job has its stressors, but here you're constantly on deadlines, watching budgets because there isn't endless money for a job, and maintaining relationships. There are a lot of days I go home thinking, "Man, that was a really long day." Eventually, I'd love to be a construction manager or project manager and take on more responsibility, even with the added stress. But I'm happy where I am. As hard as the stress is, it's rewarding to look at something and know I helped build it. Do you work at a data center and want to share your story? Email this editor, Manseen Logan, at mlogan@businessinsider.com.

artigo.texto: SP vai esperar regulamento do Redata para rever ICMS de data centers Vice-governador diz que São Paulo não vai mexer no ICMS antes de seis meses, prazo no qual acredita que o decreto regulamentador das isenções federais - sem qualquer relação com os estados - sairá. O vice-governador de São Paulo, Felicio Ramuth, afirmou hoje, 6, na Futurecom 2026, que o estado só deve rever a incidência de ICMS sobre equipamentos para data center após a publicação do decreto federal que regulamentará o Redata. A seu ver, este decreto vai demorar ao menos seis meses para sair. “Não adianta a gente discutir ICMS se o Redata vai acabar com isso”, afirmou durante conversa com jornalistas na Futurecom. Vale lembrar que o Redata mexe em imposto de importação, PIS/Cofins. ICMS é imposto cobrado pelos estados, independentemente dos tributos federais. E no caso dos data centers, ele será incidente pelos próximos cinco anos, ao longo do período de transição da reforma tributária. “Então são medidas, na verdade, paliativas por certo período, porque em cinco anos a gente vai ter a reforma tributária de fato efetiva”, disse. Redata e reforma passam a conviver O regime para data centers procura reduzir custos dos novos projetos. A reforma, por sua vez, altera progressivamente a estrutura de tributação sobre consumo e investimentos. Para o ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho, o instrumento utilizado é secundário diante do efeito econômico produzido. “Se vai ser o Redata ou se vai ser reforma tributária, o importante é a gente discutir o benefício”, defendeu. Já o governo paulista enfatiza o caráter transitório de parte dos incentivos e pretende calibrar sua própria política de ICMS depois que as regras federais estiverem definidas.

artigo.texto: DeKalb County considers environmental impact study on data centers DEKALB COUNTY, Ga. - DeKalb County officials are considering a proposal to commission an independent study examining the environmental and health impacts of local data center developments. DeKalb data center proposal What we know: DeKalb County commissioners discussed a proposal Tuesday night at Dunwoody City Hall to bring in a third-party group to evaluate how large data centers impact local land, water and air. Commissioner Ted Terry introduced the measure to ensure health and environmental effects are understood before decisions are made on future developments. The board did not take a vote Tuesday, but members placed the proposal on the agenda for their next full meeting on Tuesday. Community health concerns What they're saying: Some local residents oppose hyperscale facility expansions, raising concerns over water systems, increased power demands and rising residential utility bills. Resident Gina Mangham said the issue centers on resident health, quality of life and rising noise pollution. Resident Rosalind McIntyre warned about heat islands and air pollution. Terry emphasized that he wants to limit the scale of future developments, require renewable energy, ban diesel generators and enforce buffer zones around neighborhoods. Existing development freeze The backstory: DeKalb County currently operates under a moratorium that pauses new data center applications through March. According to Terry, no applications for zoning or building data centers can be received while the moratorium remains active. DeKalb data center study What we don't know: Commissioners have not yet selected an outside firm to conduct the third-party study. It remains unknown whether the board will officially approve funding for the environmental study during their upcoming vote on Tuesday. The Source: The information in this story was gathered from a broadcast report by FOX 5 reporter Christopher King, who covered the DeKalb County Commissioners meeting in Dunwoody, as well as on-record statements from DeKalb County Commissioner Ted Terry and local residents Gina Mangham and Rosalind McIntyre.

artigo.texto: Galileo secures approval for 250 MW of battery storage in Italy Renewable energy developer Galileo has secured permits for two battery energy storage system (BESS) projects in Italy, totaling 250 MW of power capacity and 1.5 GWh of energy storage. The company expects approval for a further 100 MW of battery storage projects in the coming weeks. The approvals mark another step in Galileo’s expansion in Italy, where grid-scale battery storage is becoming increasingly important for integrating renewable energy and balancing electricity supply and demand. For Europe’s energy storage and power electronics sectors, the projects highlight growing opportunities for battery technologies, power conversion systems and grid infrastructure as Italy accelerates its energy transition. Two large-scale battery projects The newly approved developments comprise two 125 MW BESS installations, one with 1,000 MWh of storage capacity and the other with 500 MWh. The first project will be capable of delivering its rated power output for eight hours, while the second offers four hours of storage duration. Located in Italy’s North and Centre-South electricity market zones, the projects are positioned in areas where energy storage can help manage fluctuations in renewable generation and support grid stability. Both projects were originated, designed and developed by Galileo’s Italian team, which managed the entire permitting process from site identification through to authorization. According to the company, the developments incorporate advanced technology and safety standards, alongside measures to reduce environmental impact through site selection, natural screening and landscape mitigation. Local municipalities were consulted during the permitting process, with agreements reached on territorial compensation measures. More than 650 MW approved in 18 months The latest consents add to Galileo’s growing portfolio of renewable energy projects in Italy, where the company has secured approvals for more than 650 MW of solar PV and battery storage capacity over the past 18 months. Francesco Dolzani, Managing Director for Galileo in Italy, said: “Securing consent for a further 250 MW of BESS projects is another important milestone for Galileo in Italy, where in the last 18 months we have secured consents for over 650 MW of solar PV and BESS projects. We are now focusing on progressing these projects towards construction and continue working very closely with our local stakeholders.” Galileo targets independent power production Galileo’s Italian development pipeline now exceeds 3 GW, covering utility-scale solar PV, battery storage, and onshore and offshore wind projects. Across Europe, the Zurich-based company is developing approximately 17 GW of renewable energy and storage capacity. The latest approvals also support Galileo’s plans to expand its role as an independent power producer (IPP), moving projects from development toward electricity generation and storage operations. Ingmar Wilhelm, co-founder and CEO of Galileo, said: “These latest BESS consents further strengthen Galileo’s multi-technology pipeline of more than 3 GW in Italy. We will embark on our IPP trajectory in Italy, one of Europe’s most energy dependent countries, with a selection of high-quality green energy projects in the near future.”

artigo.texto: Um projeto em análise na Câmara dos Deputados pretende permitir que pequenos geradores de energia comercializem créditos de carbono correspondentes à redução de emissões obtida por suas atividades. A proposta trata da participação de empreendimentos de menor porte em operações com ativos ambientais e busca reconhecer, dentro das regras do mercado de carbono, resultados climáticos que possam ser comprovados. Na prática, a iniciativa relaciona duas atividades que normalmente são analisadas separadamente: a produção de eletricidade e a geração de benefícios ambientais mensuráveis. Caso avance, o texto poderá criar uma possibilidade adicional de remuneração para unidades que reduzam emissões em comparação com uma alternativa mais intensiva em carbono, desde que essa redução seja demonstrada pelos procedimentos exigidos. A medida ainda está em tramitação e não produz efeitos imediatos. Para que um crédito de carbono seja negociado, não basta a existência de uma instalação de geração de energia. É necessário comprovar a redução de emissões, aplicar uma metodologia reconhecida e cumprir as etapas de validação, registro e certificação previstas para esse tipo de ativo. O que a proposta pretende mudar O projeto prevê a possibilidade de que pequenos geradores tenham acesso à comercialização de créditos de carbono. A ideia é considerar a redução de emissões associada à geração de energia em menor escala como resultado passível de reconhecimento no mercado de carbono. O texto não transforma automaticamente toda unidade de pequeno porte em uma geradora de créditos. O reconhecimento dependerá da comprovação de que houve uma redução efetiva, adicional e mensurável de emissões, conforme os critérios aplicáveis ao projeto. A negociação também dependerá do atendimento às exigências previstas para o registro do ativo ambiental. Esse ponto é relevante porque créditos de carbono não correspondem simplesmente à quantidade de energia produzida. Eles estão relacionados à diferença entre as emissões que ocorreriam em determinado cenário e as emissões verificadas depois da implantação ou da operação de um projeto. A conversão dessa diferença em crédito exige regras para evitar dupla contagem e assegurar que o benefício ambiental seja atribuído a uma única iniciativa. Como funcionaria a geração do ativo ambiental Em linhas gerais, um projeto de energia precisa estabelecer uma referência para as emissões que seriam produzidas sem a atividade analisada. Em seguida, são calculadas as emissões efetivamente associadas à operação do empreendimento. A diferença entre esses dois cenários pode servir de base para a emissão de créditos, desde que o resultado atenda aos critérios técnicos e regulatórios. O processo costuma envolver a definição da metodologia, a coleta de dados, a elaboração de documentos do projeto, a avaliação por entidades habilitadas e o registro dos créditos em sistemas reconhecidos. Também é necessário acompanhar os resultados ao longo do tempo para demonstrar que a redução declarada ocorreu de fato. O projeto em análise na Câmara trata da possibilidade de participação dos pequenos geradores nesse sistema. As exigências técnicas e os mecanismos específicos para a comprovação dos resultados continuam condicionados às regras que venham a ser aplicadas ao modelo e à regulamentação correspondente. Participação de unidades de menor porte A discussão alcança geradores que, pela escala, podem enfrentar mais dificuldades para participar de operações estruturadas no mercado de carbono. Projetos menores tendem a produzir volumes individuais reduzidos de créditos. Por isso, os custos de medição, elaboração de documentos, auditoria, certificação e registro podem ter peso maior na viabilidade econômica de cada empreendimento. Ao admitir a possibilidade de comercialização por pequenos geradores, a proposta abre espaço para que esses projetos sejam considerados de forma específica nas operações com créditos de carbono. O texto, porém, não elimina a necessidade de comprovação nem estabelece que a geração de energia, isoladamente, seja suficiente para produzir um ativo negociável. A eventual participação poderá exigir a organização dos dados de diferentes unidades, a adoção de procedimentos padronizados ou a contratação de estruturas responsáveis pela gestão dos créditos. Essas condições dependem do conteúdo final da proposta e das regras que venham a disciplinar sua aplicação. Relação com o mercado de carbono O mercado de carbono reúne mecanismos pelos quais reduções ou remoções de gases de efeito estufa podem ser convertidas em unidades negociáveis. Essas unidades podem ser usadas por compradores interessados em compensar emissões, cumprir compromissos ambientais ou atender obrigações previstas em determinados sistemas regulatórios. Há diferenças entre créditos gerados por projetos e permissões de emissão vinculadas a um sistema regulado. O projeto em análise trata do reconhecimento da redução de emissões atribuída a pequenos geradores e de sua possibilidade de comercialização como crédito de carbono. A efetiva utilização desses ativos dependerá do mercado em que forem aceitos e das regras aplicáveis a cada operação. Para que o crédito tenha validade e credibilidade, o resultado ambiental precisa ser verificável. Entre os aspectos normalmente observados estão a existência do projeto, a metodologia usada para calcular a redução, a consistência dos dados, a ausência de dupla contagem e a permanência do benefício quando esse fator for relevante para a atividade. Tramitação ainda pode alterar o texto Como a proposta está em análise no Legislativo, seu conteúdo pode ser modificado durante a tramitação. O projeto ainda terá de passar pelas etapas previstas para sua apreciação, com avaliação pelos órgãos e comissões competentes, antes de eventual votação e transformação em norma. A aprovação não significaria a emissão imediata de créditos por todos os pequenos geradores. Seriam necessárias regras para definir quais projetos

artigo.texto: Propostas de regulamentação sobre captura e armazenamento de carbono associados às operações de petróleo e gás. (Chinhphu.vn) - No projeto de decreto que detalha algumas disposições e medidas para organizar e orientar a implementação da Lei do Petróleo e Gás, o Ministério da Indústria e Comércio propõe regulamentações sobre as atividades de captura e armazenamento de carbono (CCS) associadas às operações de petróleo e gás. O Ministério da Indústria e Comércio declarou que as atividades de CCS associadas às operações de petróleo e gás constituem uma nova disposição em comparação com o Decreto nº 45/2023/ND-CP. As regulamentações sobre CCS no Decreto aplicam-se apenas às atividades de CCS associadas às operações de petróleo e gás no âmbito da Lei do Petróleo e Gás; a proteção ambiental, os créditos de carbono, a medição, a comunicação, a avaliação, a certificação das reduções de emissões e outras questões específicas são regidas por leis específicas relevantes. O projeto de Decreto propõe a inclusão de disposições sobre a avaliação e seleção de formações geológicas que armazenam CO₂; a implementação de atividades de CCS no âmbito dos contratos de petróleo e gás; os requisitos técnicos e de segurança para a operação de instalações de CCS; o descomissionamento de instalações de CCS; os custos recuperáveis de projetos de CCS; a receita proveniente de créditos de carbono; e os mecanismos de contabilização. Especificamente: Avaliando o potencial de armazenamento de CO₂ A minuta afirma que o relatório que avalia o potencial de armazenamento de CO₂ inclui os seguintes conteúdos principais: a) Visão geral da geologia da região, incluindo história tectônica, estrutura geológica e sistemas de falhas; b) Características geológicas e geofísicas da formação geológica que se espera armazenar CO₂; c) Resultados da simulação hidrodinâmica tridimensional do reservatório, incluindo previsões de curto e longo prazo do estado do CO₂ após a injeção; d) Calcule o potencial de armazenamento efetivo em diferentes cenários; d) Avaliar os riscos de vazamento, incluindo a análise do potencial, da probabilidade e das consequências do vazamento, e propor medidas de mitigação; e) Avaliar o impacto das operações de injeção na zona afetada pela pressão, incluindo o impacto nos reservatórios de petróleo e gás adjacentes e nas atividades de petróleo e gás existentes; g) Avaliar os riscos para as pessoas, o ambiente e os recursos relevantes, em conformidade com a lei; h) O estado dos furos de sondagem existentes que penetram a formação do reservatório e as soluções propostas para garantir a sua integridade; i) Conclusões e recomendações sobre a adequação da formação geológica para fins de armazenamento de CO₂. O relatório de avaliação do potencial de armazenamento de CO₂ é um componente do dossiê da proposta de implantação de CCS e é usado como base para o desenvolvimento do plano diretor de implantação de CCS ou do plano de implantação de CCS, conforme estipulado no Artigo 50 da Lei do Petróleo. Os resultados de levantamentos básicos de petróleo e gás, estudos gerais e estudos e avaliações de formações geológicas armazenadoras de CO₂ que tenham sido aprovados e aceitos por agências ou organizações competentes, e que atendam aos requisitos de conteúdo, qualidade e confiabilidade dos documentos, serão herdados e utilizados como base para a elaboração de relatórios sobre a avaliação de formações geológicas armazenadoras de CO₂ e planos de implementação de CCS, conforme estipulado neste Decreto. Implementação de atividades de CCS (Captura e Armazenamento de Carbono) no âmbito de contratos de petróleo e gás. De acordo com a minuta, o contratado propõe adicionar atividades de CCS ao contrato de petróleo e gás com base em um relatório que avalia o potencial de armazenamento de CO₂ e um plano para implementar atividades de CCS, conforme estipulado no Artigo 50 da Lei de Petróleo e Gás. O contratado está autorizado a receber CO₂ gerado por operações de petróleo e gás e outras atividades emissoras para processamento, transporte, injeção e armazenamento no âmbito do contrato de petróleo e gás. A captura de CO₂ em locais de emissão fora das operações de petróleo e gás deverá ser realizada em conformidade com as leis aplicáveis. A elaboração, avaliação e aprovação de alterações aos contratos de petróleo e gás, bem como a emissão de certificados de registo de investimento alterados para adicionar atividades de CCS aos contratos de petróleo e gás, serão realizadas de acordo com as disposições do artigo 18.º da Lei do Petróleo e Gás e do artigo 26.º deste Decreto. Nos casos em que as formações geológicas que armazenam CO₂ ou as zonas afetadas pela pressão se estendam para além da área do contrato de petróleo e gás existente, em blocos abertos adjacentes, a proposta, a avaliação e a aprovação para a expansão da área do contrato para fins de armazenamento de CO₂ serão realizadas de acordo com as disposições da Cláusula 4, Artigo 21 da Lei de Petróleo e Gás e do Artigo 35 deste Decreto. O plano geral de implementação de CCS e o plano de implementação de CCS podem ser incluídos no plano geral de desenvolvimento do campo de petróleo e gás, no plano de desenvolvimento do campo de petróleo e gás ou em planos de ajuste correspondentes, ou podem ser elaborados separadamente; a elaboração, avaliação e aprovação devem ser realizadas de acordo com os regulamentos pertinentes ao plano geral de desenvolvimento do campo de petróleo e gás e ao plano de desenvolvimento do campo de petróleo e gás. O plano de descomissionamento da instalação de CCS é elaborado dentro do plano de descomissionamento da instalação de petróleo e gás, de um plano de ajuste correspondente, ou é preparado separadamente e implementado de acordo com os regulamentos sobre descomissionamento de instalações de petróleo e gás. artigo.texto: By Hank Russell A Florida-based energy company has announced it is suspending operations of two of its battery energy storage systems (BESS) on eastern Long Island. NextEra Energy has agreed to suspend operations at the facility at Cove Hollow Road in East Hampton and the facility in Montauk near Fort Pond. Both facilities are jointly owned by NextEra Energy and National Grid. The suspension follows weeks of discussions between Suffolk County and NextEra. Under the arrangement, NextEra will suspend operations at both sites and remove the Novec 1230 fire suppression agent from both facilities by approximately October 9. “We are very grateful that this agreement has been reached,” said Suffolk County executive Ed Romaine. “The 2023 fire at the East Hampton BESS location, and the consequent contamination of the site and surrounding areas, prove that the operations must cease until changes are made that will protect our drinking water.” The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation has determined that, when water was applied to the East Hampton facility during a May 2023 fire, it mixed with Novec™ 1230 — a chemical agent used for fire suppression — and broke down into PFPrA, a short-chain “forever chemical,” which has since been detected in drinking water in the surrounding area. Two Suffolk County Water Authority (SCWA) wells have been taken offline. The county has drilled monitoring wells to investigate the contamination and supports the SCWA’s litigation against NextEra. In July, Romaine and East Hampton Village Mayor Jerry Larsen sent letters to the chief executives of NextEra Energy and National Grid urging them to suspend operations at the East Hampton facility until the investigation is completed. “We need a remediation plan immediately, one approved by the DEC, so the hard work of cleaning the site can begin,” said Romaine. “The community did not know for years that the 2023 fire had left behind PFPrA. They should not wait any longer for the situation to be addressed.” The county will continue its groundwater testing in the area. Long Island Life & Politics reached out to NextEra and National Grid for comment. NextEra issued the following statement: “We are temporarily ceasing operations at our East Hampton and Montauk battery facilities. We remain committed to working with local and state officials.” National Grid did not respond as of press time.

Energy Storage Southeast Asia locks in under a third of 2030 storage goal Region pipeline holds roughly 7GW by 2030 Shortfall may widen further by 2045 Stock video by Engin Akyurt via Pexels Oct 9, 2026 South-East Asia Faces Major Energy Storage Shortfall Amid LNG Shock A report from energy think tank Ember has found that while the liquefied natural gas crisis sparked by the Iran war is driving South-East Asia toward solar and wind, the region has locked in under one-third of the storage capacity required by 2030. According to the Wednesday report, South-East Asia's existing utility-scale storage project pipeline stands at roughly 7GW, due to come online by 2030. That amount addresses under a third of the 23 to 26GW necessary to back the region's renewable energy goals. Ember warned that if growth continues at its present pace, the shortfall will widen further by 2045. Alnie Demoral, an energy analyst at Ember, noted that the financing constraint in Asean's energy transition has moved from capital raising to the development of bankable assets. These conclusions underline the difficulties facing economies attempting to lessen their reliance on imported fuel following the Iran war's disruption of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. Before the conflict started in late February, that waterway handled nearly one-fifth of worldwide LNG. The Global Energy Monitor reported that South-East Asia obtained roughly one-third of its gas imports from the Middle East prior to the war. GEM also said Asian spot LNG prices averaged $17.50 per million British thermal units in the second quarter, marking a 45 per cent increase from the prior year. GEM data reveals that in the Philippines, which announced a national energy emergency in March, gas-fired power capacity under development dropped from 19.7GW in January to 13.8GW by August. In Vietnam, Vingroup has attempted to swap a planned 4.8GW LNG power plant for solar, wind and battery storage. Ember discovered that while large solar farms are finding it easier to draw commercial financing, battery storage, smaller renewable projects and transmission lines continue to be less appealing to investors. Given identical tariff and financing conditions, a half-megawatt solar project yields 2.6 per cent to equity, versus 13.1 per cent for a 20MW facility. Ms Demoral stated that future investment will hinge on reducing transaction costs and enabling storage and grids to generate returns matching their worth to the power system. Ember noted that present investment is below the $281 billion annually required by 2035 for the region to finish its energy transition. The International Energy Agency projects South-East Asian electricity demand will grow roughly 5.4 per cent each year through 2030. Costly gas is additionally bringing coal back, with the IEA anticipating worldwide coal demand to climb 1.2 per cent to an all-time high of 8.94 billion tonnes this year, as elevated LNG prices drive utilities in Europe, Japan, South Korea and China to consume more. Ember said the financing approaches that backed large renewable projects have not yet reached the storage and grids essential for incorporating intermittent power. artigo.texto: LEXINGTON, Ky. — The Lexington-Fayette Urban County Council voted unanimously to extend a moratorium on new data center development until Oct. 2027 after hearing three hours of public comment from residents and business representatives. Critics raised concerns about the potential impact of a massive data center on the environment, electric bills and quality of life. Several residents urged stronger limits, while representatives of businesses asked for more time to avoid unintended consequences from a proposed zoning ordinance. The council also changed the language of the proposed ordinance to limit smaller data centers to industrial zones. The proposal would keep a ban on data centers larger than 50,000 square feet, set a noise limit of 30 decibels and cap energy use at 25 megawatts, which is lower than the 50 megawatts sought by some developers for a local project. Council members also voted to ask the planning commission to create a new, separate zoning classification for minor data centers. In city terms, it would be an “exclusive use zone,” a designation currently used only for landfills. Some concerns focused on banking and healthcare, which rely on onsite data infrastructure such as server rooms or smaller data centers for day-to-day operations. “I believe we need a more intentional, responsible and equitable approach to data center regulations, one that clearly distinguished between principal uses and legitimate accessory uses, and strongly regulates both,” Councilmember Tyler Morton, Dist. 1 said. Morton and Dist. 4 Councilmember Emma Curtis led the motion that changed the city’s approach to regulating the rapidly evolving technology. “This is an emerging technology. Everything is changing so quickly that as soon as we think we have the right policy in place, something else changes,” State Rep. Anne Gay Donworth, D-Lexington, said during the meeting. Donworth said she has heard of colleagues in Frankfort who plan to propose new state regulations on data centers. Those bills could be discussed as early as January. Lexington’s Urban County Council is expected to discuss the issue again during its next regular meeting. It’s not clear when the local planning commission could take up the issue once again.

artigo.texto: Physical artificial intelligence company iiLab (307180.KQ) has developed a technology that can raise the energy density of small solid-state batteries by up to 10 times compared with existing products. The company removed the substrate that had taken up unnecessary space inside the battery and applied its own interface control technology, improving both energy storage capacity and high-rate discharge performance. Based on the technology, iiLab plans to accelerate its efforts to secure the core energy technology needed for humanoid robots. iiLab said on the 8th that it has developed a technology that completely eliminates the substrate, which accounted for more than 95% of the total volume in conventional thin-film solid-state batteries. Existing products are built on a silicon or glass substrate about 500 micrometers thick. Because the substrate takes up considerable space without contributing to energy storage, it has limited efforts to raise energy density. Instead of using a substrate, iiLab applied a hybrid structure combining thin and thick films to expand the space available for energy storage. Based on the active material in a coin cell the company actually produced, the energy density was calculated at 500 to 750 Wh/L, up to 10 times higher than the 50 to 80 Wh/L of conventional thin-film solid-state batteries. The company also improved high-rate discharge performance by combining the high-output characteristics of thin films with the high-capacity characteristics of thick-film electrodes and precisely controlling the interface between the two structures. iiLab plans to link the technology to its humanoid robot business. Humanoids must fit batteries into limited internal space while stably supplying the power needed for joints and drive units. That requires batteries with both high energy density and high output. The company's strategy is to internalize the core technologies of its physical AI business by adding battery technology to the robot operating data and AI technology it already has. "The key to this technology is that it solves the structural problem that had constrained the energy density of existing thin-film solid-state batteries, while improving both high capacity and high output at the same time," said Ko Jae-hwan, head of iiLab's battery R&D center. "We will continue to advance the performance and technological competitiveness of next-generation small solid-state batteries." He added, "As a company operating a physical AI operating data platform in South Korea, iiLab will strengthen the technological competitiveness of the physical AI industry by organically connecting robot operating data, artificial intelligence and core energy technology."

artigo.texto: LONDON — Britain and the European Union have successfully reached an agreement on linking their respective emissions trading systems, four people briefed on the talks told POLITICO. The negotiations, which kicked off last year, have been wrapped up and a deal is set to be unveiled at the planned U.K.-EU summit in the coming weeks. The two sides are now just “tying a ribbon” on the agreement ahead of its official announcement, according to one EU diplomat, who, like others cited in this report, was granted anonymity to discuss closed-door negotiations. Advertisement Linking carbon trading markets was one of three topics the U.K. and EU committed to negotiating at last year’s summit — and is the first file to conclude successfully. Industry groups have been pushing for emissions trading linkage because it would ensure they are exempt from the EU’s new CBAM carbon border tax — which would otherwise add cost and bureaucracy to many British exports to Europe. Talks on the other two proposals, a trade deal to remove border checks on agriculture and food, as well as new “youth mobility” visas for young people, are still ongoing. Both sides have said the three agreements come as a package and will not proceed individually. The upcoming summit, expected in November, is meant as both a deadline for current talks and potentially a springboard for even closer relations. The meeting’s date has not formally been announced, but internal discussions are based on it happening on Nov. 20. Advertisement The U.K.’s European Relations Minister Hamish Falconer told POLITICO’s Brussels Playbook Podcast on Tuesday: “I have a date in mind, but I don't want to say it just yet.” Youth mobility talks ongoing Negotiations on ETS linkage have long been seen by officials as the most straightforward of the three files. Talks on the planned agri-food agreement are also thought to be processing well, with some negotiation over the extent of U.K. “carve-outs” from EU rules. Questions still remain over the youth mobility scheme, however. The EU wants the agreement to include cuts to tuition fees for EU students studying at British universities. The U.K.’s higher education sector has warned that such a change would see them taking a difficult financial hit. The U.K. also wants the number of people able to use the new youth visas to be capped to limit its impact on politically sensitive net migration statistics. Advertisement Carbon taxes The U.K. is introducing its own CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism) from Jan. 1 2027, which would similarly hit EU firms without the new agreement. Linking the two emissions trading markets is also expected to provide more liquidity for carbon markets, improving efficiency. Critics of the agreement say it could increase the price of polluting in the U.K., at least in the short run, at a time when businesses are facing other economic headwinds. The U.K. carbon price is currently below that of the EU’s. The U.K. government and European Commission both said they do not comment on ongoing negotiations.

artigo.texto: Randolph County quorum court discusses data center possibilities POCAHONTAS, Ark. (KAIT) - The Randolph County Quorum Court met Thursday night to discuss the possibility of a data center coming to the county, and members agreed they need more time and research before moving forward. County Judge Ben Wicker said a buyer who has been shopping for property in the region reached out earlier in the week about land in Randolph County for a possible data center. Wicker said the same buyer is also considering purchasing similar centers in the surrounding area. Wicker brought the topic to quorum court and to the public to discuss what should happen next. There have been no formal moves beyond the buyer expressing interest in land for a possible data center. Michael McIntire, a barber who has worked on the Pocahontas Square for five years, said he is torn on the issue. “Data centers are good in an aspect that I do believe that can help people because everything is going to technology,” McIntire said. McIntire also said he has concerns about the tradeoffs. “A lot of data centers, they use a lot of water,” McIntire said. “So I can imagine water bills are going to go up, and they also use a lot of consumption of energy, so where is that energy going to come from?” McIntire said. McIntire pointed to this year’s drought and low river levels. “If I had a vote or a choice, I would say no to the data centers,” McIntire said. Pocahontas resident Don McGuirt said he is concerned that jobs created by a data center could go to specialists from outside the county. “That’s not going to really help Randolph County if they bring in specialists from other places. We already got a problem with that,” McGuirt said. Randolph County has already passed Ordinance 2023-16, which caps data center noise at 65 decibels from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. and 55 decibels from 10 p.m. to 8 a.m. — about the sound of a busy restaurant. Centers that don’t meet those limits could face fines or be ordered to shut down operations. Thursday’s meeting was a discussion, and the court was largely in agreement that it needs more time and research before moving forward. Wicker said any decision the county makes will be in the best interest of the future of the county and its residents. “This is the only county in the United States that I know of that has five rivers that run through it,” Wicker said. “It’s a beautiful county, and I want to keep it that way if I can at all.” Wicker said he would like his children to remember the county the same way he does: beautiful. There is no timeline for next steps on data centers from either the county or the buyer. To report a typo or correction, please click here. Copyright 2026 KAIT. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Ossoff, Collins discuss tariffs, data centers in Georgia Senate debate SAVANNAH, Ga. (WTOC) - Georgia voters heard from Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff and Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Collins during their first debate Thursday night, with the candidates exchanging personal attacks while discussing issues important to voters ahead of Election Day. The hourlong live debate covered a range of topics, including immigration, the economy, tariffs, energy and economic development. Ossoff opened the debate by criticizing Collins over his alleged ties to white nationalist figures and content. >>> Read the full transcript from the U.S. Senate debate between Jon Ossoff, Mike Collins “Imagine running for U.S. Senate while neo-Nazi propaganda is disseminated to an audience of millions from your home, that’s Mike Collins,” Ossoff said. Collins said he has condemned racism, antisemitism and hate. He countered by criticizing Ossoff’s support for individuals he said oppose Israel. “Imagine being a U.S. senator and being out there recruiting, endorsing and supporting these people that want to see Israel wiped off the map, that’s who Jon Ossoff is supporting,” Collins said. Watch the full debate below: WTOC’s Mike Cihla served on the debate panel and questioned the candidates about the Port of Savannah and data centers, two key economic development issues for the Coastal Empire. Collins said he would support communities seeking data center development while helping those opposed to such projects. “If you want a data center in your area when I’m U.S. Senate, I hope you fight to get one, if you don’t I’ll help make sure that you don’t get that,” Collins said. Ossoff emphasized the importance of the Port of Savannah while criticizing Collins’ support for President Donald Trump and his tariff policies. “Georgians deserve to know why someone who wants to serve them in the Senate voted over and over for these tariffs,” Ossoff said. Collins defended the tariffs, arguing they are working, and blamed inflation on policies supported by former President Joe Biden and Ossoff. “That Biden-nomics, that Green New Deal my opponent voted for, that’s where inflation came from. We’ve got to continue to give back to energy independence,” Collins said. With Election Day less than a month away, the debate gave both candidates an opportunity to make their cases to Georgia voters. Whether their exchanges will affect the campaigns remains to be seen. Neither campaign attended the post-debate news conference, leaving the candidates’ remarks during the debate to stand on their own. Copyright 2026 WTOC. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Meet the QS PowerBlock, QuantumScape's solid-state lithium-metal battery reference design for in-rack energy storage in AI data centers. An adaptable reference design, the QS PowerBlock fits a range of module, shelf and rack formats and can support the 800VDC architectures that next-generation AI racks will run on. SAN JOSE, Calif., Oct. 08, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- QuantumScape Corporation (NASDAQ: QS), a global leader in solid-state lithium-metal battery technology, today introduced the QS PowerBlock for AI data centers. The modular system can deliver four times the power density and five times the runtime of current data center industry standards. The QS PowerBlock brings QS solid-state lithium-metal battery technology into AI data centers, supporting safer, higher-performing energy storage and 800VDC architecture. An adaptable reference design, QS PowerBlock can fit a variety of module, shelf, and rack formats, and is designed for deployment in industry-standard power rack configurations. Paired with advanced power system components, it can provide AI data center customers with a compelling combination of power, runtime, and safety to power the 1 MW racks of next-generation data centers. In a demonstration using an expected data center training workload, the QS PowerBlock exceeded key specifications set by the Open Compute Project (OCP), the industry consortium that defines open hardware standards for data centers: 4x the power density, allowing power-hungry AI systems to integrate into compact and cost-effective data center designs. 5x longer runtime, giving data center operators more margin to smooth out power fluctuations and improve hardware productivity. Better safety compared to conventional lithium-ion batteries, helping protect billion-dollar infrastructure investments. QS battery cells have demonstrated thermal stability well over 300 °C in third-party and customer safety testing, compared to conventional lithium-ion cells, which typically go into catastrophic thermal runaway at ~180 °C. "QS solid-state battery technology offers an unmatched combination of energy, power, and safety for many different applications, from electric vehicles to AI data centers and beyond," said Dr. Siva Sivaram, CEO and president of QS. "With the QS PowerBlock, we are bringing this value proposition to AI data center customers, to enable the 800VDC designs that will power the next phase of AI growth." The QS PowerBlock design will be on display at the 2026 OCP Global Summit, October 12–15 at the San Jose Convention Center, at booth C19, hosted by Megmeet, an official partner and power system component provider for the NVIDIA MGX™ Ecosystem. QS also announced that it has joined the OCP as a member. As AI workloads push data centers toward unprecedented power density, QS is joining industry leaders to build the open standards that infrastructure providers depend on. The QS PowerBlock performance results were achieved through prototype testing and modeled system configurations under controlled conditions, with comparisons benchmarked against the OCP Open Rack V3 (ORV3) specification. Final QS PowerBlock performance will depend on product design, system configuration and real-world operating conditions. The company's next-generation solid-state lithium-metal battery technology is designed to enable greater energy density, faster charging and enhanced safety to support the transition away from legacy energy sources toward a lower carbon future. artigo.texto: It's green light for next wave of battery technology in high performance vehicles Advanced modular battery technology (AMBERS) continues to make hybrid powertrain adoption easier and more affordable across high performance applications. Ricardo’s innovative AMBERS programme is supporting this drive. Dr Temoc Rodriguez, Ricardo’s Global Technology Lead for battery development, tells us more. Q: Tell us more about the drive towards hybridisation in motorsport and high performance vehicles? "This move is being driven by multiple factors, including a more conscious approach to the environment, but also the evolution of electrification and hybrid technologies to improve performance levels over traditional propulsion systems. "Innovation has always been at the forefront of motorsport and high performance vehicles, with many of these technologies filtering down into mainstream applications. However, the switch to electrified propulsion systems has been slower to catch on. "Nonetheless, things are changing, in part due to more advanced battery technology and electric drives, leading hybrid vehicles to deliver instant torque, high energy efficiency and advanced energy management. "Although, we’re still a long way from parity across motorsport classes." Q: What are the main challenges to wider adoption in motorsport applications? "Cost is one of the biggest factors shaping decisions in motorsport, and has been a barrier influencing the wider adoption of battery technology in the industry. "If you take the pinnacle of the motorsport industry, Formula 1®, the teams are investing huge sums of money in technologies to remain competitive and meet aggressive vehicle targets. "This compares to the other race classes, who have significantly less money to invest. It doesn’t mean that they are less inventive or innovative, but the reality is that they have to manage their budgets in a way that prioritising more off-the-shelf components as opposed to bespoke, or even clean sheet designs. "This is one of the main reasons why different classes of motorsport haven’t witnessed more rapid hybridisation." Q: How does AMBERS offer a solution? "AMBERS (Advanced modular battery technology) is a platform that has been developed and designed to provide high performance power for hybrid powertrains across all race classes, where something off-the-shelf is needed, without compromising performance. "Ricardo has developed AMBERS as part of a consortium, alongside battery assembler Hyperbat and cell supplier Volklec. The design is Ricardo IP, we own the architecture and can modify it based on individual customer requirements if required. However, it’s been developed as a modular platform, with the intention to make it off-the-shelf and available by the end of 2028. "The modular design lends itself to modifications, including the number of modules in the pack, to fit customer requirements more closely, based around voltage, power and energy, so it’s fully scalable. "It provides a solution, without the need for teams to pay the design, development and test related costs of something bespoke." Q: What are some of the technical specifications of AMBERS? "AMBERS is designed to operate across high performance platforms. The pack itself will give users very high current discharge, which supports rapid acceleration and regenerative braking. It’s enabled with a clever integrated thermal management system and it’s also modular, making it fully scalable, based on customer requirements. "Very few off-the-shelf comparisons can be made, based on design, integration and performance capabilities. "In terms of baseline design, performance levels will be dependent on the battery cell that is installed, which will enable performance at a reasonable price. The more powerful the cell, the more expensive the unit becomes. That’s the customisable aspect of AMBERS; cells can be chosen based on the power and cost requirements of the customer – yet the architecture remains the same. Companies can buy AMBERS as an off-the-shelf kit and integrate it into their racing vehicles. "There’s also an opportunity for parallel applications, including in niche and boutique vehicles, both hybrid and fully electric." Q: What are the next steps for AMBERS? "We’ll have the first prototypes available in 2027, then production is planned to start by the end of 2028, which fits with planned design and development cycles associated with these markets. "Beside the advanced thermal management system, one of our key differentiators will be in our management of the wireless communications in the unit, allowing the sensing electronics to talk to the control module more easily. This eliminates the need for low voltage harnessing. We’ve also looked at how we can improve the BMS system, using artificial intelligence estimation algorithms." Temoc will be presenting on the AMBERS programme at the upcoming PMW Expo on 11th November 2026 in Cologne, Germany. artigo.texto: A Azul Conecta, subsidiária da Azul Linhas Aéreas, compensará emissões de voos de 2026 com créditos de carbono de projetos eólicos A Azul Conecta, subsidiária da Azul Linhas Aéreas, e a Auren Energia anunciaram na última quarta-feira (7), que firmaram uma parceria para compensar as emissões de carbono associadas ao consumo de combustível dos voos realizados pela companhia regional ao longo de 2026. A iniciativa prevê a utilização de créditos de carbono certificados e não terá custo adicional para os passageiros. A compensação será realizada por meio do programa Conecta NetZero, iniciativa voluntária da Azul voltada à neutralização de emissões relacionadas às operações da Azul Conecta. O volume atualmente estimado para a operação é de aproximadamente 10.000 toneladas de CO₂ equivalente (tCO₂eq) por ano. Os créditos utilizados na operação são provenientes dos complexos eólicos Ventos do Piauí I e Ventos do Araripe III, pertencentes ao portfólio de geração renovável da Auren Energia. As unidades foram certificadas pelo Verified Carbon Standard (VCS), programa administrado pela Verra. A certificação envolve processos independentes de validação e verificação dos projetos responsáveis pela geração dos créditos. Os créditos também tiveram sua elegibilidade reconhecida para a fase piloto do Corsia (Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation), mecanismo criado pela Organização da Aviação Civil Internacional (ICAO) para tratar das emissões de carbono da aviação internacional. Depois de utilizados na compensação, os créditos serão aposentados no registro da Verra em nome da Azul Conecta. O procedimento retira permanentemente as unidades de circulação e impede que os mesmos créditos sejam comercializados ou empregados novamente para compensar outras emissões. Cada crédito de carbono representa uma tonelada de dióxido de carbono equivalente que deixou de ser emitida ou foi removida da atmosfera, conforme a metodologia aplicável ao projeto que originou a unidade. Por Marcel Cardoso Publicado em 08/10/2026, às 08h54

Questionado sobre os percentuais de redução reivindicados pelo setor, ele afirmou que essa definição dependerá do conhecimento das regras federais. Não foi anunciado um percentual de benefício nem uma data para sua aplicação. São Paulo defende incentivo para equipamentos específicos Ramuth indicou que o estado pretende concentrar os incentivos em equipamentos de alta tecnologia destinados à inteligência artificial, como processadores e computadores de alta capacidade sem similares nacionais. A posição não contempla, da mesma forma, itens de uso mais amplo, como aparelhos de ar-condicionado. O vice-governador também afirmou que a proposta discutida entre os estados passou por alterações e se afastou do formato inicialmente defendido por São Paulo. União e estado têm expectativas diferentes sobre o prazo Ramuth estimou que a regulamentação do Redata poderia levar pelo menos seis meses. O ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho, apresentou uma expectativa mais curta: concluir o processo até o fim de 2026. Também presente no Futurecom, o ministro afirmou que a aprovação pelo Congresso superou a etapa mais difícil. Segundo ele, os ajustes restantes envolvem principalmente a questão energética e estão em discussão com outras áreas do governo. Os prazos mencionados pelas autoridades são estimativas. Não representam uma data formalmente estabelecida para a publicação da regulamentação ou para a concessão de um incentivo estadual. Redata não reduz automaticamente o ICMS O Redata foi instituído pela Lei nº 15.504, de 15 de setembro de 2026. O regime prevê suspensão de tributos federais sobre determinados equipamentos destinados ao ativo imobilizado de empresas habilitadas, com conversão em alíquota zero conforme as condições legais. A legislação contempla PIS/Pasep, Cofins, suas modalidades incidentes na importação, IPI e Imposto de Importação. Para este último, exige produtos sem produção nacional equivalente, relacionados em ato do Executivo. O ICMS não integra essa lista. Assim, a regulamentação federal não concede, por si só, redução do imposto estadual. A concessão de benefícios de ICMS segue regras próprias. A Lei Complementar nº 24/1975 prevê convênios celebrados e ratificados pelos estados e pelo Distrito Federal e exige decisão unânime dos estados representados para conceder benefícios. Por isso, a posição paulista faz parte de uma discussão que também depende da coordenação entre as unidades da Federação no Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz). Regulamentação terá de detalhar habilitação e contrapartidas A lei atribui ao Executivo federal a definição das condições de habilitação e coabilitação, concedidas pela Receita Federal. Também prevê compromissos relacionados à sustentabilidade, à oferta de capacidade ao mercado brasileiro e a investimentos em pesquisa e desenvolvimento. Há ainda um limite relevante para o calendário: os benefícios relativos a PIS/Pasep, Cofins e IPI têm efeitos previstos até 31 de dezembro de 2026, observadas as regras da Reforma Tributária. Para empresas e profissionais contábeis envolvidos em projetos de data centers, o acompanhamento deve considerar separadamente as condições federais do Redata e os eventuais atos sobre ICMS. Uma redução ainda em discussão não deve ser incorporada como economia garantida ao orçamento de aquisição dos equipamentos. Leia mais: Redata é sancionado e cria incentivos fiscais para instalação e ampliação de data centers no Brasil. artigo.texto: Principais Conclusões - As ações da Microsoft ganharam 37,5% no terceiro trimestre, e Jim Cramer diz que a empresa está "começando a recuperar seu investimento monstruoso em data centers". - O retorno está aparecendo na receita da Microsoft, mas seu fluxo de caixa livre caiu por dois anos consecutivos, então a recuperação está apenas começando. - Os gastos de capital da Microsoft subiram de US$ 23,9 bilhões no ano fiscal de 2022 para US$ 116 bilhões no ano fiscal de 2026, e 30 milhões de usuários do Copilot não podem cobrir essa conta sozinhos. - O ponto a ser observado é se os gastos atingem o pico enquanto a receita continua subindo em direção aos US$ 467 bilhões que os analistas esperam para o ano fiscal de 2028. No episódio de quarta-feira à noite do Mad Money, Jim Cramer, da CNBC, revisou tudo o que preocupava os investidores em junho, no início do que tem sido uma corrida incrível para a Microsoft (MSFT). Desaceleração do Azure. Muito envolvimento com a OpenAI. Clientes que supostamente não pagariam pelo Copilot. "Todas essas preocupações acabaram sendo ou erradas ou falsas", disse ele. Mas Cramer guardou o que chamou de "a maior mudança" para o final: "A Microsoft está começando a recuperar seu investimento monstruoso em data centers." Se ele estiver certo, isso muda tudo. Quão monstruoso estamos falando? O CapEx da Microsoft quase quintuplicou em quatro anos, de US$ 23,9 bilhões no ano fiscal de 2022 para US$ 116 bilhões no ano fiscal de 2026, o ano até junho… Só esse último ano foi um aumento em relação aos US$ 64,6 bilhões do ano anterior. Se é que dá para dizer, eu diria que "monstruoso" é pouco. (Claro, se você quiser se aprofundar... como meu colega explicou na terça-feira, há uma manobra contábil por trás de como os números de capex da Microsoft são relatados, o que vale a pena ler.) O argumento de Cramer para o retorno começa com o Copilot, que tem "30 milhões de usuários e crescendo. Eles estão pagando." A Microsoft claramente quer muito mais usuários do Copilot também. Na sexta-feira passada, o CEO Satya Nadella anunciou "nossa maior atualização do Copilot até hoje", apresentando-o como "um novo sistema operacional para o trabalho que abrange todos os modelos, todos os fatores de forma e todas as tarefas". O que soa bem, mas obviamente não é suficiente para justificar os gastos com capex. Pelo menos ainda não. A receita está aparecendo Mas, ao ampliar o foco do Copilot para toda a empresa, o retorno fica muito mais fácil de ver… A receita cresceu de US$ 245 bilhões no ano fiscal de 2024 para US$ 332 bilhões no ano fiscal de 2026, e os cerca de 50 analistas que cobrem a ação esperam US$ 391 bilhões no ano fiscal de 2027 e US$ 467 bilhões no ano fiscal de 2028. Esse é um crescimento sólido, mas, mais importante, desafia uma lei da gravidade: empresas desse tamanho não deveriam acelerar, mas é exatamente isso que o Wall Street espera que a Microsoft faça. Com a receita da Microsoft Cloud subindo 27% ano a ano no último trimestre (e o Azure subindo 43% – e ultrapassando US$ 100 bilhões pela primeira vez!) – há todos os motivos para pensar que tal aceleração é possível. E só é possível graças à expansão dos data centers. Agora, Cramer está um pouco mais confiante do que eu. Ele acha que os gastos com data centers "podem estar até mesmo atingindo o pico e a lucratividade está à vista", e que Nadella e a CFO Amy Hood sabiam que "esses data centers durarão muito mais tempo do que as pessoas pensavam". Se o capex se estabilizar enquanto a receita se capitaliza na taxa que os analistas esperam, o fluxo de caixa livre finalmente deve começar a subir. Essa é a aposta que os investidores fizeram neste trimestre. Então, sim, o investimento monstruoso da Microsoft está começando a dar retorno, pelo menos na linha de cima. Claro, nada nesses gráficos mostra o capex atingindo o pico ainda, e os US$ 116 bilhões do ano fiscal de 2026 são a maior conta até agora. Então, qual é o valor real da ação da Microsoft? artigo.texto: Taylor City Council greenlights 664-Acre Data Center Project TAYLOR, Texas — A major new data center project east of Taylor is moving forward after the City Council unanimously approved an agreement to annex the 664-acre development following months of heated debate and negotiations. The proposed agreement passed 5-0. The Taylor Technology Campus, formerly known as Project Mustang, will bring data centers and on-site power generation to land between FM 112 and U.S. 79. The project is being developed by Big Watt Digital and PowerHouse Data Centers. Developers and residents have spent months discussing the plan, with concerns about noise, water use and impacts on nearby neighborhoods halting progress last September. Developers withdrew their original annexation and zoning requests at that time, but negotiations continued. According to city leaders, the new agreement includes strict requirements governing water use, noise, lighting and setbacks. The plan also includes $28.2 million in commitments to benefit city programs, Taylor Independent School District and local nonprofits. Some residents, along with the advocacy group Halt Taylor Data Centers, have opposed the project. They argue that the campus could lead to overindustrialization and place additional demands on local water supplies and infrastructure. City officials say the agreement brings the property within Taylor’s city limits, giving the city authority to enforce the new requirements and oversee the development. Officials estimate the project could generate $1.38 billion in gross tax revenue for the city over the next 20 years. The council’s unanimous vote ends a prolonged period of uncertainty and clears the way for the Taylor Technology Campus to move forward under new city oversight, following months of negotiations over the project’s potential benefits and impacts on the surrounding community. Following the City Council’s vote to advance the proposed agreement, Big Watt Digital and PowerHouse Data Centers released the following statement: “Big Watt + PowerHouse welcomes the Taylor City Council’s unanimous vote to advance the Taylor Technology Campus. The decision reflects our commitment to developing a responsibly planned data center campus that aligns with Governor Abbott’s data center standards. We recognize that responsible development means being a good neighbor and an engaged community partner. The Taylor Technology Campus is designed to expand the city’s tax base, create workforce opportunities and support quality-of-life improvements for local residents. The project includes $28.2 million in community commitments, including ongoing support for local nonprofits, schools and community initiatives. We thank the City of Taylor and its elected leaders for their consideration of the project. We look forward to continuing to work collaboratively with the community as the campus moves forward and are excited about the opportunity to call Taylor, Texas, home.”
