artigo.texto: The global building boom of power-hungry data centers is straining electrical grids, causing greater reliance on energy from polluting fossil fuels. Christina Delimitrou, a newly tenured associate professor at MIT, is fighting this environmental threat by rethinking how the computer servers and networking equipment inside those data centers operate. She and her group apply machine learning to make large-scale data centers more efficient, secure, and reliable. They redesign outdated cloud computing systems, develop methods to manage shared hardware resources, and create streamlined server architectures. These advances allow data center operators to coax more computational power out of existing hardware. “If data centers are not utilized to the best of their capabilities, then they will burn much more power than they need to meet growing user demand,” says Delimitrou, the KDD Career Development Associate Professor in Communications and Technology in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and a member of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). “There is a lot of bloating, especially on the software side of these systems. If we can remove that bloating in a way that doesn’t compromise performance, then we won’t need to build as many new data centers.” She also harnesses AI to help programmers find and fix problems in cloud-based applications, like music-streaming services or video conferencing systems. This eliminates application downtime that hampers performance and drains computational resources. “By managing resources more effectively in the cloud, the end user gets more predictable performance from the application running on their smartphone,” she adds. Mathematical beginnings Delimitrou grew up in a midsized town within the vast plains of northern Greece. Her early interest in math and science was sparked, in part, by the ancient history of her homeland, where Euclid and Pythagoras studied mathematical problems more than 2,000 years ago. “In Greece, there is a long tradition of geometry,” she says. She also drew scientific inspiration from her parents. Her mother worked as a chemical engineer and her father as a pharmacist — and both encouraged their daughter’s innate curiosity. Her early affinity for math led Delimitrou to study computer engineering at the National Technical University of Athens, even though she didn’t know much about the field. She quickly gravitated toward courses that focused on the applied science of engineering. For her diploma thesis — a project all students complete during their fifth and final year of study — she studied resource management in a computer when multiple applications are running at once. “A lot of the challenges I was looking at then would get much harder if, instead of a single system, you had 100,000 of these systems. That was a problem that piqued my interest,” she says. Seeking to make a bigger impact as a researcher, Delimitrou pursued a graduate degree at Stanford University. She began tackling inefficiencies in cloud computing systems and large-scale data centers, which was a rapidly growing area of research. Through that work, Delimitrou and her research mentor, Christos Kozyrakis, the Leonard Bosack and Sandy K. Lerner Professor of Engineering, realized many large computing systems were underutilized. “You would expect, with all the demand for these systems, that they should be running close to 100 percent capacity. But we found that most were running at only about 15 percent capacity,” she says. “This is not a resource-efficient or sustainable way of scaling these systems.” Applying AI To push that utilization closer to 100 percent, she began investigating machine-learning solutions to streamline cumbersome computational processes. Machine learning could automate resource management operations in the cloud, identifying solutions that developers might miss on their own. “Applying machine learning to solve a large-scale system problem was a novel approach at the time. It was a bit risky because people had not yet shown that these techniques would work,” Delimitrou says. “But empirical approaches require a lot of expertise, and the scale of the system is so large that it is difficult for users to manage. This is why machine learning is often the best solution.” After earning her PhD, Delimitrou continued this line of work as an assistant professor at Cornell University. One tool her group developed, Seer, uses deep learning to anticipate and prevent problems in web applications before they happen. This averts widespread slowdowns that may occur if a developer tries to fix a problem manually. As she delved deeper into cloud computing, Delimitrou observed that cloud applications were changing. Developers were now splitting applications into smaller pieces to spread across multiple servers, which increases the speed of deployment. “But the servers were not built for this new style of application design. So, I rethought some of my earlier work to build machine-learning systems for this new class of applications,” she says. To tackle these new challenges, she found herself collaborating more often with faculty members who had different software and hardware expertise. Those collaborations opened exciting new research areas. A few years later, she decided to join MIT because of the opportunity to collaborate with researchers at the top of their fields in hardware and software engineering. She became an assistant professor in EECS in 2022. Creative approaches At MIT, Delimitrou also enjoys the teaching aspect of her role. One of her favorite courses to teach is 6.191 (Computation Structure), a popular undergraduate class with about 350 students each semester. artigo.texto: As ações da LG Electronics registravam forte valorização no pregão desta terça-feira (6) após a companhia fechar um novo contrato plurianual para o fornecimento de sistemas de resfriamento de grande porte (chillers) a data centers focados em inteligência artificial (IA) nos Estados Unidos. A operação reforça o reposicionamento da sul-coreana de eletrônicos de consumo no mercado B2B de gestão térmica para infraestrutura crítica de dados. A subsidiária da empresa nos EUA firmou um acordo de longo prazo com a AIR Control Concepts, plataforma de data centers sediada na Virgínia. A parceria prevê o fornecimento de soluções de refrigeração para instalações que somam mais de 5 gigawatts de capacidade computacional. Embora os valores financeiros não tenham sido revelados, a LG destacou que o contrato consolida sua entrada na cadeia de suprimentos de infraestrutura essencial para IA na América do Norte. A reação dos investidores foi imediata. Na Bolsa de Seul, os papéis da LG Electronics chegaram a subir 8,8% no início da sessão, registrando a maior alta diária em cerca de dois meses. A valorização reflete o otimismo com a diversificação de receitas da companhia para além de eletrodomésticos e telas, aproveitando o boom global de demanda por capacidade de processamento intensivo. Para dar conta do volume de pedidos, a LG anunciou planos de expansão capacidade fabril nos Estados Unidos e na Coreia do Sul. A empresa construirá uma nova planta industrial na Virgínia focada no atendimento ao mercado norte-americano, com início de operações previsto para o primeiro semestre de 2027. Em paralelo, a produção será ampliada nas unidades sul-coreanas de Changwon e Pyeongtaek. Além dos contratos norte-americanos, a divisão HVAC (aquecimento, ventilação e ar-condicionado) da empresa vem conquistando espaço em projetos de infraestrutura corporativa no Oriente Médio e na Indonésia. A LG projeta que as novas encomendas anuais de resfriamento para data centers alcancem múltiplos bilhões de dólares até o encerramento de 2026, impulsionadas pelos US$ 426 milhões já garantidos no primeiro semestre do ano. Com o ritmo acelerado de fechamento de negócios, a gestão da companhia afirmou que deve superar antecipadamente a meta estipulada para 2027, que previa R$ US$ 680 milhões em faturamento anual exclusivo na unidade de chillers.

artigo.texto: The voluntary carbon market (VCM) continued to move away from a volume-driven model in the third quarter of 2026, with carbon credit retirements falling even as buyers spent more on the credits they purchased. - Carbon credit retirements reached 30.6 million in Q3 2026, down 9% from 33.7 million a year earlier, according to carbon market data provider Sylvera. However, the value of those retirements rose to $211.8 million from $190.6 million in Q3 2025. The difference points to a market where buyers are becoming more selective. The report reveals that the average price paid for a retired credit climbed to $6.92 in Q3, compared with $5.66 a year earlier. For the first nine months of 2026, the average reached $6.12, up from $5.40 during the same period in 2025. The trend also builds on what Sylvera identified earlier this year. In the first half of 2026, retirement volumes were down 9% year over year, while market value increased. By the end of Q3, however, cumulative retirements had edged above 2025 levels at 130.3 million credits, compared with 129.1 million through the first three quarters of last year. Meanwhile, year-to-date retirement value reached $798 million, 14% above the $697.3 million recorded a year earlier. Quality Is Taking a Bigger Role in Carbon Credit Pricing The strongest signal from the latest data comes from the widening gap between higher- and lower-quality credits. Credits rated BBB or higher represented only 18% of rated retirement volume in Q3. Yet they generated 42% of rated market value. This suggests buyers are willing to pay significantly more for credits that meet stronger quality expectations rather than simply purchasing the cheapest available supply. The premium becomes even clearer across individual project categories. - For afforestation, reforestation and revegetation (ARR), BBB+ credits averaged $23.47 per tonne in Q3, compared with $12.80 for credits rated BB or below. Improved forest management (IFM) showed a similar divide. BBB+ IFM credits reached $21.07, while lower-rated credits averaged $12.79. - REDD+ also saw a sharp quality-driven price difference. BBB+ REDD+ credits averaged $7.75 in Q3, up 58% from $4.90 a year earlier. Lower-rated REDD+ credits increased from $2.70 to $3.56 over the same period. As a result, the REDD+ price gap between the two quality groups nearly doubled from $2.20 to $4.19. The trend suggests that buyers are not abandoning nature-based credits altogether. Instead, they appear increasingly willing to distinguish between projects based on perceived quality. - RELATED: Carbon Credit Prices Explained: What Determines the Value of a Carbon Credit? - LIVE PRICES: Carbon Credit Prices Today 2026 | Live Chart, EU ETS & VCM Renewables Still Dominate, But Their Market Position Is Changing Renewable energy projects accounted for 41% of Q3 retirements, giving them the largest share among project categories. However, Sylvera cautions that the increase in market share does not represent renewed growth in renewable credit demand. Renewable retirements totaled 40.7 million credits during the first nine months of 2026, roughly unchanged from the same period in 2025. That remains far below the 77.1 million credits retired during the first three quarters of 2022. Full-year renewable retirements peaked at 99.7 million in 2022 before falling to 49.3 million in 2025. The quality issue is particularly important here. Sylvera does not rate renewable projects above C because many grid-connected renewable projects face additionality concerns. As a result, renewables accounted for 76% of B/C/D-rated retirement volume in Q3. That helped push the share of B/C/D-rated credits across the entire retirement market to 66.1%, the highest level since Q3 2023. In other words, renewable credits continue to provide substantial market volume, but their presence also weighs on the overall quality profile of retirements. REDD+ Demand Normalizes While Agriculture Gains Ground REDD+ accounted for 18% of Q3 retirements, down sharply from 38% in Q2. However, the comparison needs context because Q2’s unusually high share was largely driven by one major retirement. Beyond that temporary spike, REDD+ demand appears relatively stable, with retirement activity spread across Colombia, Brazil, Cambodia, Peru, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Agriculture was a more notable growth area. Its share of retirements increased from 2.55% to 7.82%, while retirement volume more than doubled. Energy and utility companies played an important role in that shift, with agriculture representing 28% of their Q3 retirement mix, compared with 6.8% a year earlier. This diversification matters because the market is gradually moving beyond a small group of traditional project categories. Buyers are showing greater interest in credits tied to agriculture, forest management, and other project types where measurable climate and environmental benefits can support stronger pricing. Corporate Buyers Are Still Active Despite the overall decline in quarterly retirement volumes, major corporate buyers continued to transact at scale. Yamato Transport and Corpay each retired about 2 million credits in Q3, making them the largest retirees during the quarter. Primax Colombia followed with just over 1 million. For the first nine months of 2026, Eni remained the largest retiree with nearly 9 million credits. TASC, Organización Terpel, Engie and Lenovo also ranked among the largest buyers. At the same time, Shell’s retreat remains significant. The company retired only about 496,000 credits through the first three quarters of 2026, compared with roughly 7 million during the same period in 2025. Sylvera first highlighted the decline in its Q2 report, and the latest numbers suggest the pullback has continued. artigo.texto: The second-gen BYD Seagull electric hatchback became available for pre-orders in China. The all-new car has grown by 425 mm in length to compete with the current domestic bestseller, which is the Geely EX2 (Xingyuan / E2). Customers can place a reservation for the new Seagull in the BYD App for 2,000 yuan (~300 USD). The price of the new car remains undisclosed, which is a common practice in China. It allows automakers to attract attention to the model and to assess potential sales volume based on booking statistics and user interest. A refund can be issued at any time before the order is locked. According to BYD, the 2,000-yuan deposit is only used to confirm the intention to purchase the car. However, it doesn’t act as a purchase contract, as the car’s configuration, trim levels, and prices have yet to be revealed. After the official release, clients can revise their reservations, modifying the vehicle according to personal preferences. It was officially revealed that the second-gen Seagull will be available in six exterior colors: green, orange, white, pink, blue, and gray. As mentioned, the new BYD Seagull has significantly grown in size. Its dimensions are 4205/1810/1570 mm with a wheelbase of 2,650 mm. It is 425 mm longer than the ongoing first generation. The exterior styling looks more mature as well. The new Seagull has a five-seat cabin. The left part of the center screen acts as an instrument panel. Another highlight is a 94-liter storage compartment under the bonnet. The car’s trunk offers up to 1,380 liters with the rear seats folded down. The second-gen BYD Seagull has a 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor in the rear axle and two battery options for 30 and 39.2 kWh. Its CLTC range is 320 – 420 km under CLTC conditions (262 – 344 km WLTP). It is expected that the new Seagull will adopt the flash charging function, suitable for charging from 10% to 97% in nine minutes. There is also an optional roof-mounted LiDAR, which is part of the DiPilot 300 (“God’s Eye B”) ADAS. The BYD Seagull is expected to cost below 100,000 yuan (14,915 USD) in China. For clarity, the ongoing BYD Seagull delivered 74,087 units from January to August 2026, down 66.5%, according to China EV DataTracker. Its price range lies between 69,900 and 85,900 yuan (10,425 – 12,810 USD).

artigo.texto: Pennsylvania governor candidates debate data centers and education Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and Republican state Treasurer Stacy Garrity debated key issues, including data center development and education, during a gubernatorial debate at the state Capitol in Harrisburg. Video above: Top news stories, weather forecast. Candidates clash over data center development The development of large data centers has been a major political topic this year, with Shapiro and Garrity expressing differing views on the issue. Shapiro defended his decision not to implement a moratorium, instead using an executive order to protect communities. "If a local community does not want that data center to be built in its community, it will not be built. That policy won't even be heard. That proposal won't even be heard by the Commonwealth when it comes to permitting," Shapiro said. Garrity, who earlier this year called for a pause on hyperscale data center development, did not commit to a specific timeline but emphasized collaboration with stakeholders. "Real leaders don't need that long of a pause. You get all the stakeholders around the table and you find out what you need to protect ratepayers and protect communities. So as long as it takes," Garrity said. Education funding and achievement take center stage Education funding and student achievement were also key topics during the debate. Garrity stressed the importance of ensuring students meet academic benchmarks. "By the third grade, your child needs to be able to read, and if they can't, there are a lot of steps you can take to make sure that they're not falling behind. They need to stay at that grade level. By the time they get to the eighth grade, they need to read and do math at grade level," Garrity said. Shapiro highlighted public school investments during his term and expressed support for both public education and private school vouchers. "It is not an either-or... either we invest in public education or we make those investments in educational opportunities. It's both/and. I want to see investments in public schools like we have done, and I'm open to seeing the Democrats and Republicans come together to be able to provide that opportunity," Shapiro said. Budget challenges ahead Shapiro also addressed his veto of lifeline scholarships during his first year in office, explaining that it was due to lawmakers not having a deal in place that would have upheld the state budget. The candidates are expected to share their thoughts on budgeting challenges in what could be a tighter year for Pennsylvania’s savings.

artigo.texto: - Carbonzero has been acquired by Gitxaała Enterprises Corporation, the economic development arm of Gitxaała Nation. - The transaction makes the Canadian climate consultancy 100% First Nations-owned, according to the companies. - The deal gives GECO a platform in both voluntary and compliance carbon markets, including British Columbia’s industrial carbon-pricing system. Carbonzero, Gitxaała Enterprises and carbon markets are coming together in a deal that gives the Canadian climate consultancy a new ownership structure and gives a First Nations economic development corporation a larger foothold in the climate economy. Gitxaała Enterprises Corporation, the business arm of British Columbia’s Gitxaała Nation, announced Oct. 6 that it had acquired Carbonzero. The company said Carbonzero will retain its existing name, clients, contracts and services, while Jeff Calvert takes over as chief executive. A bigger role in carbon markets The transaction comes as governments and businesses look for ways to expand carbon-market participation and channel investment toward emissions reductions and removals. Canada has been developing its own offset-credit infrastructure while also examining ways for Canadian companies to participate in international carbon markets. The federal government said in September that it was exploring a framework for international carbon-credit transfers under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. For GECO, the acquisition also has a direct connection to British Columbia’s forest-carbon economy. The company said Carbonzero will expand its work in the province’s Output-Based Pricing System compliance market using Gitxaała Nation’s ownership of carbon credits from the Great Bear Rainforest. Indigenous ownership meets climate finance The deal reflects a broader role for First Nations in Canada’s environmental and natural-resource economy. The Great Bear Rainforest has already demonstrated how carbon finance can support Indigenous-led conservation and economic development. British Columbia says revenues from carbon offsets have helped First Nations participate in stewardship and implementation of regional conservation agreements. Carbonzero, which has operated for more than two decades, will now build on that market expertise under First Nations ownership as GECO seeks new economic opportunities for Gitxaała Nation. artigo.texto: Champaign County residents voice opposition to potential data centers The county could vote on an ordinance before the moratorium is lifted in April CHAMPAIGN, Ill. (WAND) — The repeated message heard from Champaign County residents — they don’t want a data center in their backyard. “Letting this data center come and be here in our county would detrimentally affect all businesses, and that would just be a problem for the continued survival of us as people,” said one community member during public comment. After Mahomet’s recent rally against potential data center additions, Champaign residents said they don’t want the same situation playing out in their community. “I really just wanted to reiterate how important this was before — how close things got with Mahomet,” said another resident. “That’s very scary for everyone, and I really think it lit a fire in the community to make this ordinance have as much teeth as possible.” Some board members also shared their own insight on the potential addition. “We can still cover a substantial amount of Champaign County, and other counties will look to us just like we look toward Aurora,” said Prairie Rivers Network Director of Climate Policy Andrew Rehn. “I think we have a chance to be a leader here.” No decisions were made during the meeting, but this won’t be the last chance for the public to weigh in. “Let’s just think big on this and make it as tough as possible for any data center to be built here. Thank you,” said one resident. Copyright 2026 WAND. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Li Auto’s 2026 i6 set for October 28 launch without CATL’s battery Li Auto has officially announced that the 2026 model of its i6 SUV is scheduled for market launch on October 28, with deliveries expected to commence in early November. The vehicle is set to arrive at dealerships on October 11 and will make its international debut at the Paris Motor Show on October 12. Li Auto CEO Li Xiang highlighted that the 2026 Li i6 introduces six upgrades: - Lighting: The vehicle is now equipped with ADB matrix headlights, identical to those found on the Li Mega, offering improved brightness, width, and range for night driving. - Storage: A new electric front trunk (frunk) has been added, featuring convenient “knock-to-open” and voice-control functionality. - Comfort: The front row now features dual zero-gravity seats capable of reclining to a 150-degree angle. - Display: The interior boasts a 29-inch 6K panoramic screen in the front and a 21-inch 4K entertainment screen for rear passengers. - Range: Powered by a 96 kWh fast-charging battery, the vehicle achieves a CLTC-rated range of 780 km (632 km WLTP). - Computing: The system is powered by a combination of the Qualcomm 8797 chip and Li Auto’s “Mach M100” chip. Design and dimensions The 2026 Li i6 features exterior refinements, aligning its front bumper design with the new L9 and i9 models. It adopts semi-concealed door handles compliant with new national standards and offers a choice of 20-inch or 21-inch wheels. The vehicle measures 4,950 mm in length, 1,935 mm in width, and 1,655 mm in height, with a wheelbase of 3,000 mm. The interior has been refreshed with a new design language and updated ambient lighting. Battery The i6 utilises Li Auto’s self-developed battery system, covering the entire chain from cells to Pack and BMS. The 5C fast-charging cells are produced by Sunwoda and CALB under Li Auto’s specifications, with the final battery pack assembly completed in-house. Performance The powertrain is available in single-motor and dual-motor configurations. The single-motor version delivers a maximum power of 250 kW (335 hp), while the dual-motor system features a front motor with 150 kW (201 hp) and a rear motor with 250 kW (335 hp). Li i6 is Li Auto’s best-selling model at present. In September, Li Auto sold 31,817 vehicles, down 6.3% year on year and 15.6% month on month. The i6 accounted for roughly half of September’s sales. The newly launched 2026 model is the first version to stop using CATL batteries altogether.

artigo.texto: San Gabriel Valley Residents Fighting Data Centers Hit a 12-Mile-Long Snag Community groups opposed to the projects face a tough adversary in the City of Industry, an economic powerhouse seemingly unaccountable to surrounding residents. San Gabriel Valley residents, community organizers and advocates rally at Peter F. Schabarum Regional Park in Rowland Heights on May 2 to protest a proposed data center across the street at the Puente Hills Mall site in the City of Industry. Photos by Semantha Raquel Norris for Capital & Main. Falynn Love met her husband 25 years ago at the Puente Hills Mall, a place best known as a filming location for the 1985 movie Back to the Future. Today, Love is fighting to preserve the largely vacant, 1970s-era retail center in the City of Industry, about 15 miles east of Los Angeles, as a third space for the community, and to stop plans to turn the site into a massive industrial complex with two large warehouses, a new bus transit station and a 10-megawatt data center. Those plans have sparked fierce opposition among residents of the San Gabriel Valley, where a diverse coalition of community groups across an array of predominantly Latino and Asian suburbs has mobilized to try to stop a series of proposed data centers over concerns they will worsen the area’s air quality and noise pollution and hike residents’ utility bills. “We’re going to be bearing the cost of these kinds of projects,” said Love, who joined the fight after learning about plans for the Puente Hills Mall when attending a neighborhood meeting in Rowland Heights, an unincorporated community just across the street. As with many residents in the coalition, the issue impelled Love to get involved in activism for the first time. “It doesn’t matter what race you are, what background, what religion,” Love said. “Everybody is standing for the same thing, and it’s community, it’s people, it’s environment.” The San Gabriel Valley has become a hotbed of opposition to the building of data centers for artificial intelligence, part of a nationwide backlash uniting communities across demographic groups and political parties — a Gallup poll earlier this year found seven in 10 Americans oppose construction of data centers in their area. Community groups have notched victories across several cities in this region of nearly 2 million people, including in Monterey Park, which in June became the first city in the nation to pass a voter-approved ban on data centers. Sam Brown-Vázquez, an organizer with No Data Centers San Gabriel Valley and Avocado Heights Vaquer@s, speaks at the May 2 rally against a proposed data center in the City of Industry. But community efforts to block data centers have come up against a formidable obstacle in the City of Industry, a sprawl of industrial warehouses and commercial manufacturing centers that snakes across 12 miles of the San Gabriel Valley. Though it borders a dozen communities from El Monte to Diamond Bar, with just over 200 residents, it’s a municipal oddity that has faced legal challenges since its incorporation in 1957. Public records obtained by community groups and reviewed by Capital & Main show City of Industry officials have been discussing data center proposals with developers in recent years — the largest of which is the plan for the Puente Hills Mall site. Activists say there are few means by which residents of surrounding communities can protect themselves from the impacts because the city has few actual constituents and its leaders are unaccountable to nearby residents who could be harmed. A City of Industry spokesperson reached by Capital & Main said the city has not approved plans for a data center but declined further comment for this story. The Blueprint Data centers, large industrial facilities that house computer servers to store, process and transmit digital information used by artificial intelligence, cloud computing and other digital services, require large electrical systems, enormous amounts of water for cooling equipment and other resource-intensive infrastructure. As technology becomes more reliant on these services to feed AI-powered search engines and chatbots, data centers are rapidly expanding nationwide, but so is community resistance, as residents raise concerns about the environmental and health impacts of the resource-hungry facilities and their effects on electricity and water rates. “I couldn’t believe that a data center was going to be built within a five-minute walk of my house,” said Steven Kung, co-founder of No Data Center Monterey Park and candidate for Monterey Park City Council. “It didn’t sit well with me because data centers usually get built in rural communities or deserts, and there was this cognitive dissonance in a data center coming to such a housing-dense area,” said Kung. “It felt like environmental racism.” Steven Kung speaks at the May 2 rally in Rowland Heights. Monterey Park, a predominantly Asian and Latino community of about 57,000 people just a few miles west of the City of Industry, has been leading the local data center resistance. After fierce community backlash, the Australian-owned investment firm StratCap pulled its plans for a 247,000-square-foot data center in the city. “It feels very empowering in a time when people feel powerless,” Kung said. No Data Centers San Gabriel Valley, a coalition of residents, activists and at least six community organizations from across the San Gabriel Valley, has used similar tactics in El Monte, Montebello and Baldwin Park, where city councils adopted temporary moratoriums on data centers, and Alhambra, where a citywide ban is on the November ballot. But there’s a 12-mile-long obstacle to community groups’ aspirations to keep data centers out of the San Gabriel Valley. artigo.texto: A China acelera a construção de centros de dados no interior, região rica em energia e terras baratas, para disputar a liderança global em inteligência artificial. Só em Ulanqab, na Mongólia Interior, há 89 centros de dados construídos ou planejados, segundo o Financial Times. Os centros de dados de Ulanqab pagam cerca de US$ 0,05 por kWh, menos da metade dos mais de US$ 0,08 cobrados em muitas cidades chinesas e dos US$ 0,11 de Pequim. A região também tem ligação de trem de alta velocidade de duas horas até a capital. Ao menos uma dezena de empresas já ocupam quatro campi na região, incluindo Alibaba e a Huawei, com três centros de dados. A ByteDance, maior locatária de capacidade computacional do país, também está entre os ocupantes. Uma das empresas, a ZData, converteu uma antiga escola abandonada em centro de dados. A estratégia chinesa tem nome oficial: dongshu xisuan, ou "dados no leste, computação no oeste". Mais da metade do pipeline de novos centros de dados do país já está no norte e noroeste, incluindo a Mongólia Interior. A região deve superar Pequim, Xangai e outras áreas urbanas como maior fonte de capacidade computacional da China até 2028. A corrida ocorre em paralelo a conversas entre China e EUA sobre os riscos da inteligência artificial. Publicidade A aposta em energia farta não é nova. A China já havia inaugurado um data center submerso movido a energia eólica, além de uma unidade alimentada inteiramente por fonte eólica na região de Ningxia. O avanço reforça avaliações recentes sobre o setor. O CEO da Nvidia já disse que a Huawei se destaca como líder global em inteligência artificial, mesmo sob restrições dos EUA à exportação de chips. O que acontece agora O pipeline de novos centros de dados chineses segue concentrado no norte e noroeste do país. Analistas já alertam que regiões como a Europa correm risco de ficar atrás na disputa global pela infraestrutura de IA.

artigo.texto: IMPERIAL — As part of their bus tour across 28 states, conservative non-profit organization Humans First stopped at Eager Park in Imperial to spread their message against an “unaccountable AI buildout” on Friday, Oct. 3. Despite the nationwide bus tour being called “AI Data Center Revolt,” Kylie Jane Kremer, Senior Advisor for Humans First, said the movement is not anti-AI or anti-AI data centers, but rather “America first.” “We’re definitely not anti-data center, we’re not anti-AI; we’re not anti-tech, as I said. We believe we can do this in a way that is transparent and lets communities know what they’re getting into and what’s involved,” said Kremer. For Humans First, communities facing AI data center proposals should be the ones with the authority to welcome or reject the projects while having full transparency from the project developers and local officials. “If these data centers are so great, if they’re going to bring so many jobs and be so powerful in these communities and be this economic boom, why are they not being transparent?” said Kremer. ”Shouldn’t they be able to sell this to the American people very easily and tell them all the facts? Because if they’re so great, it should be an overwhelming yes. But they know that that’s not the truth, that these are not great for communities.” “People don’t want them, and so that’s why they’re having to go about it in sneaky ways where they’re doing NDAs, payouts, and that sort of thing,” explained Kremer. The bus tour transporting the Humans First team began their cross-country trip with stops at 35 different cities in Austin, Texas, and going as far east as Washington, D.C. The tour then made its way toward the West Coast, where it will reach San Francisco as its final stop on Monday, Oct. 5. Kremer explained that each city the Data Center Revolt bus tour stopped at was at different stages of an AI data center project, but their goal to elevate community voices and make them engaged stayed the same. Some cities face an uphill battle when it comes to opposing AI data centers, such as Jonesburg, Missouri, one of the stops made by Kremer and her team. Jonesburg is located in rural Montgomery County, which currently has two data centers under development, despite local opposition. “It’s a town of, I think, 640 people. They have roughly an $18 million county budget annually. Google and Amazon are going there and bringing two massive hyperscale data centers over $25 billion,” explained Kremer. “How does a town of 640 people with an $18 million annual budget even begin to fight that? So we went there; it’s about generational land, farmers, communities that really matter just like here in Imperial.” Tom Gaitens, Senior Advisor for Humans First, praised Imperial for their success in opposing the hyperscale AI data center proposed in Imperial County, which, if built, would be the largest data center in the state. “What you did here needs to be echoed around the country. What you did here, you’re heroes. You found out the process late in the game, and they tried to hide it from you,” said Gaitens. “They did not want to disclose this information in public hearings and allow you to see what your neighbors were going to be doing, but you are the heroes who stood up, faced this giant, a $10 billion giant, and you held it at bay.” Local opposition against data centers has been an issue that Democrats and Republicans find common ground on, with Kremer noting that the issue affects local communities as a whole, bringing them together against a common cause. Kremer stressed the importance of staying engaged in creating opposition to data centers, and despite meaningful victories, the issue of data centers is far from over. “We’re seeing time and time again that communities have wins, and then the people get complacent or, you know, have this victory and they kind of take a break from it. What happens when people let their guard down is that the big tech companies come back with bigger lawyers, smarter about the process,” said Kremer. “We are on track to have over 10,000 data centers in the United States by 2030. And right now we’re just roughly over 5000, so that will be doubling it. So this issue is not going away; it’s not just temporary, this is a long-term play that people need to remain engaged in,” explained Kremer.

artigo.texto: Residents had a chance to question a data center developer about two proposed data center developments planned for Swatara Twp. Haley O'Brien / WITF Several representatives from Corscale Data Centers spoke with residents Thursday evening about the proposed Highlands East and Highlands West projects at the Sheraton Harrisburg Hershey Hotel. Residents who live nearby raised concerns about increased traffic flow and environmental impacts. Erik Draaisma, executive vice president of business development for the company based in Texas, called the projects responsible. “We’re ready to be completely transparent about what we’re doing here,” he said. “We’ve done our due diligence. We are proud of the project that we are putting forward.” Corscale submitted plans for the Highlands East project on Highland Street bordering I-283 in mid-September. The Highlands West project will be on the site where Dauphin Highlands currently stands. The golf course is set to close Oct. 12. Corscale confirmed grid availability with PPL and purchased both properties. Nicholas Ressetar, president of St. Nicholas Serbian Orthodox Church, said the information session was his first opportunity to look at renderings of the proposals. “What’s very upsetting to me and our congregation… is that the data centers themselves are almost directly across from the homes and our church,” he said. “It’s really a slap in the face to the people in the community.” The proposed developments will be set at least 210 ft. from the road with a 70 ft buffer zone of trees. Draaisma reminded concerned residents that those plans exceed legal requirements. “We’re very familiar with architecture, we’re familiar with being inside a community,” he said. “So this is not like some of the other data centers that you’ve seen that are highly industrialized and haven’t taken that into account.” The projects totaled at $14.5 billion are projected to be completed in 2029. They will create 2,000 jobs during the construction phase, which is expected to begin in 2027, and more than 250 permanent jobs. Katherine Pelley, a resident of Steelton, attended with a list of questions. She learned about other developments in Pa. and had concerns that they will dimmish home values or strain the power grid. “A lot of them have been answered both by the core scale representatives and by some other people, residents who have gone to more meetings,” she said. She is one of many residents who came from other neighborhoods. “I think it’s better to protect ourselves by trying to fight this and fight for residents protection as much as possible. Before it becomes something that is irreversible.” Thomas White lives in Middletown and came to the meeting to gather information to bring back to his community. “I want to get as much information here so that I can take that to Middletown and get an ordinance in place in Middletown,” he said. “I just don’t see a benefit in AI, and I avoid it at all costs.” Draaisma acknowledged that some residents oppose data centers, particularly those who live nearby. But he said Corscale intends to develop the properties within the limits of what is allowed. “I understand not everyone’s in favor of development,” Draaisma said. “Especially if you’re in the immediate vicinity but we want to develop what is allowed on this site to the best of our abilities and be a good neighbor within that context.” The projects have both been confirmed to be within the intended zoning use. The developer will now work to ensure that they are meeting all regulations moving forward. “I want to get people over the hump of that initial fear of the unknown and hopefully show them what I know is that they’re quite boring, these buildings, once they’re up and running,” he said. “There’s not an awful lot going on. artigo.texto: San Francisco approves, other cities consider bans and reviews on data center growth SANTA CLARA, Calif. - As artificial intelligence and digital services rapidly expand, several California local governments are stepping back to evaluate the footprint of data center development in their communities. Cities across the Bay Area and Southern California are considering pauses or reviewing long-standing policies to address rising concerns over energy demand, water usage, and environmental impacts. High demand prompts policy evaluation The City of Santa Clara stands as one of California's primary data center hubs. Despite its population of roughly 133,000 residents, Santa Clara currently hosts 56 data centers, with two additional projects in development. The industry has proven highly lucrative for Santa Clara, contributing $35 million annually in taxes directly into the city's general fund. However, high power demand prompted the city's municipal utility, Silicon Valley Power, to stop accepting new data center applications in 2023. Santa Clara officials are launching a year-long interdepartmental review of environmental, water, power, and quality-of-life impacts before updating local development rules. Regional moratoriums and community pushback Local perspective: In Oakland, City Council members are considering a 45-day temporary moratorium on new data center construction. Protesters gathered at Oakland City Hall ahead of a council vote scheduled for Tuesday night to voice concerns about local neighborhood impacts, high water consumption, and energy efficiency. Similarly, San Francisco supervisors unanimously approved a 45-day moratorium on data center approvals, declaring an immediate threat to public health, safety, and welfare without comprehensive regulations in place. Supervisor Shamann Walton noted the pause allows the city time to study energy, water, air quality, land use, and community effects. Meanwhile, Southern California is taking a similar approach. The Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors received a proposal to permanently ban massive "hyperscale" data centers—frequently built to support resource-intensive AI workloads—while leaving allowances for smaller operations.

artigo.texto: Denver is taking its next step toward deciding where data centers can operate — and under what conditions — as concerns mount over their demands on electricity, water and surrounding neighborhoods. Mayor Mike Johnston and three Denver City Council members announced Wednesday the selection of 26 people to a working group tasked with developing recommendations for regulating the facilities. Recommended Stories “It will be Denver — not corporations — that decide if and how data centers may operate in our city,” Johnston said in a statement. “This group brings together people with different perspectives to help us get this right: setting clear rules, protecting Denver’s resources, and putting the interests of Denverites first. Let’s get to work.” The working group is comprised of wide swath of individuals representing utility, academia, healthcare and air quality as well as community members. The group is expected to create policy suggestions. Among those serving are Ean Thomas Tafoya, with GreenLatinos; Rev. Terrance D. Carroll, former speaker of the Colorado House of Representatives and Melissa Almond of Xcel Energy. More than 250 people applied, according to the mayor’s office. The first meeting is expected to be held Friday, with sessions streamed in English and Spanish. The community is encouraged to submit questions and comments. Privately owned, a data center houses IT infrastructure for building, running and delivering computer applications and services. It also stores and manages the associated data. Data centers date back to the 1940s with the U.S. military and one of the world’s first digital computers, which was developed at the University of Pennsylvania during World War II and required a dedicated space to house the machines. With the advent of microcomputers in the 1990s, data centers today dramatically reduce the amount of space required for IT operations. These microcomputers filled mainframe computer rooms, or servers, that became today’s “data centers.” The Denver metro area has 54 data centers, according to the Data Center Map. Nearly 2,800 data centers are planned or under construction nationwide, according to a 2025 American Edge Project report, which identified another 4,149 already operating. Fueled by America’s AI boom, the rapid expansion of data centers has drawn comparisons to the railroads of the 19th century, highways of the 1950s and broadband of the 1990s — even earning the description of a “modern-day Moonshot moment.” Dan Diorio at the Data Center Coalition said data centers are a positive investment for communities, adding that data center success goes hand-in-hand with the success of the community it’s built in. “It matters how a company responds, and overwhelmingly you’ll find good actors in this space,” he said about community concerns. “Transparency and trust matter.” But public opposition to data centers is mounting because of the water and electricity demands and other strains associated with them. More Americans believe data centers have a negative effect on the environment, energy costs and the quality of life than say they have a positive impact, according to a Pew Research Center poll earlier this year. In May, the Denver City Council unanimously voted to impose a one-year moratorium on permits and site development applications for data centers. Data centers permitted before May of this year are not subject to the moratorium. Other cities are also pushing back. Aurora Mayor Mike Coffman has said that the proposed Trident Data Center near Green Valley Ranch “must be stopped.” And the 170,000-square-foot CoreSite DE3 data center in Denver’s Elyria-Swansea neighborhood has sparked fierce protests from residents who have complained about the lack of notification prior to the city approving the project. Johnston’s working group also includes representatives from Globeville, Elyria and Swansea. “We will take our time and use this opportunity to ensure we are establishing protections for our communities and resources today and in the future,” Councilwoman Serena Gonzales-Gutierrez said in a statement. “I am grateful to the people who took the time to apply and are going to devote additional time and expertise to this process.” Reporters Deborah Grigsby and Kyla Pearce contributed to this report.

artigo.texto: Data centers pedem redução de 90% do ICMS para equipamentos Brasscom relata resistência dos estados à proposta discutida no Confaz; entidades também cobram regulamentação do Redata. As entidades do setor de data centers negociam com o Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz) uma redução de 90% do ICMS sobre equipamentos contemplados pelo Redata. Segundo Walter Wolff, diretor de projetos da Brasscom, a proposta enfrenta resistência dos estados e busca complementar os incentivos federais do regime. A discussão foi apresentada durante a abertura do Data Center World, nesta terça-feira, 6 de outubro. De acordo com Wolff, o setor trabalha com uma lista de 25 equipamentos, concentrada em eletrônicos. A relação está em discussão com outras associações, incluindo representantes dos fabricantes brasileiros. O dirigente explicou que o foco da negociação está nos equipamentos de tecnologia, sem abranger toda a infraestrutura física dos empreendimentos. A Brasscom defende que o tratamento estadual acompanhe os benefícios federais para aumentar a competitividade do Brasil na disputa por projetos. Na avaliação de Wolff, a negociação deve considerar a concorrência com outros países pela instalação de data centers. A Conexis também participa da mobilização. Seu diretor jurídico, Bruno Cavalcanti, afirmou que a entidade assinou, com outras associações, um manifesto dirigido ao Confaz. “Não existe um Redata completo sem esse endereçamento do tema no Confaz”, declarou. Regulamentação ainda em discussão Além do ICMS, as entidades aguardam a regulamentação do Redata. Wolff afirmou que a expectativa é concluir essa etapa nas próximas semanas, mas reconheceu os obstáculos nas negociações. “Tem sido uma discussão extremamente difícil”, disse o dirigente da Brasscom. Segundo ele, as condições de fornecimento de energia aos data centers estão entre os assuntos discutidos. A definição dos equipamentos beneficiados também permanece pendente. Renan Lima Alves, presidente da Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC), explicou que a lista de classificações fiscais dos produtos ainda precisa ser divulgada, assim como os procedimentos para apresentação de pedidos de inclusão. Alves destacou a dificuldade de aproveitamento dos créditos tributários da aquisição de hardware na prestação dos serviços. Por isso, a entidade considera o tratamento do ICMS parte relevante da política de redução dos custos de implantação. Wolff também apontou a previsibilidade dos benefícios para os próximos cinco anos como um elemento importante para decisões de investimento de longo prazo. Incentivo à transferência de processamento Para o presidente da Equinix, Victor Arnaud, a combinação entre regulamentação do Redata, tratamento dos tributos estaduais e compatibilidade com a reforma tributária determinará as condições de aplicação do incentivo. O executivo identificou como oportunidade imediata a transferência para o Brasil de cargas de processamento que atendem ao mercado brasileiro, mas estão hospedadas no exterior. Segundo ele, a redução da diferença de custos pode estimular empresas a manter esses dados em território nacional. Arnaud ressaltou, porém, que a demanda por data centers já cresce independentemente do regime. Na avaliação do executivo, os incentivos podem ampliar esse movimento e melhorar as condições de atração de novos projetos.

artigo.texto: New battery chemistry could help lithium-sulfur batteries store more energy Lithium-sulfur batteries are an experimental alternative to today’s lithium-ion batteries that could store considerably more energy for their weight but have proved difficult to make durable and practical. Now, researchers at Vanderbilt University and the University of Maryland have demonstrated a new approach that could push their energy-storage potential further. In a study published in Nature Energy, the team developed a battery chemistry that allows sulfur to participate in an additional energy-storing reaction. The result is a sulfur-based battery that operates at a higher average voltage while also storing more charge. De-en Jiang, the H, said: The traditional way of thinking about lithium-sulfur batteries leaves some of sulfur’s redox power untapped, Eugene McBrayer Professor of Chemical Engineering and Professor of Chemistry. He is also a co-corresponding author of the study. “We wanted to see whether we could expand sulfur’s redox capability and use it to store more energy.” Getting more energy out of sulfur Sulfur has long attracted battery researchers because of its abundance and lower cost. Plus, it can store far more charge by weight than the materials commonly used in lithium-ion battery cathodes. The challenge has been that most lithium-sulfur batteries operate at a relatively low voltage. And the amount of energy a battery can store depends on both how much charge it holds and the voltage at which it operates. The researchers found a way to improve both functions. In a conventional lithium-sulfur battery, each sulfur atom can exchange two electrons as the battery charges and discharges. The new system extends that chemistry by introducing chlorine, allowing sulfur to exchange a third electron. That additional reaction also takes place at a higher voltage. In laboratory tests, the new chemistry increased sulfur’s charge-storage capacity by about 58% and raised the battery’s average operating voltage from about 2.05 volts to 2.54 volts compared with standard lithium-sulfur chemistry tested under the same conditions. The combination of the higher charge-storage capacity and the higher voltage allowed one kilogram of sulfur to store more than 1,700 watt-hours of energy in their experimental cell. Designing an electrolyte to make it work Making the new reaction reversible presented another challenge. The team needed chlorine to interact with sulfur during charging without allowing the resulting sulfur-chlorine compound to travel through the battery and react with its lithium-metal electrode. Researchers used molecular simulations to understand how lithium and chloride ions behave inside different electrolytes. Those calculations led to the design of an electrolyte in which chloride remains available to react with sulfur. The team also selected an electrolyte in which the sulfur-chlorine reaction product does not readily dissolve. That helps keep it where it belongs—inside the battery’s positive electrode—so the reaction can be reversed when the battery discharges. Experiments using several different spectroscopy techniques confirmed that sulfur repeatedly moved through the newly accessible chemical state as the cells were charged and discharged. An early demonstration The researchers ultimately built a small, single-layer pouch cell to show that the chemistry could work outside the coin cells commonly used for early battery experiments. The pouch cell retained 78% of its initial capacity after 100 charging cycles. Considerable work remains before the approach could be used commercially. The prototype uses a lithium-metal electrode, relatively modest amounts of sulfur and more electrolyte than would be desirable in a commercial battery. But Jiang said the larger significance is the possibility of expanding the chemistry available to sulfur batteries rather than simply improving the conventional reaction. The researchers estimate that, after accounting for major battery components rather than the electrode alone, the approach could enable a stack-level specific energy of 477 watt-hours per kilogram, about 37% higher than the conventional lithium-sulfur system used for comparison in the study. artigo.texto: Sudeste Asiático enfrenta grande déficit de armazenamento de energia em meio ao choque do GNL Um relatório do think tank de energia Ember constatou que, embora a crise do gás natural liquefeito deflagrada pela guerra do Irã esteja levando o Sudeste Asiático em direção à solar e à eólica, a região garantiu menos de um terço da capacidade de armazenamento necessária até 2030. Segundo o relatório divulgado na quarta-feira, o pipeline atual de projetos de armazenamento em escala de serviços públicos do Sudeste Asiático é de aproximadamente 7GW, com entrada em operação prevista até 2030. Esse volume atende a menos de um terço dos 23 a 26GW necessários para sustentar as metas de energia renovável da região. A Ember alertou que, se o crescimento continuar no ritmo atual, o déficit aumentará ainda mais até 2045. Alnie Demoral, analista de energia da Ember, observou que a restrição de financiamento na transição energética da Asean deixou de ser a captação de capital e passou a ser o desenvolvimento de ativos bancáveis. Essas conclusões evidenciam as dificuldades enfrentadas por economias que tentam reduzir sua dependência de combustível importado após a interrupção dos embarques pelo Estreito de Ormuz provocada pela guerra do Irã. Antes do início do conflito, no fim de fevereiro, essa rota marítima respondia por quase um quinto do GNL mundial. O Global Energy Monitor informou que o Sudeste Asiático obtinha cerca de um terço de suas importações de gás do Oriente Médio antes da guerra. A GEM também afirmou que os preços spot do GNL asiático ficaram em média em US$ 17,50 por milhão de unidades térmicas britânicas no segundo trimestre, um aumento de 45 por cento em relação ao ano anterior. Dados da GEM revelam que, nas Filipinas, que anunciaram emergência energética nacional em março, a capacidade de energia a gás em desenvolvimento caiu de 19,7GW em janeiro para 13,8GW até agosto. No Vietnã, a Vingroup tentou substituir uma usina a GNL planejada de 4,8GW por solar, eólica e armazenamento em baterias. A Ember descobriu que, embora grandes fazendas solares estejam encontrando mais facilidade para atrair financiamento comercial, o armazenamento em baterias, os projetos renováveis menores e as linhas de transmissão continuam sendo menos atraentes para os investidores. Sob condições idênticas de tarifa e financiamento, um projeto solar de meio megawatt rende 2,6 por cento ao capital próprio, contra 13,1 por cento de uma instalação de 20MW. A Sra. Demoral declarou que o investimento futuro dependerá da redução dos custos de transação e da capacidade de armazenamento e redes gerarem retornos compatíveis com seu valor para o sistema elétrico. A Ember observou que o investimento atual está abaixo dos US$ 281 bilhões anuais necessários até 2035 para que a região conclua sua transição energética. A Agência Internacional de Energia projeta que a demanda de eletricidade do Sudeste Asiático crescerá cerca de 5,4 por cento ao ano até 2030. O gás caro também está trazendo o carvão de volta, com a AIE prevendo que a demanda mundial de carvão suba 1,2 por cento, para um recorde histórico de 8,94 bilhões de toneladas neste ano, à medida que os preços elevados do GNL levam concessionárias na Europa, no Japão, na Coreia do Sul e na China a consumir mais. A Ember afirmou que as abordagens de financiamento que sustentaram grandes projetos renováveis ainda não chegaram ao armazenamento e às redes essenciais para incorporar energia intermitente. Este relatório fornece uma análise aprofundada do mercado global de gás natural liquefeito (GNL), cobrindo tamanho de mercado, crescimento, demanda, oferta, fluxos comerciais, preços, cenário competitivo e previsões até 2035. O estudo é projetado para fabricantes, distribuidores, importadores, exportadores, investidores, equipes de compras, consultores e equipes de estratégia que precisam de uma visão consistente e orientada por dados da dinâmica do mercado e de uma definição analítica transparente do escopo do produto. Cobertura do Produto Este relatório abrange o Gás Natural Liquefeito (GNL), que é o gás natural resfriado ao estado líquido para facilitar o armazenamento e o transporte. O escopo engloba o mercado global de GNL em suas principais etapas da cadeia de valor, incluindo liquefação, transporte marítimo, regaseificação e comércio atacadista. A análise é segmentada por tipo de produto, aplicação e principais atividades comerciais. Incluídos - GÁS NATURAL LIQUEFEITO (GNL) COMO PRODUTO PRIMÁRIO - BIO-GNL E GNL SINTÉTICO - GNL EM PEQUENA ESCALA PARA DISTRIBUIÇÃO DESCENTRALIZADA - GNL PARA GERAÇÃO DE ENERGIA E COMBUSTÍVEL INDUSTRIAL - GNL COMO COMBUSTÍVEL PARA TRANSPORTE MARÍTIMO E RODOVIÁRIO DE CARGA PESADA - GNL UTILIZADO COMO MATÉRIA-PRIMA QUÍMICA - ATIVIDADES DE LIQUEFAÇÃO, TRANSPORTE MARÍTIMO, REGASEIFICAÇÃO E OPERAÇÕES DE TERMINAIS - COMÉRCIO ATACADISTA E TRADING DE GNL Excluídos - GÁS NATURAL EM ESTADO GASOSO TRANSPORTADO POR GASODUTO - GÁS NATURAL COMPRIMIDO (GNC) - ATIVIDADES DE EXPLORAÇÃO E PRODUÇÃO A MONTANTE DE GÁS NATURAL - DISTRIBUIÇÃO VAREJISTA E COMERCIALIZAÇÃO DE GÁS ENCANADO PARA CONSUMIDORES FINAIS - LÍQUIDOS DE GÁS NATURAL (LGN), COMO ETANO, PROPANO E BUTANO Cobertura do Relatório e Módulos Analíticos O relatório combina a base padrão de estatísticas de mercado com capítulos estratégicos úteis para planejamento comercial, decisões de sourcing, entrada no mercado, monitoramento de concorrentes e priorização de portfólio. - Tamanho do mercado, desenvolvimento histórico e previsão até 2035 - Arquitetura da demanda por aplicação, grupo de clientes e comportamento do comprador - Estrutura de oferta, papel da produção quando aplicável, sourcing e restrições da cadeia de valor - Exportações, importações, balança comercial, dependência de importação e principais corredores comerciais - Níveis de preço, corredores de preço, efeitos de especificação e lógica comercial de preços - Panorama competitivo, presença de empresas, foco no portfólio de produtos e posicionamen

(TSX-V: LMR, OTC: LMRMF, FSE: DH8C) (“Lomiko” or the “Company”) is pleased to announce the successful completion of the previously announced plan of arrangement (the “Arrangement”) under the Business Corporations Act (British Columbia) involving Global Battery Materials Corp. (“GBM”) and the Company, pursuant to which GBM, among other things, acquired all outstanding shares of Lomiko (the “Shares”) for cash consideration of $0.13 per Share, all in accordance with the terms of the Arrangement. artigo.texto: Alarm.com Extends Intelligent Video Protection to More Entryways with New Battery-Powered 781B Wire-free video doorbell brings intelligent video, relevant alerts, and proactive deterrence to entryways where traditional doorbells aren't practical TYSONS, Va.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 6, 2026-- Alarm.com (Nasdaq: ALRM), the leading platform for intelligently connected properties, today announced the Alarm.com 781B Battery Video Doorbell, giving homeowners and businesses a new way to bring video security to entryways throughout their properties. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261006740792/en/ Alarm.com announces the release of the Alarm.com 781B Battery Video Doorbell (ADC‑VDB781B). The 781B combines a rechargeable battery, Wi-Fi connectivity, and intelligent video capabilities in a doorbell designed for locations without existing doorbell wiring. Customers can install the 781B at a front door, side door, back door, detached garage, gate, shed, or other entryway where running new wiring may be impractical. As part of the Alarm.com platform, the doorbell works alongside the broader connected property system, unlocking a range of intelligent features that go beyond basic video coverage. "The 781B brings intelligent video, proactive deterrence, and connected actions to more entryways," said Dan Kerzner, President of Platforms Business at Alarm.com. "It gives our service providers another strong wireless option for delivering comprehensive video coverage across a property." Intelligent Awareness at More Entryways A square 1:1 view captures visitors from head to toe, while Advanced Video Analytics can identify people, animals, vehicles, and packages to help deliver more relevant alerts. As the first Alarm.com battery video doorbell to offer animal and vehicle detection, the 781B helps customers distinguish different types of activity around their property. Familiar Face Analytics can recognize up to five familiar people and support customized notifications, while Package Alerts help customers stay aware of deliveries and removals of packages. When a response is needed, customers can interact with visitors remotely through crisp two-way audio and Call Screen Actions, allowing them to unlock doors, turn on lights, and more through the Alarm.com platform without leaving the doorbell screen. For unwanted visitors, Perimeter Guard® combines attention-grabbing lights and audio alerts with the ability to trigger connected lights throughout the property. AI Deterrence can also deliver AI-generated verbal warnings when a person is detected at the door. Flexible Protection Without Doorbell Wiring The 781B is designed to make video protection possible in more locations without requiring an existing doorbell power source. Its battery-powered, Wi-Fi-connected design allows customers to install the doorbell where traditional wired models may not be an option without requiring connection to a hub or base station. Specially designed Energy Saver Video Analytics help conserve battery power during periods of inactivity. When it's time to recharge, the removable battery can be swapped out, or customers can use optional wiring for continuous trickle charging. The removable universal rechargeable battery is also compatible with the Alarm.com Volt Series™ V731B Battery Camera, giving customers a common battery solution across compatible devices and a simpler way to expand battery-powered video throughout a property. Designed for Everyday Security From monitoring a side entrance to keeping an eye on packages delivered near a garage, the 781B extends the role of the video doorbell beyond the front door. Customers can see activity, communicate with visitors, and respond to unexpected activity from the Alarm.com platform, wherever the doorbell is installed. The 781B also supports Bluetooth® Enrollment, designed to make device setup faster and easier for service providers. Availability The 781B is compatible with a range of Alarm.com residential and commercial video service packages, with feature availability varying by service package. To learn more about the Alarm.com 781B Battery Video Doorbell, visit www.alarm.com or contact an Alarm.com service provider. About Alarm.com Alarm.com is the leading platform for intelligently connected properties. Millions of homeowners and businesses rely on Alarm.com’s technology to secure, monitor, and manage their environments from anywhere. Our comprehensive suite of solutions—including security, video surveillance, access control, active shooter detection, intelligent automation, energy management, personal safety and awareness, and fire—is delivered exclusively through a trusted network of thousands of professional service providers and commercial integrators across North America and worldwide. Alarm.com’s common stock is traded on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ALRM. Alarm.com delivers serious security for serious people. To learn more, visit www.alarm.com. artigo.texto: Fisk Electric Awarded $24 Million Data Center Electrical Project, Expanding Prefabrication Capabilities in Houston LOS ANGELES--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 6, 2026-- Tutor Perini Corporation (NYSE: TPC) (the “Company”), a leading civil, building and specialty construction company, announced today that its subsidiary, Fisk Electric Company (“Fisk”), has been awarded an electrical services contract for a confidential data center customer in Houston, Texas. The contract value is approximately $24 million. Fisk’s scope of work includes prefabrication and assembly of modular containment systems and related electrical infrastructure, including liquid-cooled components and piping, for a new ground-up data center. These units will be built at Fisk’s new 75,000-square-foot prefabrication/manufacturing facility in Houston. This new emerging prefabrication market is in high demand due to the nationwide shortage of electricians, enabling Fisk to increase its prefabrication work when serving as the prime electrical contractor supporting data center owners, developers, and general contractors in refining offsite manufacturing to ensure schedules are met with the limited resources available nationwide. Electrical construction work is expected to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026 with substantial completion anticipated in the first quarter of 2027. The contract value will be reflected in the Company’s backlog for the third quarter of 2026. About Tutor Perini Corporation Tutor Perini Corporation is a leading civil, building and specialty construction company offering diversified general contracting and design-build services to private customers and public agencies throughout the world. We have provided construction services since 1894 and have established a strong reputation within our markets by executing large, complex projects on time and within budget while adhering to strict safety and quality control measures. We offer general contracting, pre-construction planning and comprehensive project management services, and have strong expertise in delivering design-bid-build, design-build, construction management, and public-private partnership (P3) projects. We often self-perform multiple project components, including earthwork, excavation, concrete forming and placement, steel erection, electrical, mechanical, plumbing, heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC), and fire protection. artigo.texto: Renesas Expands GaN Portfolio with First Low-Voltage GaN FETs for AI Data Centers and Robotics New 100V E-mode GaN Advanced Power Transistor Family Delivers Higher Power Density and Industry-Leading Figure-of-Merit Performance TOKYO--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 6, 2026-- Renesas Electronics Corporation (TSE:6723), a premier supplier of advanced semiconductor solutions, has expanded its GaN portfolio into low-voltage applications with its first family of 100V enhancement mode (E-mode) GaN-based discrete power transistors. The RTP100E005G1FL, RTP100E2P6G1FL, RTP100E1P8G1FL-DSC and RTP100E1P2G1FL-DSC low-voltage GaN FETs deliver ultra-fast switching speeds and enhanced thermal performance in efficiency-critical, high power density applications, including AI data centers, humanoid robotics, factory automation and industrial motor drives, power tools and solar microinverters. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261006989457/en/ The new GaN FETs achieve industry-leading hard- and soft-switching figure-of-merit (FOM) performance, delivering up to 35% lower hard-switching FOM and up to 63% lower soft-switching FOM than comparable GaN devices. The low-voltage GaN devices also maintain a silicon-compatible footprint that allows for easy adoption into existing designs. Power converters in today's data centers generally operate at switching frequencies of a few hundred kilohertz. But as AI servers and industrial infrastructure transition to 800 VDC power distribution and 48V bus architectures, many converter stages are moving toward megahertz-class switching to shrink magnetics, increase power density and improve overall efficiency. Using low-voltage GaN in 800V high-voltage direct current (HVDC) power architectures simplifies power conversion design, significantly reducing passive component size, switching losses and cooling requirements. At the system level, this translates to better efficiency, fewer thermal management requirements and lower energy and BOM costs. Broad GaN Portfolio Yields Greater Efficiency, Power Density and Design Flexibility Built on Renesas’ recently expanded low-voltage E-mode GaN technology platform, this new transistor portfolio features ultra-fast GaN switching with low total gate charge (Qg) and output charge (Qoss) to minimize the overlap between voltage and current. It reduces energy lost in each conversion cycle across AI power supply units, motor drives and DC-DC power stages. The devices also offer zero reverse recovery (Qrr = 0), which eliminates energy losses for immediate switching efficiency gains. Fast switching increases power density and yields higher frequency operation by shrinking PCB footprint and reducing the size of magnetic and passive components, while low RDS(on) improves operating efficiency by curtailing conduction losses. Available bottom- and dual-side cooling configurations provide added heat dissipation and design flexibility. Depending on application requirements and power-conversion architecture, the low-voltage GaN devices can achieve up to 40–70% lower switching losses and up to twice the power density at the system level. The new GaN transistors are offered in multiple standard MOSFET-compatible packages, allowing customers to quickly migrate from silicon MOSFET layouts for faster design implementation without significant PCB rework. The package options, combined with a wide RDS(on) range (5 mΩ-1.2 mΩ), enable designers to scale across power levels and applications, including synchronous rectification, multiphase buck conversion and motor drives. "Customers adopting next-generation GaN technology for AI servers, robotics, industrial motor drives and renewable energy systems are looking for ways to deliver more efficient power conversion performance from increasingly compact systems,” said Akhil Nair, Senior Director, Low-Voltage GaN at Renesas. "Our low-voltage GaN family delivers the efficiency, switching performance and power density designers expect from GaN while making it significantly easier to transition from existing silicon MOSFET designs.” High GaN Performance in Silicon-Compatible Footprints The new GaN family is built on E-mode (normally off) GaN technology, which offers the performance advantages of GaN in a convenient silicon-compatible footprint. This helps designers capture the efficiency and power benefits of GaN and simplifies migration from existing silicon-based designs. Key features of the new low-voltage GaN family - 1 to 3% higher efficiency over silicon-based designs, eliminating Qrr loss - Drastic 40 to 70% reduction in switching losses - Doubled power density by reducing switching energy per cycle and supporting high frequency operation - Smaller system footprint with higher switching frequency reducing magnetics size and lowering overall system losses - Optimized thermal management reduces fan and active cooling requirements, cutting system complexity and BOM cost Additionally, with its lower total energy consumption per power stage, the new GaN family helps designers meet sustainability objectives. This is achieved by reducing the size of fans required for thermal and airflow management, enabling the use of smaller magnetics and shrinking overall PCB footprint, which contributes to AI data center and industrial energy efficiency targets.
