artigo.texto: Europe’s solar and battery storage sectors supported nearly one million jobs in 2025, highlighting the growing contribution of clean energy to the European Union’s economy. According to the latest industry assessment, solar photovoltaics and battery energy storage systems (BESS) together provided approximately 982,000 full-time equivalent (FTE) jobs across the EU. Solar PV accounted for the largest share with 874,000 FTE jobs, while BESS contributed 108,000 FTEs. Battery storage employment was assessed separately for the first time in the report. Solar employment grew by 1% during the year, twice the pace of overall EU employment growth. Indirect employment across supply chains represented 56% of the total workforce, while direct jobs accounted for the remaining 44%. Strong deployment of renewable energy and storage capacity was the primary driver behind this employment growth. The EU installed 69 GW of new solar capacity and 27 GWh of battery storage in 2025. Deployment activities generated around 742,000 solar FTE jobs, representing 85% of total solar employment. For battery storage, deployment accounted for approximately 90,000 FTE jobs, or 84% of the sector’s total workforce. Operations and maintenance activities also recorded significant employment gains. Solar O&M supported a record 78,000 FTE jobs, while battery storage operations and maintenance contributed another 8,000 FTEs. The increase reflects the expanding installed base of solar and energy storage projects across Europe. However, manufacturing continued to face challenges from strong international competition, low factory utilization and plant closures. Solar manufacturing supported only about 37,000 FTE jobs. Inverter production dominated this segment, accounting for around 90% of solar manufacturing employment. Battery manufacturing supported approximately 64,000 FTE jobs across the broader battery industry. However, only about 7,000 of these jobs were directly linked to stationary energy storage, as electric vehicles continued to account for the majority of battery manufacturing activity. Germany and Spain emerged as the largest solar employment markets in Europe, each supporting nearly 165,000 FTE jobs. Italy followed with approximately 85,000 FTEs. Together, the three countries represented nearly half of total solar employment in the EU. Utility-scale solar projects also overtook rooftop installations for the first time, accounting for 50.2% of solar jobs. Large projects in Spain, Germany, Italy and Romania contributed significantly to this shift. By 2030, the EU solar workforce is projected to decline by 12% to around 766,000 FTEs. The decline is expected to reflect greater industry productivity and market maturity rather than a contraction of solar power. Annual installations are projected to stabilize at around 70 GW under the medium scenario. Deployment-related employment could fall by 22%, while O&M jobs are expected to increase to 109,000 FTEs. Manufacturing employment could reach 49,000 FTEs if planned projects are completed, while decommissioning and recycling jobs could nearly double to 30,000 FTEs. The report recommends stronger access to training funds for SMEs, updated vocational education covering digital technologies, smart grids and storage, and implementation of installer measures under RED III. Apprenticeships, new career pathways and reskilling programmes for former fossil-fuel workers are also expected to help Europe maintain a skilled workforce for its clean energy transition. artigo.texto: America is hopelessly divided along party lines. That’s a stubborn fact, we’re told, and the polling bears it out: Democrats dislike Republicans and Republicans dislike Democrats, in almost precisely the same proportions. But every election produces surprising coalitions that defy entrenched partisanship. In these midterms, left and right have found something so commonly loathed that politicians across the country are flip-flopping in real time. Mother Jones has been tracking the backlash to data centers on the ground long before the water-guzzling behemoths became the country’s bête noire. The AI boom, with its insatiable need for computing, has unleashed a power grab by tech billionaires. “Data centers have replaced megayachts as the preferred theater of oligarchic status signaling,” national correspondent Tim Murphy wrote in his big Mother Jones investigation into hyperscale data centers and the communities they land on. “Oligarchy is now more than an idea; it is a place.” On today’s episode of Stress Test, Tim joins host Garrison Hayes to discuss how data centers—and other AI-boom technologies, like Flock cameras—have upended political fortunes and ripped up the partisan playbook ahead of November’s vote. “It’s maybe the single most toxic issue in the midterms this side of, you know, gas prices,” Tim tells Garrison. “It’s like a three-to-one opposition among voters. Nobody wants data centers. Everybody’s fired up about it.” Take Texas. Republican Gov. Greg Abbott promoted the state as a place where companies could build almost anything. Then rural and suburban communities got the facilities, and the gas plants that power them, in their backyards, along with strained water supplies, pollution, and rising utility bills. “People are complaining about what they have to live next to,” Tim says. “And it just builds and builds and builds.” Under pressure (and running for reelection), Abbott made a stunning reversal, announcing steps that amount to a moratorium. And he’s not the only one feeling the heat. So what changed? Data centers used to be half the size of an Amazon warehouse; now they’re measured in “multiples of Manhattan,” says Tim, who explains how we got here and what to expect next. He heads back to Texas in the coming weeks, and we’ll follow what he learns right up to Election Day. For more, read Tim Murphy’s road trip through the towns living in the shadow of the AI boom: “How the American Oligarchy Went Hyperscale,” from our May+June issue. artigo.texto: Marquette residents ask questions at data center presentation MARQUETTE, Mich. (WLUC) - Lake Superior Community Partnership and the Northern Michigan Chamber Alliance hosted nearly two-hour informational presentation at the Peter White Public Library on data centers. The presentation covered a variety of topics including what data centers need to operate, how many are in Michigan, what they look like and the different types, and the economic impacts of having a data center nearby. Audience members were given the opportunity to ask questions following three speakers. Dakota Baker, NMCA’s director, said the goal was to provide factual information to the community. “It’s really important that people in our communities - the leaders, the residents, everybody - have the best access to factual information that sort of gets away from all of the potential misinformation on social media and opinion profiles and different things,” Baker said. “So that when projects are considered, if they are considered, these community leaders and members can make the best decision for their unique community.” Some members of the audience believe important information was missed, especially regarding the environmental impact of data centers. Lucy Miller, an NMU professor, said environmental topics were not covered in-depth. “It was touched upon but not elaborated upon in a way for folks to enter a basic literacy and understanding those conversations related to noise pollution, water use, environmental energy concerns,” Miller said. Miller said she would’ve liked to have seen an environmental expert on the panel. Nick Gualazzi, a community member, said he attended for information on the topic. “I’m not for them, I’m not necessarily against them, I just wanted more information, and we got a lot of that,” Gualazzi said. According to the panel, there are no current known plans for data centers in the Upper Peninsula. artigo.texto: Lexington-Fayette Urban County Council votes to extend data center moratorium LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT) - The Lexington-Fayette Urban County Council voted Thursday night to extend its data center moratorium. The moratorium will now expire on Oct. 31, 2027. It was previously set to expire at the end of the month. The vote came after an hour of public comment, with residents raising concerns about data centers. Three items on the agenda Three data center related items were placed on the agenda for first reading: - Extending Lexington’s data center moratorium for one year - Initiating a new zone specifically for data centers - Adjusting language in the original zota to enhance future regulation A resident said, “Everyone in this city is making it very clear that we don’t want these data centers in Lexington now or ever.” The council’s committee of the whole voted Tuesday to advance the proposal to extend the moratorium. Council member Emma Curtis, who represents council district four, moved to suspend the rules for all three items, to go immediately to a second reading and a vote. “To me there are some things that matter more than us doing things the way they’ve always been done when we have the flexibility to treat them in a slightly different way,” Curtis said. Two items fail to advance The council suspended the rule requiring a second reading at Thursday’s meeting, leading to a final vote on the moratorium extension, which passed with relative ease. The vote for a second reading on the language for regulation failed 6-5. The resolution to initiate a zone specifically for data centers did not receive a second and failed. A resident said, “We’re not talking about a quiet office park with cubicles and laptops, we’re talking about massive energy loads, rotating industrial cooling towers, and diesel backup generators pumping toxins into the air.” Council member Liz Sheehan, who represents council district five, said moving to a second reading within the same meeting rushes the process when more public input is needed. “The rule that we have on two readings where they are spaced out is to increase transparency for the public, and to give more opportunities for the public to weigh in,” Sheehan said. Next steps Curtis sees Thursday’s results as a net-positive and a step in the right direction. The remaining two items are set for their second reading in two weeks, on Oct. 22. “Seeing as council member Morton was the primary sponsor of those items, I am looking forward to him being present for our discussion. I do suspect both motions will pass at the next council meeting that we have when they’re given second reading,” Curtis said. Under the moratorium extension, Lexington-Fayette County won’t accept or review data center development plans, approve zoning changes for data center projects, or issue permits for data centers. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no EPE adia estudo de data centers no RS para dezembro Publicado 06/10/2026 • 18:17 | Atualizado há 13 horas KEY POINTS Informe trimestral reorganiza 47 estudos de transmissão: nove estão concluídos, 28 em andamento e dez ainda serão iniciados. Alterações de prazo não significam atraso automático em obras. A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) atualizou o calendário da Programação de Estudos da Transmissão de 2026. O informe trimestral de setembro reúne 47 análises: nove finalizadas, 28 em andamento e dez ainda por iniciar. Uma das mudanças alcança o estudo sobre o atendimento a grandes cargas de data centers no Rio Grande do Sul. A conclusão, antes indicada para agosto, passou para dezembro de 2026. O trabalho examina a integração dessas cargas à rede de transmissão; a nova data é do estudo e não representa, isoladamente, adiamento de um empreendimento privado ou de uma obra específica. Também foi ampliado o horizonte do estudo de compensação dinâmica de potência reativa no Sistema Interligado Nacional, de dezembro de 2026 para abril de 2027. A análise sobre controle de tensão no Norte foi dividida em duas partes: a primeira segue para outubro de 2026 e a segunda, incorporada agora à programação, tem término previsto para fevereiro de 2027. A segunda parte do trabalho do Norte está associada à consulta tecnológica da EPE sobre recursos avançados para controle de tensão e suporte dinâmico, aberta até 31 de dezembro. A separação indica que o planejamento pretende incorporar respostas do mercado antes de fechar a recomendação tecnológica. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC Na comparação com junho, três estudos passaram à condição de finalizados: atendimento à região da Grande Vitória, à região de Sorocaba, Indaiatuba e entorno e ao sul do Rio Grande do Sul. A finalização do estudo significa conclusão da análise técnica e não equivale a licenciamento, contratação ou entrega das instalações recomendadas. Outros cronogramas foram estendidos. Entre eles estão as análises da ilha do Marajó, da interligação Acre–Rondônia–Mato Grosso, do noroeste de Minas Gerais e de regiões de Campinas e Curitiba, agora apontadas para dezembro. Trabalhos no Maranhão, Mato Grosso, Minas Gerais, Paraná e Rio Grande do Sul também receberam novos marcos entre outubro de 2026 e fevereiro de 2027. O documento funciona como instrumento de transparência do planejamento. Os estudos podem recomendar novas linhas, subestações, transformadores, compensadores ou soluções operativas; depois, cada alternativa ainda precisa percorrer decisões setoriais, autorização ou leilão, licenciamento, contratação e implantação conforme o caso. Para transmissoras, grandes consumidores, fabricantes e financiadores, a atualização ajuda a identificar quando soluções técnicas deverão ficar maduras para as etapas seguintes. artigo.texto: The Baldwin County Commission passed a 180-day moratorium on all rezoning requests, new data centers and renewable energy projects within zoned areas. Commissioner Jeb Ball said the county has received many rezoning requests, and without a planning director or an updated master plan, he believes it's best to let the incoming commission and a new planning director decide future rezoning cases. "The moratorium will actually be enacted after we leave this meeting today. Is it going to cause some backlashes and rifts? It probably will. Don't care," Ball stated. "It's needed for mainly our staff and for the citizens of this county just to slow down a minute and catch our breath, let the new commission get a planning director in place, let them get the master plan set up and then if they feel like they're ready to go, the new commission can always undo the moratorium." RELATED: Foley puts six month moratorium on data centers to update ordinances, evaluate capacity Ball hopes developers will have time to consider more plans before presenting them to the new commission. "It shouldn't be controversial," he added. "It shouldn't be going against everybody's will around the area and stuff like that, and that's what this master plan, once it's solidified and a new planning director are going find." There are currently exceptions to single-family residential building permits on existing, individually owned lots that do not require a change in zoning or special exception approval. Exceptions also exist for previously approved renewable energy projects and data centers. "I don't disagree with the moratorium. The staff-they're going to get hit harder too once this 180 days is up and there's going to be a lot of rezoning cases coming in front of them," Commissioner Matt McKenzie voiced. "This helps out. I really appreciate it and I know the developers will be upset, but like I said earlier, when do we ever listen to developers?" Commissioner Billie Jo Underwood, who will serve on the next commission, believes the moratorium will allow for smarter preparation for growth as the master plan is updated. "I understand that master plans are just a guide. They're not statutory. But we're being asked more and more to put the brakes on things," Underwood said. "This is not about putting brakes on development at all. It's about making sure we have the proper framework in place to guide the development that is continuing to come." Underwood is unaware of any data center plans for Baldwin County but wants the commission to be prepared as the demand for data increases nationwide. The moratorium was imposed upon passage. artigo.texto: City Beats Follow Us on Google October 6, 2026 by Franca Ochigbo, Abuja Climate Change: Stakeholders urge FG to harmonise policies, boost carbon trade The Director General, National Council on Climate Change, Mrs Omotenioye Majekodunmi, in partnership with Climate Change stakeholders, have called on the federal government and regulatory agencies to harmonise policies on climate change, while urging Fiscal and monetary authorities to provide clarity on taxation, foreign exchange rules and investment incentives for carbon transactions and optimisation of domestic benefit retention. The DG made the call during a High-Level Roundtable on Operationalising Nigeria’s Carbon Markets through Robust Measurement, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) in Abuja, calling on Private Sectors and Project Developers to build a robust, bankable pipeline of high-integrity projects. She urged the private sector and developers to align their methodologies with Nigeria’s national baseline criteria and also prioritise community impact alongside financial returns, noting that from Policy Intent to Market Delivery Nigeria stands at a pivotal juncture in its socio-economic journey. According to her, “This gathering is under the auspices of the European Union Climate Dialogues programme; it is to address one of the most vital policy imperatives of our generation, which is turning Nigeria’s climate ambition into tangible, bankable, and verifiable action. Through initiatives such as the EU Climate Dialogues, we continue to foster the critical institutional momentum required to transition our climate commitments into sustained economic growth. “This is to power clean energy transitions, restore degraded lands, modernise agriculture, improve waste management, and expand clean technology access across our 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, climate finance at scale is indispensable with global carbon markets presenting one of the most promising avenues to mobilise this private capital”. She added that carbon markets are only as strong as the integrity of the underlying credits. A carbon market without rigour is merely an exercise in greenwashing a scenario that Nigeria will not accommodate. The goal is straightforward: Nigeria’s carbon projects must deliver real, additional, and permanent mitigation outcomes that benefit the communities, protect its ecosystems, and deliver fair value to project developers and investors alike. Speaking, the Director of Forestry, Ministry of Environment, Halima Bawa-Bwari, noted that the forestry sector is central to Nigeria’s climate response because forests are carbon sinks, temperature buffers, reduce natural disaster risks, important sources of livelihoods, primary food and pharmacy sources, among others. artigo.texto: A regulamentação do Encargo de Reserva de Capacidade associado aos sistemas de armazenamento não deve atrasar o primeiro leilão de baterias do Brasil, previsto para dezembro deste ano, mas o debate sobre o rateio do encargo evidencia, na avaliação da Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae), uma lacuna na legislação que precisa ser corrigida. Pelas regras aplicáveis ao certame, a regulamentação do encargo e a formalização dos contratos de uso de potência precisam estar concluídas até 30 dias antes do início do suprimento, previsto para agosto de 2028. “Há tempo regulatório para aperfeiçoar o rateio sem comprometer o certame. O que não podemos fazer é permitir que uma discussão sobre metodologia adie um leilão necessário para o sistema elétrico e já aguardado pelo mercado”, disse Fábio Lima, diretor-executivo da Absae. Para a entidade o avanço da regulamentação é necessário e deve ocorrer com consistência técnica, previsibilidade financeira e segurança jurídica. Mas a regulamentação, por si só, não elimina a distorção criada pela legislação. Consulta pública A entidade considera positiva a consulta pública aberta nesta semana pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) sobre o assunto e defende o avanço da regulamentação paralelamente à aprovação do Projeto de Lei (PL) 3.716/2026, que revoga um dispositivo da Lei 10.848/2004, incluído pela Lei 15.269/2025, que determina que os custos das contratações de reserva de capacidade com baterias sejam rateados apenas entre os geradores de energia, conforme regulamentação da Aneel. A ideia da proposta é mudar o rateio do encargo e cobrar dos consumidores. Para a Absae, a própria complexidade do debate regulatório evidencia um problema anterior à regulamentação, já que a legislação atribuiu aos geradores o custeio da contratação de sistemas de armazenamento em baterias sem estabelecer diretrizes mínimas para operacionalizar esse rateio. Na avaliação da entidade, a lei 15.269/2025 definiu quem deve pagar o encargo, mas deixou em aberto elementos fundamentais para sua aplicação, como a grandeza sobre a qual o rateio deve incidir, a periodicidade de apuração e os critérios para eventual diferenciação entre os próprios geradores. “A consulta pública é importante e a Absae vai contribuir tecnicamente para que a regulamentação seja segura e operacional. Mas o próprio debate mostra que estamos tentando resolver, pela via regulatória, uma distorção que nasceu na lei. A solução estrutural é corrigir essa assimetria sem transformar essa discussão em obstáculo para o primeiro leilão de baterias do país”, afirma Fabio Lima. Com isso, cabe agora à Aneel transformar um comando legal genérico em uma metodologia objetiva e operacional, capaz de assegurar previsibilidade de arrecadação e segurança financeira aos contratos de longo prazo associados ao certame. Necessidade contratada tem natureza sistêmica Outro aspecto do debate sobre o encargo é a própria origem da necessidade que justifica a contratação dos sistemas de armazenamento. Para a entidade, o voto do relator do processo na Aneel, diretor Gentil Nogueira, e a contribuição do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) reconhecem que o certame contrata disponibilidade de potência e que a necessidade atendida pelo produto se manifesta especialmente nos momentos de maior demanda do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Para a Absae, esse ponto é central porque evidencia o caráter sistêmico do produto contratado. A lógica é semelhante à discutida pelo Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) na consulta pública 229/2026, que propõe o rateio do encargo entre os usuários finais a partir da demanda nos momentos de máxima carga do sistema. Em ambos os casos, segundo a associação, a necessidade de potência decorre do perfil de consumo e da operação do sistema como um todo, e não da atividade específica de um único segmento. Previsibilidade e segurança aos contratos Enquanto a solução legislativa não é concluída, a Absae entende que a regulamentação do encargo deve buscar uma base de pagantes sólida e suficiente, com critérios objetivos, previsibilidade de arrecadação e mecanismos capazes de assegurar a estabilidade financeira dos contratos de reserva de capacidade. A associação também considera importante que a metodologia preveja recursos adequados para lidar com eventuais inadimplementos pontuais, evitando que esse risco seja transferido aos empreendimentos contratados. Essas contribuições, contudo, não significam concordância da entidade com o tratamento diferenciado estabelecido pela legislação para o armazenamento em baterias. Na avaliação da entidade, o próprio debate conduzido pela Aneel reforça a necessidade de uma solução estrutural por meio da revogação do § 6º do art. 3º-A da Lei nº 10.848/2004, objeto do Projeto de Lei nº 3.716/2026. A mudança elimina a excepcionalidade criada para uma única solução tecnológica e, na visão da Absae, restabelece coerência entre o custeio da reserva de capacidade e a natureza sistêmica do produto contratado.

artigo.texto: As diferentes estratégias de Equinix e Elea para ampliar data centers no Brasil Equinix prioriza mercados com demanda e interconexão consolidadas; Elea aposta na descentralização e prevê 250 MW iniciais em projeto no Rio A expansão dos data centers no Brasil está sendo conduzida por estratégias distintas de localização dos investimentos. Enquanto a Equinix mantém a concentração de empresas, redes e usuários como critério central para ampliar sua infraestrutura, especialmente no eixo Rio–São Paulo, a Elea aposta na descentralização geográfica para atender mercados regionais e criar novos polos de processamento de dados. As diferenças foram discutidas nesta quinta-feira, 8, no painel “Operators Fireside Chat: Crescendo rápido demais? Os limites reais de expandir data centers no Brasil”, realizado no Data Center World (DCW), durante a Futurecom 2026, em São Paulo. Participaram Eduardo Shuto, diretor de Estratégia da Equinix para a América Latina, Fernanda Belchior, diretora nacional de Vendas e Marketing da Elea, e Flávio Lang, CEO do Tele.Síntese e da Emerging, responsável pela mediação. Lang abriu a discussão destacando que as duas operadoras seguem estratégias distintas. A Elea construiu sua presença nacional a partir da aquisição de instalações de telecomunicações e da expansão para mercados regionais. A Equinix concentra sua atuação em ecossistemas de interconexão digital, nos quais a proximidade entre empresas, provedores de nuvem e operadoras constitui parte do valor oferecido aos clientes. O moderador questionou se, diante dessa diferença, a estratégia da Equinix seria ampliar a disponibilidade de energia no eixo Rio–São Paulo, em vez de deslocar os data centers para regiões mais distantes dos principais centros consumidores. Equinix exige diversidade de clientes para expandir Shuto afirmou que existe espaço para as duas estratégias, mas ressaltou que a Equinix avalia a expansão a partir da existência de demanda sustentável no médio e longo prazo. O executivo explicou que um grande cliente pode justificar a construção de um data center em determinada região, mas sua presença isolada não significa que haverá um ecossistema de interconexão capaz de sustentar novos investimentos. “Um cliente de grande porte até viabiliza um projeto fora de São Paulo, mas a gente também não acha que só um cliente grande, por si só, cria um ecossistema”, afirmou. Segundo Shuto, a Equinix procura mercados com diversidade de clientes, empresas de redes e demanda por troca de dados. A localização próxima dos usuários e das empresas que produzem ou consomem informações também integra essa avaliação. O executivo citou o mercado norte-americano para argumentar que, apesar da existência de instalações destinadas a aplicações específicas em regiões afastadas, os grandes centros continuam concentrando parte relevante da infraestrutura digital. Na avaliação da Equinix, essa concentração permanecerá importante com o crescimento da inferência de inteligência artificial, etapa em que modelos já treinados são utilizados para processar informações e produzir resultados. Shuto explicou que os dados podem ser gerados, processados e consumidos em locais diferentes. Essa arquitetura aumenta a necessidade de interconexão entre data centers, redes e empresas. Ao ser questionado por Lang sobre investimentos fora do eixo Rio–São Paulo, o executivo respondeu que a companhia analisa outras regiões, mas considera que diferentes mercados cumprem funções distintas. “Ainda São Paulo e Rio têm a sua função”, afirmou. A Equinix possui mais de 250 data centers distribuídos por mais de 70 mercados metropolitanos no mundo. Shuto é responsável pela avaliação de investimentos orgânicos e aquisições da companhia na América Latina. Elea aposta na criação de mercados regionais Fernanda Belchior apresentou uma estratégia baseada na distribuição da infraestrutura digital pelo território brasileiro. Criada em 2019, a Elea opera nove data centers no país e possui cerca de 300 colaboradores, segundo a executiva. A plataforma atende empresas, organizações públicas, provedores de serviços digitais e clientes de grande porte, incluindo companhias de nuvem e inteligência artificial. Fernanda explicou que a estratégia começou com a aquisição de instalações que pertenciam a empresas de telecomunicações ou já concentravam infraestrutura de conectividade. A partir dessa base, a companhia investiu em backbone próprio e na ampliação da presença de operadoras dentro de seus data centers. “A infraestrutura começa pela rede”, afirmou. Segundo a executiva, essa estrutura permite atender provedores de internet, operadoras e clientes corporativos, além de receber cargas computacionais de empresas de nuvem e inteligência artificial. A Elea também mantém investimentos em mercados consolidados. Fernanda citou a aquisição de infraestrutura em São Bernardo do Campo, na Grande São Paulo, associada ao contrato de computação de alto desempenho da Petrobras. A descentralização, portanto, não representa uma saída dos grandes centros, mas a inclusão de outras regiões na estratégia de expansão. Belém terá primeira etapa de 7,5 MW Um dos exemplos apresentados por Fernanda foi o projeto anunciado pela Elea em Belém, no Pará. Segundo a executiva, a companhia considera a capital paraense uma localização complementar a Fortaleza, que já concentra infraestrutura de cabos submarinos e conectividade internacional. A Elea também identifica demanda de empresas e instituições públicas da região Norte por serviços de processamento e armazenamento de dados. Fernanda afirmou que o projeto poderá contribuir para reduzir a necessidade de manter determinadas cargas computacionais em instalações próprias ou em outras regiões do país. A primeira etapa foi apresentada com capacidade de aproximadamente 7,5 MW, em parceria com a Axia Energia, antiga Eletrobras. artigo.texto: Trending With the November midterm elections approaching, environmental and community advocates gathered at the Capitol Rotunda in Harrisburg Tuesday to protest the impacts of hyperscale artificial intelligence data centers and urge their fellow Pennsylvanians to become more civically engaged. The demonstration was organized by several advocacy groups, including the Better Path Coalition, a grassroots organization that advocates for clean, renewable energy and government policies that prioritize public health. Attendees were encouraged to sign constituent letters representing different subgroups. Organizers said the letters are intended to show lawmakers and other decision-makers opposition to the expansion of data centers while giving frustrated voters a way to engage with elected officials. Organizers said they hope that engagement will motivate voters to participate in the November elections, even if they are angry with the elected leaders on either side of the aisle. "What we're doing is launching the campaign today to encourage people to write constituent letters so that we can send them to not only the governor and our legislators, but anyone who is making decisions about data centers," said Karen Feridun, co-founder of the Better Path Coalition. "I know a lot of people are really angry because they're not seeing an alternative ... sometimes I worry that people might stay home on Election Day." The letters represented a range of concerns, including artists worried about how generative AI could affect their work, parents and guardians concerned about the effects of data centers and AI on children, health care professionals focused on potential impacts to physical and mental health and faith leaders seeking to protect God's creation and marginalized communities, according to Better Path. Though organizers said the event was not intended to rally behind a particular candidate, some attendees held signs that read "Senator Katie Muth: Write-In for Governor." Muth, a Democrat from Montgomery County, introduced Senate Bill 1349 in June. The legislation would impose a three-year moratorium on hyperscale data center development. Speakers criticized Democrat Gov. Josh Shapiro for initially "rubbing elbows" with Amazon Web Services (AWS) executives before calling for greater scrutiny of the data centers supporting AI development. AWS operates hundreds of data center facilities worldwide, though the company does not publish an official count. "Pennsylvania lawmakers, particularly Governor Shapiro, put communities across the state in a very difficult position when it came to hyperscale data center development," said Stuart Day, co-founder of Ohio Valley Allies. "The governor enthusiastically promoted the AI and data center boom, supported these companies, pushed fast track permitting and talked about Pennsylvania working at the speed of business, but while he was cheerleading for this industry, communities -- real communities like mine -- were burdened with figuring out the consequences in real time." Shapiro's administration has sought to regulate that infrastructure through its GRID standards, which set requirements for data centers related to energy, environmental protections and community engagement. A subsequent executive order signed in August requires developers to meet those standards as part of the state permitting process. Speakers at the rally raised concerns about the long-term environmental and health impacts of data centers and what their expansion could mean for future generations. "Communities across the state see the horrific consequences of these data centers on our health, including air pollution, which damages the heart and the lungs, and light pollution, which does not sleep and leads to chronic stress," said Parker Studebaker, director of the Phoenixville Liberation Center. The speakers urged lawmakers to prioritize the health and interests of Pennsylvania communities over the economic incentives driving data center development. "Our parents are not just numbers in the study. Our children are not just a profit margin. Our friends and neighbors are not just a check to be cashed," said Anneke van Rossum, advocacy and advancement coordinator at the Delaware Riverkeeper Network. "I'm tired, but more than anything, I'm angry. The people are angry, and we are not going to let them get away with it this time." Lawmakers advanced several bills last week related to data centers in both chambers ahead of the rally. The bills address issues including the facilities' energy and water use, environmental impacts and how their development is regulated, as lawmakers face increasing pressure to respond to communities concerned about the effects of these facilities.

artigo.texto: ”Agriculture and blue carbon are the next frontier; this means carbon financing will extend to farmers, fishers, and coastal communities—not just large corporations," Coordinating Minister for Food Affairs Zulkifli Hasan remarked at the Indonesia Sustainability Forum (ISF) 2026 in Jakarta, Tuesday. Hasan, who chairs the Carbon Economic Value (NEK) Steering Committee, explained that carbon economic mechanisms serve as an instrument to assign direct monetary value to environmental preservation while channeling financial benefits to grassroots community managers. Indonesia's annual carbon market potential is estimated to reach US$7.7 billion. The national carbon ecosystem is governed under Presidential Regulation No. 110 of 2025 on Carbon Economic Value, supported by six implementing regulations and the Carbon Unit Registry System (SRUK). The market framework incorporates carbon trading, carbon taxation, and result-based payments. To date, the government has issued registered carbon units for four forestry projects, representing an emission reduction capacity of approximately 30 million tons of CO2 equivalent. These four projects carry an estimated total transaction value of Rp5 trillion (approximately US$279.3 million) and have the potential to generate Rp500 billion (US$27.9 million) in non-tax state revenue. Hasan stressed that carbon market development must prioritize inclusivity, ensuring that localized agricultural and coastal conservation activities generate tangible economic improvements for rural populations. artigo.texto: Power Maryland Backs Two BESS Projects Amid PJM Capacity Push Industrial Info Resources is tracking nearly $3 billion worth of active and proposed BESS projects across Maryland, more than half of which is attributed to grassroot developments Released Thursday, October 08, 2026 Reports related to this article: Written by Will Ploch, Assistant Editor-in-Chief for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary As part of a broader effort to address rising capacity prices, Maryland recently awarded two battery-storage projects with generous capacity credits. Backing Up the PJM The Maryland Public Service Commission recently awarded two battery energy-storage system (BESS) projects under its Energy Storage Capacity Credit (ESCC) program, during the first round of the state's Next Generation Energy Act procurement. Both projects are designed to be connected to the broader power grid. Industrial Info Resources is tracking nearly $3 billion worth of active and proposed BESS projects across Maryland, more than half of which is attributed to grassroot developments. Under the ESCC, Maryland will provide long-term capacity payments--based on stable, flat pricing for a 15-year term--to energy-storage projects that would help to curb market price volatility in the PJM Interconnection. Electricity providers within the state are required to purchase these storage capacity credits at a monthly fixed price, which is proportionate to each provider's capacity obligations. The ESCC program is intended, in part, to address rising capacity prices on the PJM. The PJM Interconnection is the grid manager for an estimated 67 million people living in parts of 13 Mid-Atlantic and Midwestern states, including Pennsylvania, Ohio, Illinois and New Jersey, among others. The two projects selected are Hull Street Energy's Chalk Point Storage Project in Aquasco, which is about 25 miles southeast of Washington, D.C., and LS Power Group's Jade Meadow III Storage Project in Westernport, which sits in the northwestern corner of the state. According to Industrial Info Resources data, both projects currently are expected to begin construction in 2028. The Chalk Point BESS unit would be built next to the operational Chalk Point Power Station, which produces 1,744 megawatts (MW) of gas-fired electricity. The BESS unit would carry 400 MW via lithium-ion batteries and associated facilities. Industrial Info Resources offers more information on this project in its Global Market Intelligence (GMI) Power Plant and Project databases, where readers can find details--including construction schedules, investment values and necessary equipment--in a project report a profile of the Chalk Point Power Station. The Jade Meadow III BESS unit, which would carry 100 MW, is being developed as part of the Jade Meadow Solar III Plant, which is designed to generate 300 MW from photovoltaic (PV) panels provided by ZnShine PV-TECH Company Limited. Like the Chalk Point project, the BESS unit would use lithium-ion technology. Readers can learn more from a project report and plant profile. The Maryland Public Service Commission said these two ESCC awards will incur a total cost of 6.98 cents per month for the average Maryland residential customer. By the Numbers - Nearly $3 billion: Total investment value (TIV) of active and proposed BESS projects across Maryland - 15 years: How long Maryland will provide capacity payments based on stable, flat pricing for projects awarded under ESCC - 67 million: Estimated number of people living in the PJM area, which covers parts of 13 Mid-Atlantic and Midwestern states More Awards on the Horizon By law, the Maryland Public Service Commission must open bidding for the second round of awards under the ESCC program by January 1, 2027, and it must announce the results by October 1. Among the project developers it has invited to participate is Tenaska Incorporated, whose Oystercatcher Battery Storage Project in Maryland Line was not awarded in the first round. Maryland Line sits on the Pennsylvania border, about 35 miles north of Baltimore. The Oystercatcher project would be a stand-alone unit connected to the 500-kilovolt (kV) Conastone Substation, which is managed by Baltimore Gas & Electric Company. It would carry up to 500 MW for the power grid. Readers can learn more from a project report a profile of the Conastone Substation. Other Maryland BESS projects in the works include RWE Renewables Americas LLC's Fourth Quarter Battery Storage Project in Dickerson, which is about 30 miles northwest of Washington, D.C. The stand-alone project, which is proposed to be built at the now-closed coal-fired units at the Dickerson Power Plant, would carry 300 MW. Readers can learn more from a project report a profile of the Dickerson plant. The Industrial Info Resources GMI Project and Plant databases offer a full list of detailed reports for projects mentioned in this article, and a full list of related plant profiles. Industrial Info Resources also offers a full list of reports for active and proposed BESS projects across Maryland. Key Takeaways - Maryland awarded two BESS projects under the first round of its Energy Storage Capacity Credit program. - Both projects currently are expected to begin construction in 2028. - The Maryland Public Service Commission must open a second round of bidding for the ESCC program by January 1, 2027. artigo.texto: Brookwood City Council backs $3.2 billion Applied Digital data center project BROOKWOOD, Ala. (WBRC) - The Brookwood City Council voted Tuesday to support a resolution backing the Tuscaloosa County Economic Development Authority’s (TCEDA) agreement with Applied Digital for the company’s “Delta Forge 2” AI data center project. The TCEDA signed off on Applied Digital’s “Project Highlands” last month. The council’s decision comes after weeks of concerns from the community about environmental impacts and a lack of transparency surrounding the project. Applied Digital says the project would bring thousands of construction jobs, just over 100 full-time jobs, and hundreds of millions of dollars over time for schools and community projects. Brookwood Mayor Joe Barger believes the project is going to be a game changer for the city. “This has been a long time coming. It’s a project that our city has long been fighting for as a community leader. We are excited about what this economic impact comes to for our police, fire, education, infrastructure and a town as a whole,” Barger said. The Alabama Public Service Commission will vote on a power agreement between Applied Digital and Alabama Power. Barger said that vote could happen within weeks. artigo.texto: Oklahoma residents seek answers on data center costs, cooling and accountability TULSA, Okla. — As data center development draws attention across Oklahoma, residents interviewed by FOX23 said they want clear answers about electricity costs, water use and what it could mean to live near one. For Tulsa resident Barbara Coleman, the concern is whether new development could leave households paying costs they cannot afford. "I don't mind them being around," Coleman explained. "I am concerned that they might find a loophole and say 'okay well, sorry. You're going to have to pay for some of the electric we're using' and put a different fee on the bill." Coleman, who said she cares for her elderly grandparents, wants transparent, written commitments that residents can use to hold companies accountable. She said people already struggling with bills need reassurance about who will pay for a project's electricity and infrastructure. In Yukon, Charlie Scott said a proposed data center would be about 1,500 feet from his home. Scott said he retired from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service in 2012 after 38 years as a wildlife biologist. His career included 23 years in a Tulsa field office, as well as work in Washington D.C. and Columbia, Missouri. He said his work included assessing federally funded or permitted development projects and identifying ways to reduce their environmental impacts. His experience also included endangered species and environmental toxicology work. That background informs the questions he's asking about the development, although he described his data center research as something he pursued after the proposal near his home made the issue personal. Scott said neighbors began seeking his help because of his environmental science background. He has since become involved in community organizing and said residents in other Oklahoma communities have also asked him for information. "I have a problem putting it in close location to where people live because of just the traffic, the work, the construction, the noise, the light," Scott said. Those concerns are addressing the potential impacts of a proposed facility, rather than conditions he reported experiencing from an operating data center next to his home. Scott said his concern is not simply whether data centers should exist. According to Scott, he wants attention paid to where they are built, the technology they use and the information residents receive before decisions are made. He acknowledged that projects can bring substantial revenue to communities, but said secrecy and late communication can undermine public trust. He expressed concern about nondisclosure agreements and residents learning about projects after discussions between developers and local officials are already underway. Scott said he has seen increased attendance at local government meetings as residents seek answers about the development. He said he is helping collect signatures for a proposed change to Yukon's city charter that would require residents to vote on data center proposals. He said the effort is intended to give residents a greater role in decisions. "We're just saying the citizens should have a right to vote on something that's so significant," Scott explained. The petition seeks a change to the charter, but such a requirement is not established by the petition effort itself. Coleman said she also wants officials to examine the benefits and drawbacks of individual projects before making decisions about their location. "Do the research on it," said Coleman. "See what the pros and cons are." FOX23 spoke with Henry Cubillan of Kelvion, a manufacturer of data center cooling equipment at the Port of Catoosa. The company supplies the data center industry, giving it a specific business interest in its growth. Cubillan said Kelvion also provides thermal solutions for other industries including oil and gas, and power and transportation. Cubillan explained that cooling designs vary depending on a facility's location, outdoor temperatures, size, computing demand and available space. "There's a lot of factors that go in it: location, average ambient temperatures," Cubillan shared. "The space available is also a factor that we consider." He said the equipment used in a smaller, conventional data center can differ from the systems required for a larger facility designed for high-density artificial intelligence computing. Cubillan described a closed-loop system in which liquid absorbs heat, carries it outside to be cooled and then returns through the system. He said the system requires an initial fill of treated water, typically mixed with glycol to prevent freezing. The liquid is designed to remain in circulation for years, although maintenance or leaks may require replacement. "They're designed to go in there for a very long time—years." Cubillan said one misconception he encounters is the assumption that all data centers use the same amount of water or rely on the same cooling methods. He contrasted water-consuming evaporative cooling towers with systems that recirculate liquid. He said Kelvion has adapted cooling equipment used in oil and gas and power applications for data centers. In the closed-loop design he described, the initial fill can be significant, depending on the facility's size. The recirculating liquid is intended to remain inside the system rather than being continuously consumed. However, he said buildings do still need water for uses such as restrooms and landscaping. Cubillan compared modern facilities' water consumption with golf courses, saying a modern data center uses less. He did not provide site-specific figures for that comparison during the interview. Recirculating liquid in one part of a cooling system does not, by itself, establish the total water demand of an entire facility. The full design matters. artigo.texto: Geraldo Campos Jr., da Agência iNFRA O desembargador Rafael Paulo, do Tribunal Regional Federal da 1ª Região, determinou que a ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) conclua em 48 horas a análise de pedidos de medida cautelar relacionados ao acesso ao sistema elétrico de três data centers da Pahlavan. A empresa saiu vencedora da 1ª Temporada de Acesso de 2026, finalizada nesta semana, mas tenta desde já ter a garantia do aumento do montante de energia a ser usado da rede em 2029. A decisão, expedida na segunda-feira (6), ainda assegura que, até a deliberação da reguladora, não sejam adjudicadas propostas vencedoras na 1ª Temporada de Acesso de 2026 para conexão à rede na Subestação Replan, em São Paulo. Conforme a liminar, eventual capacidade remanescente do barramento na proporção dos montantes de uso de energia solicitados pela Pahlavan não poderá ser comprometida até a decisão da ANEEL. Segundo o desembargador, o restante do procedimento competitivo “prosseguirá regularmente quanto a todas as demais margens” e a determinação em questão não se trata de “reconhecimento de prioridade, reserva de capacidade ou autorização para contratação, energização ou incremento de carga”. Assim, os efeitos da liminar encerrarão após com deliberação da ANEEL, independentemente do resultado. A Pahlavan já tinha entrado com um primeiro pedido de cautelar na agência para ter a garantia do aumento do MUST (Montante de Uso do Sistema de Transmissão), que foi negado. Um recurso foi interposto na ANEEL em setembro, com novo pedido de cautelar, mas ainda não foi analisado pela reguladora. A empresa alega que seus três projetos de data centers são de grande porte, situados em Paulínia (SP), e que foram estruturados sob o regime anterior de acesso à transmissão, antes da Pnast (Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão). No entanto, após o novo modelo, o ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico) apontou a inviabilidade dos incrementos de acesso pretendidos pela empresa. Os projetos entrariam em operação de forma escalonada, com uso da energia do sistema indo de 71 MW (megawatts) para 157 MW por unidade em 2029. Os empreendimentos já tinham portaria do MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia), atos autorizativos da ANEEL e pareceres de acesso e CUSTs (Contrato de Uso do Sistema de Transmissão) assinados.

artigo.texto: BYD Da Han EV to launch October 13 with 0.197 Cd drag and 1,008 km range BYD will launch the Da Han EV on October 13, 2026. Ahead of the launch, Autohome reported a 0.197 Cd aerodynamic drag coefficient and official energy consumption of 11.5 kWh/100 km for the 1,008-km RWD version. The Da Han opened pre-sales in August at 249,900 to 299,900 yuan (35,300 to 42,400 USD). Customer deliveries are scheduled to begin within two weeks of launch. Aerodynamics and powertrain efficiency The Da Han measures 5,256 mm long, 1,999 mm wide and 1,510 mm tall, with a 3,130 mm wheelbase. Its 0.197 Cd drag coefficient is among the model’s key efficiency figures. All versions use a 102.3 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) second-generation Blade Battery. The EV is offered in three configurations: - 1008km RWD Premium: 370 kW (496 hp), 500 Nm, 0–100 km/h in 4.9 seconds, 11.5 kWh/100 km, and 1,008 km CLTC range (approx. 820 km WLTP). - 1008km RWD Flagship: It uses the same 370 kW RWD powertrain with additional rear-seat equipment, delivering 1,008 km CLTC range (approx. 820 km WLTP). - 880km AWD Flagship: Dual motors producing 570 kW (764 hp) and 910 Nm, 0–100 km/h in 3.3 seconds, 13.1 kWh/100 km, and 880 km CLTC range (approx. 715 km WLTP). The battery can charge from 10% to 97% in nine minutes at compatible high-output charging stations. Standard DiSus-A and ADAS coverage BYD confirmed that chassis and driver-assistance hardware will be standard across the range. Every Da Han has rear-wheel steering and a 4.95-meter turning radius, along with dual-chamber DiSus-A air suspension. Driver assistance uses BYD’s DiPilot system, marketed in China as the God’s Eye 5.0 driver-assistance system. The roof-mounted LiDAR-equipped system supports high-speed and Urban Navigation on Autopilot (Urban NOA), as well as automated valet parking. BYD also provides a one-year full damage coverage guarantee. Under the policy, BYD covers specified economic losses from qualifying legally liable accidents while Urban NOA is being used in compliance with applicable regulations. The coverage also applies to intelligent parking, subject to the stated conditions. The system remains classified as Level 2+ driver assistance. Cabin technology The cabin features a 17.3-inch floating 3K central display running the DiLink 300 interface with BYD’s in-car AI voice agent, named DiDiXia in the domestic market. Audio uses a 7.1.4-channel Devialet sound system with 31 speakers. Other equipment includes Nappa leather upholstery, front seats with zero-gravity positioning and an active fragrance system. Market positioning BYD positions the Da Han above the existing Han EV in the Dynasty sedan lineup. Domestic sales of BYD’s existing Han sedan lineup have weakened substantially through 2026. The standard Han averaged roughly 7,000 to 8,900 monthly deliveries in late 2025, but monthly volume fell to around 3,000 units during 2026. It delivered 2,997 units in August, down 61.4% year over year, reducing its share of BYD’s domestic sales to 1.6%, according to China EV DataTracker. The higher-spec Han L has declined more sharply. After reaching 2,934 units in December 2025, monthly deliveries fell throughout 2026 to 205 units in August, down 90.7% year over year and accounting for 0.1% of BYD’s domestic sales. BYD will announce final retail pricing and delivery details at the October 13 launch.

artigo.texto: Big Island Wants To Ban Big Data Centers, Once They Agree On What They Are Giant data centers have become the latest bogeyman for residents across the nation wary of industrial development. So far, none are based in Hawaiʻi. Hawaiʻi County is discussing a bill that would restrict large-scale data centers on the island. But the public, officials and state representatives can’t agree on how to define one — or whether they are even a threat. Under Big Island zoning rules, residents and businesses can only use their land in the ways outlined by the county’s code. If it’s not listed as a permitted use, then it’s not allowed. Currently, the code allows for data processing centers in an area with a mouthful of modifiers: industrial-commercial-mixed-use-zoned. Translated, that means if a data center developer wants to build in an industrial area, they would just need to apply. There aren’t any so-called “hyperscale” data centers in Hawaiʻi yet. Zoning codes for Maui, Kauaʻi and Honolulu counties also have a not-listed-not-allowed rule for land use. Some of their codes currently permit data storage and processing facilities. But no other county has put forward regulations and the state is only just beginning to study the issue. Bill 170, introduced by Councilwoman Heather Kimball, seeks to make sure data centers like the ones ruffling feathers across the continent are not permitted anywhere on the Big Island. If it passes, construction of large data centers would be banned with one caveat: they can apply for a special use permit. The bill was heard for a second time by the Windward Planning Commission on Thursday. The Leeward Planning Commission will take up the issue on Oct. 15. So far, however, the biggest hurdle is figuring out how to define what would qualify as a data center under the proposed new rules. “If we get a really good definition, I think that could solve a lot of things,” said Louis Daniele, chair of the Windward Commission. “We keep calling things data centers, data processing facilities – That’s kind of confusing for the layperson.” ‘We Don’t Want It’ Powerful technology corporations are rapidly putting up data centers across the country to power the artificial intelligence boom. The rush has sparked significant backlash from communities over concerns about the impact on the environment, the power grid and their neighborhoods. Hundreds of counties from California to Maine have already introduced regulations or instituted moratoriums on data center construction. The centers, which can cover thousands of acres and consume entire city blocks, are the latest target for those wary about new industrial development, such as Amazon megawarehouses and microwave cellphone towers. “I wanted to make sure we got ahead of the issue,” Kimball said. “I think it’s better to do it now,” she added, before developers start knocking on the door. Her primary concern is the effect a data center could have on the island’s already strained grid and aquifers. The massive centers being built across the country require equally massive amounts of energy and water. A typical hyperscale data center can use up to 100 megawatts of electricity annually, for instance. That could power 100,000 households, according to The International Energy Agency. The increased demand on the grid and the added infrastructure required to support it are raising utilities’ costs to produce electricity elsewhere, and those costs are being passed on to residents. In Maryland, customers pay $168 to $216 more per year on their electricity bills primarily due to the data center boom, according to estimates. Across Hawaiʻi and the country, residents are not only concerned about higher bills. They’re also worried that the energy demand increases the use of fossil fuels and thus pollution, which drives climate change and threatens health. Christina Holt, a Hilo resident who recently ran unsuccessfully for state representative, is leading the local charge against the centers. She’s hosted community Zoom meetings and posts regularly on social media to inform residents and urge them to speak out. Dozens of Big Island residents have shown up at planning commissions meetings. In hours and pages of testimony, residents have made clear that they support an outright ban. “We don’t want it,” Holt said, “and we, as a community, have every right to say no.” Defining ‘Data Center’ No Easy Feat For Bill 170 to be effective, advocates say, it needs to clearly define data centers and distinguish them from a data processing center. Data processing center use was added to the county code in 1996 when the council undertook numerous amendments to the zoning rules. The addition reflected emerging technologies and business activities at the time. It generally referred to office-oriented businesses that used computers to process information, maintain electronic records, or provide administrative and technical services. These types of centers don’t require much electricity and are vital to business and research operations. Today, the state has more than 20 data processing centers, two of them on the Big Island. A Hawaiian Telecom facility in Kawaihae is one of them. Jeannine Souki, manager of government and regulatory affairs for Hawaiian Telecom, testified in front of the Windward Commission, one of two planning commissions on the island, in September. Advocates have two related worries. A definition that’s too broad could exclude necessary infrastructure. Being too specific could create loopholes developers can exploit. Souki urged commissioners to consider whether the way Bill 170 defines data centers could unintentionally ban these essential telecommunication facilities Lawsuits by developers against towns elsewhere in the country that have attempted to prevent construction are adding further pressure to get the definition right. “They’re going to lie, cheat and steal to get what they want,” Chuck Flaherty, secretary of the Hawaiʻi island Sierra Club, said

artigo.texto: Oracle is using a novel power strategy to keep several data centers on track: trucking natural gas directly to the server farms. The truck deliveries kept a data center on the outskirts of Salt Lake City moving forward for more than a year as Oracle waited for a gas pipeline to be built and integrated with its machinery, according to people familiar with the work. The company also is using this approach to get initial work done at one of its campuses being built for OpenAI in Shackelford County, Texas, one of the people said. Now, Oracle is considering using the same strategy in New Mexico, where a gas pipeline to help power one of its most crucial data centers is delayed and threatening the project’s timeline, according to people familiar with the project. A plan to use trucks to deliver compressed natural gas to the data center, called Project Jupiter, would let the company get the early stages of it online before the pipeline enters service, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the strategy hasn’t been made public. The stakes are high. Last month, Oracle sent a notice citing force majeure to the New Mexico project’s developer, which may shield the company from making some payments in case of further delays. Oracle didn’t respond to a request for comment. The shares dropped 5.5% to $135.69 at the close in New York, the worst single-day decline since July 16. Power has emerged as a major bottleneck to the AI data center boom. Many of the significant server farm developments are using on-site power plants that burn natural gas to provide electricity. The gas would typically be delivered by a pipeline, which can take months to design and build. Pipelines can also be delayed by regulatory action. In New Mexico, pipeline operator Energy Transfer LP had to reroute the project that will ultimately power Oracle’s data center after a proposed route was rejected by state regulators. That pushed the pipeline firm’s targeted in-service date to next year, rather than this summer. Given the challenges to quickly ensure a supply of gas, a cluster of companies that specialize in compressing gas and transporting it via truck have seized on the frenzy by data center developers to start generating computing power as quickly as possible. These firms, including Superior Plus Corp.’s Certarus and VoltaGrid LLC, are pitching their so-called virtual pipeline services as a transitional power solution while waiting for a pipeline to come online. Delivering compressed natural gas via truck is not easy nor cheap. When including the cost of labor, specialized equipment and fuel to move the trucks themselves, the delivered cost is roughly four times the price of gas sent through a major pipeline hub, according to Jack Weixel, senior director of energy analysis at East Daley Analytics. Gas must be taken from a pipeline, compressed into a trailer, driven sometimes multiple hours to a site, and then decompressed to fill generators. Even a relatively small AI data center requires trucks making deliveries constantly throughout the day. This cost and complexity is part of the reason why compressed gas has mostly been relegated to specialized industrial operations, such as mining or oil drilling, that take place in remote areas far from interconnection points with the electric grid. Still, it may be the best stopgap for a company like Oracle, which has put billions of dollars and its reputation on quickly delivering data centers for customers including OpenAI. Oracle’s free cash flow is currently negative and expected to remain that way until more of its AI data centers are completed. At the Utah project, Oracle’s gas deliveries were powered by Certarus. In Texas, they are provided by VoltaGrid. “Shoutout to the VoltaGrid team for finding cost-effective power solutions to ensure our customers can access OCI capacity on schedule,” Oracle wrote on social media shortly after receiving a request for comment on this story, referring to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. VoltaGrid, similarly to Oracle, didn’t respond to a request for comment, but posted on social media about the partnership. Certarus declined to comment on specific deals, but said the extended timelines for data centers to secure connections with pipelines and the grid “have created a growing need for rapidly deployable and scalable energy solutions.” The big question is how far this solution can expand. Given Project Jupiter’s size, even powering a small fraction of its full capacity would require dozens of truck deliveries a day. If Oracle powered just 100 megawatts — about 4% of its ultimate 2.45-gigawatt footprint — with CNG deliveries, each large trailer would only provide about 40 minutes of electricity, said Ellie Holbrook, an energy analyst at SemiAnalysis. artigo.texto: Novo regime tributário busca impulsionar data centers, infraestrutura energética e inteligência artificial no Brasil O REDATA cria incentivos tributários para infraestrutura digital, vinculados a energia limpa, sustentabilidade e investimentos em pesquisa e inovação. quarta-feira, 7 de outubro de 2026 Atualizado em 6 de outubro de 2026 15:01 A lei 15.504/26 instituiu o REDATA - Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter, criando um conjunto de incentivos voltados à instalação e à expansão da infraestrutura de processamento de dados no Brasil. A medida insere-se em um cenário de crescimento da demanda por computação em nuvem, processamento de alto desempenho e, especialmente, pela infraestrutura necessária ao treinamento e à inferência de modelos de inteligência artificial. O novo regime permite a suspensão de PIS/Pasep, Cofins, PIS/Cofins-Importação, IPI e Imposto de Importação incidentes sobre determinados componentes eletrônicos e produtos de tecnologia da informação e comunicação destinados ao ativo imobilizado das empresas habilitadas. No caso do Imposto de Importação, o benefício fica restrito aos bens sem produção nacional equivalente e relacionados em ato do Poder Executivo. Cumpridas as condições previstas na legislação, as suspensões poderão ser convertidas em alíquota zero. A criação do REDATA procura enfrentar um dos principais componentes econômicos dos projetos de data centers: o elevado volume de investimentos necessário à implantação e expansão da capacidade computacional. A redução do custo tributário associado à aquisição e importação de equipamentos pode contribuir para aumentar a competitividade do País na atração de novos projetos e para ampliar a infraestrutura digital disponível no mercado brasileiro. O regime, entretanto, estabelece contrapartidas relevantes. Entre elas estão a disponibilização de, no mínimo, 10% da capacidade instalada com os benefícios para o mercado interno; o atendimento a critérios de sustentabilidade; a observância de Índice de Eficiência Hídrica (WUE) igual ou inferior a 0,05 L/kWh; e a realização de investimentos em pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação correspondentes a 2% do valor dos produtos adquiridos ou importados com o incentivo. Energia passa a integrar a estratégia tributária dos projetos Um dos aspectos mais relevantes do REDATA está na relação direta entre o benefício tributário e a matriz energética utilizada pelos empreendimentos. Para usufruir do regime, a empresa deverá atender à totalidade de sua demanda de energia elétrica por meio de contratos de suprimento ou de autoprodução provenientes de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão, nos termos que ainda serão definidos em regulamento. A exigência aproxima definitivamente três agendas que, até recentemente, eram analisadas de forma relativamente independente: tributação, infraestrutura energética e economia digital. Data centers possuem elevada demanda de energia elétrica e exigem segurança e continuidade no fornecimento. Consequentemente, decisões relacionadas à localização de novos empreendimentos deverão considerar não apenas incentivos tributários e disponibilidade de conectividade, mas também acesso à energia, capacidade da infraestrutura de transmissão, estruturação dos contratos de suprimento ou autoprodução e atendimento aos critérios ambientais estabelecidos para manutenção dos benefícios. Nesse contexto, a análise de viabilidade de novos projetos tende a exigir uma abordagem integrada entre planejamento tributário, estruturação energética, infraestrutura e regulação. Inteligência artificial amplia a relevância dos data centers A própria lei 15.504/26 inclui expressamente no conceito de serviços de data center as atividades de computação em nuvem, processamento de alto desempenho e treinamento e inferência de modelos de inteligência artificial, demonstrando assim que o REDATA ultrapassa uma política tributária destinada exclusivamente ao setor tradicional de armazenamento de dados. O regime está diretamente relacionado à expansão da infraestrutura computacional necessária ao desenvolvimento da economia digital e da inteligência artificial no País. O crescimento da IA vem ampliando significativamente a necessidade de capacidade de processamento, armazenamento e energia. Nesse ambiente, a disponibilidade de infraestrutura passa a representar elemento estratégico para empresas de tecnologia, provedores de serviços em nuvem, operadores de data centers e demais agentes envolvidos na cadeia digital. A legislação também procura estimular o desenvolvimento da cadeia tecnológica nacional ao exigir investimentos em pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação, além de prever tratamento diferenciado para empreendimentos localizados nas regiões Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste, onde determinados compromissos previstos no regime são reduzidos em 20%. Implementação ainda exige regulamentação Embora o REDATA já tenha sido instituído, parte relevante de sua operacionalização ainda depende de regulamentação do Poder Executivo, principalmente quanto a definição dos critérios para caracterização das fontes de energia de baixa emissão, a relação dos equipamentos elegíveis aos benefícios, os procedimentos relativos à inexistência de produção nacional equivalente e as regras para comprovação das contrapartidas assumidas pelas empresas. A habilitação e a coabilitação ao regime serão realizadas pela Receita Federal, observadas as condições estabelecidas na legislação e na regulamentação subsequente. Tudo isso só é possível porque a LC 237/26, publicada na mesma data, que incluiu o REDATA entre as exceções às limitações aplicáveis à concessão de benefícios tributários no exercício de 2026, desde que observadas a compatibilidade com a meta de resultado primário e a previsão na lei orçamentária anual. artigo.texto: Researchers in South Korea and Saudi Arabia have engineered a new electrode material that could push a class of hybrid energy storage devices known as supercapatteries closer to the sweet spot between batteries and supercapacitors. In a study published in the journal Ionics, Sohail Mumtaz of Gachon University and Hasan B. Albargi of Najran University describe an oxygenated carbon nanotube-interlinked heterostructure combining chromium oxide and magnesium cobaltate, a three-component composite that delivers unusually high charge capacity, fast electrochemical kinetics, and remarkable durability over tens of thousands of charging cycles. Supercapatteries occupy a deliberately hybrid position in the energy storage landscape. Supercapacitors charge in seconds and survive millions of cycles, but they store relatively little energy per kilogram. Batteries store far more energy but charge slowly and degrade faster. A supercapattery blends the two: one electrode behaves like a battery electrode, storing charge through faradaic reactions in which electrons cross the interface during chemical transformations, while the other behaves like a capacitor electrode, storing charge electrostatically at the surface. The challenge has always been finding positive electrode materials that can deliver battery-like capacity without sacrificing the rapid, reversible kinetics that make the capacitor side so attractive. The new material, designated Cr₂O₃/MgCo₂O₄@OCNT, is built from three ingredients chosen for complementary roles. Chromium(III) oxide, Cr₂O₃, contributes structural stability, holding its framework together through repeated charge and discharge. Magnesium cobalt oxide, MgCo₂O₄, a spinel-structured mixed metal oxide, supplies the high faradaic activity, with cobalt centers participating in redox reactions that pack large amounts of charge into small masses of material. The third ingredient, oxygenated carbon nanotubes, forms a conductive network that threads through the oxide phases, providing highways for electrons and oxygen-containing functional groups that improve wettability and add extra pseudocapacitive charge storage sites of their own. Structural and surface analysis confirmed the successful synthesis of the heterostructure. Two numbers from the characterization stand out. The composite exhibited a specific surface area of 87.69 square meters per gram, a figure that indicates abundant electrolyte accessibility, meaning ions from the electrolyte can reach a large fraction of the electrochemically active material rather than being blocked by dense, poorly connected agglomerates. Equally important, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy revealed a charge-transfer resistance of just 31 ohms, an exceptionally low value showing that electrons move across the electrode-electrolyte interface with minimal resistance, which translates directly into faster charging and better power delivery. When tested in a three-electrode configuration with a 1 M potassium hydroxide electrolyte, the Cr₂O₃/MgCo₂O₄@OCNT electrode posted specific capacities of 1963 coulombs per gram at a scan rate of 10 millivolts per second and 2214 coulombs per gram at a current density of 2 amperes per gram. These are impressive figures for a positive electrode material. Coulombs per gram is a measure of total charge stored per unit mass, and values above 2000 C g⁻¹ indicate that the material combines the high capacity typical of battery-type oxides with the ability to release that charge quickly, a combination few single materials can achieve. The real test, however, comes when the electrode is paired with a counter-electrode in a full device. The researchers assembled a hybrid supercapattery using their composite as the positive electrode and activated carbon as the negative electrode, a configuration written Cr₂O₃/MgCo₂O₄@OCNT//AC. The device operated across a voltage window of 0 to 1.4 volts, delivering specific capacities of 370 C g⁻¹ at 10 mV s⁻¹ and 423 C g⁻¹ at 2 A g⁻¹. From these values, the team calculated a maximum energy density of 96.2 watt-hours per kilogram and a maximum power density of 2494 watts per kilogram. For context, conventional supercapacitors typically manage energy densities in the range of 5 to 10 Wh kg⁻¹, so a device approaching 100 Wh kg⁻¹ while retaining supercapacitor-grade power represents a substantial advance. Durability is where many high-capacity electrode materials stumble, since the mechanical stress of repeated ion insertion and removal tends to crack and pulverize oxide structures over time. The new device retained 90.31 percent of its initial capacity after 10,000 charge-discharge cycles, with a Coulombic efficiency of 94.58 percent, meaning nearly every electron pumped into the device during charging came back out during discharge. That combination of high capacity and long cycle life suggests the Cr₂O₃ scaffold and the carbon nanotube network are doing their structural jobs, buffering volume changes and maintaining electrical contact even as the active spinel phase cycles through its redox reactions. Perhaps the most scientifically interesting part of the study is the kinetic dissection of how the device actually stores charge. Using b-value analysis and Dunn’s method, a standard technique that separates surface-controlled capacitive contributions from diffusion-controlled faradaic contributions by examining how current scales with scan rate, the researchers showed that the charge storage mechanism is genuinely hybrid. At higher scan rates, the surface-controlled capacitive process dominates, allowing the device to charge and discharge rapidly. At lower scan rates, the faradaic diffusion-controlled process takes over, letting ions penetrate deeper into the oxide and extract the full battery-like capacity. This rate-dependent shift between mechanisms is precisely the behavior a supercapattery is designed to exploit, and having it confirmed quantitatively validates the design philosophy beh

artigo.texto: DeLAND, Fla. — The Volusia County Council is moving forward with a ban on data centers after the first reading of the proposed ordinance. Residents in favor and against them spoke out at the podium, but it wasn't easy to change commissioners' minds. As they reviewed an ordinance written by staff, county commissioners listed concerns discussed two months ago during a meeting in August — like possible sinkholes, public safety and environmental impacts, like water usage. The ordinance said the county will not review or approve any applications, permits, amendments or construction about them. “I, for one, am pleased with what we have in front of us, and unless someone can change my mind, I’ll be voting in favor of it,” District 4 Volusia County Council Member Troy Kent said. The 26-page ordinance references Florida Senate Bill 484, which went into effect in July. The bill allows local governments to regulate large-scale data centers through land development regulations. The proposed ordinance also references studies that say data centers consume large amounts of water, affect the environment and pose health risks for residents. “And if we vote for this ban, it’s not a statement that any of us up here are against data centers," Volusia County Chair Jeff Brower said. "We use them every day. It just means not here.” Council members voted unanimously to move the proposal forward. It is expected to be discussed by the Planning and Land Development Regulation Commission on Oct. 15. Then it’s up for the second and final hearing on Oct. 20. If approved, the ordinance would take effect once filed with the Florida Department of State.
