artigo.texto: THE PHILIPPINES and South Korea are negotiating two cooperation agreements involving joint work on carbon market mechanisms, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources said. Environment Secretary Juan Miguel T. Cuna said the two governments are expediting talks on a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on environmental cooperation and another on climate change cooperation, both of which meet the requirements of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. They hope to conclude talks before a bilateral summit in November, to be held during the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila. According to Mr. Cuna, the MoUs will also cover greenhouse gas emissions reduction, water resource management, and ecosystem-based disaster risk reduction. Article 6 of the Paris Agreement sets out how countries can cooperate through carbon markets, including the cross-border transfer of emissions reductions. Mr. Cuna met with South Korean Deputy Minister for Climate Change Jongho Kyun on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly High-Level Week and Climate Week NYC 2026 in New York. “As we move toward COP31, we see the priority increasingly shifting from commitments to implementation and delivery, translating climate goals into policies, investments, technologies, and measurable outcomes,” Mr. Cuna said. Mr. Cuna also thanked South Korea for its official development assistance through the Korea International Cooperation Agency, for its support for marine plastics reduction, emergency aid during the Mindoro oil spill, and the recent transfer of the marine clean-up vessel MV Nilad for use in Manila Bay. The two officials also discussed the need for a clear pathway for vulnerable countries to access the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, following the floods in Nepal. Mr. Cuna said access arrangements are particularly important for the Philippines, which continues to face significant climate-related hazards. Mr. Cuna said partnership with South Korea will remain important for regional sustainability. — Moureen Ylessandra B. Dizon

artigo.texto: ‘It’s a nuisance’: Harlem neighbor raises concerns over data center noise HARLEM, Ga. (WRDW/WAGT) - Construction at Google’s Pumpkin Center data center in Harlem is running around the clock, according to a neighbor, raising questions about whether the project is following county rules on construction hours. Gregory Guido, who lives near the more than 3,000-acre site, said he moved to the area for peace and quiet, only for the noise to begin almost as soon as work started. “I moved out here to the country, where it was going to be nice and quiet, a nice place to settle down and raise families,” Guido said. A county ordinance allows construction sites to operate only between 6 a.m. and 11 p.m. Developers can apply to the Inspection and Permit Department for a permit to work beyond those hours. Guido said the noise continues well outside those hours and questioned why it isn’t regulated more closely, given the impact on families with children and people who work. Augusta leaders set hearing on major rewrite of zoning ordinance Augusta residents will get a chance to weigh in on a rewrite of the city’s zoning rules later this month. “If there’s kids that have to go to sleep and they have to wake up early to go to school or if somebody’s working and they got to get up and they got to go to work, they should not have to hear this,” Guido said. “Twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week, where’s the protection?” A county spokesperson said they were not able to confirm by the end of the day Wednesday whether the Pumpkin Center site has applied for or received a permit to work beyond normal construction hours. Guido said he expects the noise to continue for some time as the project moves forward. “It’s a nuisance,” Guido said. “This is just the start, this is just the beginning, right, we haven’t even had any data centers go up yet.” He hopes for a change, as the construction scene near the Harlem exit seems to grow with each passing night. “This is all night and it does not stop,” Guido said. “Now that the weather’s cooled off, right, October, everybody’s outside, we got trick or treating coming up. When all the kids are outside trick or treating, this is what they are going to hear.” There is no further information available on the project’s permit status at this time. Copyright 2026 WRDW/WAGT. artigo.texto: City council meeting erupts into chaos after planned data center vote postponed See more of our coverage in your search results. Chaos erupted at the end of a Tennessee city council hearing when officials postponed a vote on Elon Musk’s data centers, sparking a fistfight and protesters taking over the meeting hall. A mob of enraged protesters harassed members of the Memphis City Council Tuesday night after they had just voted to delay the vote on a moratorium of data centers in the city. Councilors voted 7 to 5 Tuesday night to table the remaining items on the agenda for a later date before the meeting devolved into a loud disarray of shouting between council members and the residents. One protester broke out a bullhorn and began to lead a chant of “ain’t no power like the power of the people.” Council Chairwoman Jana Swearengen Washington had called for a recess to the meeting and ordered police officers to clear out the hall, according to a livestream. The frenzied mob worked its way to the dais and began shouting at the city councilors who were huddled around. The protesters accused the elected officials of being “sellouts,” according to video from KWAM News Radio. Officers had successfully removed the protesters from the meeting hall as the mob continued to shout “this is our city” and “show me what democracy looks like.” At least two women engaged in a fight near the exits during the chaotic meeting, but no arrests were made, WREG reported. Roughly 100 protesters had attended the meeting for the scheduled final vote on the data centers that sit south of the city on the Memphis, Tenn.-Southaven, Miss. border. Two large data center facilities, named Colossus and Colossus 2, are run by Musk’s artificial intelligence company SpaceXAI. The original Colossus facility was built to serve X’s Grok AI bot but was later part of an agreement in May that will see Anthropic use the full computing power of the facility The delayed motion was rescheduled to October 20, Action News 5 reported. If passed, a 12-month moratorium would be enacted on data centers to allow for a study on the impact the facilities have on the city’s health, engineering, power and water infrastructure. City council infighting occurred amid the chaos as one councilor accused another of confusing people. “That’s all he does; he brings up mess, he… that’s all you do, JB Smiley, confuse the people over, over, over and over! Anytime there is an election,” Councilwoman Yolanda Cooper-Sutton, according to Action News 5. Councilman Smiley, who voted against delaying the vote, called for a civilized discussion on the subject instead of the shouting and fighting. “When the community shows up, we just have to listen to them. I’m disappointed that we didn’t listen with ears, okay, I hear you, I understand. Let’s figure out how we can do what you want, but also what we believe would be in the best interest of the community,” said Smiley, who was the lead sponsor on the moratorium proposal. Councilman Jeff Warren, an opponent of any moratorium, warned that the year-long pause would give incentive to companies to not do business with the city and find another area to build the complexes. “If we pass a moratorium, there’s not reason for them to think they need to come here. They get the same benefit from going to Desoto County, Crittenden County, Fayette County, Tipton County,” said Councilman Jeff Warren Tuesday.

artigo.texto: Trending WHEELING - Business and economic experts told members of the Ohio Valley’s business community that data centers would be beneficial to the economic future of the community. Data centers, a hot topic in the region, was discussed at length Tuesday morning at the annual Economic Outlook Conference sponsored by the Wheeling Area Chamber of Commerce. The conference was held at the Wheeling Island Hotel-Casino-Racetrack. David H. McKinley, president and chief investment officer at McKinley-Carter Wealth Services, supported construction of data centers locally, pointing out the financial success in Loudoun County, Virginia. There are 234 data centers located in the county, and the collective property tax on them comes in at $1.8 billion, according to McKinley. This accounts for 38-40% for the county's tax base. "Technology investments are huge. We take them all for granted," he said. "The ramp up is significant and not to be overlooked. "I'm disappointed there is so much negativity about data centers." Former Delegate Erikka Storch, R-Ohio, now external affairs manager for American Electric Power, and James Bailey, a member attorney at Spilman, Thomas and Battle, participated in a panel discussion pertaining to the energy industry in the state that was led by John Deskins, assistant dean at the WVU John Chambers College of Business and Economics. both Storch and Bailey indicated support for data centers. "From our perspective, data centers operating in our area would help our customers," Storch said. "It would give us a larger population in which to spread our costs, and we would welcome them. "It would send the message that it would diversify the economy when there are opportunities, and it would increase tax revenue." The money has been "very transformational” for counties that already have data centers or are building them, such as in Putnam County, she added. Google is developing a multi-billion-dollar hyperscale data center campus in Buffalo, West Virginia. "There are incredible opportunities, but unfortunately there are tons of misinformation out there," said Bailey, whose law firm represents those wanting to build a data center in Ohio County. "The water use isn't nearly what you hear. These things are self-contained now." Newer technology allows the water at the plant to be recycled and it uses about the same amount of water as any industrial facility, he explained. "You never hear from people who are for something. You only hear from people who are against it," Bailey said. Deskins provided a statewide economic outlook, and said that West Virginia needs more working-age adults in the workforce and a more diversified business climate if it is to grow economically. Deskins predicts there will be economic growth in West Virginia in the coming years, though it will happen at a slower rate than is typical. "We still have uncertainty ... over tariff policy, the war in Iran," he said. "Certainly, we have uncertainty around interest rates, but that uncertainty has diminished and that's a good thing. "Here in West Virginia, we think the state is going to remain stable over the next five years. There will be growth in some regions, but stability overall statewide." West Virginia has many successes, but they are "too concentrated geographically," Deskins noted. These are occurring in Jefferson and Berkeley counties in the Eastern Panhandle, and in Putnam County near Charleston and Kanawha County. "We have a lot of regions that are stagnant, and we need to find ways to have growth in those regions that are healthy to broaden out geographically," he continued. Despite the fact that West Virginia has low unemployment rates and people are working, the state continues to rank last in the number of adults actively participating in the workforce. The national workforce participation rate is 64%, while West Virginia continues to lag at 54.5%. "It is the biggest economic challenge we face," Deskins said. "There is no way West Virginia can achieve the prosperity we hope for until we get more people in the workforce. It is virtually a mathematical impossibility to imagine that West Virginia would have some form of economic prosperity on par with the nation... and have mathematically the smallest share of adults in the workforce. "It should be our biggest economic development challenge, and it should be our biggest priority. But fixing this is very hard." Among West Virginia counties, Wetzel County has the lowest workforce participation rate at 47.9%, according to U.S. Census statistics. This reflects a measurement of people between the ages of 16 and 64 who are not in school. Sharon Campbell, executive director of the Wetzel-Tyler Chamber of Commerce, suggested workforce participation in the region is lower because of a lack of any childcare facilities there and a lack of public transportation. These factors particularly affect women in the workforce, she added. The area also has been hit hard with drug addiction issues, Campbell noted. Deskins noted the years West Virginia has outperformed the nation in gross domestic product growth were when oil and gas industries performed strongly. The healthcare industry, led by WVU Medicine, also has been growing in the state, he added, as has the information industry. More diversification among businesses located in the state would lead to more economic growth, Deskins said. He also suggested the state should make more effort to retain and attract people to increase population. West Virginia Treasurer Larry Pack spoke about "how inefficient state government is," and how when a bad decision is made, "government keeps going on." "West Virginia is at a crossroads, and this demand is being brought to us by the demand for electricity nationwide," he explained. "Most of it is needed by AI (artificial intelligence and data centers). "America cannot produce that electricity for West Virginia. They have to have us." artigo.texto: ContactExisting Customer SupportLogin Key takeaways: The companies announced on Monday September 28 that they will establish three joint ventures covering lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cell production in Spain and Slovakia, alongside cathode active material (CAM) production in Morocco. The agreement also includes joint procurement and sales activities in Europe. The largest component of the agreement centres on PowerCo’s battery plant in Valencia, Spain, which will be transferred into a joint venture in which PowerCo will retain a 51% stake while Gotion holds 49%. The companies said the site is intended to become a European production hub for LFP-based battery cells. Under the agreement, Gotion’s battery factory in Šurany, Slovakia will also be transferred into a joint venture, with Gotion retaining a 51% controlling stake and PowerCo holding the remaining 49%. The facility is expected to focus on LFP battery cells for electric vehicles and energy-storage applications. In 2023, Gotion had announced a joint venture to build a gigafactory in Šurany with Slovak company InoBat. Volkswagen has now been folded into these plans via PowerCo, as a means of developing its continental cell production capacity. The companies also plan to establish a joint venture in Kenitra, Morocco, to produce cathode active materials for LFP batteries, which they said would help diversify supply sources and expand a regional battery value chain. Financially, PowerCo is expected to contribute around €470 million total toward the Slovakian and Moroccan projects by 2030, while Gotion is expected to invest approximately €1.1 billion to acquire its stake in the Valencia facility. Separately, Volkswagen announced plans to sell a 5.3% equity stake in Gotion while remaining a strategic investor in the company. The announcement follows Volkswagen and Gotion’s strategic partnership beginning in 2020, when Gotion began supplying cells to Volkswagen Group, as well as contributing as a strategic partner for PowerCo. Interested in prices, news and analysis for the commodities used in EV and ESS batteries? Discover Fastmarkets’ battery raw materials suite. At Fastmarkets’ recent Battery Raw Material Conference in Budapest, market participants referred to an increasingly common development strategy known as “near-shoring”: European stakeholders utilizing Morocco’s phosphate resources and lower operating costs. “The near-shoring of LFP CAM manufacturing to Morocco via this partnership is a welcome change from the status quo of sourcing LFP CAM from China, and will likely help Volkswagen to comply with future EU regulations surrounding local sourcing requirements,” Fastmarkets battery demand analyst Connor Watts said. In July, the African Development Bank (AfDB) approved a €100 million loan for Gotion’s Moroccan subsidiary to support the development of the integrated LFP battery project in the Rabat-Sale-Kenitra region. At the aforementioned conference, panelists on the future of the European battery midstream supply chain were wary of the European battery supply chain facing similar outcomes to failed projects such as Morrow Batteries and Northvolt. One suggestion from panelists was to move a step beyond the framework of being supplied by Chinese expertise and instead, develop joint ventures with shared ownership structures. These partnerships are beginning to be announced, with Stellantis’ joint venture with CATL to produce LFP batteries in Spain an example of joint ventures with overseas expertise facilitating the European supply chain’s pivot to lower-cost chemistries. “Volkswagen and Gotion expanding their strategic partnership by converting their respective facilities into joint ventures is emblematic of Europe’s deepening reliance on Chinese battery technology companies. While from a strategic perspective relying on Chinese partners for technology likely isn’t the first preference of legislators in Brussels, the shift away from whole Chinese ownership seen in Chinese Eastern European battery facilities towards equal joint ventures is a step in the right direction towards a more co-dependent industrial relationship,” Watts added. The announcement reflects growing appetite for a complete LFP battery supply chain within Europe. Volkswagen said LFP’s share of the European battery market could increase from around 10% currently to between 40% and 60% by 2030, while noting that Europe currently lacks significant LFP production capacity. The companies said the partnership is intended to expand regional battery production and strengthen supply security for the sector. LFP remains the dominant battery chemistry for the fast-growing battery energy storage system (BESS) market, due to its lower cost and longer operating life. In July, Italian energy major Eni entered the battery manufacturing sector with the construction of an LFP battery hub in southern Italy, targeting a production capacity of 16 GWh by 2030. Announced in 2025, German LFP CAM producer IBU-tec announced a supply and development agreement with PowerCo to expand its production capacity to 15,000 tpy by 2028. The agreement comes as European policymakers seek to accelerate domestic battery manufacturing following previous regional failures. Earlier this year, the European Commission launched its €1.5 billion Battery Booster Facility, designed to help battery producers scale commercial production capacity in Europe. artigo.texto: Jinko ESS, a leading global energy storage company and a subsidiary of JinkoSolar Co., Ltd., is advancing a 135MWh green battery energy storage project in Germany. Connected with a photovoltaic plant and structured to support a hybrid power purchase agreement (PPA), the project is designed to strengthen the delivery and commercial value of renewable electricity. As Germany expands its renewable energy capacity, co-located and connected storage is becoming increasingly important. Battery energy storage can capture surplus solar generation, shift renewable electricity to periods of higher demand, and help create a more stable delivery profile for customers and the grid. By integrating 135MWh of green BESS capacity with the PV plant, the project is intended to support more effective use of solar generation and provide the flexibility required for a hybrid PPA. The approach brings together renewable production, energy storage, and contracted energy delivery within one coordinated project concept. The project is built on the Jinko Tera liquid-cooled energy storage system (5.01MWh). With a tested 94.1% conversion efficiency, the system captures surplus solar output with minimal charging and discharging losses, while its mirrored AB-cabinet layout reduces footprint by 17.7% and DC cabling by 50%, significantly shortening on-site delivery and grid-connection cycles — enabling storage capacity to enter service alongside the PV plant faster and supporting the reliable execution of the hybrid PPA. Roberto Murgioni, General Manager of Jinko ESS Europe, said: “We are delighted to continue strengthening our cooperation in Germany through this 135MWh project. By bringing together PV, storage and a hybrid PPA structure, this project reflects the kind of integrated approach that will make renewable energy more flexible and dependable.” Looking ahead, Jinko ESS will continue to collaborate with partners across Europe to deliver high-quality battery energy storage solutions that enhance renewable energy utilisation, strengthen grid flexibility, and support new routes to market for clean power.

artigo.texto: During their first face-to-face debate, candidates for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, Democrat William Lawrence and incumbent Republican Tom Barrett, faced off on immigration policy, the Iran war and data center development. Throughout the debate on Tuesday, Barrett continually referenced old statements posted by Lawrence on social media, while Lawrence repeatedly took a stance of connecting Barrett to President Donald Trump. A 'humane' immigration policy Upon being asked about budgeting for the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Lawrence said border security and ICE personnel should be regarded as separate. Lawrence said he supported a “secure border” paired with a “humane, efficient and orderly” immigration system. The congressional hopeful referenced the deaths of two Minneapolis, Minnesota, residents, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during Operation Metro Surge in January, saying the current immigration system is “un-American.” “We need to remember the words on the Statue of Liberty, which call us to our high values and remind us that we should welcome immigrants because we are immigrants,” Lawrence said. Barrett also established a desire for a “humane” system of immigration that is also “firm” and “fair.” He further advocated a need for a “secure border,” saying current border security legislation has reduced fentanyl overdose rates. The Department of Homeland Security's renewed focus on immigration enforcement under the second Trump administration led to a 31% decrease in the number of hours spent on fentanyl-related criminal investigations, according to a recent DHS Office of the Inspector General report. “We have to start with the border security first policy,” Barrett said. “Then we can have a conversation about the remaining immigration questions that are out there that we need to continue to work on.” Barrett also referred to Lawrence’s old social media posts advocating for “free and open migration” and “amnesty to all 12 million illegal immigrants in the country,” saying Lawrence’s plan would make “communities less safe.” Lawrence said they were “hypothetical statements" and later said he has since changed his mind. Future data center development Data centers have been a bipartisan source of strain in the Greater Lansing Area, with residents concerned about the hyper-scale projects' toll on the environment and the job market. Barrett said local governments should be in charge of data center development projects. The incumbent Republican candidate disparaged the pursuit of the Green New Deal due to it “taking away local control" from future development. “I've been on the side of local control,” Barrett said. “I've been on the side of local residents for this.” Lawrence, who co-founded the Sunrise Movement, championed his “nationally recognized” fight against data centers and advocacy for “safe AI.” He referenced past appearances at local council meetings where Lawrence condemned data center development, calling out Barrett’s lack of presence in such areas. “Residents across the political spectrum — Democrats, Independents, Republicans — have been fighting back and saying, ‘No, we don't want this in our communities,’” Lawrence said. The Iran War Barrett said he was “one of the very first Republicans” to vote against continuing the war in Iran. He said this “continued vote” was not of "convenience" but "conviction,” advocating for "separating" himself from Trump with regard to the nation’s part in the war. “Our national leaders, whether it's the president or anybody else, (have) to be contemplating the downstream effects of every decision that we make,” Barrett said. While Lawrence also supported an end to the conflict, he emphasized the economic impacts, saying, “We can’t afford for this war to continue.” Lawrence also criticized Barrett’s initial support of Trump, condemning his decision to “arm the Israeli government.” Support student media! Please consider donating to The State News and help fund the future of journalism. “We have got to put a stop to this,” Lawrence said. “I am a strong supporter that we should bring our money home, stop arming Israel and stop these endless wars that are not making us any safer.” Lawrence called for Barrett to “condemn the president for his words” in reference to recent comments suggesting that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego if cleared to develop nuclear weaponry. While Barrett agreed that this language “wasn’t acceptable,” he fired back, challenging Lawrence to denounce leftist streamer Hasan Piker’s remarks that “Americans deserved 9/11.” Lawrence denounced Piker's comments, saying, “It was a despicable statement.” The event was livestreamed through WKAR’s YouTube channel on Tuesday and will air on Oct. 7 at 7 p.m. through local news outlets.

artigo.texto: Três data centers ficaram com os 228 MW de capacidade da rede básica de transmissão ofertados em São Paulo no primeiro processo competitivo da Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão (Pnast), realizado na terça (6/10). Dois deles são da norte-americana CloudHQ. O resultado foi divulgado nesta quarta (7/10) pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS). A CloudHQ venceu com a Pahlavan One e a Pahlavan Three, empresas pelas quais desenvolve um campus de data centers em Paulínia (SP). O terceiro projeto é da Digital DC Brasil, que opera no país sob a marca NextStream. A disputa envolveu a margem de escoamento em quatro pontos de conexão no estado. Sete empreendimentos participaram, com 451 MW de demanda habilitada, quase o dobro da capacidade disponível. Os lances médios ficaram na ordem de R$ 800 por kW, segundo a Associação Brasileira das Empresas de Transmissão de Energia Elétrica (Abrate). Foi a primeira vez que a capacidade remanescente da rede básica foi alocada por meio de um mecanismo competitivo, segundo o ONS. O processo era a etapa final da 1ª Temporada de Acesso de 2026, encerrada nesta quarta em cerimônia na sede do operador. O diretor-geral do ONS, Marcio Rea, avalia que o primeiro ciclo comprovou a efetividade do novo modelo de acesso. “Além dos volumes expressivos de capacidade analisada e viabilizada, realizamos com sucesso o primeiro Processo Competitivo da Pnast, consolidando um ambiente mais previsível, transparente e eficiente para investidores, consumidores e para o planejamento da expansão do sistema elétrico brasileiro”, disse. Para a Abrate, que representa as transmissoras de energia, a política é necessária para disciplinar a fila de pedidos de conexão à rede básica diante, de um lado, da expansão das fontes eólica e solar e da geração distribuída (GD) e, de outro, da chegada de grandes cargas, como data centers, projetos de hidrogênio verde e a eletrificação da demanda. A associação avalia que o modelo coloca o Brasil à frente de outros países no atendimento à demanda dos data centers. “Enquanto diversos países enfrentam dificuldades para atender à crescente demanda computacional, recorrendo com frequência à geração própria local para evitar a dependência da rede elétrica tradicional, o Brasil tomou a dianteira”, afirma a presidente executiva da Abrate, Talita Porto, em nota. Segundo a entidade, Rea foi convidado a apresentar os resultados da política em Washington (EUA), no início de novembro, em evento que reunirá operadores elétricos de todo o mundo. Quem levou a capacidade A Pahlavan Ventures One e a Pahlavan Ventures Three aparecem, em lista de solicitações de acesso publicada pelo ONS (.pdf), como controladas pela CloudHQ e associadas a um data center em Paulínia. A CloudHQ lançou o campus de Paulínia em março de 2023, com investimento anunciado de até US$ 3 bilhões. O projeto prevê três prédios com 48 MW de capacidade de TI cada, com possibilidade de expansão para seis. A Digital DC Brasil tem um data center no campus de Tamboré, em Santana de Parnaíba (SP), e pediu ao Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME), em maio de 2025, a conexão de nova carga para ampliar a estrutura. A NextStream opera 11 data centers, quase todos na América Latina. A empresa surgiu depois que a gestora britânica Actis comprou, em 2023, ativos da Nabiax, construídos originalmente pela Telefónica. ONS analisou 43 GW em pedidos Na temporada, o ONS registrou 367 cadastramentos de empreendimentos de geração e consumo, que somam mais de 20 GW em solicitações de acesso, distribuídas por 64 barramentos do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Somada a fase transitória da política, o operador analisou mais de 43 GW em pedidos de acesso à rede básica. Desse total, cerca de 30,7 GW foram viabilizados ou habilitados. A experiência da primeira temporada servirá de base para ajustes nas próximas edições, segundo o diretor de TI, Relacionamento com Agentes e Assuntos Regulatórios do ONS, Maurício de Souza. A partir de 2027, serão duas temporadas de acesso por ano. O cronograma da primeira delas já foi publicado pelo ONS (.pdf). A Pnast foi instituída pelo decreto 12.772/2025 e reorganiza a fila de pedidos de conexão de grandes projetos ao SIN. O ministro de Minas e Energia, Alexandre Silveira, afirmou que a política substitui a lógica de espera por “planejamento, critérios técnicos e processos competitivos”. Editado por Gustavo Gaudarde

artigo.texto: Backlash as American tech giants look to build data centers in Australia Facing legal challenges and public backlash at home, American tech giants are looking abroad for new opportunities in Australia. But the reception down under may not be quite as warm as they hope. MARY LOUISE KELLY, HOST: Facing legal challenges and public backlash at home, American tech giants have been looking abroad for new opportunities, and Australia is high on their list. But as Kristina Kukolja reports from Melbourne, the reception down under may not be quite as warm as they would hope. (SOUNDBITE OF BIRDS CHIRPING) KRISTINA KUKOLJA, BYLINE: The sound of native birds as they fly over fields as far as the eye can see, these were once Australia's largest goldfields. Now, the vast farmland outside Melbourne is the setting for a medium-sized data center being proposed by Australian developer RV Energy. ALAN FORD: We know nothing. No one has told us anything to do with this data center. We've heard it by hearsay in the media. KUKOLJA: That's Alan Ford, a fifth-generation farmer whose land borders the planned site, an abandoned quarry that also faces a residential area. FORD: For us, it's going to be a real eyesore to start with, but the biggest problem is going to be noise and the energy. Where's this energy going to come from? We're talking about a massive amount of energy. KUKOLJA: Fellow farmer John Drife fears the project could affect local water supply. JOHN DRIFE: Well, a lot of people do rely on that creek for stock water. Some use it for irrigation. There's obviously an on-flow effect if they deplete the creek in the dry months. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) UNIDENTIFIED PROTESTER: What about the data center? KUKOLJA: Concerns about land, water and energy use have flared up in city neighborhoods, too, where data center projects are planned or already underway. Residents in Melbourne's west called for a pause in their rollout in August, captured here by The Westsider newspaper. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) UNIDENTIFIED PROTESTER: We don't want expansion. But we don't want any more data centers at all. (CHEERING) KUKOLJA: But data center construction in Australia is booming, with the Commonwealth Bank of Australia estimating investment could exceed $100 billion by 2030, trailing only the U.S. and China. Microsoft and Amazon have already pledged funding. Johanna Weaver, a former Australian lead negotiator on cyber issues at the United Nations, says American companies are drawn to Australia for its... JOHANNA WEAVER: Geographical location, our access to clean and renewable energy, the availability of land and our democratic stability - plus, our alignment, which is important. KUKOLJA: Other factors are in play, too, says John Quiggin, a professor of economics at the University of Queensland. JOHN QUIGGIN: It's just headlong expansion, and of course, they're running into barriers in the U.S. So in some sense, they all believe that the one who spends the money fastest will be the one who gets the monopoly. KUKOLJA: And the national government is keen to attract their investment, promising economic benefits will flow from companies like OpenAI and Anthropic. From next year, though, large-scale developers will face tougher regulations over things like water efficiency and power supply. But the biggest barrier to investments, says the former U.N. negotiator Weaver, are Australia's strict copyright protections. WEAVER: The challenge is the companies say, well, we will come and train in Australia, but we need regulatory certainty that we are not going to be prosecuted for breaching copyright. KUKOLJA: And adding fuel to the fire, she says, is last month's revelation that an OpenAI agent accessed Australian government websites without authorization. WEAVER: If you have products that cause harm, you are held accountable. I think it's important that we don't treat AI companies like a separate and distinct class. KUKOLJA: The question is, she asks, who will hold them to account? For NPR News, I'm Kristina Kukolja in Melbourne. (SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. artigo.texto: A Researcher in Denmark Aims to Reduce AI Reliance on Data Centers New Technology Can Move AI Calculations to the Electricity Grid The EU [European Union] wants to make data centres a more sustainable part of the energy system. A researcher from the leading energy research university in Europe, Aalborg University, has developed a technology that can allow existing energy plants to take over part of the AI calculations and thus relieve both data centers and electricity grids. Data centres are crucial for Europe’s digital development, but their increasing electricity consumption is also putting pressure on the energy system. This summer, the European Commission published a strategic roadmap for digitalisation and artificial intelligence in the energy sector. Among other things, it will promote digital solutions for optimising the electricity grid and ensure that data centres are integrated more sustainably into Europe’s energy system. According to the European Commission, data centers already account for 2.5 percent of the EU’s electricity consumption. Therefore, a model for tripartite agreements between data center operators, energy players and public authorities is being worked on to support a more sustainable integration of data centers. The European agenda hits directly at the challenge that Associate Professor Subham Sahoo from Aalborg University in Denmark is trying to solve with the technology Power to Compute, P2C. Instead of letting all AI calculations take place in data centers, he will use parts of the existing energy infrastructure to carry out part of the calculation work. “We are facing a challenge where both the green transition, electrification of companies and digital development pull in the same direction. Everyone needs more power and more capacity. Therefore, we also need to think about how we can use the existing infrastructure more wisely,” says Subham Sahoo, associate professor at the Department of Energy at Aalborg University. Energy Plants Can Help Data Centers The basic idea of P2C is that some of the electronic devices that are already connected to the electricity grid can also contribute to calculations. For example, it can be control electronics in a solar cell system. Instead of just handling power, the device can receive a small computational task from a data center, solve it, and send back the response. In this way, P2C will not replace data centers, but distribute part of their computational work on equipment that is already in the energy system. The technology thus links two tracks in the EU’s new strategy: the use of AI and digital solutions in the energy sector, and a more sustainable integration of data centers. “We do not see P2C as a competitor to the data centers. We see it as a supplement. The data centers will continue to be necessary, but if we can move some of the computational work to existing energy infrastructure, we can reduce the need for new physical infrastructure,” says Subham Sahoo. Can Reduce Power Consumption and Cooling Preliminary calculations indicate that P2C can lower data centers’ energy consumption by about 10 percent and reduce the cost of cooling the servers by 10 to 20 percent. The results are early, and it is still too early to draw definitive conclusions about the large-scale effect. The perspective is that the data centers can solve more tasks without a corresponding expansion of their physical capacity, while at the same time making better use of existing equipment in the energy system. The Next Step Is Testing Outside the Laboratory P2C has so far been tested in the laboratory. Several Danish companies have already shown interest in participating in a large-scale trial, and according to the researcher, the technology can be brought closer to practical application if the right partners and data are in place. “This is not something we see as a distant vision far into the future. Our preliminary results are promising, and the ambition is to get out of the laboratory and into real test environments as soon as possible,” says Subham Sahoo. artigo.texto: Council moves to extend Lexington's pause on data center development, restart zoning process In a lengthy public hearing, Council heard from dozens of residents who pressed for more time to get Lexington data center regulations right. Following a lengthy public hearing Tuesday, Lexington’s Urban County Council moved to extend Fayette County’s pause on data center development until October 31, 2027, as the body continues working to regulate them. Spurred on by the sale of a former Lexmark property to a data center developer, Council has spent the last few months studying the facilities, along with their environmental and electrical grid impacts. In June, the body unanimously passed a moratorium – or temporary pause – on their development in Fayette County, effective through October 31, 2026. Council had also directed the Planning Commission to develop a zoning ordinance text amendment (updates to Lexington’s zoning laws) so it could modernize its regulation of data centers. Councilmembers discussed the Planning Commission’s recommendations Tuesday after a public hearing that lasted for several hours and saw nearly 60 residents and individuals sign up to address the Council. From representatives of Lexington’s business community to members of the Bluegrass Democratic Socialists of America, their message was clear: Lexington needs more time to properly regulate data centers, including determining where they should go and what types of restrictions they should have. Most speakers opposed data centers or wanted much stricter limits on the facilities. Many in the room called for a ban on hyperscale data centers (those with an energy capacity exceeding 25 megawatts) and some supported a complete ban on new data centers in Fayette County. Speakers raised several concerns about data centers’ potential land use impacts, from electricity and water consumption to higher utility bills, strains on the electrical grid, noise, pollution, waste heat and potential negative health effects for nearby residents. Representatives of Commerce Lexington, banks, telecommunications companies, and the University of Kentucky stressed that smaller data centers and server rooms already exist in Lexington and support local businesses and institutions here, particularly those that rely on data storage and processing, from hospitals to schools. They cautioned against overly broad restrictions that could hurt Lexington’s economic development. The deciding motions came from District 1 Councilmember Tyler Morton and District 4 Councilmember Emma Curtis. Morton successfully moved to remove most of the Planning Commission’s recommendations for data centers and server rooms from the draft zoning ordinance text amendment (ZOTA), allowing the Council to move forward with its own approach to regulating data centers in Fayette County. Morton had previously questioned the fairness of the recommendations, which proposed allowing smaller-scale data centers in Lexington’s industrial and commercial zones – which are concentrated in District 1 and on the city’s northside. Morton also successfully moved to advance a resolution launching a new zoning ordinance text amendment process that will look at creating a separate zoning category for data centers. The new process will not be under the tight timeline Lexington’s Planning Commission faced to deliver its recommendations to Council, and it will include more opportunities for residents to engage, Morton told CivicLex in an interview after the hearing. Curtis moved to advance a resolution extending the current data center moratorium through to October 31, 2027. Morton and Curtis’ resolutions will move through Council’s regular legislative process, with final votes expected at an upcoming Council meeting.

artigo.texto: Raleigh leaders voted to put a pause on developing new, larger data centers for six months, as community advocates push for a 32-month pause to study the impacts and give residents more say. The measure passed in a 7-1 vote, with councilmember Christina Jones voting against the moratorium. A group advocating for a longer moratorium expressed frustration after the moratorium passed, saying it wasn't long enough. Other WRAL Top Stories The moratorium is shorter than the 12-month pause Apex approved in April and the 18-month pause Cary adopted in August. Raleigh’s draft sets aside 60 days for research and drafting rules, followed by 120 days to move proposed changes through the legislative process. Mary Black, who served on Raleigh City Council from 2022 to 2024 and is now a community organizer for the Raleigh Anti-Data Center Coalition, says that leaves too little time to involve people who could live near the facilities. “What we want is transparency and input in the process, and that’s going to take more than six months,” Black said. WRAL contacted Mayor Janet Cowell and every council member on Monday and Tuesday morning to ask why six months was chosen, whether that would be enough time, and whether they would support an extension if new guidelines were not ready. They had not responded as of publication. Why six months? The draft ordinance says Raleigh needs time to address the development, infrastructure, and environmental impacts of larger data centers. It identifies potential concerns, including electricity and water demand, noise, light pollution and heat islands. While Raleigh has general industrial development rules, the draft says it lacks standards specific to larger data centers. It also warns that infrastructure needed to serve those facilities could create significant burdens for the city’s water utility and its ratepayers. During the first 60 days, staff would study impacts, draft proposed changes and examine how other communities regulate data centers. A team of staff experts would coordinate that work. The final 120 days would be used to propose code amendments and follow the legislative adoption process. The draft calls that six-month period necessary to complete the work. It does not explain why Raleigh’s schedule is shorter than those in Cary and Apex. Black said adopting regulations within six months may be possible, but meaningful community engagement would take longer. She said the coalition’s request for 32 months would allow more time for research, rulemaking and public involvement. In September, Cowell told WRAL the pause would allow a conversation about an issue that had become highly emotional. She also said Raleigh wanted to protect residents while preserving its role as a technology and research hub. “This is a tech center,” Cowell said. Neighboring towns have longer timelines Cary unanimously approved an 18-month moratorium Aug. 27 to study power demand and grid capacity, water consumption, noise and vibration, site design and buffering. Staff will provide progress updates, with a decision on an ordinance expected in February 2028. Cary’s schedule includes technical studies, community engagement and regional coordination through spring 2027, followed by draft ordinance review that summer and public hearings and board consideration before a council decision. Apex unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on April 14 after a developer withdrew a proposed data center near the Shearon Harris Nuclear Plant. Mayor Jacques Gilbert previously told WRAL the pause would allow more research into water and electricity use and potential costs to residents. Pushback over neighborhood impacts and transparency Raleigh’s debate follows substantial opposition to a proposed data center near Jones Sausage and Rock Quarry roads in Southeast Raleigh. In August, 30 of the 32 people expected to speak at a public hearing had signed up in opposition, according to a sign-up sheet WRAL obtained. The developer subsequently withdrew its annexation request. Mayor Pro Tem, Jane Harrison, said in August that she wanted residents to better understand the approval process and wanted more notice when larger projects came before the Board of Adjustment. “I just want to make sure that we all understand how this process currently works,” Harrison said. Black said public hearings alone do not provide enough opportunity to reach residents and understand their concerns. She wants council members to engage people where they live, work and play. Supporters point to jobs, tax revenue and innovation Data center supporters say the facilities can generate investment and tax revenue while supporting the technology behind modern services and artificial intelligence. During a recent visit to Duke Energy’s Roxboro coal plant in Person County, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright described data centers as “intelligence factories” and linked their growth to the Trump administration’s economic agenda. “So we can spur economic growth, generate revenues for local communities, drive up wages for workers,” Wright said. “To do that, you need more energy, not less energy.” In a statement to WRAL, the Data Center Coalition, an industry group representing companies including Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Meta, urged local leaders to pursue regulations instead of moratoriums. “Rather than enacting moratoriums, which will discourage investment and send signals that the community is closed for business, local leaders should work with the industry and all stakeholders to establish reasonable regulatory frameworks that meet the needs of the community without deterring the industry and the benefits it can bring,” said Christy Tarallo, the group’s Southeast director of government affairs. artigo.texto: Romania’s renewable energy associations have called on the country’s energy regulator, ANRE, to slash the required financial guarantee for standalone battery projects sixfold, from EUR 30,000 per MW of installed capacity to EUR 5,000 per MW. They claim the “excessive” guarantee amount hinders investment in energy storage amid increasing flexibility needs. The current regulation, issued by the Romanian Energy Regulatory Authority (ANRE) this summer, treats energy storage projects and new power generation plants equally, despite considerable differences in investment profile, revenue structure, and economic risks, according to the Romanian Wind Energy Association (RWEA) and the Romanian Photovoltaic Industry Association (RPIA), Economica reported. “Independent (standalone) electricity storage facilities have a distinct technical and functional specificity compared to electricity generation capacities. Consequently, the investment profile, revenue structure, and related economic risks differ considerably and require a proportionate approach in terms of the financial guarantee related to the issuance of the establishment authorization,” according to RWEA and RPIA. Battery projects would face a disproportionate financial burden if treated equally as power generation plants The uniform treatment creates an unequal financial burden for standalone storage projects, which may affect their economic viability and create an additional barrier to their development, amid the increased need for flexibility and at a time when more and more investors plan to install large-scale batteries, they claim. The two associations have sent an amendment to ANRE calling for the required financial guarantee for standalone battery energy storage projects to be set at EUR 5/kW of installed capacity, down from EUR 30/kW. Romania has tightened the rules for energy projects in an attempt to filter out “serious” investors from “speculators.” Other measures include raising the financial guarantee for grid connection from 5% of the connection fee to 20% and introducing auctions to allocate grid capacity. Romania’s total battery storage capacity currently stands at about 2.31 GWh and is expected to reach 4 GWh by the end of 2027, according to Economica’s report.

artigo.texto: Manatee County Commissioners have unanimously approved a 12-month moratorium on new data center applications. The move puts large-scale projects on hold while the county weighs whether the rapidly expanding AI infrastructure industry has a place in Manatee at all. The moratorium blocks new applications and development orders tied to data centers and other large-load customers while the county considers what permanent policy should follow, including potential changes to its comprehensive plan, land development code and other regulations. County planning staff said investment in data centers has surged alongside growing demand for artificial intelligence products and services. Large-scale facilities can require substantial amounts of electricity and water to power and cool computer servers, creating infrastructure demands that can rival those of small municipalities. Future regulations could address water and power consumption, noise, environmental impacts, design standards and where the facilities could be located, while Thursday’s vote ensures no proposal can move forward before those rules are in place. But several Commissioners suggested Thursday that the eventual answer could be more restrictive than simply writing new development rules. Commissioner Jason Bearden raised concerns about Manatee County’s water supply and questioned whether the county should ultimately allow large data centers at all. “I understand we need them. I’m in AI, so I get it,” Bearden said. “But I just don’t think that the state of Florida or even Manatee County has the capacity, especially with the water situation that we have right now, for data centers.” Commissioner Bob McCann said he also favors keeping large-scale data centers out of Manatee. “You know, AI is out of control. If you read about AI there’s lots of worries about it. There’s lots of worries about it taking over a lot of things,” McCann said. “There’s also worries about it being out of control by humans at some point in time. So, you know, are the data centers necessary? Yes. Are they necessary here? No. Would I be for them? I’m for the permanent ban.” Commissioner George Kruse urged caution on a permanent ban. He said overly broad rules could incidentally sweep in manufacturers, cryptocurrency mining operations and other high-power users and advised treading lightly. Still, he said a moratorium gives the county essentially the same immediate protection while leaving time to determine what permanent policy makes sense. Commissioners also stressed that approving the moratorium should not be interpreted as preparing Manatee County to eventually welcome data centers. “It’s not a precursor to approving data centers,” Board Chair Tal Siddique said. “It is a good measure to ban any applications from coming through today to scare them off now.” The issue is not entirely hypothetical. Planning staff said no data center applications are currently pending, but one earlier development proposal included a data center among its potential uses before the applicant withdrew that request. Thursday’s vote does not set a deadline for permanent regulations. Kruse argued against rushing the process as the technology and laws continue to evolve, noting that Commissioners could extend the moratorium if necessary.

artigo.texto: Finlândia interrompe construção de data centers do Google pelo impacto ambiental De acordo com a Agência de Supervisão Finlandesa, mais de 300 hectares de floresta foram cortados sem avaliação de impacto A Agência de Supervisão Finlandesa (LVV) ordenou nesta terça-feira, 6, que o Google suspenda a construção de novos ‘data centers’ em dois municípios da Finlândia até no máximo 23 de outubro de 2026, à espera de uma avaliação de seu impacto ambiental. Estes projetos fazem parte de um investimento de 13 bilhões de euros (R$ 72,7 bilhões) anunciado na Finlândia, o maior investimento da gigante tecnológica americana na Europa no âmbito da inteligência artificial. Durante uma visita na semana passada à cidade de Muhos, uma jornalista da AFP observou o ir e vir de retroescavadeiras. Em frente à fazenda de um dos moradores com quem conversou, a floresta tinha desaparecido de um terreno adquirido pelo Google. A agência finlandesa de supervisão exigiu, em um comunicado, que sejam suspensas “todas as medidas preparatórias suscetíveis de modificar de forma significativa o meio ambiente no âmbito dos projetos de ‘data centers’ previstos em Muhos e Kajaani”, no noroeste do país. A agência abriu uma investigação pela suspeita de que a empresa Tuike Finland, que representa o Google, cortou mais de 300 hectares de floresta em Muhos sem realizar previamente a avaliação de impacto ambiental. As obras devem ser interrompidas até que seja feita esta avaliação, detalhou a agência. “Entendemos as preocupações expressas e reconhecemos que, neste caso concreto, não estivemos à altura de nossos próprios padrões, que são elevados”, admitiu Sondre Ronander, porta-voz do Google, em uma mensagem enviada à AFP. “Estudaremos as conclusões da agência e seguiremos suas recomendações”, acrescentou. Graças a um clima ameno, uma eletricidade relativamente estável e barata, produzida majoritariamente mediante energia nuclear, além de uma ampla capacidade eólica e hidrelétrica, a Finlândia experimentou recentemente um auge dos investimentos em ‘data centers’. (com AFP)

artigo.texto: Residents of a Northern Virginia neighborhood say a data center just steps from their backyards cuts into their quality of life with too much noise and light pollution. Those residents on Cocquina Drive in Reston say the company CoreSite’s data center expansion near Fairfax County Parkway has been an issue over the past 10 years. Stream NBC4 newscasts for free right here, right now. “I’m ticked off, upset,” said one resident who wished to remain anonymous. “The noise level, electricity, and, oh, randomly people that come from here and come across your property and expect you to understand,” he explained. “Drilling, blasting, chipping at metal, excavation,” his list went on. “Lights at night during the construction.” Video taken from a neighbor's backyard shows bright lights from the data center at night. It even peaks through blackout curtains, residents said. Other neighbors shared videos of what they say are cracks in their homes from the vibration from the drilling for the expansion. “It does absolutely nothing to mitigate the noise, which goes on all day long,” resident Maggie Urbanik said. “When you look at the size of the building that is behind these people’s home and the lights shining into their bedrooms.” Residents say that last year CoreSite planned to expand its data center with a 75-foot-tall facility 97 feet away from those living in the neighborhood. Residents say they were unable to challenge the expansion due to prior approval the development went through before the county’s new data center regulations, which prohibit facilities within 200 feet of residential neighborhoods. Residents who’ve lived there for decades told News4 they never wanted the data center to be so close. CoreSite broke ground on the building more than 10 years ago, and since then, neighbors say, the construction has led to quality-of-life issues. Homeowners say they have met with CoreSite and Fairfax County leaders and would like to see changes. “I was clear to let them understand that the noise, the vibration and the light, the light bill, it rendered our property almost completely useless,” said the anonymous resident. News4 reached out to CoreSite and awaits a response.

artigo.texto: This piece was originally published at MLK50: Justice Through Journalism, a nonprofit newsroom focused on poverty, power and policy in Memphis. I visit the hospital rooms of my family and church elders relatively regularly. I have never been to the hospital to visit any of my young cousins, but that changed a week ago. As a heat dome covered Memphis and the Mid-South, my 21-year-old cousin, Ra'Kelle Miller, was struggling to breathe after five minutes outdoors and was rushed to the emergency room. Neither her nebulizer nor asthma pump worked to open her airways. She lives a few miles away from Colossus I and only a couple of miles away from the Valero Oil Refinery. The pollution from these facilities, and the power plant with the illegal gas turbines in neighboring Southaven, are having a real impact on our community's health now. Politicians and talking heads are leaving the people impacted by hyperscale data centers behind when discussing the "economic development" they think data centers can bring. Memphis is becoming a testing ground for the future of artificial intelligence. But before we rush into that future, we need to pause and ask: What will it cost the people who live here? SpaceXAI's Colossus data center arrived in Memphis under the cover of NDAs and secret meetings that never included people from the community. That rush to secrecy and to market has led to tons of harmful pollutants being emitted into our air and lungs. SpaceXAI is raking in billions of dollars a month, and all we have to show for it is $30M in city and county tax revenue and temporary construction jobs filled by people from out of town. The tax money is a pittance compared to SpaceXAI's value and profits. We should be ashamed, not celebrating how we are being treated. SpaceXAI's Colossus data center has put extraordinary demands on Memphis for electricity, water and other infrastructure. To power those demands, SpaceXAI's founder, Elon Musk, has relied on dozens of methane gas turbines that emit nitrogen oxides and other pollutants with well-documented health risks. The full health and environmental consequences for Memphis residents continue to worsen. The Memphis City Council has an opportunity to help us learn from this colossal mistake by pausing to think, learn and act in the best interest of the people of Memphis. The council is scheduled for a third reading and vote on Ordinance 5982 on Tuesday. The ordinance proposes pausing new large-scale data center development for 12 months to give Memphis time to study the impact of facilities like SpaceXAI's Colossus, allow for community input on where they are built, and develop regulations that protect our air, water, land and jobs. Musk's Memphis xAI data center and the making of a 'Digital Delta' A fierce political struggle is brewing in Memphis. On one side is the world's richest man, Elon Musk, whose company xAI quietly set up shop in an abandoned factory this past summer. On the other side is a broad cross-section of Memphis residents, led by the low-income, historically Black neighborhoods located nearby. There's more than enough reason to pause and research this before expanding the existing facilities or allowing more. The environmental concerns are substantial. A recent Reuters report found that Musk's company has installed many more gas turbines than it claimed, and without proper permitting. The majority of those turbines are in neighboring Southaven, near predominantly Black communities of Whitehaven and Westwood that already face elevated rates of respiratory illness. The five-mile affected area extends across the state line into Memphis, including John P. Freeman Middle School. The Reuters report calculated that 30 methane gas turbines with available emissions data could produce nearly 2,500 tons of nitrogen oxides, 4,000 tons of carbon monoxide, and 22 tons of formaldehyde annually, assuming they operate continuously at 80% capacity. The report says that the EPA states that these turbines typically operate around the clock at 80% capacity or more. The American Lung Association states that nitrogen dioxide, one of the nitrogen oxides produced by these turbines, increases toxic smog, which is proven to reduce lung capacity and increase airway inflammation, coughing and wheezing. Toxic smog also worsens asthma and can cause asthma in children, leading to hospital and emergency room visits. Carbon monoxide deprives the body of oxygen, and formaldehyde is a human carcinogen. Cancer rates in South Memphis are already more than 4 times the federal cancer limit. Memphis has become the sacrifice zone for a billionaire's wealth and profit. An investigative report by ProPublica exposes that this highly elevated cancer rate is due to cancer-causing pollution from industrial sites. Beyond the proposed economic effects of this industrialization are the effects on the lives of the people living in Memphis. People like my cousin, Ra'Kelle. Further, Memphis residents are being asked to not only put themselves in harm's way for these and future data centers, but also to accommodate this massive land use without the necessary regulation. The current Unified Development Code doesn't specify regulations for these massive data centers that so heavily consume our water, burden our electrical infrastructure, and threaten our health. The real question isn't whether Memphis should participate in the AI economy. It's whether we should allow this unprecedented data center growth to continue under rules written before this technology existed and its adverse health effects were known. We need courage from our City Council to put people at the forefront of these policy decisions. Our lives matter more than hyper-scale data centers. I urge the council to pass Ordinance 5982, which identifies the regulatory gaps and would impose a temporary 12-month moratorium on specified permits for new and expanded data-center development while the city studies and develops permanent regul

artigo.texto: Publicidade O avanço dos investimentos em data centers no Brasil pode abrir uma nova frente para o mercado de fundos imobiliários (FIIs). De um lado, a AZ Quest Panorama estruturou um fundo temático para financiar ativos da Scala, uma das principais empresas do setor no país. De outro, a Alianza mantém no radar a possibilidade de transformar seus ativos de data center em um veículo próprio, em um movimento que poderia ampliar o acesso de investidores de varejo a esse mercado. A estratégia ganhou força em um momento em que o Brasil busca se posicionar como um polo regional para infraestrutura digital. A regulamentação do setor, especialmente com o Redata, é vista pelas gestoras como um passo importante para aumentar a competitividade brasileira e destravar novos projetos. Para Marcos Freitas, gestor de fundos imobiliários da AZ Quest Panorama, o modelo de fundo de data centers funciona como uma nova fonte de capital para empresas que precisam financiar uma expansão intensiva em investimentos. A estrutura criada pela gestora envolve a aquisição de ativos da Scala, que permanece como locatária por meio de contratos de longo prazo. Atualmente, a Scala opera 13 unidades no Brasil, com cerca de 200 MW instalados, e é controlada pela DigitalBridge. Segundo ele, as empresas de data centers já utilizam equity, dívida corporativa e project finance, mas o modelo imobiliário acrescenta uma nova alternativa. “A gente traz uma nova fonte de capital, que é usar os ativos imobiliários que elas possuem como forma de financiamento do capital de giro e dos investimentos dessas companhias” explica o gestor ao InfoMoney. No caso, a AZ Quest estruturou um fundo imobiliário cetipado com prazo determinado de dez anos e remuneração previamente definida. Continua depois da publicidade A Scala aluga os ativos adquiridos pelo fundo durante o período e, ao final, tem a obrigação de recomprá-los. A remuneração, segundo Freitas, parte de IPCA + 9,5% ao ano no cenário de permanência até o décimo ano e pode chegar a IPCA + 10,5% em determinadas hipóteses de recompra antecipada. Leia Mais: FIIs sobem forte após 1º turno da eleição presidencial; veja maiores altas FIIs de data centers buscam combinar renda previsível e exposição à expansão da infraestrutura digital Segundo Freitas, o AZ Quest Panorama Data Centers (AZDC) foi desenhado para oferecer ao investidor uma exposição ao setor sem que ele precise assumir diretamente os riscos de desenvolvimento de um novo data center. Continua depois da publicidade O fundo captou R$ 482 milhões na primeira emissão de cotas e reuniu mais de 7 mil investidores. “A gente achou que seria interessante levar para o mercado um produto temático desse setor, que pudesse dar um pouco para o investidor a sensação de que ele está participando do segmento, mas com ativo real, não tendo que entrar em projetos com uma incerteza mais alta”, afirma. O gestor destaca ainda que o prazo determinado pode ser uma característica atrativa para investidores que buscam previsibilidade. “É um fundo que tem começo, meio e fim”, diz. Para a pessoa física, diz ele, a proposta é oferecer uma renda de longo prazo com isenção fiscal, sem a volatilidade diária típica dos fundos imobiliários listados. Continua depois da publicidade A tese da AZ Quest não depende, necessariamente, da expansão do fundo para outros ativos imediatamente. A gestora avalia conversas com outras empresas de data centers para estruturas semelhantes, mas mantém a característica temática do produto como parte central da estratégia. “Eu acho que nesse momento de mercado, o nosso plano é seguir com fundos cetipados, que é um fundo temático, com uma empresa específica para comprar data centers”, pontua Freitas. Leia Mais: Galpão perto do consumidor vale mais: FII BRCO11 explica força do “last mile” Continua depois da publicidade Alianza mantém plano de spin-off de data centers do ALZR11 A estratégia da Alianza segue uma direção diferente. A gestora já possui exposição a data centers dentro de sua estrutura e mantém a possibilidade de realizar, no futuro, um spin-off dos ativos, transformando a carteira em um veículo listado dedicado ao segmento. Segundo Fabio Carvalho, sócio da Alianza, a ideia continua de pé, mas depende principalmente de uma melhora das condições de mercado. O tamanho dos projetos e o nível dos juros são hoje os principais obstáculos para uma operação desse tipo. “O interesse do spin-off ainda existe, mas em um momento de juros mais baixo, pra conseguir evoluir com outro ativos”, comenta Carvalho. O executivo explica que o próprio crescimento dos data centers tornou a estrutura mais desafiadora. Projetos que antes exigiam algumas centenas de milhões de reais passaram a ter dimensões muito maiores, dificultando a aquisição integral de determinados ativos por um único fundo. “Os data centers estão ficando grandes, isso é um problema também. Os projetos estão ficando cada vez maiores. (…) Antigamente tinham data centers médios, que eram de R$ 200 milhões, agora você tem um médio de R$ 700 milhões, isso é um negócio enorme”, diz. Nesse cenário, a Alianza avalia alternativas para participar de projetos maiores sem necessariamente comprar 100% dos ativos. Contratos longos podem transformar data centers em ativos de renda Para Carvalho, a principal característica que pode tornar os data centers interessantes para um eventual fundo dedicado é a duração dos contratos. Segundo ele, os ativos já existentes possuem contratos longos e novos projetos podem ser estruturados com prazos ainda maiores. Segundo o executivo, há contratos com mais de uma década restante e novos ativos poderiam ser adquiridos com contratos de 15 ou até 20 anos. A Alianza já possui exposição ao segmento por meio de fundos com estratégia mais ampla. O ALZR11, por exemplo, é citado por Carvalho como um dos fundos de perfil multiestratégia que poderia ter maior flexibilidade para adquirir ativos de data center. artigo.texto: Electricity and Energy Minister Dr Kgosientsho Ramokgopa has confirmed that South Africaâs first section 34 determination under the Integrated Resource Plan 2025 (IRP 2025) will prioritise 4,600MW of battery energy storage systems (BESS) and 5,000MW of gas-to-power. Electricity 1Min South Africa Ramokgopa prioritises battery storage and gas-to-power in new electricity plan Electricity and Energy Minister Kgosientsho Ramokgopa says the first section 34 determination under the Integrated Resource Plan 2025 will prioritise 4,600MW of battery energy storage and 5,000MW of gas-to-power to reduce curtailment and strengthen reliable electricity supply. Electricity and Energy Minister Dr Kgosientsho Ramokgopa has confirmed that South Africaâs first section 34 determination under the Integrated Resource Plan 2025 (IRP 2025) will prioritise 4,600MW of battery energy storage systems (BESS) and 5,000MW of gas-to-power. The combined 9,600MW allocation is aimed at addressing the electricity systemâs immediate need for energy storage, flexibility and dependable, dispatchable power. The first determination will not include new wind or solar capacity. According to the Department of Electricity and Energy, a subsequent determination will address additional wind and solar projects, including hybrid developments paired with energy storage, as well as longer-term pumped storage options. Ramokgopa said the IRP 2025 should be viewed not only as an electricity planning framework but also as an infrastructure investment blueprint. He said new investment must deliver electricity that the system can accommodate and supply when households and businesses need it, while keeping costs as low as possible. The department said rising electricity curtailment was placing additional pressure on system costs. Curtailment occurs when available electricity generation cannot be accommodated because of network constraints or operating conditions, including periods when supply exceeds demand. This means electricity that could otherwise be supplied to consumers is left unused, while infrastructure and contractual costs remain. The procurement approach will therefore first focus on making better use of electricity that is already available before additional variable generation is added through the next determination. Batteries to reduce curtailment Battery energy storage will be central to the government's approach. The batteries will be able to charge using electricity that would otherwise be curtailed and discharge that electricity during evening peak periods or when demand increases. The department said this would help convert surplus electricity into usable power while providing rapid balancing and grid-support services. Storage projects will be located and operated in areas where they can access surplus electricity and discharge it without creating the same network constraints. Procurement will be aligned with the requirements of the System Operator, with enforceable availability and performance obligations. The department said the effectiveness of battery storage would be measured by the amount of electricity shifted into periods when it is needed and the reliability services provided to the grid. South Africa already has a foundation for expanding battery storage. By June 2025, all five projects in the first battery storage bid window, totalling 513MW, had reached commercial close and entered construction, attracting R15.4 billion in investment. The proposed 4,600MW allocation would significantly expand the country's procurement of storage services. 5,000MW gas-to-power allocation The proposed 5,000MW gas-to-power allocation will complement battery storage by providing dispatchable electricity when renewable generation declines or demand rises. Unlike batteries, gas generation does not absorb surplus electricity. Instead, its role will be to operate flexibly, allowing renewable energy to meet demand when output is high and supplying the remaining electricity requirement when renewable generation falls. The procurement design will consider factors including plant start-up times, ramping capability and minimum operating levels. The department said fuel availability, delivered gas prices, port and pipeline infrastructure, grid connections and commissioning schedules would also need to be assessed together. The affordability of gas-to-power projects will be evaluated against their expected operating profiles. The battery storage and gas procurement programmes will form part of a broader strategy involving transmission expansion, new industrial electricity demand and regional electricity trade. While battery storage can help reduce curtailment, the department said sustained progress would also depend on delivering the grid infrastructure needed to transport electricity to consumers. The procurement programme is also expected to support local manufacturing, engineering, construction, skills development and broader ownership of energy infrastructure through measurable commitments. âThis approach advances the seventh administrationâs priorities by improving the use of available electricity, supporting dependable supply for industrial production and employment, and addressing avoidable costs that place pressure on electricity affordability,â Ramokgopa said.

artigo.texto: CHARLESTON, Ill. (WCIA) — The Charleston City Council approved an ordinance establishing a temporary moratorium on data centers and battery energy storage systems Tuesday night. City Manager Steve Bennett confirmed with WCIA over email that the council approved the moratorium in a 5-0 vote. According to city documents online, Charleston has determined data centers, battery energy storage systems and related battery uses have “unique characteristics” that warrant “consideration of appropriate regulations.” Currently, the City’s Unified Development Code does not have specific regulations addressing the location, development, and operation of data centers or battery energy storage systems. With this moratorium, the city plans to conduct research and update the code, before considering related applications. The Board of Zoning Appeals and Planning had a public hearing Sept. 24. During that hearing, the board recommended the council approve the moratorium. You can read more details about the ordinance online.
