artigo.texto: Governor and Representatives Ocasio-Cortez and Ryan Hold Roundtable in Dutchess County With Farmers and Community Stakeholders To Discuss Impacts of Potential Data Center Development Governor Highlighted Key Policies from Data Center Moratorium and AI Safety Regulations Governor Kathy Hochul and U.S. Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Pat Ryan today toured Fishkill Farms, a family-owned, multigenerational farm in East Fishkill, Dutchess County and held a roundtable discussion with several local farmers, advocates and businesses to discuss the impacts of hyperscale data centers. Today’s discussion highlighted New York’s nation-leading moratorium on hyperscale data center construction, which is helping to protect local communities amid concerns over water and land use, energy costs, and proposed data center development, including in East Fishkill. New York State is experiencing an unprecedented surge in proposals for data center development driven by artificial intelligence and other computing operations that could require massive amounts of energy and water to run and cool thousands of computer servers. This summer, Governor Hochul signed an Executive Order hitting pause on new hyperscale data center development. This action has temporarily paused discretionary State environmental permits for up to one year in order to build a regulatory framework that will protect ratepayers, the environment, the energy grid and communities across the state. By pausing discretionary state environmental permits for new hyperscale data center construction for up to one year and imposing strict new rules that hold data center developers accountable and ensure benefits for local residents, Governor Hochul’s moratorium is addressing the ongoing concerns being raised by communities statewide. “As artificial intelligence grows more powerful and transforms our world as we know it, I’m standing up for New York’s farmers, small businesses and families — ensuring they aren’t left behind,” Governor Hochul said. “I enacted a nation-leading data center moratorium to protect our communities and hold developers accountable because I believe New Yorkers deserve a say in the decisions that affect their future. I’m proud to stand with Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Pat Ryan as we deliver a government that’s committed to fighting for working families across New York.” Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, “Across the country, Silicon Valley billionaires are trying to impose data centers on communities that don’t want them. Today, Governor Hochul, Representative Ryan, and I heard directly from Hudson Valley farmers on the impacts these data centers have on the farming communities in New York State. In July, Governor Hochul took action to protect farmers and working New Yorkers by instituting a one-year moratorium on data center construction. New York is once again showing Americans what is possible when we put working people at the center of our agenda.” Representative Pat Ryan said, “I’m so proud that here in the Hudson Valley we’re standing together and fighting back against these data center projects. We’re not going to let anyone — especially not a bunch of billionaire tech oligarchs — come in here and poison our water, drive up our utility bills, and build this powerful technology that even they acknowledge could have devastating impacts for humankind. This is a fight that transcends so many of the divides in our country right now because we’re all united in putting our community ahead of corporate profits. From our town boards, to the Governor’s nation-leading moratorium, to urgently needed action at the federal level, we’re going to continue our fight to ensure that we the people are the ones to decide what happens in our lives and in our communities.” State Senator Michelle Hinchey said, “Tech companies are racing to profit off the AI boom, building data centers wherever they can and leaving communities to bear the costs through increased pressure on water supplies, energy infrastructure, and utility bills. New York is responding the right way — with Governor Hochul’s nation-leading moratorium, which is critical to giving the state time to understand the risks involved and, above all, protect ratepayers from higher bills and our natural resources from depletion. New York has an opportunity to lead in responsible innovation, and I thank Governor Hochul for her leadership and Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez for bringing this fight to the federal level.” State Senator Kristen Gonzalez said, “Across New York State, communities are struggling with the impacts of unchecked data center development from demands on our natural resources to strains on our energy grid. On my New York Fights AI Data Centers Statewide Tour, I visited 13 proposed or existing data centers and met with communities, just like East Fishkill, fighting to protect their air, water, and land. I want to thank the Governor for her first-in-the-nation moratorium on the largest data centers and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez for her work introducing federal data center legislation.” “As artificial intelligence grows more powerful and transforms our world as we know it, I’m standing up for New York’s farmers, small businesses and families — ensuring they aren’t left behind.” Assemblymember Didi Barrett said, “It’s clear there is still more work to do in regulating data centers, and I look forward to working with Governor Hochul and her team to address many of the priorities in the Responsible Data Center Development Act, which includes ratepayer protections, robust host community benefits, renewable energy requirements and strong labor standards. artigo.texto: A inteligência artificial vai gerar bilhões em ganhos de eficiência. Para o bolso de quem? O dinheiro poupado pela IA pode ir para consumidores, empresas ou sumir numa briga de algoritmos. A inteligência artificial está redefinindo o valor no mercado acionário, com o setor de software caindo para a 31ª posição no ranking da BCG. A demanda por infraestrutura física, como chips e energia, impulsiona fabricantes de hardware. Paulo Mattosinho, da BCG, e Moisés Cona, do GRI Institute, destacam a necessidade de infraestrutura para IA. O estudo Value Creators Rankings 2026 mostra que empresas de infraestrutura têm bons retornos, enquanto software enfrenta desafios para monetizar a IA. A inteligência artificial está mudando o mapa de criação de valor no mercado acionário. O setor de software e serviços de tecnologia, que antes estava entre os quatro que mais geravam retorno aos acionistas, agora está na lanterna do ranking da Boston Consulting Group (BCG). Os novos dados mostram que a área caiu para a 31ª posição entre 35 segmentos. Enquanto isso, chips, componentes elétricos, energia e outras empresas ligadas à infraestrutura física da IA ganharam espaço. “Por mais de uma década, o segmento de tecnologia dominou o topo das nossas classificações. Agora, porém, o setor de software e serviços de TI despencou 27 posições. Isso acontece porque a IA, na sua fase atual de implantação, é altamente intensiva em infraestrutura (física e computacional)”, explica Paulo Mattosinho, diretor executivo e sócio do Boston Consulting Group (BCG). Segundo o estudo Value Creators Rankings 2026, a atual fase de implementação da inteligência artificial demanda investimentos em chips, data centers, energia e conectividade. Neste contexto, fabricantes de hardware, produtores de componentes elétricos e empresas de energia ganham espaço. “A capacidade computacional para treinar e rodar modelos de IA em escala relevante não existe sem chip, data center, energia e conectividade”, diz Moisés Cona, sócio e managing director do GRI Institute Infrastructure. Por isso, o dinheiro começa chegando às empresas que fornecem a estrutura necessária para a tecnologia funcionar. O executivo afirma que esse padrão não é inédito e já foi observado em ciclos tecnológicos anteriores. “O boom de investimentos em fibra óptica e infraestrutura de telecomunicações antecedeu o aumento de valor das empresas de internet que passariam a rodar sobre essa infraestrutura. Décadas atrás, investimentos em rede elétrica precederam os ganhos de produtividade das fábricas”, exemplifica Cona. Software e TI em baixa O estudo mostra que, enquanto as empresas de infraestrutura garantem bons retornos aos acionistas, as companhias de software ainda não conseguiram transformar o avanço da IA em crescimento de receita. “Elas enfrentam incertezas e custos elevados para monetizar a IA em escala sem perder suas margens”, complementa Mattosinho. “A própria IA começou a mudar a cadeia de valor do mercado de software: modelos de IA generativa e ferramentas de automação avançada começam a substituir licenças, processos e serviços de TI tradicionais”, acrescenta. Veja mais - Como a IA vai dar dinheiro? Empresas buscam modelo lucrativo apesar dos altos custos - Meta AI, Grok, Gemini e ChatGPT espalham desinformação e imprecisões sobre eleições, mostra estudo - Empresas brasileiras podem movimentar R$ 500 milhões com vendas de data centers Os números da Morningstar ajudam a ilustrar esse movimento. Em 2025, o índice que acompanha as empresas de tecnologia dos Estados Unidos subiu 21,4 pontos porcentuais, dos quais 11,9 pontos vieram da indústria de semicondutores. Fabricantes de chips que impulsionam a computação de IA, como a Nvidia e a Broadcom, registraram forte crescimento em 2025. Em contrapartida, as empresas de software tiveram dificuldades. A empresa de gerenciamento de relacionamento com o cliente (CRM) baseada em nuvem, Salesforce, por exemplo, registrou uma queda de 20,2%. A provedora de serviços de TI corporativos ServiceNow teve queda de 27,8%. “O grande desafio para os executivos de software é equilibrar duas exigências: precisam continuar investindo no desenvolvimento de soluções de IA para não perderem relevância no longo prazo, mas precisam entregar metas de curto prazo e margens saudáveis”, afirma o sócio da BCG. O economista Felipe Araújo, doutorando em economia pela FGV, afirma que existe um hiato entre a adoção da inteligência artificial e conseguir, de fato, aumentar a produtividade. “Muitas organizações estão incentivando a implementação de IA, mas ainda estão descobrindo exatamente onde a tecnologia consegue gerar ganhos efetivos. Algumas dessas experiências vão funcionar e aumentar a produtividade, mas existe um processo de aprendizado sobre quais aplicações realmente geram valor”, diz. Criação de valor ou euforia do mercado A ruptura tecnológica promovida pela inteligência artificial impulsiona uma movimentação significativa entre empresas de todos os segmentos. Uma projeção da consultoria Gartner diz que o gasto global em IA deve superar US$ 2,59 trilhões em 2026. Segundo Araújo, essa não é a primeira vez que se observa uma euforia em torno de uma ruptura tecnológica. “Eu teria cautela em afirmar que estamos diante de uma migração estrutural da criação de valor do software para a infraestrutura física”, contrapõe. “Falaria mais em um possível overshooting (excesso de investimento): existe uma corrida para antecipar uma transformação potencialmente muito grande, e o risco é que o investimento em capacidade se antecipe à velocidade efetiva de monetização da tecnologia”, afirma. No Brasil, um relatório da GRI mostrou que 76% dos investidores do segmento planejam ampliar os investimentos. “O próprio mercado reconhece que essa é uma janela de cerca de dois anos, e que, uma vez fechada, dificilmente se reabre na mesma dimensão”, afirma Cona. “Se falharmos em enfrentar os desafios necessários para garantir atratividade, que passam, entre outras, pelas e

artigo.texto: Aligned Data Centers files court documents regarding Pataskala's rejection of data center PATASKALA, Ohio (WSYX) — Aligned Data Centers has filed court documents with the City of Pataskala to appeal the city’s ruling to block a proposed data center from being built near Mink and Broad Streets. This comes after Pataskala City Council members sided with residents and rejected the proposed data center at a council meeting in August. The proposed Aligned Data Centers facility was planned as a 200-megawatt, three-building site. The project had been at the center of community discussion for months, drawing concerns from residents who said a large-scale development would change their neighborhoods. Pataskala voters will still have the chance to weigh in on a potential data center ban during the November election. ABC6 reached out to city council on Aligned Data Centers plan to appeal and if this could impact the potential the data center ban. Council said they have no comment right now. This story will be updated.

artigo.texto: Marcelo Francisco de Oliveira O Redata, programa federal que suspende tributos na compra de equipamentos para data centers, já começa a estimular novos investimentos destinados para a construção de operações, que podem chegar a R$ 20 bilhões. Quatro gigantes do segmento – as americanas Ascenty e Scala, a britânica Terranova e a brasileira Takoda – com operações em cidades da Região Metropolitana de Campinas (RMC) – já teriam manifestado interesse no desenvolvimento de novos projetos ou expansão de centros de processamentos já existentes, segundo o Portal Veja. Odata projeta novos investimentos na região de Campinas A RMC é vista como a “Faria Lima” dos data centers pela Odata, em uma alusão ao maior centro financeiro do País, na Capital paulista. Com 25 operações em vários países, incluindo a RMC, a empresa brasileira fundada em 2014, prepara uma segunda onda de investimentos no Brasil. O foco de grande parte dos recursos será a RMC, segundo Ricardo Alário, CEO da companhia, em entrevista ao portal NeoFeed. “Nossa Faria Lima dos data centers é a região de Campinas, Hortolândia, Sumaré e São Paulo”, disse, sem revelar valores. Após concluir obra em SP, Twenty Four Seven negocia operação em Campinas Outro grupo que planeja construir centro de processamento de dados na Região de Campinas é a 247 Datacenters, conhecida como Twenty Four Seven, de capital nacional e que tem estre seus sócios a Kinea Investimentos, do Itaú. A empresas construiu recentemente uma operação na Capital, em fase de ligamento com o sistema nacional, e vai expandir os negócios com uma unidade em Campinas. Para montar operação em Campinas, a empresa vai receber benefícios do município, como redução ou isenção do Impostos Predial e Territorial Urbano (IPTU), sobre Serviços (ISS), de Transmissão de Bens Imóveis (ITBI) e ISS na construção civil, além de taxa de aprovação de projetos, emolumentos e alvará de uso. A unidade terá potencial de até 300 megawatts de capacidade instalada. Além dos imóveis: Airbnb passa disponibilizar aluguel de carro na região A plataforma online Airbnb está expandindo seus negócios no Brasil. Além de aluguel de imóveis ou quartos, a multinacional passa a oferecer aluguel de carros em 300 cidades brasileiras, incluindo a cidade de Campinas nesta primeira fase. O plano da Airbnb tem como foco principal os turistas, incluindo o novo serviço para complementar e ampliar a experiência dos viajantes. Retração na construção: número de unidades lançadas na região cai 31,8% no primeiro semestre O setor da construção civil registou forte retração em número de unidades lançadas no primeiro semestre de 2026, segundo números do Secovi-SP. De janeiro a julho, as construtoras e incorporadoras colocaram no mercado regional um total de 4.016 novas unidades. Número esse que representa uma retração de 31,8% ante o mesmo período do ano passado. A quantidade também está bem distante do total lançado no segundo semestre de 2025, quando foram registradas 8.085, unidades. Segundo a pesquisa do Secovi, no acumulado dos últimos doze meses, 12.101 imóveis foram lançados na Região de Campinas. Esse número representa 18,1% na participação total dos lançamentos ocorridos no Estado no período. A região de Campinas só foi superada pela Região Metropolitana de São Paulo, onde foram lançadas 12.643 unidades, ou 18,9% da participação total.

artigo.texto: PIERCE TOWNSHIP, Ohio — A new data center proposal in Pierce Township turned what was scheduled to be a regular Zoning Commission meeting into an hour-long referendum on how the controversial facilities should be regulated Tuesday. People packed the Locust Corner Elementary School gymnasium to get their turn telling Zoning Commission members what they'd like to see done to limit the potential impact on utility rates, water consumption, noise levels, lighting and more. To get inside, just about everyone had to pass through a net of Pierce Township residents passing out fliers against them being welcomed to town. Kathy Cummins told us she was against the facilities being built in Pierce Township for many reasons, but the location of Crane Data Center's 300-acre proposal directly across US 52 from the now-closed Walter C. Beckjord Generating Station, still contaminated with toxic coal ash, was the most concerning. "That's what makes this site particularly challenging," Cummins told us before the meeting began. WATCH: Pierce Township residents pack a meeting on data center rules with a proposal looming A Crane representative told us after their presentation to Pierce Township Trustees that they had considered building on the Beckjord site, but ruled against it due to the ongoing contamination. We asked another member of the group passing out fliers, Bruce Cummins, what he thought about a deal allowing Crane to move in if they agreed to clean up Beckjord. "If the site was remediated, the coal ash was removed, I think that's a different conversation," he said. Bob Hucker told us he attended the meeting because he was against any new large-scale data center construction. "People need to know about this," Hucker said. Zoning Commission Chairman Jeff Stitt told the crowd before public comment began that they have been tasked with establishing data center rules for the entire township, and no official application had been submitted. Therefore, he said there was no specific project they could address directly. When asked about Crane's proposal, Stitt said that was not a formal submission they could review. "There is no one who has submitted an application, so there is no area planned," he said. "That was just an area someone expressed concern in." That sentiment was echoed weeks earlier when Pierce Township Trustee Allen Freeman talked with our I-Team. "It's basically a sales pitch, but it was not a proposal. It wasn't a zoning request. It doesn't even rise to that level, so we're not entertaining it," he said. At Tuesday's meeting, Freeman pledged transparency as the Zoning Commission built data center regulations and the trustees considered them. "This stays open. This stays transparent. Anything that we discuss, you're not going to see an NDA (non-disclosure agreement) that's going to block it," he said. Stitt urged patience as the process could take months to complete. "We don't want to make a snap decision because we live here," he said. Pierce Township has a moratorium on data center construction through May 31, 2027. Stitt said if the rules aren't prepared by the time the moratorium expires, it could be extended. Click here to see Crane's full presentation.

artigo.texto: UKIAH, CA., 10/6/26 — Mendocino County’s ban on new data centers will run until August 2028, with an exception about the size of a shipping container. The ban was put in place while a committee works with staff on a permanent ordinance that would govern how and whether the county permits data centers in the future. Supervisors voted 4-1 Tuesday to extend the moratorium they adopted Sept. 1 by 22 months and 15 days, to Aug. 21, 2028, the longest stretch state law allows. They also narrowed the terms. As Supervisor Ted Williams described the change to the board, facilities that draw less than 3 megawatts of electricity are no longer subject to the moratorium. The ad hoc committee of Williams and District 3 supervisor John Haschak met with county staff over lunch, worked out the change, and the board adopted it the same afternoon. Supervisor Maureen Mulheren voted no, calling the threshold “not fully developed.” “This idea that we’re having three megawatts coming up during a meeting as a path forward,” she said, was something she would’ve wanted staff and the community to work out first. The first version of the moratorium, a 45-day urgency ordinance, was set to expire Oct. 16. Deputy County Counsel Matthew Kiedrowski told the board the next meeting would’ve fallen outside the 45-day limit. Why 3 megawatts Williams, reporting for the board’s two-supervisor ad hoc committee of Haschak and himself, said 3 megawatts is roughly what PG&E will deliver through standard service before a project needs its own transformers or a substation. “3 megawatts would allow a data center the size of a shipping container,” he said. The point, he said, was to let local businesses use small data projects without tripping over the ordinance while the county spends the next 20 months writing a permanent rule, and still keep out “gigawatt-size facilities.” Richard Angley, the interim director of Planning and Building Services, said he believed the ordinance his staff has been drafting uses 20 megawatts as a threshold, a figure drawn from other jurisdictions. “The three megawatts came up today,” he said. Supervisor Madeline Cline said she was “not particularly in love with this arbitrary setting” of a number, but preferred allowances to a blanket ban. Williams, who proposed the figure, said it was “still somewhat arbitrary.” The board took the item up at 9:33 a.m. and couldn’t finish it before lunch break. Williams and Cline wanted a power threshold so telecommunications facilities wouldn’t be caught by the ban. Mulheren said she wouldn’t vote for any megawatt figure that day. “I do not know what that should be,” she said. “From a politics standpoint, a ban on data centers is great politics,” Cline said. As actual policy, she said, a flat-out ban is problematic. A two-year clock The board also asked whether two years was too long. Interim CEO Sara Pierce said Planning and Building is short-staffed and anything sooner than two years “would be stretched.” Later in the same discussion, senior planner Mark Cliser said the permanent ordinance “is just about done,” and a first draft could reach the Planning Commission in six or seven months. However, in the afternoon, Angley said 10 months was possible “in an absolute perfect world,” but “the likelihood of that is very slim.” Supervisor John Haschak said these things can take a while, explaining that the county has worked on an ordinance for low-intensity camping, the Hipcamp model, for about five years and still doesn’t have one. Adam Gaska, executive director of the Mendocino County Farm Bureau, told the board the bureau opposed the blanket ban. “We believe a ban is a knee-jerk reaction stemming from fear and not out of a real and actual present threat,” he said. Eileen Russell of Mendocino Forest Products, who asked the board in September to leave room for a data center at the Ukiah sawmill, said in the morning that “people have stopped the conversation” about investing here since word of the moratorium got out. In the afternoon, after the 3-megawatt change, she said a data center the size of a storage container is “not really allowing the type of development or innovation that could take Mendocino Forest Products into the next generation.” She described a power plant burning forest residuals next to the sawmill, selling its power to a data center. Doug Stewart, president of the Anderson Valley Winegrowers Association, said he wanted a limit, not a two-year moratorium. After the change, he said it “did address what I came here to discuss.” Dolly Riley, chair of the Redwood Valley Municipal Advisory Council, supported the full extension. “Mendocino County does not have the water to spare,” she said. What else changed over lunch The lunch rewrite made two other changes. The ordinance had exempted ordinary office, retail, school, hospital and industrial computer equipment. Williams said that under that wording a large retailer could have built a data center for its own operations. That exemption is gone. Hospitals and healthcare facilities are now exempted as public safety and emergency facilities, and the requirement that those be owned and operated by a public agency was dropped, because the county’s hospitals aren’t. The ordinance doesn’t name a project. It says the county “anticipates receiving” inquiries and applications. The moratorium can end sooner than 2028. Kiedrowski said the board can terminate it once it adopts a permanent data center ordinance. Haschak moved the amended ordinance with two conditions: a report back to the board every four months, and a new ad hoc committee to work with staff on the permanent ordinance. Chair Bernie Norvell named Cline and Williams to it. Mulheren said she assumed that committee would take up the question she voted no over. “If three megawatts is too small, what isn’t too small?” she asked.

artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia 7 de outubro de 2026, às 12:20 Por Ana Paula Machado São Paulo, 07/10/2026 – A BYD depende de uma mudança na regra sobre conteúdo local de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) para definir investimentos de R$ 500 milhões no País. O vice-presidente sênior da empresa no Brasil, Alexandre Baldy, disse à Broadcast que a companhia tem conversado com o governo para aumentar o porcentual de localização dos equipamentos. Pelas regras atuais, é considerada nacional uma bateria que tenha até 15% de componentes produzidos no mercado brasileiro. Segundo Baldy, na estrutura de uma bateria para armazenamento de energia elétrica, os packs contêm entre 80% e 83% dos componentes. Já os inversores, onde se concentram os transformadores, respondem por 15% a 17% das peças. “Do jeito como está, isso não estimula a fabricação de BESS, porque posso trazer da China, onde é mais competitivo”, disse o executivo. “Queremos fazer aqui no Brasil os packs de bateria não somente os inversores. O plano é importar a célula da bateria, porque isso envolve transferência de tecnologia e é uma decisão de governos, não de uma empresa.” Baldy ressaltou ainda que, caso a regra seja mudada, a BYD vai instalar a fábrica de BESS na Zona Franca de Manaus (ZFM) e poderá gerar entre 400 e 500 empregos. A unidade, de acordo com ele, teria capacidade para produzir até 10 gigawatts (GW). “Não posso passar o que passei com a fábrica de painel solar em Campinas (SP), que hoje trabalha com 82% de ociosidade. Lá já tivemos 700 funcionários, hoje, trabalhamos com 300 empregados em um turno de produção e mais de 50% de capacidade ociosa”, disse Baldy. Isso aconteceu, segundo ele, porque o governo anterior zerou as tarifas de importação de painel solar e a medida, completa Baldy, prejudicou os investimentos realizados pela companhia. “Quando se mudou a regra do jogo, quebrou o nosso planejamento. Por isso, vamos aguardar um retorno do governo para decidirmos se vamos ou não investir em uma fábrica de BESS no Brasil.” O executivo ressaltou que os recursos, de R$ 500 milhões, são próprios e garantidos pela matriz, mas disse que a China só vai liberar o investimento após essa definição e com todos os documentos assinados para a instalação da unidade. “Nós precisamos que o BNDES financie os nossos clientes, aqueles que devem participar do leilão (armazenamento de capacidade de potência) de dezembro. Dinheiro nós temos.” Quanto ao pedido de aumento de carga na fábrica de Camaçari, na Bahia, Baldy disse que a companhia teve de pedir à Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) um reforço para sustentar os investimentos de expansão da unidade. Segundo ele, a empresa havia pedido uma elevação de fornecimento somente para a distribuidora local, a Coelba, mas teria de fazer o pedido também à Aneel por comprar energia no Mercado Livre. “Hoje, a fábrica usa 1,5 megawatts (MW) e precisamos de 13 MW com a estimativa de chegarmos a 22 MW”, disse Baldy. “Sem energia não tem indústria.” Contato: ana.machado@estadao.com Veja também

artigo.texto: Cisco's Jeetu Patel: AI Agents Are Coming, and Data Centers Are a National Security Issue Jeetu Patel is bullish on AI, especially AI agents. He also thinks the technology brings real national security stakes. Patel is Cisco's president and chief product officer. He was in Austin for WebexOne, Cisco's major user conference, where the company showed off its next wave of AI tools. Cisco has a significant presence in Austin, including an innovation hub. "One of the most seismic shifts in history" Patel says AI is moving fast. He believes it can help solve some of the world's biggest problems, including disease, poverty, and education. "This technology is one of the most seismic innovations and shifts that we have experienced in the history of humanity," Patel said. "But it also has a meaningful amount of risk that we have to make sure that we mitigate." His outlook is optimistic, with a clear view of the downsides. "I am, on balance, a net optimist," he said. "I feel like this is going to be one of the most amazing technologies that allows us to do things we could never dream of doing before. But I don't wear rose-colored glasses." ALSO| This vest simulates getting shot in the line of duty so officers can train for it before What are AI agents? Patel says the next big wave is AI agents. These are tools that take on tasks, make decisions, and do more work on our behalf. Cisco sits on the front lines of cybersecurity, and Patel says the company is working to reduce the risks that come with that shift. As agents get more powerful, he says, they create new challenges. One is network strain. "Agents consume about five times more network bandwidth for conducting the same exact task as a human does," Patel said. The data center debate Data centers have become a hot topic across Texas. Patel says the stakes go beyond the economy and changing the landscape. His warning is that if the country does not keep up with demand for computing power, it could face a national security problem as AI agents and bad actors multiply their capabilities. "You're going to have trillions of agents around the world, and they can start attacking critical infrastructure if we're not careful," Patel said. "That could cost lives. The only way you can defend against it is by making sure that your defenses are also at machine scale." Machine-scale defense takes computing power, and computing power takes data centers. "So I feel like for the safety and security of humanity, data centers are actually a very essential ingredient," he said. "It's not something that's an elective that we can either choose to do or not do, because it actually won't keep us safe." Texas and the AI buildout Patel says Texas is well positioned for the AI buildout. He adds that the country as a whole will need more power, computing capacity, network bandwidth, and security to keep pace.

artigo.texto: CAMINUS Signs Contract Manufacturing Agreement with Amprius Technologies for US Pouch Cell Production Agreement covers Amprius silicon-anode pouch cells from partial assembly through full cell production at CAMINUS’s Indianapolis facility INDIANAPOLIS, Oct. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — CAMINUS (formerly EnPower), a U.S. manufacturer of lithium-ion battery cells and electrodes, today announced a contract manufacturing agreement with Amprius Technologies, Inc. (NYSE: AMPX), a developer and manufacturer of silicon-anode lithium-ion batteries. Under the agreement, CAMINUS will manufacture Amprius-designed pouch cells at its Indianapolis facility, adding domestic production capacity for Amprius customers in aviation, defense, and uncrewed systems. The agreement spans the cell production process, from partial assembly of Amprius-supplied components to full cell production, allowing various cell formats to be produced in a staged manner that fits each format’s volume and qualification status. The structure supports Amprius’s contract manufacturing strategy, which enables rapid capacity expansion with minimal capital investment. Qualification builds are already in progress, and volume production is planned for 1Q27. Adrian Yao, founder and CEO of CAMINUS, said: Manufacturing execution is a critical bottleneck in Western supply chains and is increasingly a differentiating right to win, “This agreement highlights the productive synergies within our domestic battery ecosystem: Advanced product designs combined with established manufacturing capabilities enables unprecedented speed to market for domestically designed and produced cells. We are happy to provide near-immediate capacity for companies like Amprius.” Ronnie Tao, Chief Business Officer at Amprius Technologies, said: Building a resilient, NDAA-compliant supply chain is central to how Amprius serves its defense customers, “CAMINUS shares our commitment to American manufacturing, and its pouch cell expertise fits our needs very well. Together, we’re strengthening the domestic battery base that mission-critical systems depend on.” CAMINUS operates a 92,000-square-foot (and expanding), vertically integrated powder-to-cell facility in Indianapolis, with end-to-end production capabilities spanning slurry mixing, high-quality electrode coating, automated cell assembly, and formation. This rare domestic capability supports an NDAA Section 842-conforming supply chain for defense and uncrewed systems. Contract manufacturing is one of CAMINUS’s two lines of business, alongside manufacturing of its own cell and pack products. artigo.texto: Clearway Energy, a United States-based renewable energy owner, has agreed through a subsidiary to acquire three BESS projects in Utah with a combined capacity of about 210 MW. The transfer will not take place immediately, however, because the closing depends on customary conditions and on certain third-party actions. It is expected to occur in the fourth quarter of 2027. artigo.texto: Cabinet Secretary for Environment, Climate Change and Forestry Deborah Barasa speaking during the launch of the Kenya Guide for Strategic Engagement in Carbon Markets 2026./KNA Kenya has moved to strengthen its participation in global carbon markets with the launch of a new guide aimed at attracting high-integrity climate investments while protecting communities, ecosystems and the country’s national climate targets. Cabinet Secretary for Environment, Climate Change and Forestry Deborah Barasa said the Kenya Guide for Strategic Engagement in Carbon Markets 2026 would provide a framework for ensuring that carbon-market investments generate genuine environmental benefits and lasting value for Kenyans. The guide was officially launched in Nairobi on Monday in the presence of Environment and Climate Change Principal Secretary Dr Eng Festus Ng’eno and senior representatives from Switzerland, South Korea, the European Union, the United Kingdom and Norway. Barasa said the guide marked a critical milestone in making Kenya’s engagement in carbon markets more strategic, transparent and aligned with national interests. “Kenya is open to responsible and high-integrity carbon investment. We are seeking quality, integrity and lasting development value,” she said. She noted that carbon markets presented a major opportunity to mobilise private capital into renewable energy, forestry, agriculture, waste management and clean cooking, while creating jobs, supporting innovation and facilitating technology transfer. However, she cautioned that such investments must not come at the expense of communities or the environment. The guide is expected to provide greater clarity and predictability for investors, project developers and communities, while complementing ongoing reforms, including the establishment of the National Carbon Registry and strengthening of Kenya’s legal framework for implementing Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Barasa called for partnerships that deliver measurable climate benefits, strong environmental and social safeguards and equitable sharing of benefits generated by carbon projects. She said the government’s priority was now to translate the new policy framework into concrete action and position carbon markets as a credible pathway towards a low-carbon, climate-resilient and inclusive economy. Environment and Climate Change Principal Secretary Dr Eng. Festus Ng’eno said Kenya was moving beyond viewing carbon markets as a future opportunity and was positioning itself as a key player in shaping the emerging global carbon trading system. “For years, carbon markets were discussed as a future opportunity. That future is now here,” Ng’eno said, noting that international trading frameworks under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement were becoming operational. He said the new guide would strengthen Kenya’s strategic, transparent and high-integrity participation in international carbon markets. A key provision of the guide is a 10 million-tonne cumulative ceiling for international transfers of carbon dioxide equivalent between 2025 and 2030. Ng’eno said the ceiling would help safeguard Kenya’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) targets and minimise the risk of the country overselling its carbon credits. He said Kenya’s carbon-market strategy was anchored on four principles: predictability, uncompromising integrity, putting people before carbon, and creating value beyond carbon. Under the framework, carbon projects will be expected to provide tangible benefits to local communities through equitable benefit-sharing, technology transfer, skills development, employment and local value creation. The government said the approach would ensure that carbon markets contribute to national development without undermining Kenya’s climate commitments or the rights and livelihoods of communities hosting carbon projects. The launch brought together Switzerland’s Ambassador to Kenya Mirko Giulietti, South Korean Ambassador Kang Hyung-shik, EU Deputy Ambassador Ondrej Simek, British Deputy High Commissioner and Development Director Diana Dalton, and Norwegian Minister Counsellor and Deputy Head of Mission Christian Gahre. Kenya is now expected to focus on implementing the new framework as it seeks to attract climate finance while maintaining strong safeguards against environmental degradation, inequitable benefit-sharing and risks to the country’s carbon budget.

artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia 7 de outubro de 2026, às 15:50 Por Aramis Merki II São Paulo, 07/10/2026 – O avanço da inteligência artificial está levando empresas a rever como armazenam e processam dados, em um movimento que combina a busca por soberania da informação com a necessidade de controlar custos de infraestrutura. No caso da B3, ter data center próprio é uma escolha para proteger informações do mercado financeiro, de acordo com o líder da área responsável por alocar equipamentos de processamento de dados em data centers externos (colocation, no termo em inglês), Eduardo Yukio Kashiwakura. Segundo ele, a B3 armazena informações de brasileiros e de clientes institucionais, incluindo dados sobre carteiras de investimentos, posições e operações no mercado financeiro. “Para nós, ter um data center próprio, é questão de soberania dos dados”, disse durante painel no evento Data Center World Brasil, em São Paulo. Já empresas que não têm escala para operar estruturas próprias buscam alternativas híbridas para garantir segurança e governança sobre os dados. É o caso do Grupo Santa Cruz Distribuidora de Medicamentos, segundo o diretor de informação da companhia, Jorge Stakowiak. Ele afirma que a empresa não tem capacidade para manter um data center próprio e, por isso, busca combinar diferentes ambientes de infraestrutura, com regras de governança para determinar quais dados podem ser utilizados em aplicações de inteligência artificial. Para o diretor, a arquitetura de infraestrutura precisa ser flexível e pode combinar ambientes próprios, terceirizados e híbridos, de acordo com o tipo de informação e as necessidades do negócio. A definição de onde cada dado será armazenado e processado passa, nesse contexto, por critérios de segurança, governança e custo, e não apenas pela propriedade do data center. Foss & Company, which was founded in 1983, has deployed more than $11 billion in tax equity since its inception. artigo.texto: A diretoria da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) decidiu, nesta terça-feira (6/10), abrir consulta pública de 30 dias para o aprimoramento da proposta de custeio da contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), na modalidade de reserva de capacidade. A consulta ficará aberta de 8 de outubro a 9 de novembro de 2026. A área técnica da agência apontou, em parecer de agosto, que a melhor alternativa para os custos da contratação de baterias é o rateio entre todos os geradores de energia. Contudo, a proposta é que o pagamento seja modulado em função do chamado Índice de Flexibilidade (IF). Com esse critério, aquelas usinas com maior flexibilidade pagariam menos (25% do encargo), enquanto aquelas com menor flexibilidade pagariam 100%. A alternativa, ainda de acordo com a área técnica, apresenta o “melhor equilíbrio entre aderência à finalidade do encargo, estabilidade do custeio, objetividade técnica e viabilidade regulatória”. O tema é controverso, especialmente porque há projetos de lei no Congresso buscando derrubar essa previsão de rateio dos custos. A Lei nº 15.269/2025, de modernização do setor elétrico, previu expressamente que os custos decorrentes da contratação de baterias sejam rateados apenas entre os geradores de energia elétrica, excluindo a possibilidade de custeio pelos consumidores. Os dois leilões de baterias, inéditos, estão previstos para dezembro deste ano. O diretor Gentil Nogueira, relator, comentou que a proposta em discussão trata da “norma perene”, que, se aprovada, poderá ser utilizada para o custeio dos sistemas de armazenamento que devem ser contratados no leilão de baterias marcado para dezembro. No entanto, ele salientou que o próprio edital do leilão, ainda a ser aprovado, pode trazer disciplina para esse custeio específico. O edital precisa ser aprovado até o fim de outubro, de maneira a cumprir a regra de publicação com 30 dias de antecedência. Por Renan Monteiro e Luciana Collet

artigo.texto: BYD is ahead of Tesla in battery-electric vehicle sales through September 2026, but the competition extends beyond vehicle volumes. Battery costs, international manufacturing, charging access and recurring software revenue are shaping how the two companies pursue growth. BYD sold 1,629,957 passenger battery-electric vehicles (BEVs) during the first nine months of 2026, compared with 1,324,681 global Tesla deliveries. That puts BYD ahead by 305,276 vehicles, or approximately 23 percent. The companies are competing in an expanding market. The IEA’s Global EV Outlook 2026 forecasts 23 million electric-car sales in 2026, representing 28 percent of global car sales. This market forecast includes battery-electric cars and plug-in hybrids. BYD vs Tesla Sales: The 2026 Comparison A meaningful comparison must separate BYD’s battery-electric vehicles from its plug-in hybrids. Tesla sells fully electric vehicles, while BYD’s wider sales totals include both technologies. BYD’s third-quarter lead reached 275,946 vehicles, accounting for most of its cumulative advantage through September. Its quarterly passenger-BEV sales increased 36.87 percent sequentially, indicating a substantial acceleration. Tesla recorded faster percentage growth over the nine-month period, although its Q3 deliveries remained below the corresponding quarter of 2025. These results show why quarterly momentum and cumulative sales should be assessed separately. BYD’s EV Portfolio Supports Manufacturing Scale BYD competes across multiple price categories through battery-electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids. That breadth gives it more opportunities to serve buyers with different budgets, driving patterns and access to charging. Plug-in hybrids also provide a route into markets where charging infrastructure remains limited. However, their sales should remain separate when assessing which company leads the fully electric segment. Tesla’s business is more concentrated. Model 3 and Model Y accounted for 478,237 of its 486,532 Q3 deliveries, approximately 98.3 percent, according to Tesla’s Q3 2026 production and delivery results. Tesla Investor Relations This concentration supports production standardization but makes demand for those two models particularly important. BYD’s wider portfolio spreads its commercial opportunities across more vehicle segments, while adding complexity to manufacturing, distribution and inventory management. Battery Integration Strengthens BYD’s Cost Strategy Battery economics remain central to electric-car affordability. Cell costs, pack design, energy efficiency and manufacturing yields influence how competitively automakers can price their vehicles. BYD combines battery development with vehicle and component manufacturing. Its Blade Battery technology forms part of a broader approach that integrates batteries, electric powertrains and vehicle platforms. That integration can help coordinate product design and production costs. During price competition, manufacturing efficiencies create room to reduce prices, improve specifications or protect margins. However, integration alone does not prove superior profitability. Factory utilization, warranty costs, product mix and selling prices determine how much of any manufacturing advantage reaches the bottom line. Tesla also brings substantial experience in electric powertrains, vehicle efficiency and large-scale manufacturing. Comparing the companies’ cost positions ultimately requires financial results alongside delivery figures. Tesla’s Charging Ecosystem Adds Customer Value Tesla’s charging infrastructure and integration of navigation, charging and vehicle software remain important elements of its ownership proposition. For drivers, charging convenience depends on more than maximum charging speed. Station coverage, reliability, waiting times, pricing and compatibility can all influence whether an electric vehicle suits everyday travel. BYD’s battery and vehicle technology strengthens its product offering, but international growth also requires dependable charging arrangements, service networks and spare-parts availability. As competing charging networks expand, both companies must demonstrate how their vehicles reduce the time, cost and inconvenience associated with electric-car ownership. Energy Storage Broadens Tesla’s Growth Opportunities Tesla deployed 13.7 GWh of energy-storage products in Q3 2026, demonstrating the scale of a business that operates alongside vehicle manufacturing. Energy storage gives Tesla exposure to demand from utilities, renewable-energy developers and customers seeking backup power. Its software and autonomous-driving investments could also generate additional revenue beyond the initial vehicle sale. Those opportunities require separate evaluation. Storage deployments do not establish storage profitability, while autonomous-driving revenue depends on technical performance, regulatory approvals, customer adoption and commercial execution. Tesla’s Q3 financial results are scheduled for October 21, 2026. Until then, delivery and deployment figures provide an incomplete picture of quarterly margins and cash flow. BYD’s Overseas Expansion Brings New Execution Risks The supplied report states that BYD’s September global vehicle sales reached 463,561, up 17 percent year on year. Overseas passenger-vehicle and pickup shipments increased 153.9 percent to 179,877. These broader figures include categories beyond passenger BEVs and should not be compared directly with Tesla deliveries. International expansion can diversify BYD’s demand and increase manufacturing scale. Local production may improve delivery times and help address market-access requirements. Nevertheless, export shipments are different from sales to final customers. Sustained growth requires dealers to sell inventory, customers to receive reliable service and factories to operate at commercially viable utilization levels. artigo.texto: Data Centers: Dalton Utilities details water usage, power costs, citizens repeat pause request Published 3:01 am Wednesday, October 7, 2026 City officials said Monday night that work is continuing behind the scenes to examine issues surrounding data centers and other large power users, while Dalton Utilities offered new details about the financial safeguards and revenue associated with serving the rapidly growing industry. The discussion came amid repeated calls from some residents for the city to impose a six-month moratorium on new data center development while it considers regulations specifically governing the facilities. Before the public comment portion of Monday’s meeting, Mayor Sams said city staff are continuing work the council has requested involving large power users. “I want to make [clear] that our staff are continuing to work on doing their due diligence as we have asked of them as it relates to large power users, which would include but not be limited to data centers,” Sams said. Sams did not announce a decision on a moratorium or a data center-specific ordinance. City Administrator Andrew Parker said he had invited Dalton Utilities CEO John Thomas to speak because of the amount of public comment council members have heard about data centers during recent meetings. Parker cautioned that the utility’s role represents only one part of the broader discussion and that some issues surrounding large power users and data centers fall outside Dalton Utilities’ purview. “We’ll continue to provide more information as we move forward,” Parker said. Water use Thomas addressed water use, electricity supply and rates, financial protections for other utility customers and revenue generated by data center customers. On water, Thomas said the large data center being developed in Whitfield County is being built with a closed-loop cooling system in which water is initially added and then recirculated rather than continuously replaced. Thomas said some water can be lost through evaporation or other means but said the amount is expected to be small. “It’s not expected to use really much more water than a restaurant, two restaurants or so that you might think of around town,” Thomas said. Thomas also said Dalton Utilities has water capacity available because its industrial customers now use about one-third as much water as they once did. Power and protecting other customers Thomas said Dalton Utilities has always purchased some of its electricity from the regional wholesale market and has never supplied its entire electric load solely from resources it owns. As population, manufacturing and other economic activity grow across the Southeast, increased demand can constrain that regional market and put upward pressure on wholesale electricity costs, he said. Thomas emphasized that electric providers do not all have the same mix of owned and purchased power and therefore may experience those pressures differently. When Dalton Utilities serves a data center directly, Thomas said, the utility uses several measures intended to protect its other customers from financial exposure created by the enormous electric loads involved. Data center customers are subject to what Thomas described as exceptional deposit requirements. They also pay a fixed monthly demand charge tied to the amount of electric capacity available to them, regardless of whether they use that full capacity during a particular month. Dalton Utilities’ largest data center customer is treated differently still. Thomas said the customer is billed weekly for electricity rather than monthly and maintains a prepaid account. Each week, the customer pays for the amount of electricity Dalton Utilities expects it to consume during the following week. Data center customers also pay upfront for local infrastructure Dalton Utilities must construct to connect their facilities to the electric grid, Thomas said, rather than leaving the utility to recover those costs through rates over time. Millions in revenue Thomas also put numbers Monday night to the financial benefits Dalton Utilities says data centers provide. According to Thomas, the utility’s two largest data center customers generated just under $5 million in state and local sales tax revenue in 2025. Data center revenue has also substantially increased the amount Dalton Utilities transfers annually to the city’s general fund, according to Thomas. Dalton Utilities transfers 5% of its revenue to the city. Thomas said that in each of the past four years, the annual transfer would have been approximately $3.5 million to $4 million lower without revenue from data center customers. The city’s adopted 2026 General Fund budget includes $15.55 million from the Dalton Utilities transfer, compared with $9.1 million in budgeted property-tax revenue. Councilmember Steve Farrow noted that the utility transfer reduces the amount of revenue the city must raise through property taxes. Parker said the city’s 2026 budget includes approximately $15.5 million from Dalton Utilities transfer payments, compared with approximately $9.1 million in budgeted property tax revenue. Resident renews call for moratorium The presentation did not resolve the broader questions that have brought residents to recent city and county government meetings. During public comment, Carmen Shuler again asked the city to adopt a six-month moratorium on data center development while officials develop a data center-specific ordinance. Shuler said a group of concerned residents has submitted a proposal seeking the moratorium and argued that a temporary pause would give the city time to research standards and best practices. “A moratorium is a pause, not a ban,” Shuler said. She asked whether city officials have made decisions on either the requested moratorium or development of a data center ordinance and questioned whether the city has sought consultants or impact studies to help evaluate future development. Oct 7, 2026 Foss & Company Closes $58 Million Tax Equity Deal for GridStor Battery Storage in Hidalgo County, Texas Foss & Company has finalized a $58 million partnership flip deal to fund a utility-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) in Hidalgo County, Texas, constructed by GridStor, as announced in a press release. This transaction, which yields Section 48 Investment Tax Credits, is the second collaboration between the tax equity syndicator and the battery storage developer. The battery storage asset remains on track to be operational in October 2026, according to the release. Bryen Alperin, Partner and Managing Director at Foss & Company, stated that the deal highlights the strength of the firm's partnership with GridStor and its ongoing confidence in utility-scale battery storage as an asset class. He added that with grid operators increasingly depending on storage to balance supply and demand, the firm is pleased to assist in bringing projects like this one in Hidalgo County online, and anticipates expanding its pipeline with GridStor in the coming years. Spencer Mash, SVP of Finance and Head of Capital Markets at GridStor, expressed satisfaction with completing the financing with Foss and gratitude for their backing of the BESS asset class. He noted that the transaction mirrors the sector's continued maturation and the rising confidence of financing partners in the role battery energy storage can play in supporting grid reliability and flexibility where it is most needed. The deal adds another utility-scale battery storage asset to Foss & Company's expanding renewable energy tax equity portfolio. Established in 1983, Foss & Company is a national tax equity investor and fund sponsor that has allocated over $11 billion in tax equity for insurance, banking, and other large corporate clients into historic rehabilitation projects, renewable energy, and advanced energy production facilities. The firm positions itself as a full-service advisor with demonstrated expertise in guiding partners through tax equity investments. GridStor builds and operates battery projects aimed at enhancing the reliability of America's power system by storing electricity for delivery when and where it is most needed. The company develops, acquires, builds, and operates utility-scale, standalone battery storage projects primarily across North America. artigo.texto: A gigante sul-coreana LG Electronics assinou um contrato de longo prazo para fornecer sistemas de refrigeração industrial a data centers de inteligência artificial nos Estados Unidos. O acordo, que impulsionou as ações da empresa em Seul, visa atender à demanda crescente por infraestrutura térmica eficiente para o boom de IA no mundo. As ações da LG Electronics avançaram no mercado financeiro depois que a companhia fechou um novo contrato plurianual para fornecer sistemas de resfriamento a data centers de inteligência artificial (IA) nos Estados Unidos. A gigante sul-coreana de eletrônicos de consumo vem expandindo rapidamente o negócio de equipamentos de refrigeração industrial, conhecidos como "chillers", impulsionada pelo boom global de data centers, que aumenta a demanda por soluções eficientes de gestão térmica para infraestrutura de IA. Pontos-chave sobre o contrato - Contrato plurianual firmado com a AIR Control Concepts, plataforma de data centers com sede na Virgínia. - O acordo prevê o fornecimento de "chillers" para data centers de IA com mais de 5 gigawatts de capacidade. - As ações da LG subiram 8,8% no início do pregão em Seul, marcando a maior alta diária em dois meses. - A LG planeja construir uma nova fábrica na Virgínia, com início da produção no primeiro semestre de 2027. - Encomendas anuais podem chegar a bilhões de dólares até o fim de 2026, após US$ 426 milhões no primeiro semestre. A LG informou nesta terça-feira (6) que sua subsidiária nos EUA firmou um acordo de longo prazo com a AIR Control Concepts, plataforma de data centers com sede na Virgínia, para fornecer "chillers" a data centers de IA com mais de 5 gigawatts de capacidade. A empresa não revelou o valor exato do contrato, mas afirmou que o acordo acelera a expansão da LG no mercado global de resfriamento para data centers de IA. Em Seul, as ações da LG Electronics chegaram a subir 8,8% no início do pregão, caminhando para a maior alta diária em cerca de dois meses. A LG disse que, apoiada por vitórias recentes na América do Norte, também está ampliando sua presença em projetos relevantes de data centers no Oriente Médio e na Indonésia. Expansão industrial e metas de receita No início deste mês, a empresa anunciou que vai aumentar a produção de "chillers" tanto nos EUA quanto na Coreia do Sul. A LG planeja construir uma nova fábrica na Virgínia para atender à demanda crescente de data centers americanos, com início da produção previsto para o primeiro semestre de 2027. Paralelamente, pretende elevar a produção em unidades já existentes em Changwon e Pyeongtaek, na Coreia do Sul. Segundo a LG, as novas encomendas anuais de soluções de resfriamento para data centers podem chegar a vários bilhões de dólares até o fim de 2026, após a companhia garantir US$ 426 milhões no primeiro semestre. A empresa também afirmou esperar atingir, antes do prazo, a meta de 2027 de US$ 680 milhões em receita no negócio de "chillers".

artigo.texto: There’s a growing need for long-duration storage to meet energy demand and balance out renewables on the grid. Energy Dome uses compressed carbon dioxide gas in its massive grid batteries, which can deliver power for up to 24 hours. As the world races to meet growing electricity demand, solar and onshore wind power have become the cheapest and quickest-to-deploy sources to install on the grid. But, despite their upsides, both are subject to variations in weather patterns, which means supplies can be intermittent. Energy Dome is using stored carbon dioxide to help smooth out gaps between supply and demand. Advertisement The key component of an Energy Dome plant is a huge white dome that covers an area about the size of seven soccer fields and holds about 2,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide. When energy is available—say, from a connected solar farm—compressors squeeze the gas, turning it into a liquid that’s then stored in carbon-steel tanks. That process generates heat, which the system holds in a proprietary thermal storage material. Then, when the grid needs power, the carbon dioxide is released from the tanks and warmed with the stored heat, turning it back into a gas. That gaseous carbon dioxide then passes through a turbine to generate electricity and flows back into the dome, ready to begin the cycle again. This story is only available to subscribers. Don’t settle for half the story. Get paywall-free access to technology news for the here and now. Compressing gas to store energy isn’t new—utilities have been using compressed air in underground caverns to hang on to reserves for decades. But Energy Dome’s approach doesn’t require any specific geology to work, so it could be more easily scaled to help grids around the world. Energy Dome turned on its first commercial plant in Sardinia, Italy, in 2025. The facility has a capacity of 200 megawatt-hours. That’s enough to power about 18,000 Italian homes for 10 hours. Key indicators Industry: Energy storage Founded: 2020 Headquarters: Milan, Italy Notable fact: Energy Dome has plans for 30 gigawatt-hours’ worth of projects across five continents. Potential for impact Cheaper energy storage could help wind and solar meet more of the world’s electricity demand. Today, lithium-ion batteries dominate new installations for short-duration applications of up to four hours. But the economics aren’t competitive for longer durations: A lithium-ion system that provides eight hours of storage at the same power output requires doubling the number of cells. Energy Dome estimates that its technology is roughly 10% to 15% cheaper than lithium-ion batteries for an eight-hour system, and that the economics are even better for longer-duration systems of up to 24 hours. The company says its ability to scale bigger and faster than lithium-ion boils down to the fact that its design uses existing commercially available equipment like compressors and storage tanks. Its plants that are either operational or under contract have eight or 10 hours of capacity. Caveats Energy Dome only has one commercial project that’s operational. It’ll need to build many more to provide the 30 gigawatt-hours of storage it has planned. The technology also isn’t quite as efficient as lithium-ion. Overall, Energy Dome’s process can return about 70% of the electricity it stores to the grid (a measure known as roundtrip efficiency). Lithium-ion batteries average roughly 90%. But some other long-duration storage techniques clock in lower; some iron-air batteries, for example, are around 50%. Advertisement Energy Dome’s plants may not all be benign from a planet-warming perspective. The company offers a version of its system that pairs its carbon dioxide battery with natural gas turbines. That version replaces internal heat storage with waste heat from the gas turbines to help evaporate carbon dioxide. That helps the plant run more efficiently but ultimately results in greenhouse-gas emissions from the natural gas turbines. Next steps Energy Dome has a pipeline of about 30 gigawatt-hours’ worth of plants in the works around the world, and many of these projects could come online by the end of the decade. Because the company uses off-the-shelf components, the time from a signed contract to delivered capacity is only two years. In June 2026, for example, it signed a deal with Google to build a 200 MWh plant in Ireland, which is expected to come online in 2028.

artigo.texto: This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, independent news organization that covers climate, energy, and the environment. It is republished with permission. Sign up for their newsletter here. Environmental groups and citizens are urging Pennsylvania regulators to increase the minimum amount of protective buffer space between gas wells and homes, schools and water sources. The issue has taken on new urgency as the AI data center buildout spurs more demand for natural gas. On Wednesday, a coalition of environmental and community groups held an event at the state capitol to draw attention to their concerns. They complain they’ve been waiting two years for the Department of Environmental Protection to move forward with a petition they filed in 2024, urging the agency to increase minimum setback requirements. Katie Weber lives in Hanover Township, Washington County and went to Harrisburg because she’s concerned about plans to build a large cluster of data centers powered by an on-site natural gas plant near her home. “We are united and our message is clear,” Weber said. “We do not want data centers, and we do not want fracking anywhere near our homes, our schools or our daycares.” The day before, activists argued for a three-year moratorium on data centers in another rally at the capitol. Gov. Josh Shapiro had been an early proponent of the AI buildout in the state, but shifted his stance earlier this year as public opposition mounted. He has signed executive orders aimed at putting some limits on data centers, including having them “build, bring online, or buy incremental electric capacity” to power their facilities. The goal is for data center builders to foot the bill for the increased power demand instead of Pennsylvania ratepayers. More Data Centers, More Natural Gas Environmental advocates, like Lisa Graves-Marcucci of the Environmental Integrity Project, worry Shapiro’s efforts will push data center builders to rely more heavily on natural gas to power the facilities—leading to more pollution on site and negative environmental and health impacts from increased shale gas production. “We’ve realized now that fracking will fuel the data centers,” said Graves-Marcucci. “Communities that already have a lot of fracking could see an increase, or communities that don’t have fracking may get some. It’s all the more reason we need these protective setback distances.” Environmental groups argue a growing body of peer-reviewed research shows more space would provide more protection from potential health harms, including chronic stress, excessive noise and light, poor air quality, vehicle accidents, explosions and chemical spills. Two years ago, the coalition of groups filed what’s called a petition for rulemaking with the state Department of Environmental Protection’s Environmental Quality Board— asking regulators to evaluate whether the existing setback requirements could be expanded. For example, under current law, a gas well could be 500 feet from a home. “We are looking for a common-sense protective setback of one kilometer, which is a little over 3,000 feet,” said Gillian Graber, executive director of Protect PT, a community group for Westmoreland and Allegheny counties. “The current setback is very old and out of date.” Their petition also calls for greater distances between gas wells and buildings serving vulnerable populations like schools or hospitals. David Hess, a former secretary of the Department of Environmental Protection, who authors a blog covering state environmental issues, views the push to increase the setbacks as reasonable. “We’ve been shale gas drilling here in Pennsylvania for more than 20 years, and to not look at those kinds of issues, like setbacks and other things, would be a huge oversight,” Hess said. “We’ve learned a lot from these operations and how they impact people living next to them. If anyone thinks 500 feet is adequate to deal with any of the issues, I think they’re kidding themselves.” In 2018 Colorado expanded its oil and gas well setback requirements to be 1,000 feet from schools. A 2020 grand jury report about fracking in Pennsylvania led by then Attorney General Josh Shapiro recommended 2,500 foot setbacks for buildings and 5,000 feet for schools and hospitals. DEP spokesman Neil Shader said the agency is continuing to review the petition. “DEP thoroughly reviews all petitions submitted, along with the other associated materials submitted with the petition, before delivering a recommendation to the EQB,” Shader wrote in an email. “This particular petition included several scientific studies, which DEP is reviewing using in-house experts (including a toxicologist) to be able to deliver a fully informed recommendation to the EQB.” The Marcellus Shale Coalition, a natural gas industry trade group, argues the DEP lacks the legal authority to increase the setback requirements via this rulemaking petition, because those limits are already spelled out in state law, and any changes would have to go through the legislature. Patrick Henderson, vice president of government affairs and communications at the Marcellus Shale Coalition, previously worked in Republican Gov. Tom Corbett’s administration and helped update the state’s oil and gas law in 2012, in response to the drilling boom. “That process Governor Tom Corbett put forth was the product of an advisory commission that he appointed with environmental, industry, local government officials and academia to develop,” said Henderson. “Those setback requirements derived a lot from that input.” Lisa Graves-Marcucci of the Environmental Integrity Project, said the environmental groups are hopeful DEP will respond to them before the end of the year. “There is no draft rule,” she pointed out. “We’re just waiting for the formality for them to say they’ve reviewed the petition. We believe it merits the full process of rulemaking.” BEFORE YOU GO… If you learned something from this article, pay

artigo.texto: JUWI GmbH, based in Wörrstadt, has recently signed contracts with three leading companies in the energy sector for the technical operation, servicing and maintenance of six further battery energy storage systems (BESS). The facilities are currently under construction and are due to be commissioned within the next six months. For more than five years, the JUWI Group’s O&M experts have been managing battery storage systems in Germany and Belgium. With these newly secured contracts, JUWI is expanding its portfolio of managed battery storage systems to around 700 megawatt-hours of storage capacity. The new projects are being carried out for three different companies and involve storage capacities ranging from 4 to 100 megawatt-hours. JUWI’s services include technical operations management as well as servicing and maintenance for the first few years of the plants’ operational phase. The new contracts underscore the growing importance of battery storage systems for a secure and flexible energy supply, as well as market participants’ confidence in JUWI’s long-standing expertise in operations management and service provision. Oliver Otte, Head of O&M at JUWI GmbH, explains: “We are delighted that three renowned companies in the energy sector have chosen us as their O&M partner for the servicing, maintenance and technical operation of their battery storage systems. With our many years of experience in operating battery storage systems, we create real added value for investors and operators. Our aim is to operate the systems reliably, safely and cost-effectively throughout their entire life cycle.” By further expanding the BESS portfolio, JUWI is strengthening its position as an experienced operations management and service partner for battery storage and renewable energy systems in Europe.

artigo.texto: Indiana has heard plenty about the data center boom: billions in proposed investment and construction jobs. The more consequential question is whether the benefits will extend beyond the project site and be shared by all Hoosier families and businesses. One early answer is coming from Indiana Michigan Power, which has proposed a rate reduction plan to the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission. The proposal would reduce Indiana customer bills by about $59 million in 2027, freeze all rates on the monthly bill for three years and, by I&M’s estimate, save its average residential customer about $100 annually. I&M explains why: “This rate decrease is made possible by the load growth and increased revenue it is experiencing from large customers including data centers.” I&M’s proposal offers a concrete early indication of how the economics can work. Large customers bring more than new demand. Their steady, substantial revenue can create room for utilities to invest in transmission, substations and the technology that makes the grid stronger. That means more capacity, fewer and shorter outages, and a system prepared for the factories, homes and businesses that will need dependable electricity in the years ahead. South Bend Mayor James Mueller called the proposal “the power of growth and getting more for less.” It is a concise description of how growth can work for the people of Indiana. Indiana is only beginning to see these investments reach the system. As projects move to construction and operations, the benefits of growth should become easier to recognize: stronger infrastructure, greater capacity and, if I&M is a guide, lower bills for Hoosier households. Data center investment can generate significant local tax revenue to help communities pay for schools, police and fire protection, infrastructure and amenities. A larger tax base can also mean less pressure to raise property tax rates on homeowners and businesses. Water use is changing, too. A new data center planned for Lebanon will use a water-efficient closed-loop system designed to use zero water for most of the year. The developer says a typical AI-optimized data center using this kind of system uses less water annually than two full-service restaurants. Just as important is the people side of this growth. Last month, Indianapolis celebrated the first graduating class of Meta’s America’s Workforce Academy. Indiana is one of four states in the initial pilot for Meta’s $115 million nationwide initiative, which trains people for the skilled trades needed to build and maintain digital infrastructure, power generation and grid modernization. Participants need no prior experience. They are paid while completing the program and graduate with industry credentials and a guaranteed job with a Meta partner. Ethan Blake, a graduate from Fishers, put its value more directly: “They gave me an on ramp to success in a way, and they gave me the tools that I needed to be able to navigate this new workforce. They gave me the knowledge that I needed to be able to navigate the new workforce, and they gave me a job.” That is why this moment matters. Indiana has abundant energy resources, a skilled manufacturing tradition, strategic location and workers ready to build. The data center boom can create jobs for electricians, fiber technicians, equipment operators, construction workers and the many local businesses that support them. It can also catalyze the grid improvements that help every employer and family. I&M’s proposed rate reduction is not the end of the conversation. It is a promising early sign of what Indiana can achieve through new investment, a growth-oriented mindset, and confidence in ourselves and the future. Jim Merritt of Carmel is a former Indiana state senator.

artigo.texto: Jupiter Wagons Limited (JWL), through its energy business arm JEM Energy, has strengthened its presence in India’s battery energy storage system (BESS) market by securing a 41 MW/102.5 MWh standalone BESS project in Uttarakhand in partnership with Madhav Infra Projects Limited. The joint venture emerged as the L1 bidder for Cluster C of the Uttarakhand Power Corporation Limited (UPCL) tender issued under the Tariff-Based Competitive Bidding (TBCB) mechanism. The project includes the supply and commissioning of BESS systems with an estimated value of approximately ₹100 crore. The award marks JEM Energy’s entry into the Uttarakhand energy storage market. JWL has also received a formal Letter of Award (LoA) from the West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Limited (WBSEDCL) for a 50 MW/200 MWh standalone BESS project. The project will be located at the Jeerat 132 kV substation in North 24 Parganas, West Bengal. JWL had originally secured the project in August 2026, while the latest LoA formalizes the award. Together, the two projects represent a combined BESS capacity of 91 MW/302.5 MWh and strengthen JEM Energy’s pipeline in the rapidly expanding energy storage segment. The company’s expansion comes as India accelerates investments in battery storage to support renewable energy integration and improve grid flexibility. The Union Cabinet’s approval of the Green Energy Corridor Phase-III includes plans to add 50 GWh of battery energy storage capacity along with the development of stronger intra-state transmission infrastructure. Substation-level storage projects such as those being developed in Uttarakhand and West Bengal are expected to support this broader grid modernization strategy. Vivek Lohia, Managing Director of Jupiter Wagons Limited, said that winning the Uttarakhand project and receiving the formal award for the Jeerat project represent important milestones in scaling JEM Energy into a significant energy storage business. The company has set a target of building a BESS order book of approximately ₹1,000 crore by FY27. JWL also expects its electric mobility business to turn EBITDA positive in the third quarter of FY27 and achieve profitability by FY28. JEM Energy plans to continue a disciplined bidding strategy for utility-scale as well as Commercial and Industrial (C&I) energy storage opportunities across India. The company’s growing presence in BESS reflects JWL’s broader strategy of diversifying beyond its traditional railway and mobility operations and participating in high-growth segments linked to India’s energy transition.
